The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address· to the Grand
Lodge, ea follows:BBETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA~The Annual Communications of this body are the grand festivals of the moral,
socia.l, a.nd intellectual fa.cul ties; and I gladly welcome the auspicious day which
bring11 us together a.gain in peace, harmony, and frat.emal love. The months which
have passed since, here in this goodly Temple of benovolence, we exchanged our farewell greetings, may have been attended with sorrows and Inisfortnnes. Noble ambitions may have been wrecked, and the hopes of yea.rs scattered a.nd overthrown.
The holiest ties may have been rudely broken, and pa.in, weariness, and tears may
have hung on your footsteps to da.rken a.nd embitter your journey hitherward.
These, my brethren, a.re the insepe.re.ble elements of human life. Trial is the furnace blast which exalts and puri1ies-which consumes the evil and developee the good·
in humanity, a.nd through which mortals must ever adva.nce toward the better conditions of imlii.orla.lity. But while it becomes us not to indnlge in vain regrets, nor
murmur or repine a.t apparent hardships, but rather be thankful that fortune has
not been still less kind, it would be a fa.Jae a.nd hollow pretense to congratnla.t.e
yon to-day on another season of abundance a.nd prosperity. The yea.r has not been
one of genera.I prospt)<ity to this commonwealth, as empty gra.nariee, idle hands,
diminished incomes, and unusual calls for charity, have too often testified; a.nd I do
not propose to mock your intelligence, nor my own sense of truth and propriety, by
the a.ssertion of abundant harvests a.nd a.mple rewards for honest industry. What
causes, other tha.n natural ones-what mistaken notions of st.ateemanship a.nd politica.l economy- what false theories of government, of commercial intercourse, of taxation, of priva.te right a.nd public policy, have contributed to bring upon our noble
St.ate, so boundless in resources a.nd so blessed with all the elel!lents of ma.teria.1
greatness-this general paralysis under which we a.re to-day staggering, a.re questions
fit only to be considered iii another forum.
I do not propose to ent.er upon a discussion which, however rationa.lly conducted,
Inight seem to partake of a political and pe.rtisa.n cha.racter, with which Masonry could
have no possible pa.rt or lot. But with those other questions so interwoven with
these- with the corrupt a.nd evil influences a.nd motives which have induced these
mistaken theories of government, of public policy, and political economy, Masonry
has everything to do ; and I do not propose to be frightened from a, calm and dispaa_
sionat.e criticism of public a.ffaire, nor from pointing out to you the public duties of
Masone in a period of general moral infection, by the mistaken cry that I should
thereby encroach upon the arena of politics. Masonry owes an allegiance to the
State, to its Government, and to society at la.rge; and Masons have public, as well as
private, duties to perform.· A moral leprosy seems to steal pei;iodica.lly upon nations
a.nd communities. There are seasons when the whole social fabric and body politic
a.re eaten a.nd gangrened with corruption-when high official position is prostituted
to the be.seat purposes, and the most sacred of public duties a.re betrayed and violated
with open a.nd sha.meless effrontery-when licentiousness, unblushing, walks the
highways unrebuked at noontide-when honesty in public and priva.te life ceases
to be regarded as a virtue, and betrayals of trust become so common that men no
longer give them a passing considera.tion, butrege.rd them rather as the to be expected
and legitimate events of the day. Public serva.nts are bought a.nd sold, a.nd the betrayed cease to cry out against it. Miserable theories of free love a.nd domestic
infidelity are openly practiced, and the a.ctors in the wretched drama are welcomed
a.nd courted with all the bla.ndishments of the beet society. Public revenues are
Inieappropriated by the cuetodia.ns thereof, and the courts of the la.nd refuse to punish the criminals. The. worst of vices a.re fostered and encouraged by those who
should be the zealous guardians of public morals, a.nd examples destructive of all

correct principle'are furnished by those whose social e.nd official position gives them a.
fearful influence for evil. Gambling ha.a been ga.lva.niud into respectability by official patronage, and we have witnessed the distressing spectacle of the State herself
inviting her own citiY.ens to perdition, by casting a.round that worst, because most
insinuating of vices, the glamour of legislative and judicial protection. Through all
your borders the evil contagion of that one pernicious example ha.a swept like a.
devouring fta.me, until lotteries, rs.files, and the whole shameless brood of chance
entertainments, have stifted the moral sentiment of the people and stimulated that
restless, feverish passion for sudden wealth which is the destroyer of all patient application e.nd solid prosperity. To what depth society has desC!lllded-how fa.r gambling
ha.a been ma.de respectable by this public indorsement a.nd the tolerance of communities, Ma.sons will readily comprehend when they a.re informed that a Ma.sonic
Lodge, even, has asked the advice of the Grand Master a.a to the propriety of discharging its liabilities through the medium of a gift concert. I need not repeat to you the
a.newer ma.de to this application, for the spirit of Masonry would permit but one.
But the mere fact that advice on such a subject should have·been sought from such a
source, is painfully suggestive of moral e.nd social dep~sion. Better that all the
libraries on earth should have perished than society have suffered the moral evil
which that example has wrought I Yet thus will it ever be when correct principles
a.re departed from for mere expediency.
·
We have indeed fallen on troublous times; a.nd in the midst of this genera.I deeay
of all that is good e.nd commendable, Freemasonry ha.a a public mission to perform.
Never has there been presented so grand an opportunity for the displa.y of your
power, and never ha.a the vigorous exercise of that power been more needed the.n at
.present. You should be the conservators of public as well a.s private morals---0f political integrity as well as personal fidelity. Let every Mason, mindful of his individual
responsibilities e.nd true to the Divine teachings of the ancient Craft, wage eternal
war on vice e.nd wrong wherever found, e.nd in whatever guise they present themselves. Scattered far a.nd wide, every denizen of the St!te is within the persona.I
influence of some one of you. Let that infiuence be ever wielded for the right, and,
by this unity of purpose and of action, you will present a nucleus around which the
moral power of communities may be gathered and consolidated, to arrest the epidemic which threatens to overwhelm e.nd destroy us.
With the n ew-fangled dogma.a of a loose mora.lity, Masonry must have no intercourse or sympathy; but in the midst of these growing evils- this threatened triumph of vice e.nd immora.lity-it should stand like the beacon-Ugh t on some tall cliff
or jutting headland, unshaken and unscathed, in.the midst of, yet above and beyond
the war of elements,-whose golden sheen shall catch the first gla.nce of the imperiled wanderer, to light him in peace e.nd safety home. But the lessons of morality
must be taught, and this influence on society must be wielded, if at all, by your
example rather than by precept- by acts, not words-deeds, not promises to do. You
must yourselves obey the mora.l law in every particular, and be scrupulously observant of all your obligations. The Ma.sonic relation does not require or permit you to
shield a brother in the practice of any vice or -wrong, and the temples.where Justice
is proclaimed as a cardinal virtue must never be converted into asvlums for criminals.
•
Imbued with these views of the public e.nd private duties of Ma.sons, I have never
hesitated to exercise the power of my official position with prompt and unsparing
hand when departures from that standard of excellence have come to my knowledge.
I have never felt called upon to deal t.enderly with willful a.nd persist.ent wrong-doers.
That is a. mistaken notion of Masonic charity which leads to the toleration of vice
through a series of months and years, in the hope that, at some indefinite period in
the future, reformation may.be accomplished. I have but little patience with such

treatment of such diseases, and have chosen to bring in requisition the remedies
which Masonic jurisprudence a.ffords, to hasten the cleansing of the Masonic household.
But it is the right of this Grand Lodge to know to what extent I have exercised
the prerogative of a. Grand Mast.er in enforcing these views and purposes ; and that
will perhaps be best exhibit.ed by presenting a case or two of actual occurrence. Some
months since I was advised that a. member of a certain Lodge was living in the very
shadow of its temple in open prostitution with a. vile a.nd abandoned woman. In
another instance a. member was the proprietor of a gaming house, himself the dealer
of the games, corrupting the morals of the community and luring his own brethren
to destruction. I directed the Ma.sters of these Lodges to demand of these brethren
the immediat.e abandonment of these shameless practices, a.nd, unless these demands
were promptly and fully complied with, to proceed as speedily as possible to the
expulsion of the offenders. To this they r eplied, with evident sorrow a.nd regret, that
though the accusations were conceded to be true, and the offenses public and notorious, yet such was the condition of the Lodges, and such the personal popula.rity of
the offending brethren, that trial commissioners would certainly be elect.ed who, in
spit.e of the obvious facts, would pronounce in favor of the accused. To this I
replied in turn : that, though the commissioners who would return such a verdict,
under such circumstances, would be primarily liable to the severest penalties an4
would be promptly dealt with accordingly, yet there was a.n ultimate responsibility
on the part of the Lodge which I should neither ignore nor forget; that, in my judg·
ment, a Lodge which would or could elect tria.l commissioners who, upon such a state
of conceded fa.eta, would persist in acquitting the guilty parties, was hardly worthy of
its charter ; a.nd I directed them again to proceed at once, a.nd exhaust every remedy
against the accused, and if the occasion arose, against the trial Commissioners as
well, or surrender into my hands the charter so unworthily held. In brief, that the
Lodge must properly punish the offenders, or be punished itself for the omission.
I t maybe urged.t hat this would have been an·extraordina.ry exercise of power a.nd
a dangerous prececlent to establish-an attempt to coerce the judgment and destroy
the independence of the trial commissioners, and practically to pass upon the guilt
of the accused by the Grand Master rather than by the legitimate tribunal. Concede
all this to be true ; and still, when the usual methods of discipline thus fail, through
the obvious indifference or culpable neglect and connivance of those charged in the
first instance with that duty, there must be some ulterior resort, or a complete a.nd
hameful failure of justice. This Grand Body must reserve, a.nd in my judgment
has reserved, to itself, while in session, a.nd to its executive head at all other times,
the power to compel its subordinates to properly discipline their recreant members.
And, unless otherwise instructed by you, I should in all cases of such open and ftagra.nt disregard of those virtues which lie at the very r oot of the Masonic structure,
and constitute all its grandeur a.nd excellence, the facts being obvious and conceded,
do again as I have done in the pa.st. I should exercise this power of suspension a.nd
arrest, when milder means had failed, a.a often as the occa.sion for it might arise, unless int.erdict.ed by you ; and I report these cases as illustrations, for your consideration, that I and my successors in this office may know how far we are to be suRtained in such proceedings. My badge of Masonry is a mockery and a cheat if it
implies nothing. It is worse than idle to bear that name unless the obligation it
imposes. can be always enforced by some power, promptly and effectually.
Other cases less fie.grant than these, but still involving moral turpitude, have come
to my knowledge during the year. But in most of them it has only been necessary
to advise Masters how to proceed, a.nd they have hastened with cheerful alacrity to
the performs.nee of their duties. These reported cases are of course exceptional ones,
and generally there is a growing disposition to exact from all a rigid compliance with
the ethics of Masonry. The moral advancement of the Frat.ernity at large has more

That we have been heretofore too tolerant of
transgressions, I apprehend all \~ill now concede. But I understand well enough
why this baa been. t know how unpleasimt it is to be the promoter of a prosecution,
especially in small communties, where every member has social and business relations
with every other member. It is a disagreeable thing' to i:riau!;iµ-ate a trial. It brings
the interruption of personal relations and kindly offices, and very often the loss of
business patronage, where such loss would be a serious inconvenience. And so each
has waited for another to take the first l!tlip, and the duty' hail thereby been neglected
by all. In some instimces I haw no doubt the inquiries have been made for the sole
plll'p<>se of procuring from me an order to proceed; whieh would shift the responsibility to my shoulders. I have always been very willing to accept that responsibility
when 'the good of the Fraternity seemed to require action. In this connexion let me
add, that the system of inspection adopted at your last Communication, though not
yet perfected, has ve;stly accelerated the work of purifying and reforming. It has
unearthed and exposed whatever was reprehensible, and 'by senaing into the Lodges
an officer clothed with. the authority of the Grand Lcidge, and specially charged with
the correetiori of abuses, has everywhere led to the prompt refonhation, or equally
prompt expulsion, cif tlie wrong doers. Bad Masons have been taught that they can
not violate the Masonic oode·and escape its 'penalties·; and good ones have been gladdened by the elevation of our moral standard.
In other respect.ti, toci, the system has proved grandly efficient. It has c9rrect.ed
the loose manner of transacting the general business of the Lodges, brought about
a strict eompliance with the constitution. and regulations of the Grand Lodge, and
forced upOh those inspected uniformity in the Work and Lectures. In brief, it has
snooeeded beyond my most sanguine expectations, and the good already accomplished
can :b.ot be estiinated. So satisfactory has been the result of the expEirinient where fairly
tried, "that I am do"ubly pained in ~ihg obliged to r'ep<irt that in two of the districts
no inspection has yet been had, because of my fuability to find fit and competent·
persons who would e.cCept the positions in time to make the visitations this year. For
the purpose of observing for myself the operation of the system, and discovering its
defect.a, I have visited nirie 6f the districta personally, accompanied in ea.ch case by
the Grand Secretary and Grand Lecturer. In each case a Convention of e.11 the
Lodges in the district was called at the most convenient and accessible 'ple.ce; and as
these meetings ha1ve been generally well attended by the officerS', a large proportion
of the Lodges in the State have been in practical effect visited during the year.
Without detmcting from others, I can not refrain from especially commending the
zeal and interest manifested by the brethren in the southern portion of the jurisdiction: At the meeting held in Los Angeles, in June last, every Lodge in that vast
district was fully represented, and I am happy in being able to report that in that
remote region Masonry is in a most satisfe.ctory co;,dition. These visita have been, I
believe, sources of profit, as well as pleasure, to the Craft; and while my brethren
gener&lly seem to have a'ppreciated them highly, and have given me most cordie.l weloome, I have been not a little distressed by the fa.ct that a few discontented ones, who
saw fit to absent themselves from these gatherings, have openly ascribed my visitB
to the most unworthy motives. If I know my own heart, I have had nothing in view
but the good of the Frat.enrity; and I have only compassion for those who are themselves so tempered and oonstitnted that they can discover in another no motive inlluences save selfish and personal ambition; and I hope the day is not far distant when
better information and a more fraternlll and kindly spirit shall lead them to more
j_nst and charitable conclusions.

Some time since severol gentlemen residing in Alpine County, in this State, asked
permission to apply to Doug/(s.' Lodge, under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of
Nevada, for the degrees of Masonry. About the same time the Master of IJouglas
Lodge asked permi•sion to entertain such applications. Though the petitioners reside
in California, they are within a few miles of Douglas Lodge, which is of easy access,
and whither their business relations often lead them; while they are seventy miles
from any Lodge in California, and separated therefrom by a lofty monntain range. I
replied that I knew of rio authority to r<'linquish the jurisdiction, and that if such
authority existed at all it was vested in the subordinate Lodge within whose jurisdiction they resided, and not in the Grand Master; and that certainly, in the face of the
Constitution of the Grand Lodge of Nevada-requiring the residence of all applicants
to be in that State-l could not confer upon Douglas Lodge the right to receive and
8'!t upon the petitions; but that if they procnred the assent of our subordinate
Lodge which had jur;sdiction, and Douglas Lodge should thereupon confer the
degrne!l\ our Grand Lodge would never complain of it, and they would be treated
here as regular Ma.sons. What the result has been I know not.
·

In my former report I asked yon to settle definitely several questions on which
there seemed to be some doubt, but no decision was arrived at. I now renew the

I have also been asked several times during the year as to the physical qualifications
requisite to initiation. There seems to be a growing desire to have the present rigid
nle re.Jaxed • and it must be conceded that, since Masonry has become a purely spec~lative scien~e, the mental and moral qualifications are the most important features,
and mrich of the reason for the rule has ceased to exi~t. One of the cases, rece?tly
presented, forcibly illustrates the app11rent hardship of the requirement of physical
perfection. The individual was a gentleman of wealth, culture, and cha~acter, and
from his evident eagerness and solicitude, his nobll! nature and ?ure motive•, would
have been a valuable member of and an ornament to the Fratermty. But he bad lost a
leg. Bo completely, however, had art.supplied the loss, that he was able fully _to
comply with all the ceremonial requirements of Masonry, and men who had met him
almost daily for years did not even suspect his infirmity. Whether the rule could be
modified to meet such a case, without encroaching upon a landmark of Masonry,
and whether, if competent, it would be advisable for th~ Grand Lodge to adopt such
modification, is for you, and not for me, to determine. It wou~d pe:haps be v~ry
difficult to change the rule, and yet preserve its certainty and nmform1ty of application; and the work of modification once entered upon, we should perhaps ha:dly
know where to ~top. I pre.sent the matter because estimable brethren have desired
me to do so· rather than from a desire on my part to see any change.
I again r:new the recommendation made by my i_mmed~ate predecessor, and repeated by me last year, that the affiliation fee be abolished in toto. Bo long _as. yon. r~­
qnire Masons to be members of some Lodge and punish them for non-~ffiha~1on, it 1s
wrong in principle to tax them for becoming members. These two _thmgs itr,e utterly inconsistent; they mar .the beauty and symmetry of your Masomc code, and one
or the other should be dispensed with.
I also renew the recommendation that the rule of one ballot for the three degrees
be made obligatory on all the Lodges. By separate ballots you _reserve to any member of the Lodge the power to arrest the progress of a candidate at any stage of

advancement. This may be done, and we know sometimes is done, from the most
unworthy and unmasonic motives, through caprice, jealousy, or pers<>nal ill feeling.
I repeat what I said on this subject last nar-that, after initiatio11, the candidate has
some rights as a Mason, and it is unjust, wrong and cruel, to leave him exposed to
this species of Masonic assassination. After initiation he should be stopped only
for cause, and the sufficiency of that cause should be determined by the Lodge, and
not by some one factious or capricious member.
In the hurry and confusion of business at your last Communication, a resolution
was adopted without much consideration, holding, substantially, that when apetitioner for the degrees had applied to a Lodge, within the jurisdiction of which he
did not reside, and been rejected, he could not thereafter within twelve months apply to the Lodge within whose jurisdiction he in fact did reside. I do not believe this
doctrine to be sound in principle, and think that it ought not to be maintained. The
Lodge which had no jurisdiction over him, by the very force of that fact, had no power
either to elect or reject him-no right to receive or act upon his petition. All its proceedings would be absolute nullities, and the candidate would remain, in contempla.tion of all law, precisely as if no proceedings had been had or attempted. Under these
circumstances he might say, with perfect truth, that he had not been rejected, for the
attempted rejectioµ was not a rejection at all, for want of authority in the Lodge
making it. If he had in fact knowingly applied to the wrong Lodge, or had been
guilty of any bad faith or wilful deception in making such application, this undoubtedly would be ample gronnd for rejecting him; but no ground for refusing to
act upon his petition. A !though it is not a matter of any great practical importance, because such cases will not often arise, yet if the resolution is wrong, it ought,
for that reason. alone, to be rescinded; and I recommend such action.
Many of the changes and provisions which I have ·suggested can only be effected
by amending your Constitution, and it has been often said that this should only be
done (or urgent cause. The Constitution should, of course, be rigidly observed. I
shall not permit any one to go before me in devotion and obedience to its requirements. But to amend is not to violate, and the thought of amending does not inspire
me with that awe and dread which some seem to indulge. On the contrary, the
Constitution itself is only a rule of conduct prescribed by the Grand Lodge, and if
it stands in the way of needed and proper legislation, it ought to be amended at once,
and without misgiving. That instrument was framed and adopted twelve years ago.
It has been amended from time to time, here a little and there a little, and it would
be strange indeed if some of these hasty alterations were not found a little crude,
and inconsistent with provisions elsewhere contained in the same instrument. In
short, it has ceased to be a complete and harmonious whole. The experience of
these years has developed its defects, and the changes which time has wrought in
the conditions of society, with our increase of Lodges and of membership, have
produced a necessity for its alteration in several particulars other than those I have
already referred to. Some of its provisions are still vague, and should be made
fuller and plainer. Some of our general regulations seem to contravene its requirements, and others might now well be engrafted upon the instrument itself. The
whole might readily be made so clear, fnll, and explicit, that no misapprehension of
ills requirements could possibly arise. I think the time has come when a thorough
revision of tbe Constitution, regnlationR, resolntions, decrees, and judgments of the
Grand Lodge would be wise and p~ofitable. But such a task Is not likely to be well
done during the hurry and excitement of your sittings; and I th~refore recommend
that a special committee be appointed for that purpose, to report to yon at your next
Annual Communication.

At your last Communication I presented somewhat in detail my own views of the
status and pretensions of the Grand Lodge of Quebec. I reached the conclusion that
it was a case of rebellion, simple and unqualified, and declared myself decidedly

against recognition. My views npon the merits of the controversy have not changed
in any particnlar. Since then, however, a large proportion of t~ose of our sister
Grand Lodges whioh have acted npon the matter at all, have recognized that body,
and others have simply taken further time to consider the matter. The current seems
to have set rather strongly in favor of recognition, and there Is now little donbt that
most of the Grand Lodges on this continent will soon be.in fraternal Intercourse
with the new Grand J,odge. How far our own action ought now to be influenced
by these facts yon can judge as well as I. On the one hand , I still cry out in all
earnestness against any sympathy with, or encouragement of, what seems to me simple
insubordination; nor should we approve a wrong, if wrong it be, simply because
other Grand Lodges have set us the bad example. On the other hand, for as alone
to place all Masons who now hold allegiance to that body under the han of non·
intercourse would perhaps seem captious and Impracticable, while it might unpleasantly complicate our Masonic relations elsewhere. I can only commend the matter
to your careful scrutiny and consideration, urging yon, however, to postpone the
subject no longer, but do something at once and unmistakably.
I am pained to report to yon .that the Grand Orient of France still persists in its
unwarrantable invasion of the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana. Under
the late N apoleooic dynasty the Grand Orient of France was scarcely an independ·
ent body. The Grand Master, at least, was practically the mere creature of the
Emperor ; and it Is more than possible that political considerations, in some measure, induced the acts complained of. Under the new regime let ns hope that Masonic
independence will be there restored, and that better counseis will prevail. With all
the other Grang Bodies of the world our relations remain unchanged since your last
Communication.
Representatives to Grand Lodges have been appointed in two instances only during the year, no other cases having arisen which came within the views which I
have heretofore expressed on that subject.
I have approved a large number of amendments to the by-laws of Lodges, and in
sev~ral .cases have refnsed to approve those proposed. In one instance approval was
given contrary to my own judgment. It was a change from one ballot for the three
degrees to separate ballots for each. The Grand Lodge having repeatedly declined
to interfere with the discretion of its subordinates in this respect, I did not feel justified in doing ·tio, although, as elsewhere expressed, I regard such an amendment
as a step backward which yon ought not to tolerate.

I d? not think it amiss to call your attention to the sit uation and claims of the San
Fr~?m•co Board of Relief. I think I understand, as well perhaps as others, the true
spmt of Masonic charity. I subscribe most cheerfully to the oft-repeated formula

To give ~t.herw1se, indeed, would scarcely be to give at all, but rather to loan. But
the cond1t1ons here are peculiar and extraordinary. This city is the entrepot of the
w~ole coast.' and in through the Golden Gate the winged mes.•engers of commerce

and th~t the Grand Lodge shoald contribu te from its funds for the relief of those t
from foreign jurisdictions who have been here nourished and maintained.
And here , niy brethren,_I close once more the report of my official proceedings.
I have not submitted the thousand questions asked during the year, which were so
simple and well settled that I could not be mistaken in my decisions; bot 1 have
presented all of genera.I interest concerning which there could be any doubt, and
now submit all my acts for your fraternal and indulgent consideration. I have
only to add that my own hand bas been continually on the helm, and for whatever
has been done a.miss I !\lone am responsible. If I have not guided the Craft arightif evil has been wrought or suffered- if the Masonic honor has been tarnished or
obscured-if our standard has not been advanced, and onr temples purified and
a.domed-it has not been from indifference, or wo.ot of zeal, or unwillingness to toil,
but because I have not been blessed with the wi•dom and judgment essential to the
11 ccomplishment of those end•. For myself, I look back upon the progress of the
year with much pride and gratification; and forward to the glowing future with high
hopes and lofty anticipations.
Twelve months more like those just passeJ will complete the reform in progress,
and place your entire jurisdiction on the very summit of Masonic excellence.
Whether 1t shall be mine or auothe1"s mission to stand in this place twelve months
hence and witness that con~nmm~tion , it• coming will be eqaally a source of unbounded joy and satisfaction to me. And now, ...with kindness toward aJ.I, and
malice toward none,'~ profoundly grateful to my brethren for the courtesy, hospitality, and attention they have ever extende!l to me,I salute yon with the parting prayer
th<lt all your deliberations may be guided by that wi>dom which can not err ; that
peace and prosperity may ever attend you; and that the labors of these days be as
productive of good to the Fraternity at large ~they must be replete with pleasure
to those who participate iu them.

Since the le.st Annual Communication eleven special dispensations have been
lssned from this office by direction of the Grand Master. Of these, seven were to
anthorize re-ballots upon petitions of rejected applicants for the degrees, within the
period of prohibition prescribed by the general provision of our laws, the petitions
therefor having been directed to be submitted to the Grand Master by the nnanimons
vote (by ballot) of the Lodges whence they came, as our law prescribes; and four
were to permit the election of officers at times other than the regular one provided
in the Constitution, the petitions therefor having been adopted in each case by a vote
of two-thirds of the members present, as ordained by our statutes. All these petitions presented reasons for the issue of the dispensations apparently sufficient to
justify the favorable consideration of' the Grand Master, and they, together with such
correspondence as relates to them, are also herewith submitted.
Four removals of Lodges from the places of location named In their several charters have occurred during the year. The petitions to the Grand Master, asking his
permission for such removals, were in every-case adopted by the Lodges after the
necessary notice of one month and hy the two-thirds vote required by the Constitn·
tion, (in three of the cases by a unanimous vote,~ and, as it was shown that I.h e sev·
eral changes of location would promote the usefulness of the Lodges and add much
to the convenience of their members, the respective permiBBions were given as fol·
lows:To Stanislaus Lodge, No. 206, to remove from Tuolumne City, in Stanislaus County,
to Modesta, In the same county, March 20th, 1871;
To Nicolaus Lodge. No. 129, to remove from Nicolaus, in Sutter County, to
Wheatland, in Yuba County, March 22d, 1871;
To Sil-oeyville Lodge, No. 201, to remove from Silveyvllle, in Solano County, to
Dixon, lo the same county, August 10th, 1871; and
To Table Mountain Lodge, No. 124, to remove from Oroville, in Butte County, to
Cherokee Flat, in the same county, September 29th, Hi71.
Sundry communications have been received from the Grand Lodge of Canada
and from officers of the body calling itself the Grand Lodge of Quebec, relative to
the assumed independence of the last, whlch are herewith presented.
.Among the unfinished business of the last Annual Communication are the following subjects, presented in the Address of the Grand Master and referred to the Com·
mittee on Jnrisprudence, but not reported upon, in consequence of the absence of
some of the members of that committee and the Illness of its chairman : First-As to the necessity for a ballot upon the application of a candidate when
an adverse report has been made by the committee of investigation ;
Second-As to the propriety of adopting some means to avoid the necessity for a
ballot {and a consequent rejection) in cases where the candidate is found worthy,
but ineligible for lack of the proper length of residence ·in our jurisdiction ;
Third- As to the requisite · physical qualifications of candidates who, having
received one or two degrees, and thereafter having suffered some maim or dismem
berment, desire to receive the remaining degree or degrees ;
Fourth-As to whether a Mason should be liable to trial for offenses committed
before his initiation ;
Fifth-As to the admissibility of candidates who are unable either to read or
write;
Sixth-As to the. legality of the establishment, within the jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge of Canada, of the so-called Grand Lodge of Quebec ;
Seventh- As to the violation or the jurisdictional rights of this Grand Lodge by
the subordinates of other Grand Lodges in the United States;·

Eighth-As to the expediency of enacting an imposition of fines for non-attend·
ance at the faneral of a deceased brother member; and
Ninth ·-As to the usefulness of a regalation forbidding the installation of any
.M aster or Warden until he shall have produced a certificate from the Deputy Grand
Lecturer of his di~trict that he is competent to confer the three degrees of Masonry,

The following questions were also snbmitted at the last Annnal Communication
and referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, but were not reported npon for the
reasons before given, viz.:First-Whether Masons who had withdrawn from their Lodges, and had remained
unaffiliated longer than the time prescribed by our laws for good standing, should not
be required to pay dues for the period during which they were not affiliated in order
to enable them to unite in the formation of a new Lodge ;
Second-Whether it is proper to canvass the character of an' applicant for the
degrees, in open Lodge, after the report of the investigating committee and prior to
the ballot;
Third-Whether a member of a Lodge, who withdraws therefrom and has asked
for and been refused a recommendatofy certificate, should receive any other document than that prescribed in the Constitution ; and
Fourth-Whether the Grand Lodge would take any action relative to the recognition of colored Lodges and Masons (so called) within thfa jurisdiction.
The following amendments ·to the Constitution were propo8ed at the last Annual
Communication, and were referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, viz.:First-That the Grand Master be authorized to issue special dispensations to
permit the reception of petitions for the degrees of Masonry from persons belonging
to the army or naty of the United States who have not the qualification of residence
required by our laws;
Second-That no Lodge in the city of San Francisco shall confer the three degrees of Masonry for a less fee than seventy-five dollars.
Of the proposed amendments to the by-l11ws of chartered Lodges which have
reached this office during the year, forty-9even have been approved by the Grand
Master, the action of the Lodges in all those cases having apparently been in consonance with the law. Of these, eleven prf>pose changes in the times of meeting;
thirteen propose to rednce, and two to increase, the quarterly dues; four propose to
decrease the fees for the degrees; two propose to increase the affiliation fees, seven
to reduce them, and two to abolish them altogether; four propose a single ballot for
the thcee degrees; one proposes a separate ballot for each degree ; and· one proposes the establishment of life-membership". The approval of the Grand Master
being bnt a temporary authorization, the amendments, as required by the Constitntion, are now·submitted to the Grand Lodge for fl1ul action; as are also copies of
the proposed .by-laws of the eleven Lodges existing under dispensation.

Agent of the WasWngton National Monument Association, accompanied with two
hundred copies of a pamphlet appealini: to the Masons of the United States for aid
in the completion of the Washington Monument, and the expression of a desire that
our Grand Lodge should authorizoi their distribution among its subordinates and rec.
ommend them to contribute, so far as their abilities may permit, in aid of that
national and patriotic work. The papen are herewith submitted, and the appeal
· ought not to pass unheeded.

Grand. Lodge of Oalifornia :In accordance with a resolution adopted at the last Annual Communication, I
herewith submit a ,report of my official acts during the past year. Immediatdy after
the close ot' that Communication I commenced the instruction of a number of br0thren, officers of interior Lodges, who desired to perfect themselves in the wol'k as
exemplified before the Grand Lodge. Those brethren manifested a commendable
degree of zeal in acquiring the work and lectures. and all strove to attain the high·
est degree of proficiency.
Soon after the officers of the San Francisco Lodges were installed, in December
last, a Lodge of Instruction was organized in that city, composed of the offi.cers of the
city Lodges, the officers of each Lodge in turn exempUfying the work"in the several
degrees, and corrections and suggestions being made by me when required during the
e.xemplification. These meetings were held semi-weekly, and were continued during a
period of nearly three months. They were well attended; and the good resulting
from them was manifested not only in the rapid improveme{l~ ms.de in proficiency in
the ritual, bot, as was natural, where nearly one hundred officers of Lodges were
l\Sl!embled together for mutual instrnction and fraternal intercourse. in the good fellowship aud brotherly friendships which such mee tings were calculated to promote. So
apparent was the good effect of these asssemblages, that I would earnestly recommend,
where Lodges are in such close proximity to each other as not to render it inconvenient,
that they meet together and in turn exemplify tbe work irJ the prese nce of each
other. By this means they will not only improve themselves in Masonry, bot will
become better acquainted with each other and learn more thoroughly to appreciate
the beauties of the noble Order of which they are members.
To the Senior Deacons of Lodges I have given separate instructions, particularly
in tbe lecture of the second degree. Deeming it necessary that some uniform monitor1al work should be adopted, in order to more thoroughly accomplish a complete
uniformity, I arranged, with the approval of the Grand Mt1-ster, a brief text-book for
that purpoae, a copy of which is herewith submitted. This was sent to the Master
of each Lodge in the jurisdiction, and it appears to have been gene tally 'adopted and
approved by them.
I have visited, in company with the Grand Master, nine districts, comprising one

36

Pr<>eeRAiin:gs of the

[Oct. 10,

hundred and fifty Lodges. The work was exemplified In each district by the officers
of the various Lodges who were present, and, judging from the manner in which It
was done, I am satisfied that the time is not far distant when the great object ·for
which we have so long labored will have been accomplished, and uniformity in the
work be an established fact in this jurisdiction. To secnre this result bas been the
desire of this Grand Body since its organization, and divers methods have been tried
hitherto without much success. The present system of dividing the State into districts, under the supervision of Inspectors and Deputy Grand Lecturers, appears thns
far to have worked admirably, bot its effectiveness wonld probably be further promoted by an increase of the number of Deputy Grand Lecturers; and I suggest that
one for each county b e appointed. By thns reducing the area of the districts and
increasing the number of lecturers, lhe labor will be greatly diminished, and the
system of instruction adopted will be much more thorough and effective.
The reports from the Depnty Grand Lecturers, so far as received, bear evidence of
faithful labor on their part, and show very satisfactory results.
In Snn Francisco there are three Lodges in which a foreign language is employed
tn conferring the degrees-Paefaite Union, No. 17, using the French; Hermann, No.
127, the German ; and &peranza Italiana, under dispensation, the Italian. The two
latter lodges have translated the work and lectures as adopted by the Grand Lodge
into their respective langnages, and the officers deserve great credit for their earnest
endeavors to render themselves proficient therein. Pa>:faiie Unum Lodge bas as
yet made no effort to acquire the law:fUI work; bot, as the Grand Lodge has for
years tacitly conse·nted to the conferring the degrees therein according to its peculiar customs, I have not felt at liberty to interfere in that case, although I believe
that the law of lhe Grand Lodge should be general in its application, and that all
should be compelled to submit to its mandates.
In conclusion, I desire to tender my heartfelt thanks to the Grand Master for the
many acts of kindness which I have receive·d at his bands, and which have made my
labors pleasant and' easy. My official visits w ith him to the various Lodges in the
jurisdiction, during the past two years, will ever be remembered with the greatest
pleasure. My thanks are also dne to the membeTs of the Grand Lodge and to the
officers and members of the subordinate Lodges with whom I have bad occasion to
bold official intercourse , for the uniform kindnesss and courtesy with which they
have constantly greeted me ; and the evident desire of the brethren to receive
instruction, the readiness with which they discarded old and, doubtless, favorite customs, and adopted the ritual prescribed, h88 made my intercourse with them a constant source of pleasure and gratification.
To specify in detail all to whom I have given instruction or with whom I have
reviewed the work, would too gr~atly extend this report. Suffice it to say, that I
have at all times been ready to instruct those who applied to me for that purpose,
and b11ve endeavored to discharge the important duties assigned me faithfully and to
the best of my ability.
All which is respectfully submitted by
JOHN WERNER SHAEFFER,
Grand Lecturer.

The Address of Grand ,1tfaster CHILTON is well written, and full of good, sound
Me.sonic precepts. We are pleased to learn, as we do from the opening paragraphs,
that bright days are age.in cheering the Craft in that important jurisdiction. May no
clouds of war or disaster ever again darken that region. These few words of the
Grand Master will repay a perusal in this latitude, and let the connsel be heeded and
followed:! am pleased to record that the progress of our glorious institution, in th~ interest
of which we have this day assembled, is steadily upward and onward. I~ has mc~ease.d
in the number of its members as fast as was desirable, the danger bemg that 1t .will
increase too fast-not that too many good. men.ati4 true will j.oi.n us, b'!t t~at, m a
desire to swell our numbers, we should fail to mstitate that ng1d scrutiny. mto the
character of applicants so necesse.~y .to prevent \lnworthy ones from becom1!1g members. Experience has shown that 1t is much easier to reiect unworthy e.pphcants at
the threshold, than to get rid of them by the discipline of the Lodge after they have

BRITISH COLUMBIA.
.We have received a small pamphlet of twenty pages, entitled "An account of.the
establishment and subsequent progress of Freemasonry in the Colony of British Columbia, from its origin in 1859 to 1871." The reason for this pampble·t, as near as we
can make out from a cursory reading, is about this : The old Lodge5 in the Province
were about eqnally divided in their allegiance respectively to the Grand Lodges of
Enghmd and Scotland. The latter (fonr in nnmber), two or three years ago, started
an independent Grand Lodge. The others did not and do not approve of this, and the
pamphlet appears to be made op of correspondence, showing the why and wherefore
ofsoch dissent. And, baving stated this, we have given all that IR of interest to the
Fraternity of California. It is none of our quarrel, and our Colonial Brethren must
settle their difficulties to suit themselves. We remember the fate of the good-natured
mau in Arkansas who interposed in a qnarrel between a man and his wife, and prefer
to " pass by on the other side."

I think the utmost care has been ex~rcised in the selection of candidates, and while

Do not receive the applicant because no brother has any objection, or no reason is known why he should not be made a Mason.. Let not the committee, whose duty it is to inqmre into the character of the appltcant, confine themselves to the inqniry, Do yon know of any reason why he ought not to be made a Mason? Let the inquiry be, on the contrary, Do yon know of any reason why he should
be made a Mason? Is he honest, tempRrate, virtuous, discreet, and mtelligent?
Would you be proud of him as a friend a.nd brother? Would you make him a COf!l·
panlon at your fireside? My brethren, if these last questions can not be answered m
the affirmative, then the candidate ought not to be r~ceived. I thlnk it was in the
Grand Lodge of Missouri that it was ~aid, "More morals and less members.'' My
brethren we do not want less members, but we do want more morals, or better morals· and' if we can only have "more morals" by leBSening the member3, let us lessen
the 'members. Ten good men in a Lodge, men who command the respect of tb:e .commnnity in which they live, are better than ten times that number of bad or md1fferent
ones. .As Masons, we profess great things. We claim to be intelli~ent, honest, upright citizens, inculcating and practicing tho~e truly commendable virtues, Brotherly
Love, Relief, and Truth.

What headway would such a Mason make with his wooden pins, hobbling to the
rescue of some unfortunate Brother iu distress, where even his own life might be in

According to Brother Doyle's theory, a: candidate might be in possession of one
wooden leg, one wooden left arm to the elbow, a glass eye, would only need the natural thumb on the right hQnd, and be a eunuch in the bargain, and still be qualified
for the degrees, physically, for he wonld have enough left of the natural to do Masonic work, pass an examination', and prove himself' to be a Mason. As we have
before said, we are yet in the dark as to exactly how much may be cut away from a
man and he still be qualified. We hop·e some Brot~er who i• skilled in surgery and
Masonry will some time whittle the thing down to a fine point ; and until we see something more tangible than has been offered yet, in defense of receiving cripples among
w, shall be opposed to departing from ancient usage.

Would it not be well for California to "go and do likewise?"
It appears that it has been customary in Connecticut to hold semi-annual Communications of the Grand Lodge, and to require all subordinate Lodges to be represented
thereat. A worthy Brother (F1sH, by name,} made a calculation that this involved a
tax upon each Lodge of not less than eight dollars, and so he introduced a resolution,
which was adopted, releasing the Lodges from this compulsion, but requiring each, in
its stead, to spend at least five dollars annually to pay th• Grand Lecturer, or one of
his Dep11ties, for visiting and instructing the brethren in the Work. Good for Bro.
FISH, but it strikes us that .Grand Lecturers must be looked upon as rather a cheap
article in our native State, if five dollars will pay the expense of a visitation and the
Lecturer for his services. Some noses that we wot of would be elevated at a considerable angle at fue bare suggestion.

To the first qnestion, I reply by the following quotation from :Mackey's Masonic
Jnrisptndence,p.29:" Landmark Fourteenth.
" The right of every Mason to visit and sit in every regular Lodge is an unquestion·
able landmark of·the Order.· This is called' the right of visitation.'"
This right of visitation has always been recognized as au inherent right, which in·
nres to every Mason as he travels through the world, &c.
Every writer of any eminence on Masonic subjects, whose works have come under
my notice, expresEes the same idea, and I believe it is not questioned any where.
..
I have, therefore, no difficulty in replying affirmatiftly to that question.
To your second ·question, I reply as foU11w~ :A. Master Mason, who is a member of a Lodge, has an unqualified right to object
to the admission of a visiting b.rother Into the Lodge of which he is a member.
·
. "The great object in al1 Masonry," says Bro. MACKEY, (~u~ence, p. 209,)
"being the preservation of harmony among the brethren, which our ntual properly
declares to'be 'the support of all well-regulated institutions,' it has been deemed by
many excellent authorities to be the prerogative of any member of a Lodge to object
to ·the admission of a visitor, when his relations to that visitor are of such a nature as
to render it nnJ>leasant for the member to sit in a :Lodge with the Visitor."
.
This principle in Masonry has .been settled by some of the most learned and reli·
able Masons in the United States, as well as by Bro. MACKEY.
To yonr third question, I reply!That, in my opimon, the objecting brother is accountable to the Worshipful Master
and the Lodge for his objections, and is bound, if required, to ·give his reasons therefor.

The Address of Grand Master PASCO is one of tile best written and most interesting docnments we have read in this our journey through Grand Lodge proceedings.
The fact that our brother drew his sword and sn!fered for a cause which has never
commended itself favorably to us, does not detract aught from the interest with which
we read this account of the benefits of Masonry in his own case; and we know our
readers will thank ns for affording them the S11me pleasure:The rich beauties and sacred lessons of Masonry were brought home to my
o_wn heart with peculiar force during the recent struggle between the opposing sections of our country. I remember when I lay a helpless prisoner, suffering from a
severe wound, f\Qring to trust the very snrgeons lest they should employ their skill
t!l my injury. As one after another came up and asked if I needed immediate attention, I put them off by telling them there were many much worse off t han myself.
On the evening of the third day, the chief surgeon came np and entered into conversation with me, and on finding from my speech that we were brethren, he pressed
my hand and assured me that he recognized the sacred tie that united us, and I put
my entire confidence in him from that moment, and I shall never forget his acts of
brotherly love towards me , nor how my heart glowed towards him when he manifested fraternal love and sympathy for me.
I remember at a later period of my captivity, when thousands of us from all
parts of oar beloved South were enduring the horrors of a bitter winter, badly sheltered, thinly clad, ill fed, sick, wounded, wretched exlleB, with no prospect of freedom to cheer our hearts, oar comrades being cat down daily by disease and famine,
how a few score of as, who were Craftsmen, found one another out, cheered each
others' hearts, and shared with each other anything we had over and above what
actual necessity re9aired. We formed a Masonic Society, proved one another, corresponded with a similar society in another prison, visited one another when sick,
and through some of those who had. authority over as, we were gratified to learn
that our sad condition moved the sympathy of our brethren in the city near by, who
would have aided as had not the severe rigor of military law prevented. But even
the severity of military law did not wholly exclude individual acts of charity and
brotherly love whi~h reached some of ns in a disguised form. And I used sometimes
to think that the Christianity of that time and place had much to learn of Masonry,
for no word of sympathy or warning, in its name, every reached inside our walls,
though the tongues of scores of church bells called together the worshippers within
our hearing as often as the holy Sabbath returned, and the city hard by boasted of
more churches, in proportion to its population, than any other in the country.
I remem)>er when I was returning home from captivity, just before the dose of
the war-I had reached a little town in the old North State, and was wandering
about the streets in search of a suituble place to rest, when I perceived in an upper
window the sacred emblems of our beloved Order, and )learning for (raternal symp!lthy, I ascended the stairs ; th.,r'yler sent in my name, and I there found brethren
from home, who were providentially in attendance that night, who took me afterwards to their camp, and we spent nearly the entire night in talking over the 11ast,
and they sent me on my way rejoicing on the morrow.
These and many other scenes come home to my mind when I think of the
beauties of Masonry. How often have we seen in our Lodges, and in this Grand
Lodge, those who have worn the blue and gray sitting side by side- the past forgotten, for here all are brethren. Peace and good will reign among us from one end of
the country to the other. The few jarring strings that marred tire harmony of the
_instrument, for a brief time, when the war first closed, were soon attuned into perfect accord, and here we have peace. Let us hope that the spirit of Masonry may
ere long indirectly exert its blessed iufiueoce over the whole country, and that all
may be brought Into one harmonious whole.
He is quite severe upon the efforts of some indiscreet brothers, who are determined to drag the question of the admission of colored persons into our Lodges.
He had granted dispensations for the establishment of four new Lodges.

of Macon, October 25, 1870-the M.-. W.". S,ulUEL LAWRENCE, Grand Master , presid ·
Ing, and the R.". W.-. J. Ell!ICET BLACKSHEAR being Grand Secretary. Representatives
were present from one hundred and ninety-eighty Lodges.
. The Ad~ress of Gr.and Master LAWRENCE, like everything that comes from his pen,
Is well w:itten, conCise, and to the point. The Grand Master is an indefatigable,
hard-workmg, and most intelligent Mason, and calls around him a band of zealous

workerll, under whose administration the Craft cannot but prosper in that ancient
Commonwealth. Deeply imbued with reverence, as all good Masons must be, it pains
his heart (and whose does it not?) to witness so much of the opposite among the
Fraternity. We quote some of his excellent words of connsel, as giveu in the opening of his address:When I last addressed you, I called your attention to the im),lortance of this faith
in God. And I feel daily more and more the necessity of remindmg you of you! obli.gation in this respect, in view of the growing tendency in tb.e profane world to ignore
the existence of a \lersonal God, and throw the mind into the seething chaos of Pantheism, or Materialism.
. .
Now, I am persuaded, that as in time past it was vouchsafed unto our Institution to
be the recoverer and restorer of' the Book of the Law, God's revealed word, long lll[!t,
so now it is given onto it to be a bulwark and defense against all such vain philo'gophy; preserving unto the Time-tossed hnman soul the comfort and peace or ·a settled
faith in a High and Holy One, all-wise, all-good, all-powerful, and ever-present, who
can and does pity and heal all its infirmities.
The attempt has been made on the trans-Atlantic shore to break down and throw
away this landmark, and, as if God's vengeance speedily followed, the scourge of war
in worst form has overtaken and is now desolating the nation where it was attempted.
Let us learn to value more and more our inestimable privileges, my brethren, and
remaining faithful and grateful unto Him for the favors H~ has freely bestowed on
us, collectively and individually, in the past, doubt not His existence, nor His promises, but believe t:hat He is and will be unto us, and unto all who trust in Him, "a very
present help in time of trouble." Let us hold fast to the landmarks our fathers have
set, for within them is our only safo pasturage.
In a notice of the laying of the corner-stone of a new edifice, at Bethesda, ten
miles below Savannah," on the original grounds donated the Society by the celebrated GEORGE WHITEFIELD, CHARLES WESLEY, SELINA, Countess of Huntingdon, and
others," we have a note of this pleasing incident:The brethren brought with them, to grace and sanctify the occasion, "the oak
chair me.de from tire-tree under which General Oo LETHORPE held the. fii·st Masonic
Lodge, at Sunbury, Georgia; also the Bible which was used on that occasion-in the
year 1733-both the property of Solomon's Lodge, No. 1, of Savanna.Ji, Georgia."
In this jurisdiction, the system of "District Deputy Grand Masters," for prescribed
districts, has been tried, with a view of more efficient supervision, securing uniformity of work, etc. From the reports of these officers, as printed in the Journal, we
should think t hat some were of the tjght kind, being faithful, he.rd-working, and at
the same time intelligent Masons and men. Others, however, we are led to infer from
hints dropped here and there, are more willing to take the honor than to do the work.
From one of these reports we copy the concluding para.gmphs,'which explain
themselves, and to the suggestions of which many in this jurisdiction wonld do well
to give good heed :Brethren, in concluding this report, yon will allow .m e to say that my intercourse
with you during the year has been. most pleasant ar;id agreeable. I . ha ye be~n met
and received almost everywhere with that marked kmdness and hospitality which are
found only among Masons, and I humbly trust that oar meetings have not been without profit to the Craft. While I have insisted upon intelligent, skillful and uniform
work as INDISPENSABLE to the prosperity of subordinate Lodges, yet the secret of
unstained honor-of unbroken Peace and H11rmony-depends not so much upon the
MANNER of the work, as upon a faithful adherence to and practice out of the Lodge of
the principles taught within it.
Brethren, I have made it the burden of my heart and prayers, an~ it has bee~ my
constant and unceasing toil to press home upon the hee:rtts and consciences of o!ficers
and brethren that no drunken or profane man be per~1tted to find an asylum 1.u our
Lodges-to pollute our altars, profane our symbols, distract our counsels, and mault
the God whom we worship. If the fallen and unfortunate WILL NOT be reformed and
upheld, then let them be expelled at once; and by so doing protect the dignity,
honor.and reputation of the Order, and our own personal self-respect. So shall the
incense that arises from our altars be from pure bee.rte, and our sacr1/ices without spot
or blemish.
Drunkenness, profane swearing, and gaming, with their concomitant vices, are the
cankerous poisons that eat us up, making us a hiss and a by-word- aye, more, the
.
merited mark for jest and contempt.

l~ccessfnl.. Bot ma". we ~ot suggest that it is a mistake to start off these institutions
with the high-soundmg _title of a "College," with a full corps of professors, tutors,
etc. It looks too much hke an army of officers without privates; and besides, it costs
as much to run a small as a large institution. Better, we think, to commence with
the more humble academy, and then, if found expedient, and there be the material
let it grow into a eollege.

Very kindly and fraternal notice is taken of the California proceedings.
The Grand Lodge of Montana had passed the following resolution:Beso!'!led, That the subordinate Lodges in this jurisdiction be i!lstructe.d not .to
allow a brother to furnish refreshments to the Lodge upon the occasion of bis rece1v·
ing any of the degrees conferred therein.
Bro. BLACKSHEAR thus comments thereon:If by refreshments is meant WBISKY, or other intoxicating drinks, thls resolution is
perhaps well enough, and particularly if any of the members have a WEAKNESS in
that way; bot if any brother made in OUR Lodge desired to invite the members thereof
to an OYSTER suPPER we should be very loth to deny him the pleasure.
Perhaps, if very hungry, we should concur, both theoretically and practically, partioularly if the oysters were cooked to suit as. But here, as it seems to as, is the inherent
vice of the practice, and we do know that serious evils have resulted. Though all is
seemingly a voluntary act on the part of the brother passed or raised (generally the
latter), it is very easy to have it generally understood that a supper will be expected,
and that none bot a mean or parsimonious fellow would refuse. Hence many are
subjected to a large expense, when their own families needed the money. Certainly
these " oyster suppers" are no part of Masonry or the third degree, do no one any
good, and we side rather with our brethren in Montana, than with oar Georgia friend.

affiliated; 792 dimitted; 206 died, and 301 rejected..
The Grand Master and Grand Secretary were both reelected.

with this? Everything go(ld-everything noble. Equ'.1-lity am01w the people, n!11versal education, the magical spread of the arts and ~c1en~es, a higher r_ange of civilization, a higher tone of personal honor, and a decided improvement m the moral

While Masonry is essentially social, and a large s_y stem of charity, 1t1.s not.bcense.

INDIANA.
The fifty-fourth Annnal Comm1mlcation of the Grand Lodge of Indiana was held
in the city of Indianapolis, May 23, 1871, the M.·. W.·. MARTIN H. RWE being Grand
Master, and the R.·. W.·. JonN M. BRAMWELL, Grand Secretary. Representatives
were present from four hnndred and two chartered Lodges, and nineteen under dispensation.
The Address of Grand Master RICE is an excellent paper, well written, and neither
too long nor too sll<>rt. We copy the opening paragraphs, not merely for the gratifying facts stated, but for the good counsels uttered :In presenting to you my report for the past year, it atfords me mnch satisfaction
to be able to say, that at no time since the organiza1ion of this Grand Lodge, has it
ever assembled in Grand Communication under mor.e propitious circumstances than
surround as this day. We have enjoyed a year of Masonic prosperity, and our
Lodges generally have been doing food work and Increasing their membership ;
althoagh the whole nnmber admitte Is not as large as in Rome preceding years, I
am satisfied that this is not because a less number of 11pplications have been presented, but is owing to the fact that greater care has been exeroised, and a more
careful inquiry made into the qualifications of those who sought to gain admission.
Our brethren are beginning to understand that numbers alone do not constitute
strength, but oftentimes the reverse; that if they would have their L<idges prosper and
become the habitations of Friendship, Brotherly Love, Relief and Troth, none should
be permitted to enter but those who are worthy and well qualified, who have given
evidence of those qualities which are essential to properly appreciate and understant!.
their deities as Masons.
In glancing back to the first organization of this Grand Lodge, in January, 1818,
we find assembled on that occasion the representatives of five chartered J,odges; today, as we assemble in fifty-fourth 4nuual Communication, we have in this Grand
jurisdiction, four hundred and twenty chartered Lodges, and twenty-four under di89
pensations, embracing a membership of over twenty·thrce thousand Masons. In a
society governed by regulations like the Masonic, where none are ever solicited to
enter, or even yermitted to, when influenced by mercenary motives, this growth is
truly wonderfu . During the last few years it has often been remarked that we were
making too many Masons,. l&Jd that too many Lodgea were being organized; while
it is true that many are madt!'Masons who are afterwards found unworthy, and occasionally a Lodge is organized that fails to prosper, yet, we believe tbat with the numerous towns, which are springing up throughout our State, and our rapidly increasing
population, that there is room for many more Lodges, and a plenty of good material
to supply all with an abundance of work.
The danger lies not in the growth and extension of our institution, so long as none
but good men are admitted, but in the failure, through a Jack of vigilance ou the part
of those whose duty it is to investfkate the character of the applicant, to detect the
impostor, who would adorn himself in the livery of Masonry, that he maynse it in
concealing his true character. Let as see to it, then, my brethren, that the door of
Masonry iR never opened unless the applicant be worthy. Let me impress it upon your
minds that personal considerations are nothing when compared with the future welfare and prosperity of the Order.
Death had invaded the inner circle, and taken away the Senior Grand Warden and
Grand Lecturer, and to the memory of both the Grand Master pays a fitting tribute.

IOWA.
We always take up with pleasure the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Iowa,
because that jurisdiction has in its veteran Grand Secretary, Bro. THEODORE S. PAR·
VIN, an officer who not only knows his duty, but does it well and minutely. We have
not to count up formidable lists of Lodges and members to find out the ungiven
result. The tables of statistics furnished by Bro. P. are always full, plain, and.easily
understood. Long may he be kept in office, to delight the hearts of Committees on
Correspondence, if no one else.
The twenty-seventh Annual Communication was held in Davenport, June 7, 1870the M.·.
JOUN SCOTT being Grand Master, and the B.-. w. .. THEO. s. PARVIN,
Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from one hundred and forty-four
chartered Lodges and eighteen under dispensation.
The Address of Grand Master SooTT is of fair length, and is mainly devoted to
local matters. Be had granted dispensatioii.s for twenty-six new Lodges. "Uniformity of Work" had almost been obtained in perfection, over which the Grand
Master congratulates· himse If and the Fraternity, bnt he forgets not to add this
wholesome admonition: "Alas l how many t here be who can, parrot-like, run elf
the. whole catechism, and who think themselves 'bright Masons,' who have never
1
learned that Masonry is a beautiful system of morality, veiled in allegory, substantiated by symbols.''
Do not understand from this that I rate proficiency in work as of little value. Not
so. The forms of Masonry are valuable as snch, but they are not Masonry; they are
but the casket which holds the jewel. The treasure is worthy of its beautiful sur·
rounding, and the husk is necessary to the safety and growth of the kernel within.
A soul, pure and true, is all the better for an accompanying body, beautiful and
strong, but still it is the soul which" is the better part of man," and is alone worthy
of our deepest love;
The Grand Master discusses at some ll!ngth the " Negro and Indian" question,
and argues that no Grand Lodge has the right to prescribe nationality or colo1-, but
only sel"llitude. We are willing to admit !.his as a general principle, but we still say,
cui bono? to all this discussion.
The receipts of the year were $12,578 81, and the expenditures $12,294 87.
The Grand Secretary's report is elaborate in its details. One page is devoted to
the reasons why that celebrated report of Bro. GUILBERT, the unapproachable, did
noi appear in the Journal, as ordered. Reading the scraps of correspondence about
· the same brought an occasional smile to our face, but we think Bro.PARVIN has fully
justified himself, although Masonic dyspeptics lost the benefit of he~rty laughs over
som~ one hundred and thil'ty pages of Bro. GUILBERT'S "Let her rip " correspond·
ence. Alas! alas! why did not Bro. G. hnrry np with that manuscript and get it to
the printer in time ?

During the year dispensations bad been granted to institute fourteen new Lodges.
In remarking upon this subject, he takes opportunity to call the attention of recommending Lodges as to their duty in the premises. He lays dows the following rules
)Vbich will answer as well for the Masonic latitude and longitude of California as of
Kansas:There are four things for the Lodge recommending to determine :First. That the petitioners are Master Masons in good standing, and member~
of Lodges in this jQCrisd!ction; or, if from another jurisdiction, that they have proper
dimits from the Lodges of which they were formerly members.
Second. That the three first named officers in the petition are competent to dis·
charge the functions of their places, if inducted therein ; and this is to be determined
by their appearing in open Lodge, and there giving a full exemplification of the
work and lectures of the three degrees of ancient Craft Masonry. In addition to
their skill in the work and levtures, they should have a general knowledge of our
laws, rules, regulations, and usages.
Third. That the petitioners have a good and secure place in which they may
safely meet, which must be above the first floor of the building to be oocupied, and
contain the rooms necessary for doing Masonic work-of this the recommending
Lodge must be 8atisfied beyond a doubt.
Fourth. That there is suitable material for buildin~ up a sound Lodge, and that
the new organization will not interfere with the material of an old, well established
Lodge.
We should neither destroy nor impair the nsefnlne88 of an already existing
Lodge, by the establishment of a new one, which necessarily will encroach upon its
proper domain and so limit its proper scope.
I trust this reminder. will arouse attention, and assure co-operation in a matter of
~tal importance to the safe extension of Masonic honors, and that hereafter none
other than good work will be sent up. Let those who aspire to further Masonic
advancement remember that work, and work alone, is the test of merit. " By their
works ye shall know them."
He favors the recognition of the Grand Lodge of Quebec.
ThN•e is th~ usual amount of talk and action about" uniformity of work,"•and
how it should be secured, but we think our readers have had a quant. sujf. of that.
Some most excellent and pointed remarks are made upon the nnmasonic vices of
intemperanC'e and profanity, which are still too much indulged in by Masons. The
"traders on· Masonic reputation," too, are honor~d with a first rate notice, which
must have made some of them squirm! And let them squirm, say we.
.Among his decisions we note the following 11s showing the "advanced ritualism"
attained by the Maaonic .. uthorities in Kansas. Such a decision would raise a howl
in California, but we query if our Kansas brethren are not nearest right after all:Q.-Is it a Masonie olfense for a Mast~r Mason to keep what is commonly known
as a saToon?
•
.A.-1 believe it is a Masonic offense for any Master Mason to keep a dram shop,
or what is commonly known as a saloon, or to sell intoxicating liquors as a beverage;
and I believe the Grand Lodge of Kansas will sustain any of its subordinates, should
·
they suspend or expel any of their members llir such offenses.
The "Custodians of the Work" and Grand Lecturers submitted reports of their
work during the year. .Among the former we note the name of Rev. Bro. JOHN .A.
ANDERSON, formerly 11 Presbyterian minister in Stockton, California.
The Grand Treasurer reports his receipts as $2,330 88; and the expenditures as
$1,434. 82. Our Kansas brethren are certainly: most economical. We could not run
the Grand Lodge for half 11 mouth for that sum.

LOUISIANA.

The proceedings of the fifty-ninth Annnal Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Louisiana come to us in a somewhat balky, but neatly printed pamphlet of over four
hnndred pages. The Communication was held in New Orleans, February 13, 1871the M.·. w.·.S.u!UEL M. TODD presiding as Grand Master, and the R.·. W.·. JAMES c.
BATCHliLOB being Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from seventy-five
Lodges.
The AddresR of the Grand Master is very long, bnt well written. A large portion
is taken up with his decisionR, and the reasons therefor. We only quote the following to express our decided dissent from such an exclusive, and, as It appears to us,
narrow·miuded rule. We would leave each Lodge to be judge In this matter, subject
always to the control of the Grand Master and Grand Lodge, if an unsuitable or
nnsafe Lodge Room was used. And this should be done, whether the same be occupied eJ1'4llnsively by the Masons or in partnephip with others :II. That it is improper for Lodges to hold their meetings in a place jointly occu·
pied with them by other secret associations. Having been asked whether I would
give my consent to the removal of a Lodge from a Masonic Hall to a room owned
and occnpied by a society of Odd Fellows, for the purpose of saving a portion of the
rent paid by them, and of having the services of the same sentinel, r refused, declaring the proposed copartnership to be improper; and as I had learned that such an
arrangement had been entered into by some other Lodges in this city, I desired the
Grand Secretary to issue a circular of inquiry 88 tg whether this was the case, and
to what extent. I advise the Grand Lodge to take action upon this question.
Death had been very busy during the year, and the Grand Master gives a long
list of those who. in chlU'ity, we trnst were called from earthly labor to heavenly
refreshment.
He had issued dispensations for the formation of e'ght new Lodges.
The Deputy Grand Masters from th.. several districts made report of their action,
showing generally a good state of feeling and prosperity among the Fraternity.
The Grand 'freasurer shows the receipts of the year to be $30, 773 83, and the
expenditures $26,lilil 45.
The Committee on Correspondence reported in favor of the recognition of the
Grand Lodge of Quebec, but after full discussion it was resolved to postpone action
until the next Annnal Communication.
They have, in Louisiana, a Relief Lodge, that does similar work to the "Masonic
Board of Relief," in San Francisco. It is called "Louisiana Relief Lodge, No. l,"
and is recognized by the Grand Lodlq' as its Almoner of general charities. We find
its report in the proceedings, and think it well worth copying at length, becanse it
Is a record of " Relief" that gloriously illustrates the practical character of Masonic
charity:NEw ORLEANS, LA., January 1, 1871.

Is not necessary to discnss it. Poets are allowed a license for their fancies ; the same
privilege should be extended to Grand Orators.''
The very complimentary terms in which Bro. Boor alludes to our own report of
that year,. and the liberal extracts made therefrom, almost disarm our criticism of
his antagonistic positions. As to that " Burial of Suicides" matter, as our own Grand
Lodge has gone back on itself, it is now a dead issue, and might better be buried
also. So we permit our brother to have the last word, only remarking that our
own opinion is not changed in the least.
Bro. Scor finds fault with our position that other orders should be permitted by
the Masons to perform their services at a Masonic funeral, subordinate always to us.
We think he is fighting one of the windmills of Don Quixote. We certainly have
never found any of them living giants to dread, in present or future times. "Policy"
may be urged as our only position, but policy may sometimes be coincident with
sterling principle. The word has no terrors for as. Attach the adjective "good" to
it, and we are ready to carry it out to any reasonable extent. We will only i:emark
farther, that we derived oar lessons in· this particular from old Father ISAAC DAVIS,
and if he was a man that would evtr sacrifice or waive a right for policy, nobody in
California was ever aware of the fact. In following his advice, we shall never be
ashamed.
The closing paragraph of this report is so well expressed that we venture to
transfer it to our own columns, and would adopt it as our Farewell Address, as this
will probably be our last report as Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence: Here we close our annual review. Our report has grown upon our hands far
beyond what we origina11(, designed. We have no space left for a" summary of subjects of special interest,' but we can congratulate the Craft that the prosperity of
Masonry continues undiminished. Whether its popularity is a cause for congratulation is not so certain. On every side we hear the remark, "too many members and
too few Masons;" and it cannot be denied that there are many in our ranks -who are
Masons only in name. An attentive perusal of the proceedings received convinces
us that the only danger which threatens our Institution lies in the conduct of thoRe
who are of our own household. The world judges Masonry not by its professions,
but by the daily walk and conversation of its members. In a Brotherhood which, In
the United States alone, numbers over half a million, composed of men snbject to all
the frailties of human nature, perfection is not to be expected, and it would be
strange if there were no black sheep in the flock; but it 1i! expected that those in
authority, and every brother who has the interest of our Institution at heart, will use
. his influence that Masonry is not made a by-word and reproach on account of the
acts of those professing to be its disciples, and that, in the decision of every trespass
against oar rules, they will" judge with candor, admonish with friendship, and reprehend with justice." It is thus, and thus only, that Masonry will exert its true influence on society and attain 11 hight of moral grandeur to which any other merely
human institution will in vain aspire.
To our sister Grand Lodges, for the sympathy and support so generously extended
to our Grand Lodge in its resistance to the encroachments of the Grand Orient of
France, we tender our grateful acknowledgments, and renew our best wishes for the
prosperity and harmony of the Craft in their respective jurisdictions.
There are one hundred aud forty-eight Lodges In the jurisdiction, with 11 membership of 7,307. There were 733 initiated; 693 passed, and 649 raised daring the year.
The Grand Master and Grand Secretary were both reelected.

setts, it should be stated that she promptly acknowledged the right and expediency
of the separation, and, in a spirit of fraternal kindness which contrasts strangely
with the proceedings of 80me other Grand Bodies in later years, paid into our treas·.
