The most friendly relations have existed between the two Grand Bodies from that
until the present time, and we see no reason to suppose that this harmony will not
always continue.
On th<1 13th of August, 1819, a circular to the Lodges was issued by Bro. SIMON
GREENLEAF, SAJIUEL BAI!:ER and ARTHUR SHIRLEY, Committee of Porlland Lodge,
proposing a Convention of delegates from the various Lodges to take the necessary
steps preparatory to the establiRhment of a Grand Lodge.
On the evening of October 14th of the same year this Convention assembled, with
the following Lodges represente·d :Portland, Ke<1nebec, United, Saco, Oumherland, Oriental, Solar, Ancient Landmark, York, Oriental Star, Maine, Freeport, Temple, Village, Adoniram, Northern
Star, Blazing Siar, Hancock, Lincoln, Amity, Rising Virtue, Orient, St. George,
Felicity and Belfast.
This Convention was called to order by the R.'. W.·. SAMUEL BAKER, Master of
Parttand Lodge ; and the
W. ·. Si:MoN GREENLEAF was chosen President, and
JOHN P. BoYn Secretary. Rev. Bro.JOHN H. INGBAHAJ4, of Thomaston, in"voked
Divine aid, after which they proceeded with their important deliberations, and unan·
imonsly decided that it was expedient to establish a Grand Lodge. A Committee,
consisting of the ll:. W.·. Bros. S!lllON GREENLEAF, NATHANIEL COFFIN, DANI:EL
GRANGER, JOSEPH M. GERRISH and W. GEOBGB THACHER, Jr., were appointed to
report the proper method for carrying the design into etfect.
This committee was favorably received by the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts,
and all that was .asked for was granted. Several adjourned meetings were held,
resulting fa the final establishment of the Grand Lodge of Maine, June 24, 1820the Grand Master of New Hampshire officiating as presiding officer. The narrative
thus continues, alluding also to the trying times of the anti-masonic excitement:After the preliminary arrangements were completed" a procession was formed
of the new Grand Lodge and about three hundred of the Fraternity, which escorted
the Grand Lodge of New Hampshire to the Rev. Mr. PAYSON'S meeting-house. On
entering, the Grand Master of New Hampshire took the chair, having the officers of
his Grand Lodge seated on the right and the Grand Master elect and other officers of
the new Gran rt Lodge on the left. The introductory prayer was olfered by the Rev.
President of Bowdoin College, and an elegant and instructive oration delivered by.
J. H. SHEPPARD, Esq., of WiscaRset, on the connection between learning and religion,
and the influence of Masonry in preserving and extending them both.''
The con•ecratioo and installation ~ervices were then completed by the Grand
J.odge of New Hampshire, and the Grand Lodge of Maine. with a constituency of
thirty-one Lodges and a mP.mbership, probably, of less than a thousand, took its
place among the Grand ,Lodges of the world. with every prospect for a. successful
future.
From this time the Institution in this jurisdiction continued to flourish. New
Lodges were erected- Hermon Lodge , at Gardiner, and Watervate Lodge, at Waterville, being chartered at the first session of the Grand Lodge. In 1829 there had
been twenty-eight new Lodges constituted, and but one charter surrendered, leaving
fifty-eight Lodges upon the roll, with a membership, as nearly as can be ascertained-,
of about fifteen hundred.
I am necessarily compelled to leave much of interest that transpired between the
time of its organization and 1829, when the anti-ma.sonic storm that had been sweeping like a whirlwind over the conntry, reached Maine. The excitement was intense,
and for a. time Ignorance and folly held full sway. Political parties and religions
societies vied with each other in their denunciations of Masonr7, and every etfort
was made to injure the Fraternity, socially, politically, pecumarily, and in every
other manner, a.or! by every device which weakness and wickedoe88 could suggest.
In looking back at the period of excitement we are filled with astonishment that so
many of the brethren of Maine remained firm in their Masonic faith, never wavering
in their devotion to tb.e institlltion which they so wa,rmly loved. The number of

boor.

MARYLAND.
In a vP<ry unpretending pamphlet of about seventy-five pages we have the proceedings of several "Grand Stewards' Lodges," a Special Communication, and the
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Maryland. The first named is a kind
of a standing committee, elected by the Grand Lodge, that acts for the latter in the
interim, and in fact performs much of the mere routine work that would else come
before the Grand Lodge at its Annual Communication, at the risk of crowding out
more important bnsineBS. The Semi-annual Communication wa.e held in Baltimore
Mayo; 1870-the M.·. W.·. Jom; S. BERRY presiding a.e Grand Master, and the B.·. W.·.
J A.COB H. MEDAIBY being Grand Ser.retary. Representatives were present from
sixty.eight Lodges.
The 9pening prayer by the Grand Chaplain is a .very fitting one for the occa.eion,
barring its too great length. Why cannot our clP,rical 'friends, both in Lodge and
chnrch, learn to be short! The Deity needs none of our long and eloquent prayers,
but has tole! us through the wise man, that in all addresses to Him onr "words should
be few." We once learned a lesson on this subject from a "profane," which we
have tried to heed and profit by. A long time ago, in our political days, we were
connected with a Legislative body in an official capacity. Its services were opened
with prayer by the city clergymen, in turns. One of them, good Dominie W., was
noted for his long-windedness, as well e.s eloquence, and full as much for the former
e.s the latter. One morning, being late, we were compelled to stand jn the crowd in
the lobby until the parson subsided. Right in front was one of the most prominent
members of the House, who wa.e also perforce kept outside of the inner door. We
watched with amusement the varied phases of his countenance, as his patience
oozed out by degrees to the very last drop. Scarcely had the ".!.men " been said
before he flung the door open impulsively, and in a tone of voice that might be heard
by the parson himself, exolaimed : "Thank God! he's got through at last." It wa.e
a brief remark, but it set us to thinking, and when in the order of time it was our
privilege to add "Rev." to our name, we mentally resolved never to give anybody
else cause of thankfnlnees on that account, if we could help it. Our Maryland
brother will take the hint in good part, and next time put on the condenser.
The Address of the Grand Master is very brief, occupying less than two pages of
the pamphlet, and only tells us that he had granted dispensations for the formation

predecessor. The receipts of the year had exceeded the expenditures some is,500,
but that had gone but little way towards liquidating the heavy debt upon the Temple.

Master, came to the rescue with temporary loans, and the wolf, in the shape of the
Sheriff, was driven from the doors. .One new Lodge had been opefled during the

MASSACHUSETTS.
We have received in a bulky, but handsomely printed, pamphlet of over five hundred pages, the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts at several Quarterly and the Annual Communications thereof, during the year 1870, the first being
held March 9, and the last December 27, in that year. But as after al~ as is custom·
ary with our Mas~achosetts brethren, these are merely " abstracts" of the proceed·
'ings, without much regard to order or connection, it is somewhat difficult for a
reviewer to know where to begin and where leave oil'. We will do our best, howev\ll, for, from the quality of the matter contained in this volume, (and it is fairly
entllled to be so designated) we have met with none of its contemporaries of eqnal
interest. Our M.assachnsetts brethren are more immediately concerned with the historical reminiscences which form a large part of the work, but, in mnch, we and
others claim almost equal interest.

The first Quarterly Communication was held March 9, and had repre.sentatives
from ninety-one Lodges. We noticed the fact, last year, that the Massachusetts
Grand Lodge claimed jurisdiction over the Masonic Lodges on the West coast of
South America, and in China. We find here the report of the "District Depnty Grand
Master for China," Brother WH. C. BLANCHARD, of Shanghai, from which we learn
that:The amount of work has not been 1large, but it has been very well done under the
able management of Brother EAMl!S and his officers, who have taken particular pains
to instruct their Lodge, and to bring the ritual to a better state of perfection than
ever I have seen worked in Shanghai. In looking at the returns for three .years
past; yon will see that the number of members remains about the same, which can
be easily accounted for, as quite a portion of the Shanghai community is a moving
one, not settling here for any length of time ; so the affiliations and dimits are about
tbe same. Number of members, 59; initiates, 9.
The Grand Master delivered an address which fills some forty pages of the pam·
phlet, it being en~irely a historical document of great interest to the Craft in Massachusetts and elsewhere. The key note of the address is the following paragraph
from the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of New Hampshire in 1869 : "In M.assachusettsthere was no legal Grand Lodge till the Union in 1792."
This is an extract from the Report of the Committeo on Correspondence, written
by Bro. BELL, who (very lnj!ldiciously, as we think,) mounted the .African hobby,
and endeavored to prove, that as the Prince Hall Lodge was in being as early as
1787, the Grand Lodge of MasYachusetts, not coming into existence until 1792, had
no right to declare it or its subordinates " clandestine," and hence all its snbieqnent
action on the subject was null and void, ab initio, and O!lr African brother bad a
righl to walk into the white man's Lodge and say: "Am I not a. man and a brother!"
Grand Master GARDNER, to refute this claim, goes into an elaborate history of
Masonry Ill Masse.chnsetts, which we ce.n only glance e.t. In the first place, he shows
that the New Hampshire Grand Lodge was organized in 1789, and by deputies from
Lodges chartered by the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts prior thereto, viz : one
Lodge In 1734 e.nd e.uother in 1784.. Further, the Grand Master shows that the system of Provincial Grand Lodges originated in the GraDd Lodge of England In 1726,
e.nd that the first deputation was granted In 1727. The Lodges in Provinces este.b·
lished and ruled by this officer were called "Deputy Grand Lodges," and reported
through him to the parent Grand Lodge of England. The Grand Lodge of Scotland
also he.d its Provincial Deputies in America e.s early as 174.7. Extracts from old documents, historical e.nd Legisle.tlve, a.re given in proof of these statements. General

The institution of Freemasonry is universal. It stretches from east to west, from
north to eonth, and embraces within itself the representatives ol' everv branch of
\he humui family. [ts carefully•tyled doors swing open, not at the knock of every
man, but at the demand of every true and worthy man, duly accepted, whatever his
religion, his race, or his country, me.,r be. This Grand Lodge stands upon the high
vantllge gronnd of this catholic society, and recognizes the great principles which
most necessarily underlie an institution which has a home on the continents and on
&he islands of the seas.

Most Illustrious Brethren: War has wasted oar poor city, and a great Pjl:rt 'of

MINNESOTA.
The eighteenth Annnal Communication of the Grat!d Lodge of Minnesota was
held in St. Paul's, January 10, 1871-the M.·. W.·. c: W. NAeH being Grand Master,
and the R.·. W.·. W. S. CoMBS, Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from
seventy-four subordinate Lodges.
Grand }faster NASH delivered an able and interesting Address, from which we
make a few selections, which will well repay a perusal. Here is one of the opening
paragraphs:There never has been a period in history when Masonry was in a condition as
fiourishing as it is at the present time. It is now supported by a p;reater numner of•
friencls, and maligned by a smaller number of enemies, than it has ever before
known. The time when it was denounced by pions sectaries and jealous patriots
seems to have forever passed away. The principle appears to be every where acknowledged, that it is not only innocent, but laudable, for men to enter into secret
associations and brotherhoods for innocent and laudable purposes ; for objects of \
benevolence and mutual improvement; to establish stronger and purer social ties;
to create new agencies in the cause of .virtue and erect new bulwarks against the
progress of vice; to promote social, individual, and ~eneral reform. These brotherhoods have become almost as ·numerous as the sects 10 religion, or the parties in pol·
!tics. Masons can forbear to criticise the p;loss of novelty which they wear, the
t emporary and local objects which they adopt, the restricted spheres of nsefolness
within which they are confined, the ambitious and sometimes tawdry forms and rhe\·
oric of their ceremonies, for their existence is a constant prop and homage to M1sonry. Imitating, in a remote degree, and at a respectfnl distance, its organizations,
and its simple yet sublime rites, they vindicate the wisdom of the system, and they

MISSISSIPPI.
We have received the proceedings of the fifty.third Annual Communication of
the Grand Lodge of Mississippi, held in Vicksburg, January 16, 1871-the M.-. W.·.
GEOROE R. FEARN presiding as Grand Master, and the R.·. w. .. J. L. POWER being
Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from two hundred and three Lodges.
The Address of tbe Grand Master is an able and well written document, which
we have perused with pleasure. We are glad to learn that matters look better
Masonically and otherwise than they did a year since. But death had been busy at
work. A Past Grand Master and Past Deputy Grand Master had been summoned
home by the grim messenger, and their memories were appropriately honored.
Proper notice is taken of the Que bee Grand Lodge and the action of the Grand
. Orient of France towards Louisiana. The legality of the former is maintained, and
the latter is unqualifiedly condemned.
Dispensations had been granted for the opening of three new Lodges during the
year.
This appeal, in behalf of the " Orphans' Home," does honor to the head and
heart of the Grand Master:I again c.a !lyonr attentio~ to the "Orphans' Home.'' A year ago this Institution was in
danger of~emg lost to ~be little ones whom itshel.~red, and to whom it was notooly in
name, but m deed and m truth, a Home. That crisis has passed. By the exertions of a
few of the orphans themselves, guided by kind friends, funds sufficient to pay for the
property have been raised, and a good title is now vested in the Trustees. But
though relieved in this respect, its necessities are still great. The inmates of the
" Home" must be fed, clothed and educated. Many of them are the children of our
· bro.thers; all of them are helpless, desti~t~ orphans. On whom have they a stronger
claim than upon the "!embers of au Inst!tut10n whose corner stone is Charity? If you
turn a deaf ear to their appeals, who will heed them? Can you not asRist them? It
is true that in the agll'regate the expenses of the" Home" are heavy, but the sum
necessary for the mamtenance and education of each child is but light, and within
the power of almost every Lodge in this Jurisdiction to contribute. Let me suggest
then, ~rethren, that each-Lodge pledge itself to the support of one of these children:
place its name npon th~ book of the Lodge, adopt it, and see that the pledge is made
good· by a prompt remittance to the Treasurer of the required amount. Do this and
the result will be .that every member will be a better man and Mason, and ther~ will
be such a flame kindled upon your altars as will illumine this entire jurisdiction and
'
your Lodges will be filled with the best men of your community.
"In Faith and Hor.e the world will disagree,
But all mankind s concerned in Charity;
All must be false that thwart this one great end
And all of God, that bless mankind, or mend." 1

The Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence submitted an elaborate report on a
great number of questions that had been referred to them. The Report, as a whole,

1871.J

Grand, Lodge of OaJ,ifornia.

was laid over for consideration until the next Annual Communication. We cull out
of the mass some of the most salient points, not for comment, but for the considera·
tion, if not the entertainment and improvement, of our readers. The Chairman of
the Committee was th1t veteran and well-known Mason, Bro. GILES H. GRAY, Ben.:The subject and questions s11bmitted by Bro. CHAMPLIN, and referred to this Committee, have al•o had due consideration, viz: "Is not Masonry, now, no longer an
operative institution, but s;1;1eculative and moral only? and is it not the moral quaJifl.
cations of a man that qualify him to become a Mason? And cannot a man, without
an arm or leg or a finger, or otherwise maimed, perform all the moral and social
duties of a Mason? And will the conferrinir the degrees on such persons violate any
landmark of the Order now obligatory on the Order?"
'fhese questions lead us to conRider whether the physical ability speoified in the
old charges constitnteR a landmark in the Masonic. organization. In our opinion, it
does inasmuch as certain parts of the human system are called into requisition and
have' to contribute their portion of labor and action in the .development of the sys~m which forms the basis of the Masonic Order.
In the practice of the ritual, the portions that are called into r~quisition cannot
be dispenRed with or substituted. If certain positions are to be as•umed-if certain
actions are required to be used in which physical power and ability are called into
requisition, and the parts or limbs required to act are wanting, the subject cannot
proceed, but must be rejected as disqualified and ineligible.
Our institntion is based upon immutable laws and principles, which are character·
istic of the Order. These fundamental principles and laws mark it.. identity, and
are termed Landmarks, which admit of no change or modification which would impair its unity as it was in the beginning, is now, and as Masonry must ever remain.
These landmarks cousist of the Moral, Phy.9icaJ, and Religious qualifications, of
peculiar rites and ceremonies, etc., which are be.vond the control of Masonic legis·
lative aSBociations, and it is not in the power of any man or set of men to make
innovations thereon. It would be as reasonable to ask that the rest.. iction as to sex
or age or condition be removed, as .there are very many females and others excluded,
who possess the moral qualifications in an eminent degree. Would not that destroy
the identity of the Order? Remove these ancient landmarks, and other demands
would be made. The foundation being sapped, the fair fabric would tumble into
ruins.
As to " non-affiliates," the Committee " roar you gently as a sucking dove." But
such mild medicine will not do in California, that is sure:The subject of affiliation and the status of non-affiliated Masons was also referred
to onr Committee, and has been considered. An elaborate disclll!sion of this subject
canuot be embraced in this report, but the ground on which our decision is based
will be set forth as briefly as possible. Before the present system of subordinate
Lodges was adopted, there was no such thing as Lodge membership; therefore, it
has no claim to antiquity. .At its adoption, each particular organization was of a
local character. It was a volunl.a.ry association of Masons for special purposes, and
the laws and regulations enacted for their government were only binding on the individual entering into the compact, so long as they remained members thereof, and
did not. nor could they, in any manner, affect or interfere with the rights and privi·
!eges of a general character which each Mason enjoyed before he united in Auch
voluntary association to form a particular Lodge. These were not surrendered to
the Lodge, nor circµmscribed to the term of membership or Lodge jurisdiction; they
were inherent, and remained unimpaired. While, by entering into this compact,
their duties and responsibilities were increased·, they, at the same time, acquired
additional rights peculiar to their organization. A Mason, by his initiation, acquires
certain g1ineral privileges, subject to the conditions of the established immemorial
Usages, Regulations, and Constitutions of the Craft. Of these he cannot be divested,
except for immoral conduct or violation of his general obligations and duties as a
member of the Fraternity. He is under no restraint to connect himself with any
particular Lodge. The Constitutions do not make it obligatory on him. It is and
must be a free and voluntary offering on his part. He enjoys all of the general beneftts of !i[asonry without it: but, if he choose to affiliate himself he becomes, thereby,
enittled to certain special ;1;1rivileges, and subjects himself to certain special regulations. Those are the conditions of his Lodge membership, not the terms on which
he holds his connection with the Fraternity. The act of affiliation is a voluntary
contract to which the individual and the Lodge are the parties. If he fails to discharge the duties required of him by the contract, the I,odge may diRsolve the con·
nection between them by discharging or excluding him, or ·declaring bis membership
forfeited. Or if the member de•ires to dissolve the connection by withdrawing his
membership, he has the right to do so, and there is nothing in the ancient charges to ·
prevent him. When his connection is dissolved, he stands as he did before-ea a

MONTANA.
We have received the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Montana, at its fifth
and sixth .Annual Communications, held in Helena in 1869 and 1870. Both make up
neatly printed pamphlets, each being ornamented with an engraved likeness of the
Grand Master, as a frontispiece. The .Annual Communication for 1869 was commenced
October 4th-the M.-. W.·. WILBUR F. SANDERS being Grand Master, and the R.·. w.·.
SOL. STAR Grand Secretary. Twelve subordinate Lodges were represented.
The .Address of the Grand Master is of reasonable length, and discusses local and
general affairs with a free and able pen. Some of the opening thoughts are so well
expressed that we make free to use our " scis•ors" (forgive us, Bro. DRUMMOND, of
"away down East,") for the benefit of oar own readers:ThPre are here no abnormal growths to be rooted out, but a fair page given us
on which to write in ineffaceable characters what manner of men we are. We are
to give tone and direction to the unborn generations with which the future shall
teem. There will never be an hour in the history of Montana when the consequences
of our action, for good or evil, will not be palpably felt, and we cannot, if we would,
escape the responsibilities of existence at the pivotal crisis in her history and
destiny.
Regardle•s of all other differences, we have organized here an institution which
iur.nlcates Brotherly Love, Relief, and Truth, and teaches Fortitude, Prudence,
Temperance, and Justice. The other issues which divide us are evanescent in their
character; but these pract.ices are cardinal, and underlie all private and public virtue. We seek to make them not merely names in our ritual, and words in our speech,
but facts in our lives and in the Jives of our people. This tribute we pay to them,
that thus we are willing to be judged in history.
We silence to-day all strifes which are of the earth earthy, and enriched with the
added experiences of a year, have come up to consult· together for the good of
Masonry. In Auch a presence hushed be all discordant voices, banished be envy and
malice and all uncharitableness. We are friends; nay more, we are brethren. The
struggle• of life. however they may strain, must not be permitted to break the bonds
of affection. Our reliance is in the "large love and boundless thought" of Him
"who is over all, God blessed forever." In· all sincerity and reverence let us turn
to Him in gratitude for mercies vonchsafed in the past, and hnmbly invoke strength
and wisdom for the responsibilities of the present and the struggles of the future.
Quite a space in this .Address Is devoted to ~ discussion of the Utah affair, in wbjoh
Kansas, Colorado, Montana, and Nevada got somewhat mixed up. But as we believe
all is settled now, if not entirely satisfactory, and" all is quiet on the Potomac" of
this'' City of the Saints," we will not prolong the discussion of .a dead issue. Our
brethren in Utah appear.to be getting along " as well as could be expected,'' and
shall receive no drawbacks from our unruly pen.
The receipts of the year were $1157, and the expenditures $1064.

The Report of the Committee on Correspondence is from the pen of Bro. CORNELIUS HimoES, and is the first of the kind in the jarisdictfon, we believe-at least the
first from the pen of this brother. Oar brother need make no apology for his production, for it is evident that be wields the pen of a r.eady writer, and the brethren
have only done .themselves justice by electing him to the Grand Master's chair for

·
Here is a little touch of satire upon the pilgrimage of our N ortb Carolina Ma.
sonic sages, in quest of thQse very naughty things called" keys and ciphers." Bro.
H. speaks our sentiment!! :·
We find in the proceedings a lengthy report on the nse of "keys and ciphers,'.'
which show a good deal of correspondence aud labor, as well as thought, on the
part of the committee. Only one State was found where the use of such things was
conntenanced, that was Rhode Island. Perhaps it may be that our Rhode Island
brethren were more frank than the rest, and possibly that is the only jurisdiction
where such things are ti> be found; but we confess to more or less skepticism, and
the reports of the controversy between !lro. WILSON and the committee, in Vermont,
rather stilfons our skepticism. We confess that we do not believe we have the exact
work as practiced by our ancient Grand Masters, nor even as wrought in England in
1721, but we do think the symbols, the grand and important features and tenets,
have been preserved pretty faithfully, and that they are pretty near the same every
where that M!loBOnry is known or practiced. It does not destroy the identity of a man
if he changes his coat, or even his whole snit. We speak thus, not to countenance
innovation, but to express our belief that the body of Masonry has been transmitted
for a long term of years with substantially few changes.

The Sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Nevada was held in
Virginia City, September 20, 1870-the },{,',
GEORGE w. HOPKINS being Grand
Master, and the R.-. W.-. WM. A. M. VAN BoKKELEN Grand Secretary. Representa·

The Address of Grand Master HoPKilllB is a well written document, of just the
right length to suit u's. He sa.ys what he wauts to say and stops, which we believe
to be the secret of good writing. He opens with a tribute to one who was so well
and favorably known to the writer that he knows he will be pardoned for quoting.
If the Masonic Fraternity, or the world at large, only had about a million such men
as N. A.H. BALL, both wonld be far better off than either is at present. He wa•
peculiar in some things, but his heart was always in the right place and his hands
ever bnsy' in doing good to all mankind, and " especially to the brethren:" Through the mercy of diiiine goodness we again meet in Annual Communication.
We assemble with un~roken ranks. While the proceedings which have reached us
from sister jurisdictions during the year have come to us laden with sorrowings for
the 1,1111ny faithful who have closed their earthly labors and gone to their re ward, the .
angel of death has not visited this Hrand Lodge. But we are called to mourn for one "
who was llforetime with u•, and of us. Bro. NA.THANIEL A. H. BALL, who was
appointed Grarid Organist at our Annual Communication of 1868, and served in that
capacity until the Ann~al Communication of 1869, died on the 2~d day of August
last. He was widely known among the Craft in this jurisdiction, as also in California.
His genial disposition, urbane manners, and useful life, endeared him to all who
)mew him. His heart was thoroughly alive to the principles of Brotherly Love and
Masonic Charity. No nee dy person, eithP.r among the Craft or among the profane ,
ever appealed to him and went away empty-handed. We who have liste ned to his
music here may well rest assured that his son! is attuned to the celestial harmony
heard in the better Lodge above.
'

yet from ocular obser vatioL1s in lSiW we know that he utters the truth only. What

We have much cause for congratulation upon the circnmstances under which . we

season ; the laborer has been re warded for his toil. Neither pestilence nor famine
hlls visite<l the land. The nations have been startled by the clash of arm" m the Old
World; the dread meetings of contending bRttnlions have there caused thousands to
mourn the loss of fathers, brothers, hu, bands, and sons, victims to the insatiiite Mo
loch of war. A mighty Empire has been shaken to its centre. But in our beloved
country, Peace and Prosperity; hand in hand, have blessed and smiled upon the land.

The Addre@s of the Grand Master is abont the usual length, .and is mainly taken
up with the notice of local matters and the action of the Grand Master. Due notice
is taken of the death of several eminent Masons. He reports the Craft in the jnris·
diction as" in a remarkable degree of prosperity," but says the frequent changes of
Worshipful Masters make it very difficult for the Grand Lecturer to diffuse generally
. and thoroughly a practical knowledge of the work of the jurisdiction.
He had Issued dispensations for the formation of eight new Lodges. He also

received, and welcomed with a speech from the Representatives and Grand Master.
Why should Bro. ABELL be made an exception, especially as he holds this honorable

at the next session, and air his blushing honors by a set speech!
Masonic imposters, craving aid, seem to be as plentiful in New Jersey as in California, and the Grand Master utters a warning word against them.
Here are some words of good counsel and advice, which we copy, believing, from
facts that have semi-officially come to our knowledge during the year, t.hat California
Lodges are as open to this censure as those in New Jersey. We like t~ see this public and just rebuke of what is nothing lint a cowardly spirit of revenge or spite, that
has no place in a Masonic Lodge :J regret that I am obliged in this report to call your attention to the factions
spirit which bas manifested itself in some of our Lodges. Indeed, it has uome to my
knowledge that this spirit has become so ·widespread in the Lodges referred to as. to
entirely prevent their growth. Men whose morality and integrity are . unquestioned
and who stand high in the esteem of their communities, have beeu excluded by th~
action of oue or mure of the members of one faction, because the petition was presented by one of another, or for the reason that the applicant was a particular friend
of some oue toward whom they felt a dislike.
It is deeply to be regretted that such an evil should be found to exist anywhere
in our midst. The spirit of revenge should never enter the sacred precincts of a
Lodge of Master Mason•. Masons are but men, snhject to the passions, temptations
and weaknesses of fallen humanity; hut shall it be said of us, that we cannot exemplify in our Lodge rooms the teachings and obligations of our Order? To my mind,
it seems that a Lodge room ought to be the lu•t place where we should expect to
find a brother seeking revenge in this cowardly manner. No man of character and
high social position is willing to have a suspicion raised as to his reputation by being
rejected in a Masonic Lodge, and simply because rejection by the Lodge in quest.ion
i• the rule. When •uch a state of thing• exists, it i• better ten-fold to pass a resolu·
tion to admit no more members, and thereby prevent the application of candidates.
I speak thu" plainly because 1 feel it to be my duty to invite yonr attention to this
serious evil. In this connection, however , I do not wish to be misunderstood. lam
as strong au ad""cate of the black-ball being used to exclude improper material as
any member of the ~'raternity. I would admit no one who did not come up to the
proper standard. Yet I would not exclude all. I would he.re remind Masters of
Lodges of the lectures required of them in their respective Lodg" rooms; and enjoin
upon them the necessity of taking advantage of these occasions to urge upon the
brethren, in a kind and fraternal spirit,. the importance c;f a faithful discharge of their
duties and obligations as Masons, that they may practice not only in the Lodge room,
but out of it, Brotherly Love and <Jharity, the virtues so prominent in our telichings;
then, making these principles the role, will all jealousies and contentions celise, our
Lodges will prosper, and the members be joined together as a band of brotherB.
We believe we have once before called attention to the fMt that in this jurisdic·
tion the Deputy Grand Master and two Grand Wardens are not the ornamental ap·
pendages they are with us and generally, but have their tasks assigned them, and
are required to return their" fall tale of bricks." We have, following the Grand
.Master's Address, the reports of those officers, which attest tbat they had been
faithful workers, and were entitled to receive the full wages of the Craft. To the
Deputy Grand Master had been as•igned thirty-seven Lodges, and he had visited
every one, and found them, with few exceptions, "in a prosperous and healthy condition." To the Senior Grand Warden had also been assigned thirty-seven r,odges,
bnt he had only visited and inspected twenty. The Junior Grand Warden had only
been able to visit four Lodges, and renders a humble apology for his remissness.
This plan seems to work well in New Jersey. How would it do in California! We
think there would be f'ar Jess electioneering for the Grand Warden's chairs, if the incumbents were expected and required to visit some fifty Lodges annually" as the
price thereof."

during the year. The expenses of his office had been $181L 36.

doors off their hinges, locks ruined, and keys lost, &c., &c.
We are glad to say that steps were taken to make things look better in the future,
but still, as appears to us, this "St. ,John's College" is rather too heavy an elephant
to be conveniently carried by our brethren, and many of them seem to think the
same.

merited compliment to.the Address of Grand Master MARSH, the report of our Grand •

as sober sense.

TENNESSEE.
The fl.fty-eixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Tennessee was held
in Na.shville, October 4th, 1869-the· M.·. w. .. JONATHAN s. DAWSON presiding as

The Address of the Grand Mast.er is brief and mainly occupied with the local

Quit.ea number of his decisions appear ill the Address, but none requiring special

H ere are some suggestions relative to the duties of committees of investigation,
which, without fully indorsing, we give as worthy of careful thought, if not adoption
in our own jurisdiction : Among the elementa of discord, in the ordinary busines~ of Lodges, none is mo!e
fruitful of bad feeling than the common method of declanng the report of committees of investigation into the character of applicants for initiation. They usually
report favorably or unfavorably, as the resurt of their iuquiries suggest, without
giving the Lodge any insight into the general charact.er of the applicant, whic.h should
ii.Jways be done. Committees appointed for this purpos!l should never s~ek mft?r~a­
tion of the members of the Lodge, for two r easons: Fust. By answe~ their mquiries he exposes his ballot; if his answers are unfavorable to the applicant, they
of co~e become known, which very frequently gives offense to his friends who are
Masons and feel solicitous for his initiation. secondly. Each member of the Lodge
has the inalienable riaht of ballot, by which he can determine the fitness or unfitness
of the applicant; in the exercise of the right, he gives no expression of his l!Bntimenta
that become public, and, therefore, no offense. The best method t<;> adopt is for committ.ees to inquire into and report the general charact.er of the applicant to the Lodge,
without an expression, whether favorable or unfavorable; th~t would leave every
member in possession of his character, to decide according to his sense of duty.

thirty-eight American Gre.nd Lodges, and sever al foreign Bodies. From the opening
paragraphs we cull the annexed, which is full of suggestive thought, as well as eloquent expression:.
Freem~sons, bound by their essential principles to be loyal and good members .of
society, observing the laws of God and their country, must also be peaceable1 while
their obligations are remembered, and their readiness to obey the calls of chanty and
to aid any brotl1cr in need and distress is a current topic of remark here and in all
countries, and among all peoples of the world.
It is this loyalty, peaceableness, and charity which causes the Order to progress ;
which has given it, as the history of the past twelve months declares, a strength and
a moral power to defy the thunders of the Vatican, and cause the sound of the gavel
to assert itself under the shadow of the dome of St. P eter's; which is to-day spreading ita punty of doctrine and sublimity of teaching over the ruins of the Acropolis,
and among ihe descendants of LEONIDAS; founding its temples of wisdom among the
ruined churches of Asia; placing its sacred Lodges on the sites of the t.emples of
Apis, Isis, and Osiris, where "forty centuries" of mystic learning " look down upon
tliem " from the rugged Pyramids and the awful majesty of the silent Sphynx;

which is now extending its moral purification in the remot.est recesses of the ·Australlim valleys, on the table-lands of Southern Africa, the miasma.tic slopes of China., in

The charter of one Lodge was suspended for this good and sufficient reason: The

We rather think that discounts anything that California could ever show, and we

Another Lodge was hauled over the coa.ls because it "occupied for Lodge meetings a Hall in the second story of a wooden building used as a grog shop, the Lodge

Masons were made in or ruled that Lodge?
Very elaborate notice is given to the action of a Lodge in initiating, etc., a candid11.te who had had his leg amputated below the knee, but possessed a.nd used an excellent cork substitute, which, as the Lodge claimed, enabled him to comply with the
Jequirements of Masonry. A bad spirit seems to have actuated the Lodge when
ca.lied to account therefor by the District Deputy Grand Master. The Grand Master
emphatically condemned the Lodge, and recommended the arrest of ita charter. An
incident of this transaction may be of some interest to Lodges and brethren in California. It was urged upon the Grand Master that " the principal officers were responsible for the bad work, and that many of the ~bers were not present, a.nd,
oonsequently, were not responsible, and that the whole Lodge should not be punished," &o., &c. The Grand Master does not see it in that light, and thus correctly
argues in reply : "This kind of reasoning would excuse any act on the part of a
Lodge. Absence from October to March on the part of many members of - Lodge, from attendance a.t Lodge meetings, argues any thing but an excess of Masonic zeal, and does not evidence such an interest in Ma.sonic matters BB to commend
itself to favorable consideration. It is right that a Lodge should suffer, because a
few of her members commit a.n error, just a.a much BB if the greater number had
been present, for it was their duty to attend the Lodge, and if continually absent all
winter, permitting the lesser number to manage the Lodge, then they certainly deserve to receive the same punishment as those who attended and committed the error.
Those who do attend act for the absent, and they a.re bound by it." We concur.
In another case, two Ma.sons, members of the same Lodge, being enemies, fought
a duel, " until both were severely wounded by pistol shota." Yet both were tried a.nd
acquiUed by their Lodge. The Grand Master justly condemns such action in most
indignant terms, and recommended the expulsion of both the brothers from all the
righta and privileges of Masonry. "lt is time," he says, "that the Grand Lodge
used its power to punish such disgraceful conduct in the past, and to prevent it in
the future." We are pleBBed to add that the Grand Lodge concurred, and so acted.

the birds were vocal among the trees, and in an holir of profound peace, a mighty
crash resounded through the walls of our State Capitol, and a host of the foremost
men of the Commonwealth were precipitated to a sudden and a.wful death, the contemplation of which froze the bfood and touched the hearts of all who heard the
dreadful story. Since then a prodigious and devastating fiood has spread gloom and
want and despondency through some of the fairest portions of our State, and given
us cause for mournful deliberation. But while the out.er world bears the marks of
political transitions and physical decay, the calm dominions of Masonry show the
immutable nature of the wise and beneficent principles on which our institution
rests, and, admonished by the contrast, we should devot.e ourselves, with a pure
bee.rt and resolute purpose, to the perpetuation of our system.

WE5T VIRGINIA.

The sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of West Virginia was held
in Wheeling, November 8, 1870--the .M.·. W.·. WH. J. BATES being Grand Master,
and the R. ·. W. ·.THOMAS H. · LOGAN Grand Secretary, with representatives from
forty-three Lodges.
·The Address of Grand Master BA'.llES is of fair length, and ably discuBBes some
very important truths. Here are some well expressed, a.a well a.a thoroughly digested
thoughts:Freemasonry is not a system of·religious faith. It ha.a neither a religious creed,
nor a ceremonial of worship. It cannot redeem from the power of sin, nor save the
soul. Nor can it even secure to man his highest spiritual enjoyment in this life. It
is of human origin, and it was instituted for human ends.
But its " doctrines are founded upon divine truth, and they involva some of the
most sacred dnties of mankind." It teaches pnnciples and enjoins duties which
concern man in his relations to God, to himself, and to his fellow men. And in
every period of its history, a " vast cloud of witnesses" have att.ested in their lives
that its doctrines and practices t.end to encourage and promot.e the highest virtues of
which man's nature is susceptible. It had its origin in a remot.e age, and hM passed
· downward unchanged, from generation to generation, "permanent in character and
undeviating in object." Its membership has included, at every period, m1my of
those to wl:iom the world has accorded the highest rank, both for "pre-eminence of
virtue and exaltation of station."
These qualities have given to Freemasonry a vitality more vigorous and enduring

"(

'

Grand La<lge of Oalifornia.

125

than was ever possessed by any other mere human organization, and have enabled
it, throughout its progreBB, to defy the malice of even its most unscrupulous. and
most powerful enemies.
May we not, therefore, brethren, cherish a just pride that we are members of •
Society whose foundations rest upon principles that have passed unscathed through
the ordeal of centuries, and stooa unharmed before the assaults of countless foes?
But while indulging this felicitation, we must remember that the unexampled
vitality of Freemasonry has been the result, not altogether of the character possessed
by its princlples, (although these, indeed, are imperis_hable i~ th~ir nature,) but
also and in a great degree, to the fact that at all periods of its history there ha.a,
most happily, existed among its members men of unconquerable fidelity, whose
faithfulness to their fraternal obligations and duties, even in the midst of the most
dangerous trials, knew neither weakness nor change. These men, of whom, in their
day "the world was not wort.by," preserved and transmitted to the generations succeeding them these great truths and wise rules of action, that, together, constitut.e
what is termed the "body of ¥a.sonry," which has come down to us.
If, then, we would aid in the perpetuation of the principles of the institution,
pure and uncorrupted, we must as Freemasons emulate in our lives the constancy
and faithfulness which distinguished these ancient worthies, from whom we have
received a knowledge of the sublime mysteries of the Craft.
The present is an age in which changElf! ~e most s~tling and r&4ical are ~1!fug
place in the laws and customs of commumties and nations, as well SB m thti opmions
and habits of thought and of feeling of individuals.
This" spirit of progress," as it is t.ermed; this desire for change and reconstruction of existing opinions and laws, has invaded almost every Society and Association
of men. Freemasonry ha.a not escaped its influence. There are certain self-styled
reformers, who are anxious to obtain such modification of the ancient landmarks of
the Fraternity as shall, in their opinion, bring them more perfectly into harmon;i:with the changed social and political sentiments, feelings and customs, which prevail
at the present day.
But the principles of Freemasonry being founded upon the divine truths of revelation, are, like these divine truths, fit for all time and adapted to every phase of
human condition or human intelligence. They address themselves alike to the
capacities of the wise and the simple; to those who occupy the lowest, as to those who
hold the highest position in hfe. To lead virtuous and upright lives, to practice
charity and sobriety; to be obedient to civil authority-to have a just regard to the
rights of others-to seek the welfare of a brother ana to be jealous of bis honor and
reputation; to sympathize with the distreBBed, and be ever ready to succor and defend the o.fllicted and the helpless, are duties which Freemasonry enjoins alike UJ>On
the poor and the rich , upon the prince and the pea.sant; upon him who received
service as upon him who renders it; and for the performance of which all are alike,
e&pe.ble.
.
If this be a truthful statement of the doctrine and requirements of Freemasonry,
then it needs no reform, no reconstruction of its principles or its laws, to adapt it to
real or alleged changes in the condition of human wants of the present day. The
good which the faithful practice of these principles effected in the lives and character
of members of the Craft in ancient times can also be accomplished in us, "if we
walk by the same rule and mind the same things."
May we then, brethren of the Grand Lodge, be distinguished for faithful adherence to the princi.Ples and landmarks in all t.lieir purity, a.a they have descended to
us from the ancient Craft.amen ; tolerating no changes to satisfy the whims of the
capricious, nor alterations to comply with the demands of bigoted sectarians or the
so=caued "-liberal and enlarged views" of modern reformers.

and Dutch Lodges now work m harmony. An application for e. new Lodge at the

PORTUGAL-Gn.u m OnIENT OF LusITANIA.-The Boletino official de Grande
Oriente Ilusitano for July, 1869, contains a report of the negotiations of the Grant
Orient with the Grand Lodge of Portugal, in relation to the union of the two bodies.
The August (1869) number of the Boletino, states that the Commission to define
the relations of the two Grand Bodies above alluded to, had brought the matter to a
satisfactory termination.
The Grand Orient hae instituted the order de Triangulo rutilante (The Brilliant
Triangle), in commemoration of Bro. Gomez Freire D'Andrade, who, many years
ego, died on the gallows a martyr to Freemasonry. Masons of merit a.re to be
invested with it.
.
It appears from a paper, Le Grand Orient Lusitanien, written by Bro. Dr. Da
Cunha.-Bellem, that the above mentioned Bro. D'Andrade, Lieutenant-General and
Master of the Lodge Vittude, at Lisbon, was elected Grand Master in 1816, and,
with eleven other brethren, was executed on the 18th October, 1817. It is then
stated that, for some time thereafter, Freemasonry, which, however, at that time
was a political association only, ceased to exist. In 1849 several old Masons met
again, and formed the Grand Orient of Portugal, with Bro. D'Oliveira as Gra.i:td
Master. He was succeeded by Bro. Alvez de Mouro Contlliho, who, by his imperious conduct, alienated many brethren from the good cause, On the 31st January,
1859, the former Grand Lodge of Lusitania was revived. with Bro. De Paraty at itB
head. Thus sprung into existence two Grand Lodges, which declined to recognize
each other. It is to be hoped, however, that the split is now healed.
The Grand Orient of Lusitania has been acknowledged since 1863 by the following
Grand Lodges: France, Ireland, Italy, Ar~entine Republic, Uruguay, Saxony, Luxemberg, New Granada, Hamburg, Brazil (dos Benedictinos), the Netherlands,
Darmstadt, Belgium, Chili, Royal York, Three Globes, etc. The Grand Orient has
now in all eighteen Lodges under her jurisdiction, at Lisbon, Oporto, Coimbra, the
Azores, and four in Spain. The Grand Orient consh!ts, besides the Grand Officers,
of the Masters and the deputies of her Lodges (one deputy for every twenty members). By the laws of the Grand Orient, the Grand Master must be a Portuguese
by birth, who is elected for the term of three years. All the officers, grand as well
as subordinate, are elective. The Grand Orient meeU! semi-monthly. Besides the
three St. John degrees, four higher degrees, composing a chapter, are recognized
and practiced.
,
Masonry in Portugal has survived innumerable persecutions at the hands of its
kings, its priests, and the Inquisition. Many of its votaries have been subjected to
torture, banishment, and even death.
Some evidence exists that Masonry was introduced into Portugal somewhere
about the year 1727. It underwent many changes and persecutions. In 1834 we
find three Grand Masters in Portugal-1.>6 Silva Carvalho, the Marquis of Saldanho,
and Man. Da Silva Passos. Carvalho left the country in 1836; Saldanho was
deposed from office in 1837, and Vialla Nova de Foz-Coa elected in his place in 1839.
The second Grand Lodge elected Da Costa Cabral as Grand Master in 1841, and the
third Grand Lodge, in the same year, chose Man. Gonsalves de Miranda as the successor of Carvalho. The French or modern Rite was practiced by these bodies.
In 1837, the Grand Lodges of Ireland chartered a Lodge at Lisbon, from which
sprung several Lodges, and which finally formed a Provincial Grand Lodge. In
1840 the above named Jose de Silva Carvalho established a Lodge at Lisbon, and
likewise a Consistory. In 1841, however, the Grand Orient of Brazil granted a
patent for an independent Gra.nd Orient, which in 1845 had eeventeefl. Lodges under
its j1:1risdiction. There existed at that time in Portugal the following four Grand
Bodies:
,
1. The last named Grand Lodge of Lusitania; 2. The Provincial Grand Lodge,
depending on the Grand Lodge of Ireland; 3, The Grand Orient of Passas-Manuel;
4. The Grand Orient of Costa Cabral, the two last entirely independent. The
French, Scotch, and York Rites were practiced by them respectively.
In 1848, the Grand Orient of Lusitania applied to the Grand Orient of France for
the establishment of mutual representation, which seems to have been declined.
The Grand Orient of Lusitania, of which De Parady is Grand Master, is now recognized by a number of Grand Lodges, as before stated.

The following resolutions were adopted : "Every Lodge retains full freedom of ritual: tbe external relations are regulated

The 150 Lodges affiliated with the Grand Orient of Italy, are distributed in the
following countries:·
In Greece (Isle of Bamos), 1; in Turkey, 9 (4 in Smyrna, and 3 Constantinople);
in Magnesia, l, and in Salonica, 1 ; in Egypt, 6, (3 in Alexandria, 2 in Cairo, and 1
in Suez); Tunis, 1; Tripoli, 1; Lima, 1; Buenos Ayres, 1 ; Montevideo,;t; Ba.Ito (Argentine), 1; Florida (Chili), 1; and in Italy, 127.
It will be observed that the Grand Orient acknowledges those only as Freemasons
who are members of one of her own Lodges, or belong to a Lodge of Masonic
authorities in alliance with it.
Article IX. of the Constitution of the Grand Orient, provides as follows: ·
"The Grand Orient of Italy has its seat at the capital of the kingdom; it may
charter Lodges in all parts of the world."
The Grand Orient, therefore, does not only not subscribe to the right of juril!diction, but a.lso recognizes those as Masons only that are members of Lodges affiliated
with Grand Lodges in alliance with it. This is certainly a claim that even the Grand
Master of Hamburg has never set up for himself.

,
. Again have we made our a11nnal visits, to the different households of the Masonic

family and witnessed their labors and progress. In our own country, the Masonic
ranks present one grand and solid phalanx, prospering and increasing beyond all
precedent. The number of Grand Lodges in the United States is forty-two; total
number of Lodges under their jurisdiction, 6,971, with a membership of 373 962,
according to the statistical reports for 1868, with the exception of nine; onti of these
is for 1H66, and seven for 1867, and our own Grand Lodge for' 186!!. The membership of two of these we have estimated, as they are not reported. If we add to this
the Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts, who, in this country, are not members of
Lodges, we increase the total by about 37,000: With the non-affiliated Ma.sons, the
grand total would undoubtedly reach 500,000. Our neighbor, the Grand Lodge of
Canada, in 1867had184 Lodges with 7,000 members; and New Brunswick, in 1807,
17 Lodges, with about 1,000 members, under their jurisdiction.
In Europe, also, the prospect for the future of our Royal Art, is encouraging. In
Germany'the annual conference of the Gre.nd Masters seem to infuse a spirit of unity
among the bod!es yarticipating therein.
The Grand Lodge rur Sonne, at Baireutb, proposes a union of the Grand Lodges
of South Germany. Two of the Grand Bodies of Italy, the Grand Lodges of Milan
and Florence, heretofore inimical to each other, have united, and now form the
Grand Orient of Italy, with ilB seat at Florence. There exist, however, two other
Grand Lodges in Italy, the Ru1;>reme Council at Palermo, with about twelve Lodges,
and the Supreme Council of Ricily, of which Prince Elia is Grand Master, composed,
it is said, of his aristocratic followers only. Its numbers are insignificant, and they
a.re not recognized by the Grand Orient.
In Spain the change in the poll tical condition of that country is followed by
sucoe!)8ful efforts to re-kindle the fires on the altars of Masonry that had been extinguished by a bigoted priesthood. Four new Lodges have been chartered in that
country by the Grand Orient of Lusitania, at Lisbon, and others are reported to be
in process of formation. There may yet be many sore trials for Masonry in that
country; but as the nations of continental Europe gradually assert their political
rights, we may predict a brighter future for the Fraternity of those countries from
which autocratic rule has heretofore excluded the practice of our Royal Art. Such
has been the ca$e in Italy and Portugal, and it is now asserting its rights in Spaiu.

The items given have all been noted down from reports before the writer, except
t'iose from British Columbia, New Hampshire, and Wisconsin, where the figures,
though representing 1870, were t:i.ken from a table furnished by Bro. DRUMMOND, of
Maine. It will be seen by a glance at the footings, that there are in the United States
and British Provinces 8258 L odges, with a membership of 511,651. The initiations
during the year, of those Grand Lodges which have ma.de returns thereof, were
44,3i3. Compared with the t:i.ble in our r eport of last year, there has been an increase in the number of Lodges of 557, and of members, after deducting deaths and
suspensions, of 18,328. The previous year 46,335 initiations were returned, being
some more than in 1870, but both represent a large army of Masonic r ecruits.
We would particularly commend this exhibit to the attention of the "Antis," who
have been holding conventions in certain cities for the purpose of annihilating Ma.sonry and all secret societies. It certainly looks as if their vindictive opposition was
the m eans of the unusual growth of our Institution. We almost feel like OBking
those sour-visaged mawworms not to hold any more conventions, if such a result is
always to follow, for we have some fears that they will bring to us such an increase
as to threaten danger from our very p opularity and growth. Please, then, Bros.
BLANCHA"!llJ, FINNEY & Co., forbear, for a little while, at least l
And here flna.lly, as we hope, do we lay down our p en as chair1X1an of this laborious committee. Our labora have, indeed, been pleasing to us, and, we hope, not
unsatisfactory to our brethren for whom we have written. We wish we could believe
-that we deserved one half of the good words our brethren of other committees have
been ple&led to say of us. But the preBSure of other avocations has been so great
and constant, that we have all along felt that we could not do justice to the position
we have held through the kind partiality of the last three Gra.nd Masters. Our reports have not satisfied us, if they have our too partia.lly judging brethren. We have,
however, done the best we could under existing circumstances, and now feel that the
time has come to give way to other and better wriW-those more expert in Masonic
law and lore than we dare to claim for ourselves.
We shall pa.rt in pelW0 and harmony wi.t h our brethren of corresponding committees
inevery jurisdiction. We have faithfully endeavored to~arryouttheresolve ma.de at
the outset, that we would not write a word that could leave a wound rankling in the
heart of a brother.. If, some times, as in the case of Bro. Gun.BERT, of Iowa, we
have occasionally poked a little.fun at the style or arguments of a brother, our excuse
is, that the temptation was too ~eat to resist. The comments were ma.de in good·
nature, and so received, we trust.
·
All which is respectfully submitted, for the committee, by
WILLIAM H. HILL, Ohairman.

To suppress, in the Craft, the spread of the contagion of prevailing vices, the
Grand Master has seen fit to exercise his power to enforce subordinate ~odges to
apply discipline to offending members. While we fully concur in the views presented by him in regard to the scope of his executive authority, yet, as a question
concerning the extent of the Grand Master's prerogative is presented, on which he
himself desires a judicial definition, we recommend that so much of the .Address as
relates to direct action by t.he Grand Master to compel trial and punishment by subordinate Lodges for breaches of moral or Masonic law by their members, be referred
to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
The congratnla.tions of the Grand Master on the success of the system of inspection adopted at the la.st Communication will, we think, find approving echo from a.II
who ba.ve watched its working or observed its effects. As suggested in the Address,
we recommend that so much thereof as relatP.e to changes in district boundaries, and
other proposed reforms in the inspecting a.nd lecturing system, be referred to a. ape·
ciel committee to consist of the Grand Lecturer and the several Inspectors a.nd
Deputy Grand Lecturers present a.t this Commnnica.tion.
The beneficial results of the system ha.ve been, in no inconsiderable degree , the consequenc &of the tonrs of persona.I visitation with which the Grand Master ha.sfavored
the various districts, a.s reported; and we deeply regret that ca.use should have been
given him to add to such report a.ny vindication of his motives. We hereby present

present Grand Master, as that your approval hereof shall be a recommendation for
the continua.nee of the practice by bis successors so fa.r as possible-an expression
of thanks to him for the zeal that prompted the undertaking of so a.rdnons a la.bora.nd a fraternal rebuke to such unappreciative brethren as have, wh~ther thonghtlessly or nncha.rita.bly, referred to selfish motives and unwort.hy considerations the

Bro. MoRRIS M. EsTEE offered the following resolution:Resolved., That in view of the fearfnl calamity which has just befallen our sister
city, it is ordered that the entire representative fund of this Grand Lodge, amounting
to five thousand "ollars, be and is hereby unanimously appropriated for the benefit
of the sufferers at Chicago, and that onr Orand Master immediately telegraph that
amount to the Grand Master of Masons in Illinois, for the purpose indicated.

Bro. Ju!ES LAIDLEY, for the purpose of facilitating the di~patch of the
aid proposed, offered the following as a substitute for the foregoing:Be3o!ved, That five thousand dollars, in coin, of the fonds of this Grand Loqge
now in the hands of the Trustees of the Reserve Fund, be donated and. immediately
forwarded to the Grand Master of Masons in Illinois, in aid of the sufferers by the
late conflagration in Chicago.

The substitute resolution was accepted by Bro. EsTEE and was referred
to the Committee on Finances, by whom it V1as immediately reported back
wit.h the recommendation that it be adopted; and it was unanimouely
adopted by the Grand Lodp:e.
·
Bro. WILLIAM H. HILL offered the following resolution:Resolved, That, as a further evidence of our practical sympathy, the box of Ma·
sonic charity be placed npoa the altar at two o'clock, this afternoon, and that the
brethren be requested then to cast their offerings therein, as God has blessed and
favored them; and that the moneys thus contribut.ed be also transmitted by our
Grand Mast11r,. without delay, to the Grand Master of Illinois, to be disbursed,
according to his own judgment; for the relief of destitute Masons and their families.

Which resolution was adopted.

~eason of \heir town having. been three times visited by disastrous conflagrations
within the present year ; therefore, be itBesolve(l., Tbat .the due~ of . Truckee Lodge, No. 2.00, for the coming year, be remitted.

Very Dear Brethren:-Surroonded by the armies commanded by the Sovereign
of Prussia, we address to you our loud cry of distress; and, in order that it may reach
yon, we entrust it to those sublime messengers whioh science-that fruitful mother-

Grand. Lxlge of CaJ,ifornia.

1871.]

[Oct. 11,

....

145

has taught na to send forth into space, as if to defy the insane efforts of these men
of spoil who foolishly imagine that Ideas can be p enned np, subdued and chained,
like criminals in a prison.
Think not, very dear brethren, that we implore a forcible intervention. The
spirit of abnegation which animates us, our consciousness that we are defending the
right, and , permit us to add, onr courage, will aid na, as we firmly trust, to conqner
those who have made themselves the abominable inatrnments or the barbarous pretension which dares to affirm that Might takes precedence of Right. As yon will
perceive by the subjoined document, our only object is to call for the assembling of
an Impartial .Masonic Jnry, of whom we shall ask whether the charges we present
agail!st Bros. WILLIA.M and FllEDERIOK, of Hohenzollern, the one King of Prussia,
the other its Crown Prince, are well or not well founded , from a .Masonic point of
view.
If yon are willing to give due consideration to the motives alleged by us In support of this demand-If, above all, you admit that they are well founded in right and •
:Masonic morality-yon will ·acknowledge , very dear brethren, that never has there
been presented an occasion when universal Freemasonry could assert Its existence
and its power in a manner so solemn and so striking. In constituting itself the
aupreme judge of the great cause brought before it, it will have proved that it does
not content itself with the m~re form of inscribing over the portals of its temples the
noble motto-Liberty, :Equality, Fraternity-but that it intends that each word of this
motto shall be earnestly applied to all its members without distinction. It will have·
done more. It will have opened that glorious path which the profane world cannot
choose but purane ere long, viz: that all differences between nations ahii.11 tie settled, not. by brnte force, bnt by international arbitration, by_the law of simple
equity, the only one in harmony with the humane aspirations or modern civilization,
of which Freemasonry is and must remain the shining light.
This circular and the document subjoined are addressed to the Orients and Lodges
throughout the world. Each of these may c'ltooae and send a delegate furnished
with full powers to represent it in the illustrions tribunal which is called to assemble
1roviaionally on the 15th of March, 1871, at Lausanne, in Switzerland.
Trusting, very dear brethren, that our appeal will be listened to, ·we offer you th11
ezpression of our fraternal devotion.
•

FRENCH MASONRY TO MASONRY UNIVERSAL.
CBAROES AGAINST BROS. WILLIA.Ill AND FREDERIOK OF HOHENWLLERN.
BRETHREN :-

Seal of t he Lodge St. Joh.!!<
{ under the title of He11<7 • v,
Orient of Paris.
·

] 871.J

Grand Lodge of ,Oalifornia.

147

barlty so far even as to lead their soldiers under the very walls of Paris, that great
city which, more than any other, has shown itself to be liberal, pacific, and opposed
to all international wars.
Brethren, the German Sovereigns have thus become guilty of the greatest of
orfmes, and this crime is even more detestable, inasmuch as William of Hohenzollern
and bis son, Chiefs of the German army, having been received in the fr;ateroity of
Free Masons, have solemnly sworn to observe its laws.
.
William of Hohenzollern and bis son are consequently accUBed of perjury and
prevarication. Universal Free.Masonry cites them to appear before the bar of its
tribunal within three months from this date.
The tribunal before which the two aforesaid are summoned to appear will be composed of delegates from all the Orients of t.be Universe.
The seBSioos of this jury will be holden in some neutral country-at Berne, or in
some other city which will in due time be deRignated.
Should they fail to appear in obedience to this citation, William of Hohenzollern
and his son will be declared traitors to their oaths, felons, and Masonic outlaws.
They will be oondemned to suffer the, penalties provided by our laws, they will be
accursed forever, and their memory will be banded down to the execration of posterity.
ORIENT OF PARIS, this 30th November, 1870.

WHBREAS, It appears that within certain portions of the State of California, near
the borders of the State of Nevada, certain settled districts are, by the nature of the
country, more accessible and convenient to Douglas Lodge, No 12, and E1rmeralda
Lodge, No. 6, of this jurisdiction, than to the nearest Lodges now organized, or likely
to be organized, within the jurisdiction of California, at any point opposite the pres·
ent extent of oonntry embraced by said Lodges; and,
WHEREAS, It appears that persons within said portion of California are desirone
of receiving the degrees in Masonry with those Lodges, and are , for the reasons
above stated, practically debarred from receiving and participating iµ the rights and
benefits of Freemasonry; now, therefore, be it
Resolved, That the M.'. W.·. Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masone of California be and is hereby fraternally requested to confer with and request such
Lodges within its jurisdiction as are situated nearest said Douglas and Esmeral.da
Lodges, to yield such portion of their territorial jurisdiction and rights as pertain to·
that portion of the State of California lying eastwaraly of the mam summit of the
Sierra Nel'ada range of mountains ; to the end that persons there residing may legally

and benefits of Free and Accepted Ma~onry•
llaolved., That, in the opinion of this Grand Lodge, such action upon the part of
the California Lodges will tend greatly to the good of Masonry in general, withi_n the
territory contemplated in this reqaest.
Resolved, That the Grand Secretary of this Grand Lodge be instrncted to forward

avail himself of the means at his command for learning what our requirements are,

A petition cannot go before a Lodge until it has received the recommendation of
at least two of its members. Those who thne recommend may fairly be presumed to know the law, and ought to know whether the petitioner whom they recommend is qualified to be a Mason. The Lodge may rightfully asoume that, not only

.
Your committee think that no petition which has been received by a Lodge should
be returned· to the petitioner, but that no ballot should be had npon any petition
where the investigating committee have shown by their report that the petitioner is
in· any way disqualified or unworthy to be made a Mason, or that, by reason of age or
residence, his petition ought not to ha'Ve been presented to the Lodge. It may be trne

rightfully apply ; and your committee think that a little time for refiection would be
useful for one who is so careless of the truth of his statements, and that a full year
is not too long for him to wait before presentin'g a second petition to any Lodge.

To the questions proposed your committee have given careful consideration, and
they now respectfnlly report:First-1'11at every rule or regulation ordained hy thiR Grand Lodge for the good
government of the craft is so far perpetual that it must continne of binding force
nntil, in Grand Lodge, it shall have been repealed or modified; and that the resolution in regard to Negro Masons is still in force as a rule of action for all Masons
reoognizing ifs jurisdiction.
Second-That it is competent for this' Grand Lodge itself to heal, or to authorize
its subordinates to hel\I, Masons who 'have received the degrees of Masonry in clandestine Lodges, and to do this at any, Annual Communication; bat whether it would
~onsider it expedient to do so, it will in its wisdom determine whenever a proper case
is presented before it.
Third,-lt is competent for any Masonic Lodge of t his jurisdiction to receive the
petition of any person who bas resided within the State of California twelve months,
and within its jurisdiction six months next preceding bis application, provided always
that he be" a man, free·born, neither a slave nor the son of a bondwoman, a believer
in God and a future existence , of moral conduct, capable of reading and writing,
not deformed or dismembered, but bale and sound in bis physical conformation,
having his right limbs as a man ought to have, and able to conform literally .to w!iat
the several degrees, respectively, r equire of him :" and provided also that be has
not been rejected by any Lodge of Masons within twelve months next preceding the·
date of bis petition. These qualiflcatioUB are indispensable, but these are all that
are r equired. Distinction of color is.no where so much as hinted at or snggested by
any word in our Constitution, Regulations, or any resolution of the Grand Lodge that
has ever come to the knowledge of your committee.
Fourth-It is competent for tb.is Grand Lodge to grant charters to·worthy brethren. authorizing them to make Masons of such good men, residing within their jnrisdlction, as poRsess the necessary qualifications and, being moved thereto by. an hon·
est purpose, express a desire to be so made; and it is competent for the Grand Lodge
to make sncb grant to Mason•, " without regard to color, " as it bas ever done. Bot
no charter can be granted by the Grand Lodge to any Lodge "until it shall have
worked a time nnder dispensation,.and shall have exhibited to the Grnnd Lodge satisfactory evidence of its Masonic capabllity." See Sec. 1, Art. I, Part III, of the
Constitution. That instrument requires only that the applicants for a dispensation
be at least seven in number, and that they be Master Masons in good standing, recommended as such by the nearest or most oonvenient chartered Lodge, or, if in any
city or town in which more than one Lodge is established, by a majority of such
Lodges.

Becond.~ec. 2, Art. II[, Part Ill, of the Constitution, provides that "no

Sec. 2, Art. IV, of the uniform code of by-laws for Lodges, provides that, if any
applicant elected to receive the degrees in this Lodge does not come forward to be
initiated within three months thereafter, the fee shaH be forfeited unless the Lodge
shall otherwise direct."
The representative of Mendocino Lodge, No. 179, desires to know whether, under
these provisions or the Constitution of the Grand I.odge and by-laws
t~e subordinates, a man who had been elected to receive the degrees of Masonry '.n his L't>dge ,
bot had been obliged by urgent business, requiring his personal attention, to leave

1871.]

ihe State before he could come forward to receive initiation, and to remain oat of the
State for six months, or a year, mustlst-Present a new petition for the degrees ; and,
2nd-Remain in the State twelve months and within the jurisdiction of the Lodge
six months, after his return, before he could present such petition.
To this your committee answer : Ordinarily the qnestion of loss of residence,
by reason of absence, depends on the intention of the party. If he leaves the place
of his residence with the purpose of abandoning it and to.king op his residence else·
where, he loses his residence at the moment of leaving; but, if he leaves for pur·
poses of business or pleasure, with the purpose to retain and return to his residence,
and his purpose remains 1u:li.,hanged during his absen~e, be will retain his residence,
though his absence be prolonged for years, and will be entitled to all the rights and
privileges of a resident immediately on his re torn. Bnt, to give a Lodge jurisdiction
to receiv.~ a petition for the degrees of Masonry, the applicant must have resided, in
fact, in this State for the twelve,months nezt preceding the date of his petition, and
for the last six of these months most have resided within the jurisdiction of the Lodge
to which. the petition is presented. The members of the Lodge ought, at least, to
have the opportnnity to know the present character and habits of the applicant, and
the Constitution has very wisely provided that he shall live among them for not less
than six months, to give them such opportnnity.
In the cnse presented, however, the party had, while residing within the jurisdiction of the Lodge, presented his petition and been elected. As he did not come forward within three months, for initlatiQll, the fee accompanying his petition was forfeited to the Lodge, under the proVislon of the by-laws quoted, unless the Lodge
should consider his excuse sufficient and order otherwise, bot his election was not
annnlled by his absence. On his return it was his right to present .himself to the
Lodge, and, if the Lodge had taken no act.ion with respect to the non-forfeiture of his fee,
t o tender the amonnt of the fee and ask to be initiated; and it would have been the
duty of the Master, if no objection were made, to proceed to confer on him the
degrees of Masonry as in other cases.
Third.-Sec. 2, Art. I, Part III, of the Constitution provides that, "upon the petition of seven or more Master Masons being presented to the Grand Master, in the form
prescribed in Art. III, Part VII, he may grant them a dispensation to open and hold
a Lodge at the place therein to be named, with power to make Masons and receive
members by affiliation; and he shaH therein appoint the Master and Wardens of the
new Lodge. Bot, in no case shall such dispensation be issued unless the petition be
accompanied by a recommendation of the nearest or most convenient chartered
Lodge, (if from a town or city where more than one I,odge exists, then from a majority or such Lodges) setting forth, in the form prescribed in Art. ID, Part VIl, that the
11etltioners are all Master Masons in good st.anding," etc.
Sec. 1, Article IJ, Part V, farther declares that "it is the duty of every Master
Mason to be a me.mber of some Lodge ; and every one who, having resided six
months within the jurisdiction of a Lodge, shall refuse or neglect to make application so to be, or who shall not have regularly contributed to such Lodge au amount
equivalent to its regular dues, while able so to do, shall be deemed unworthy of
Masonic consUU?mtion, and shall not be entitled to, nor be the recipient of, any of the
rights, pri:vueges, or charitie$ of the Order."
With these provisions before him, Bro. OasoN K. SMITH, Senior Warden of San
Simeon Lodge, No. 196, asks whether Masons who for mo;e than six months
had resided within the jurisdiction of a Lodge, bot have not been members of any
J:.odge, and have neither made application to become such nor contributed any sum
to any Lodge daring the time, most contribute a sum equal to six months' dues, or,
at least, apply to become a member before he can become a petitioner for a dispensation to establish a new Lodge?
