The Constitution declares that a Mason who so neglects bis duties shall not be
entitled to, nor be the recipient of, any of the rights or privileges of the Order. The
right to petition for the formation of a new Lodge is one of the privileges of the
1
Order, and a privilege which is only accorded to Masons in ~ood standing. Very
clearly, no Mason who has resided for years within the jnrisdiction of a Lodge, bnt
has not been nor songht to become a member of that or any other Lodge, a_nd has
not regnlarly contributed to any Lodge, Is not, under the provisions of our Constitntion, in good standing ; and before be can be recognized as a proper petitioner for the
formation of a new Lodge, he must place himself in good standing. Bro. SMITH
seems to think that the payment of a sum of money, eqnal to six months' does, to the
Lodge within whose jurisdiction the Mason resides, would immediately restore him
. to good standing. The committee do not RO understand the law. If one relies npon
contribution to maintain his Masonic standing, he must contribute regularly.
The sixteenth of our General Regulations provides that-" Non-affiliated Masons,
who are suspended by operation of Sec. 1, Art. II, Part V, of the Constitution, (before qnoted,) if they desire to restore themselves by affiliation, shall pay a sum
equivalent to six months' does, in addition to the affiliati~n fee required by the bylaws of the Lodge to which they may lipply; or, if they desire to restore themselves
by contribution, they shall pay a sum equivalent to the ameunt of the regular dues
of the Lodge within whose jurisdiction they reside, during the whole period of such
residence-unless sickness or inability to pay be shown as the reason for such nonalllliation or non-payment."
By the eighth section of the Regulations of.1721, it was provided that" no set or
number of brethren shall withdraw or separate .themselves from the Lodge in which
they were made brethren, or were afterwarc!s admitted members, nnless the Lodge
becomes too numerous, nor even then without a dispensation from the Grand ?tfa~ter
or his depnty; and when they are thus separated , they mnst either immediately join
themselves to such other Lodge as they shall like best, with the nnaaimous consent
of that other Lodge, or else they mast obtain the Grand Master's warrant to join in
forming a new Lodge." Then it was and ever since has been regarded as the duty
of every Mason to be a member of some Lodge, and oar Constitution has laid down
no new role in that regard, but has rather relaxed the strictness of the old rule by providing that a Mason's standing shall be deemed .good, though be do not join himsefr
to any other Lodge, if be regnlarly contribute to the Lodge within whose jurisdiction
be resides. Jf he will not become anll continue a member of some Lodge, or contribute, according to his ability, to help sustain the Order, he ought not to receive or
enjoy any of its benefits or privileges; and, least of all, onght he to be named as one of
the· fonnders of a new Lodge. If he is moved to contribute, only thathe may take part
in the formation of a new Lodge, the motive is suspicions, and it wonld be prnllent
always to allow him to contribute long enongh to entitle him to the credit of having
regularly contributed before he be allowed such a privilege. A new Lodge needs
live men to manage its work and give it character.

a favorable report from an investigliting committee, speak freely together of the
qna.llf!catious of the candidate and bf the propriety of r eceiving him as a member
of that Lodge. The very object of snch committees is that the Lodge and all its
members may be informed of the fitness of the applicant to be received into the Masonic family; and if any member of the Lodge knows the candidate personally, and
desires to state any reasons why he shonld be received, and particularly if he knows

action of Phceniz Lodge, No. 178, in expelling him from all the riglits and privileges

acting Master of the Lodge, commanding him to appear at a certain stated meeting
to receive a reprimand, in accordance with the judgment of a commission, dnly
elected by said Lodl(e to hear and determine npoo certain charges preferred against
him. The wilful and contemptnons disobedience to a summons should nndonbtedly
subject the otfender to the severest punishment known to our laws, bnt before this
extreme penalty is inflicted, the fact should be clearly and indnbitably established
that the failure to obey the summons aroM from wilful neglect or contempt.
In this instance the accused otfers two excuses : First, That, immediately npoo
the reception of the summons, he served npoo the Master a written notice of his io.
tention to appeal to the Grand Lodge; which notice, he says, he thought would have
the etfect to stay all further proceedings until said appeal had been heard sod adjn·
dicated by this Grand Body. In taking this view of the case the accused was in
error ; bnt, if he honestly believed that his notice would have this etfect, hew as really
guilty of no contempt, and this should Iiave had weight with the commissioners in
determining upon their verdict.
The second excuse, however, is, in the judgment of your committee, entirely
valid, and should have been so held by the commissioners. The accused states that,
on the night indicated in the summons for his appearance before the Lodge, he, being
a physician, was in attendance upon a patient who was dBngeronsly ill, and who re·
quired his constant care and 1ttention; that the life of said patient would have been
jeopardized by his absence; and that, in the care and anxiety incident to the case, he
entirely forgot the Lodge and its meeting, and only remembered it wheo reminded
of it by a member after the Lodge had closed. This statement was made to the com·
missioners upon the trial, and no testimony was adduced to controvert it. In view
of these facts your committee are of the opinion that the commissioners erred in their
jndgmeot. They therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution :Resolved, That the action of Phceniz Lodge, No. 178, in expelling J AMES A. RnusSEAU, be revoked and set aside, and that he be and is hereby restored to all the rights

Of its antiquity, Masonic literature is replete with theories, ingenious and plans·

and became his only conso!ati.on, when, yielding to the seductive sophistry of the

Leaving the theory of antediluvian Masonry, continued by NOAH and his descend·
ants, we follow the classical ARNOLD in his endeavor to fix the origin of our science,

The Osiris and Isis of Egyptian mythology, separate from mysticism, poesy, and
divine attributes, appear as two human characters, possessed of intelligence and
goodness, and consequent po)Ver to elicit attention and obedience' from the wild and
uncultivated barbarians, and to elevate them from savagery an.d Ignorance, to social
order, divine worship, and legal observance.
ORPHEUS, the poet, physician, philosopher and priest, after listening to the instroc·
tions of the Egyptian sages by the tomb of Osiris, sought to reform society by an
elevation from the rudeness and solitude of its primitive state, in the establishment of
a secret order, which inaugurated a civilization that attracted the attention and
admiration of the world, and commenced the social regeneration of Greece. These

Generally acceptable is the theory that dates the origin of Masonry at the building
of King SOLOMON'S Temple-a belief pleasing to the majority, in view of the magni·
ficence of the structure, the wisdom of its builder, and .its dedication to the Eternal
God, who manifested His presence by a protection and approbation from its incep •
tion to its completion and sublime consecration.
From the Temple to Judea, Masonry is traced to the Essenian Fraternity, an ex·
traordinary association of speculatives and operatives, existing early in the beginning
of the Christi~n era, with many doctrines and ceremonies resembling those of our
Order; and from this remarkable brotherhood some assert the descent of Masonry t o
modern times.
The earliest direct historical connection Is found between Masonry in Europe and
the corporations or colleges of Roman Architects and Builders, instituted by NuxA
POMPILIUS nearly seven hundred years before the Christian era. Under the peculiar
privileges granted by NUMA, this fraternity prospered for about twelve hundred
years, when, falling under the displeasure of the Emperor Tm:ODOSIUS, by his decree,
they ceased to have operative life. Doring their prosperity the order was introduced
into Britian, but it was not until the commencement of the seventh century that
we find the Craft employed in the erection of stately cathedrals at London, Canter·
bury, Rochester, and other places, with evidence that a congregation of the Frsternity assembled at York, on the summons of Prince EDWIN, in the tenth century, and
that the erection of au abbey at Kilwinning, in the twelfth century, gave establish·
ment to its Lodge ; at which points respectively the general meetings of the brethren

As the first crusade for the recovery of the Holy Land occurred in the eleventh
century, the theory that introduces Masonry into Europe by Knights Templar returning from Palestine is entirely untenable.
The history of the Fraternity upon the continent of Enrope is not as satisfactory
as that of Britiao, notil the beginning of the twelfth century, when it monopolized
the building of the great churches and castles, and enjoyed especial privileges under
the patron11ge of pontiffs and sovereigns, whose desire for architectural grandeur
occasioned corresponding emulous rivalry. At this period the Fraternity appear in
history under the name of Masons; an~, in consequence of their acknowledged right
. of self-government, their exemption from taxes and ordinary allegiance, they were
soon distinguished from the common builders by the distinctive appellation of Freemasons.
Immunities thus possessed afforded an independence and prosperity be!ore noknown, and rendered attractive a society composed exclusively of operatives to a
degree that membership was solicited by many not builders, bnt who, by fortune
or their own merit, could impart an advantage by their co-operation, and thus gained
admission under the name of Accepted Masons.
Io comparing the social organization, ceremooieit and principles of Masonry with
those of the guilds of the middle ages, and the Stone Mason's Associations of Co•
logoe and Strasbourg, the resemblance and historical connection are apparent ; and
a careful consideration of these relations gives acceptance to the theory that modern
Freemasons directly descended from and are the successors, in an unbroken line, of
the operative Masons of the middle ages.
Brethren, this examination of the theories as to the origin of Masonry is not
intended simply to illustrate the honor imparted to it by antiquity, for its object and
effect are as prominent whether the parchments we hold are recent or venerable
with the impress of ages-whether few or many centuries have witnessed Its existence-but to render credible the assertion that from the earliest periods men have
constituted societies for mutual aid, protection, and advancement, based upon the
recognition of the attributes of Deity, the principles of religion, and the duties of man
to man ; that these societies hi!_ve ha,d similarity In intent and result; and that organ·
ization commenced, progression continued, and the highest civilization perfected a
. system of morality comprised in a word-Masonry:
Theism was conceived by men in their primitive state simultaneously with the
recognition of God as the Organizer. This belief was progress. As man increased
in intelligence, its adaptability became Imperative-the newly acquired knowledge
became the property of all,and as one Inquiring mind may create progreSBive thoughts
in others, so the first advancement occasioned a common elevation in the acknowledgment of a responsibility, and a necessity for obedience and protection, that removed man from bis barbarism to a condition commensurate with the improvement
made· and the spirit of Masonry, thus introduced, aBBumed substance when uninterrupted progression fixed firmly an advanced system of morality, or a better civilization. Few things are more remarkable in the history of man than that Masonry
and civilization have had unity in purpose and result.
Masonry, in object, presents a universality of idea and sublimity of design impossible to depict, in all its bearings, in this limited discourse. As a skillful Mosaic
workman forms and adjusts with his various particles a bea.utifnl work of art, so does
- Masonry blend in one harmonious whole the races of mankind, forming a general
brotherhood, where each maintaining an individuality, r.ontribntes to the beauty of
• all. Masonry knows -oG country; possesses no creed; grants toleration; is universal
in extent. It unites humanity; gives one Idea of devotion ; acknowledges a com·
mon altar; and calls upon its followers to practice Iibers lity towards the faith of every
one. Yes-under the dome of its temple could be gathered a motley crowd, holding

Masonry, in clfect, presupposes a practical realization of its object, thereby rendering valid the familiar aphorism-" a good Mason must be a good man." Io general
elfects it has assisted civilization in its contest with barbarism, established beneficial
relations between nations, enlarged international union and sympathy, and by its
potent principles, extending beyond'the bounds of nationality, placed general society
under obligations for the moral and politica_l elevation of its members. Hand in
hand with civilization in its leading element of the " Brotherhood of man " and the
"Fatherhood of God," Masonry, in effect, has ·occasioned a prevalence of truth and
justice snrpaBBing that of the fabled reign of Astrea.
·
In the viciSBitudes of war, whether in battle, in camp, hospital or ptieon, its benign effect has changed the uplifted hand of the destroyer to the extended hand of
protection, respected the crushed hopes of the defeated, relieved pain, imparted comfort, and mitigated the sulferings of captivity. Superior to self-interest or the promptings of excitement, its moral force has been directed to the abatement of war and
the promotion of peace.
Undaunted by the maledictions of faoatacism, it enabled J.1.cQUES DE MoL.t.Y, with
a dignity and calmness unparalleled in history, to summon his Papal judge to appear
with him before God, their common judge, and to suffer his martyrdom with heroic
submission. Unterrified by the threats of the Inquisition, it determined JOHN CousTos
to undergo tortures too atrocious lo their cruelty almost for belief, rather than swerve
from. his imposed fidelity. These rueo were Masons.
It has aided the cultivation of the arts and sciences, encouraged the pursuit of
knowledge, aBBisted in its general diffusion, and fostered every attempt to prom'Ote
the education and happiness of all races and nations. It has extended every priv"te
and public virtue, caused the ena~tmeot of better laws, occasioned their stricter enforcement, and supported the loyal in their allegiance in the unhappy periods of political calamity.
Effective in increasing the courtesies of life, it has rendered sacred the name or
brother-a name in its aftectionate acceptance that fails not to excite solicitude for
a brother in danger, to afford him relief in the distreBBes of life, and sympathy and
consolation in death. On the day following the memorable engagement of the Kear·

In the habitual exercise of charity is the effect of Masonry realized by those with·
ont our Order-Charity that attends the bedside of a sick or dying brother, administering relief and supplying comfort; that visits the saddened home of the widow,
bestowing sympathy and assistance ; that protects the orphan with parental care and
tenderness; that provides for the helpless and aged in their declining days.
Brethren I Each of us, in our official capacity, have witneBBed the joy, the relief,
the support, attending the dispensation of our charity ; and have listened to the recipient's prayer, passionately expressive of gratitude, invoking Heaven's blessing upon
us and our Order. Blessed Charity! the virtue of virtues-elevating and refining
human nature-increasing our growth towards the goodneBB of the infinite-would that
it might in truth become "the vital principle of our souls, dear as the ruddy drops
that warm our hearts," making us what God designed we should be without the aid
of Masonry.
" Truly to love ourselves, we must love God ;

N otwith'standing the storms of persecution and the anathemas of bigotry, Masonry,
by excellence of precepts and _fixity of principles, has continued, with varied prosperity, to its present pre-eminent position among the moral institutions of the world
with a glory at once ancient, unchangeable and universal. Masonic Temples, of
architectural display and artistic adornment, are being erected. New Lodges are
constantly created, and the numbers of the Fraternity Increased with a success heretofore unknown. Proud of our inherent worth Q.nd power of doing good-confident
of a greater prosperity in the future-we have, unfortunately, one regret-a regret
with a bitterness experienced by all-a regret produced by the action of bad Masons,
who as surely mar the beauty of our institution as the unsightly blot defaces the
otherwise unsullied sheet of paper; bad Masons-bad either from natural perversity,
for a purpose, or from indifterence-eqnally effective to the injury of our reputation
.in the estimation of the uninitiated, and preventive of the admiBBion of good men,
who, from such examples, doubt the utility and peneftcence of our organization.
Bad Masons are to ns a greater injury than the dennuciations of spiritual or temporal powers; and it is sadly true that we have unconsciously.forged the weapons
that have been nsed to our detriment. For this evil there is but one remedy; it will
mitigate, but it cannot be expected that it will entirely eradicate the misfortune. We
possess the remedy, but, unhappily, are too negligent in its application. It is this. Be
scrupulously careful not to admit imperfect material into a structure otherwise perfect.
Use caution in your recommendations; in your !JOmmittees investigate the moral character and fitness of the petitioner-not alone that he is negatively good-but that he
has positive and essential qualifications ; and, above all, employ the ballot-the safe·
guard of Masonic as well as political liberty-the bailot-nndeniooly our security and
defense, its exercise should be made obligatory upon every Mason. l<'ar better that
the worthy few enter our mystic temple, and in purity of character kneel at our universal altar, exemplars of Masonic profeBBion, than the indifferent multitude, who,
from selfishness, neglect, or '}Jersonal animosity, would pe rvert 1he privileges of membershlp to the littleness of self-interests, the gratification of passion, or the. adherence to prejudice, equally baneful in result. Every brother should endeavor, by his
close walk to the rules of the Fraternity, to show our purpose to those without, so
that all recognizing his nobleness may say : Bebo! d the effect of Masonry I

To the M. ·• W.·. Grand Lodge of California :In the matter of the formation of the Grand Lodge of Quebec, and its proposed
recognition by this Grand Lodge, your committee respectfully report that they have
carofnlly examined and considered all the documents placed in their bands nuder the
order of reference, including all circulars and proceedings of tlie Grand Lodge of Can·
ada and the Grand Lodge of Quebec, in relation to this subject, forwarded to this
Grand Lodge; and have availed themselves of all the means. of inforination at their
command, to be able to arrive at the facts of the case, and to present them in each
wise that the Grand Lodge may take euch action as it shall deem just in the premises.
Through the courtesy of the chairman of the Committee on Correspondence
and the Grand Secretary, your committee have been furnished with and have consulted the reports made apon this subject to almost all the Grand Lodges of the
United States and the Dominion of Canada. Some of these reports exhibit very
thorough and ca.refnl examination of the questions involved, and among those exhibiting most careful research and study may be named the reports of Bro. DBliM·
MOND, of Maine, Bro. GOOLEY, of Missouri, and Bro. PETERS, Grand Master of New
Brunswick. Your committee here acknowledge their obligations to the brethren
named, and to those of other jurisdictions, for they have availed themselves of the
fruits of their labors, and made free· to nse the facts found and arranged by these
brethren, and of their arguments and conclusio'l8 as well, without other ackuowledgmen t than this.
The Grand Lodge of Quebec bases its claim of right upon the political subdivision
of the territory forming the Dominion of Canada, under Act of the British Parliament, called" The British North American Act, 1867 ," which went into effect on
the first of July of that year. Hence the statement of facts should properly commence
with some facts relative to the political history of the Provinces.
lb. 1791, by an Act of the British Parliament, Canada was divided into two Provinces,
then called Upper Canada and Lower Canada. The river Ottawa was the dividing line
between the two .Provinces. Under that Act each Province had its own Governor,
appointed by the crown, and its own Legislative Assembly. The lower Province
then retained and still retains French institutions, the larger portion of its people
being of French origin and speaking the French language; while the opper Province
received and still retains English institutions. In 1841, under another Act of Parliament, a Governor General was appointed, whose authority extended over both
Provinces, and the legislative power for both was vested in one legislature. Still

Grand Lodge of California;

1871.J

177

each Province retained its o~n territorial limits and its own pecnliar institntiona,
religious, educational, and judicial; and the legislation for the Prpvinces was, for the
most part, as distinct as if there had been a legislature for each. In l8ti7, by another
.Act of the British Piuliament, the Dominion of Canada was created, composed of Upper Cari.ada, (called Ontario,) Lower Canada, (qalled Q11ebec,) Nova Scotia, and New
Brunswick. Under this Act a Governor General is appointed, in whom, as representative of the Q11een, is vested the executive authority of the Dominion ; while the legislative power.is vested in a Senate, appointed by the Governor General, and a House
of Commons, elected by the people, a certain number of the members being apportioned to each Province. For each Province a Lieutenant Governor is appointed by
and holds at the pleasure of the Governor General. Each Province has also a Pro·
vlncial 1..egislature. That of Ontario consists of the Lieutenant G~vernor and one
Honse of Assembly, r.lected by the people ; while that of Quebec consists .of the
Lieutenant Governor and two Houses-a Legislative Council, appointed by the Lieutenant Governor, constituting the Upper House, and an Assembly, elected by the
people, constituting the Lower Honse.
rhe Parliament of the Dominion has exclusive legislative authority over most of
the subjects of legislation, including the raising of money by any mode or Rystem of
taxation; banking, and the issue of paper money; savings banks, bills of exchange,
and promissory notes; interest, marriage, and divorce ; criminal law, exoept constitution of co~rts of crimina~ jurisdiction, but including criminal procedure; peniten_.
tiaries, and ID fact, all subJects, except snch as are expressly given to Provincial
Leglslatares.
·
To the Provincial Legislatures is given authority to make laws on certain enumerated subjects, which are1. Amendment of fts own Constitution, excep~ as to office of Lieutenant Governor.
2. Direct taxation for revenue for Provincial purposes.
s. Borrowing money on the credit of the Province.
''· EstabJighment of Provincial offices, and payment of officers.
6. Management and sale of public lands belonging to the Province.
6. Establishment and management of public and reformatory prisons for the
Province.
7. Establishment and management of hospitals, asylums, and eleemosynary institutions in and fnr the Province.
8. Municipal institutions in the Province.
9. Licenses of shops, saloons, &c., for raising revenue.
10•• Local works and undertaking~, other than lines of ships, railwayg, telegraphs,
and canals, connecting the Province with other Provinces, or extending beyond Its
own limits.
lL Incorporation of companies for Provincial objects.
12. Solemnization of marriage in the Province.
13. Property and civil rights in the Province.
14.. Administration of justice in the Province, including the constitntion of courts
and civil procedure.
16. The imposition of fines, penalties, and imprisonment for the enforcement of
Provincial laws.
16. Generally, of all merely local or private matters in the Province.
All the judges are appointed by the Governor General, and the Queen retains an
absolute veto over every legislative act.
Provincial legislation is confined to the subjects specified. The range of.s ubjects
le a little, but only a little, greater than that conferred by our own Legislature on the
Board of Supervisors of the City of San Francisco.

Previous to 1855, the Grand Lodges of England, Ireland, and Scotland had estab·
lished in the two Provinces of Upper and Lower Canada a considerable number of
Lodges, and at least three Provincial Grand Lodges. In October of that year, the
representatives of forty-one of those Lodges-twenty-seven from the Upper and fourteen from the Lower Province-met in convention at Hamilton, and, after preparing
a sort of declaration of independence, in which they set forth their grievances,
resolved that it was "expedient, right, and our bounden duty to form a Grand Lodge
of Canadl\ ;" and they did form such Grand Lodge. Within two years, the new
Grand Lodge was recognized by the Grand Lodge of Ireland, and by a considerable
majority of the Grand Lodges of the United States. .At our .Annual Commnnication,
in 1856, the circular of the new Grand Lodge was presented in this Grand Lodge, and
we.s referred to a special committee of which Past Grand Master CrrRTIS was chair·
man. nro. CrrRTIS, on behalf of that committee, presented an able report, recommen<!ing that no action be taken at that time in the matter, which was adopted. 'l'he
proceedings of the Canadian J,odges were revolutionary, e.nd the Gr11nd Lodge of
Cane.de. was then in open revolt against the mother Grand Lodges, and at war with
the Provincial Grand Lodges of Canada, holding under the Grand Lodge of England.
If the revolution should prove successful, and the independence of the new Grand
Lodge be acknowledged by the mother Grand Lodges, then we might and ought to
recognize It, but not before, unless the best interests of Masonry should require it. In
1857, the Provincial Grand Lodge of Upper Canada, over which Sir ALLAN N. McNAB
presided as Provincial Grand Master, renounced its allegiance to the Grand Lodge
of England and formed the "Antient Grand Lodge of Canada "-all its snbordinRtes,
twenty-eight in number, surrendering their charters to the Provincial Grand Master
and receiving new charters from the ".Antient Grand Lodge." The next year, a compromise we.s effected, e.nd the ".Antient Grand Lodge" united with the Grand Lodge of
Ce.ne.d~. By tb.e.t union, a.II the Lodges in the upper e.nd lower provinces, except two
or three in Upper Ce.ne.da, and seven in Lower Ce.no.de., (five of English, e.nd two of
Scotch 1·egister,) were united in the Grand Lodge of Ce.no.de.. In 1859, e. compromise
we.s effected between the Grand Lodge of England e.nd that of Canada, by which It we.s
agreed that the Lodges at that time holding charters under the Grand Lodges of Eng·
land and Scotland should be allowed to continue work nuder their original charters,
so long e.s they should choose to do so. Upon the consummation of that agreement,
the Grand Lodge of Canada was recognized by the Grand Lodge of England, and from
that time to the pe.sse.ge of" The British North American .Act, 1867 ,".it was recognized
by all the Me.sonic world aa havingexclnsivejnrisdlction overall the territory embraced
in the two provinces of Canada, and over a.II Masons wlthiII that territory, exc.e pt the

under their original charters.

Graud Lodge is, whether or not a new Grand Lodge can be lawfully CormP.d wi~hin
any territory over which au established Grand Lodge has long claim~tl and exercised
exclusive jurisdiction, without the consent of the latter body ; and, 1! one can be so
formed, were the circumstances of the case such as to justify the formation of a new
Grand Lodge within the Province of Quebec, without the consent of tbe Grand Lodge
of Canada?
Yonr committee are of opinion that a new.Grand Lodge may, under certain conditions or political affairs, be formed, rightfully, in territory over which another Grand
Lodge has exercised exclusive jurisdiction, but that the circumstances in this case
did not justify the formation of the Grand Lolge of Quebec. Prior to the Revolutionary war, the Grand Lodge of England had established Lodges and Provincial
Grand Lodges in many of, if not in all, the thirteen Colonies, and had exercised exclusive jurisdiction over most, if not all of them. The people of the Colonies revolted
against the Government of England, and, after a long war, were acknowledged by
it as independent and sovereign States. Then it was proper that those States
should, as they did, declare themselves Ma~onlcally independent, as well as polltlcally so. If the Province of Que bee had revolted and secured its political independ·
ence, and organized a government for itself, then its Lodges might very properly
have said that in Masonic, as In pol.itlqal alfairs, the ties that formerly bound theDl
were severed.
But the Province of Quebec was not; in 1869, ani is not now, any more ·an i:idependent State than it was iu 1855, under the name of Canada East or Lower Canada.
The British Parliament, in 1791, made it a distinct Province; in 1841, united it with
Upper Canada, under one Governor and one Legislature; and, in 1867, united the tw~
Provine.es of Canada with New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, under one Governor and
one Legislature, giving to it legislative power restricted to certain local matte~.
Next year, or at its pleasure, the same Parliament may take away the names Outar10
and Quebec, unite the two provinces into one, and call them Huron-or by another
name. It stands in much the same relation to the British Government that one of our
counties stands to the government of the State-liable, at any time, to have its name
or its boundaries changed, or to be consolidated with another county, or to be sob·
divided, at the pleasure of the Legislature; and possessing just such legislative power
over its local and domestic concerns as the Legislature gives it- and no more.
It would hav• been much more reasonable for the Grand Lodge of Canada to have
claimed ihat by the .Act of 1867, creo.ting the Domiuion of Canada, it had the right to
extend its jurisdiction over the two new Provinces, aud over all the territory embraced in that Dominion, tho.n for the Lodges of the Province of Quebec to claim that,
by reason of the .Act, they were at liberty to throw oft' their allegiance and form a new

justify the formatiou of a new Grand Lodge In Quebec, it would equally justify the
formation of one in Ontario; and if it absolved the Masons of Quebec from their

Lodge of Canada-neither restricted nor enlarged Its territorial jurisdiction. It .
acquired jurisdiction over the territory now composing the Provinces of Ontario and
Quebec by the consent of the brethren residing iii those Provinces, and by the recognition and acknowledgment of the whole Masonic world; it has the absolute right
to retain that jurisdictiou, if it so desire to do ; aud no other Masonic power can law.fully interfere therewith.

privileges of Masonry.

18'1

The appellant, in this case, appeals from the" mild punishment iofftcted npon the
accnsed," viz : suspension.
Your committee, while it does not desire to animadvert upon the action of the commissioners, in only suspending the accused for the crime charged and prove~ against
him, feel constrained to believe that personal friendship, only, could have actuated
them. If it be a crime meriting expulsion for a Secretary of a Lodge to " cheat,
wrong, or defraud " it of a few hundred dollars, what should be the punishment of
one elevated to the high and honorable position occupied by the accused, when, In
violation of his sacred honor and the confidence reposed in him, he defrauds ns of
thousands? The crime of embezzlement is one of the greatest. Masonry can make
no distinction among its members. The Grand Secretary of the Grand Chapter of
Royal .A.rch Masons of California, when found guilty of a Masonic crime, is no greater
than the humblest member of the Craft.
Your committee feel admonished, from the high moral tone of the Grand Master's
Address, that Masonry seeks to attain a higher object than that of glossing over the
misdeeds of its members; and they therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution :Resolved, That the action of .Euel.sior Lodge, No. 166, in finding LAWRENCE C.
OwEN guilty of the charges preferred against him, be approved, but that the sentence
prononnced against him be reversed, and that the said accused be expelled from all
the rights and privileges of Masonry.

To the M:.

Grand Lodge of Galifornia.

;

Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the Grand Master's Address
relating to the Masonic Board of Relief o;if this city, have given the subject serious
consideration and report as follows:The views expressed by the Grand Master, that it is not fair or equitable that the
Masons of San Francisco should be compelled to aid and assist, out of their own
means entirely, the poor end needy brethren who naturaily center here from all
parts of the globe, are eminently sound and judicious. In the very nature of things
the sick and distressed upon reaching the borders of California, whether from the
Atlantic side, from the great West, or the islands of the Pacific, flnd here their
asylum. Even from the inte1·ior of our own State many Masons find their way to
Sa.n Francisco, seeking employment or help, and here become recipients of that
noble charity, the Masonic Board of Relier. Is it right that in such cases as the last,
~Jeter Lodges, if able to respond, should a9ow their members to receive benefits
without just recompense? It is believed by your committee that the simple expression by the Grand Lodge that snch action is not only nnjust, but devoid of that
Me.sonic spirit o'I' equity which should pervade every true Me.sonic heart, will prevent
the recurrence of such events a.nd render complaint on that score unnecessary
hereafter.
But your committee believe that more positive measures are necessary in reference to the cases of strangers who come hither, poor and helpless, from distant
lands. Such should have the care and protection of the Grand Lodge of the State
of California; and, in the absence of such an organization.as a Grand Lodge Board of
Relief, the least it can do will be to set aside some portion of its r eceipts for the re.
lmbnrsement of those who devote time, labor, and money for the benefit of any
and all worthy Masons whom misfortune.may have overtaken.
The subject might be continued indefinitely, but your committee feel that U is
unnecessary to expatiate on so self-evident a proposition. They therefore simply
offer the following resolutions and recommend their adoption :Resolved, That this Grand Lodge expects every Lodge within its jurisdiction, so
far as it is able so to do, to see that the needy of its own membership and neighborhood a.re not made a burden to others.
•
Reaolved, That the ~um of one thousand dollars be and the same is hereby appropriated to the Masonic Board of Relief of the city of San Francisco, to be used by
It as a special fund for the relief of such worthy distr~esed brethren, not belonging to this jnriedie.tion, as may regularly come before it for BBBistance.
• •
All which is respectfully submitted by
JOSKl'H B. BcOTOBLER,
JAMES H. LANDER,

7b the M. ·. W .•• Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, in recommending the remission of the dues of Hawaiian Lodge,
No. 21, as has been the custom during some fifteen yea.rs or morti, desire to explain,
to those members of the Grand Lodge who may not be familiar with the facts, the
reasons why those dues have heretofore been thus remitted. Hawaiian Lodge is lo·
cated at Honolulu, in the Hawaiian Islands, entirely·excluded from immediate asso·
eiation with any other Lodge, and sitnated in a port so frequented by vessels from all
parts of the world that of necessity the claims upon its resour ces must be excessive,
Bapecially has Hawaiian Lodge ever extended the hand of charity and Masonic
courtesy to Masons of California, and, as a continued acknowledgment of such kind
ness, your committee recommend that, as heretofore, the dues of Hawaiian Lodge
No. 21, for the year ending July Sl, 1871, be remitted.

7b the M.-. W. •. Grand Lodge of California :The special committee to whom were referred so much of the Grand Master's Address as relates to the system ofinspectioo, a. revision of the districts of the jurisdiction, and the report of the Grand Lecturer, have had the same under careful consid·
eration and report as follows:-

13

194

Proceedings qf the

[Oct. 14,

We do not recommend, for another year at least, the separation of the offices of
"Inspector" and" Deputy Grand Lectnrer." We freely admit that many advantages
might result from such division, but at present we believe they would be counterbalanced by the great additional expense to the Lodges-especially to those in
the more sparsely settled portions of the country. At the same time we would recommend that, in all localities where the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer deem it advisable, suitable brethren, without limit as to numbers, be appointed to instruct Lodges
in the work; but th!l.t no official position should attach to such appointment, whereby
unnecessary expense would be thrown upon the Lodges.
We recommend an increase of the number of districts to twenty-one, and report
subdivisions for that number-having regard to the convenience of travel, access, and
business relations, rather than to the mere number of Lodges, or boundaries of
counties.
We recommend th1it hereafter no Master of a f,odge be installed, nnless he has
been first proved to be competent for the position in the manner provided for in the
resolution on such subject which will be presented at the conclusion of this report.
We do not now include the Wardens in this recommendation, leaving that for future
consideration, flfter a fall practical trial of the provision relative to-Masters.
With these imggestion8, we recommend a further and faithful trial of the plan
lnangnrated at the la.st Communication, believing it to be the best that conld be
adopted for the purposes designed thereby, and present the following resolutions for
adoption:.Re.JJol1'ed, That, for the purposes of inspection, this jurisdiction shall be divided
into twenty-one districts, each to be composed as follows:1st-The counties ot' Del Norte, Klamath, and Humboldt, comprising five Lodges;

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

. 1b the],[.-. W.·. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee find that the several Lodges, to which charters were granted at
the last Annual Communication, were all duly constituted by the brethren specially
appointed by the Grand Master for that purpose, and that doe reports thereof have
been made to the Grand Secretary.
Jn regard to that portion of the Address of the Grand Master, relating to Lodges
which do no Masonic work, yonr committee respectfully report that they have not
now sufficient information upon which to base a recommendation for the immediate
,accomplishment of the object desired. They therefore recommend that the matter
be referred to the Inspectors of the several districts, and that it be made the special
duty of each one to examine and report thereon at the next Annnal Communication.
All which is respectfully submitted by

JOHN W. HARVILLE,
JACOB H. NEFF,

Bro. JoHN W. HARVILLE, from the Committee on Charters, preRented •
the following reports : -

To the M. •. W.·. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee have carefully examined the records and papers submitted by the
following Lodges under dispensation, viz :-Rocklin, Friendship, San Benito, South
San Francisco, Bodega, San Buena'IJentura, Oak GroTJe, Dorie, Monterey, Pleasanton,·and Speranza Italiana. In each case the petition for a dispensation has been
accompanied by the di mi ts of the petitioners and the proper recommendations and
certificates; and all the papers and books have been prepared and kept in proper
form, with some few exceptionR, which have been pointed out to the delegates and
Inepectors.
The records of Frirodahip, South San Francisco, Oak Gr<nJe, and Doric Lod!!;es,
are particularly worthy of commendation. Plea.,anton and Speranza Ital.iana Lodges
have not yet completed any work, not hBvinrt had sufficient time since their dispen.
sations were received. b'or reasons uot upon the record, your committee are of the
opinion that Rocklin Lodge should be discontinued ; and they offer the following
resolutions, with the recommendation that they be adopted:Re1olved, That charters be issued to Friendship Lodge, at San Jose, in Santa Clara
County; San Benito Lodge, at Hollister, in Monterey County; South San Francisco Lodge, at San Francisco, in San Francisco County; Bodega Lodge, at Bodega Corners, in Sonoma County; San Buenaventura Lodge, at San Buenaventura,
in Santa Barbara County; Oak Grove Lodge, at Alameda, In Alameda County; lJoric
Lodge, at San Francisco, in San Francisco County; and Monl.erey Lodge, at ¥onterey, in Monterey County; and that they be numbered in the order of the dates of
their several dispeneation~.
Resowed, That the dispensations to Pleasanton Lodge, at Pleasanton, in Alameda
County, and Speranza Italiana Lodge, at San Francisco, in San Francisco County,
be continued until the first day of October, A.L. 6872.
Resolved, That Rocklin Lodge, at Rocklin, in Placer County, be declared'extinct,
and that the Grand Secretary be and is hereby directed to take· charge of and settle
its affairs.
All .which is respectfnlly submitted by
JOHN w. H.!.RVILLE,

Bro. JonN F. BNow, from the Committee on Returns, presented the following report:-

>

'.lb the M.-. W. ·• Grand Lodge of Califon.ia :Yonr committee, to whom was referred the examination of the annual reports of
the Lodges in the jurisdiction, have endeavored carefully to perform that duty, and,
as the result of their inquisition, report that, while it is gratifying to be enabled to
state that the returns of every Lodge have been received by the Grand Secretary, and
that most of them have been handsomely prepared, (some with remarkable beanty
of penmanship ) it is unhappily the fact that the punctuality in sending the reports
within the period named in our Constitution, accompanied with the dues, which, for
some years past the Secretaries generally have been credited with, have this year
•omewhat failed. There does not appear any good reason why (except perhap11 in
case of sickness or some unusual contingency) the repod of a Lodge conld not as
well be prepared and transmitted between the first and fifteenth days of Ang11st, as
our law prescribes, as during a month or two thereafter; and it is suggested to the
Secretaries-some of them-that they bear this in mind hereafter. Nearly all the
Lodges have complied, or have apparently endeavored to comply, with the regulation of 1869, reqniring the full names of all borne npon their respective rolls, though,
In some cases, it appears to have required considerable persistence in c orrespondence on the part of the Grand Secretary to effect that result; and, generally, it may
be stated that the reports are very creditable.
The returns of the following named Lodges were transmitted, with their does,
within the period of time prescribed in the Constitution, and were in every respect

From the foregoing it will be seen that the amount levied last year for account of

deeds, so is the gratitlcatiou of that passion among the most exquisite of enjoyments.
You can not fail to experience a deep sensr. of pleasure in receiving from us these
tokens of our esteem and regard ; and, because of this, ·1 rejoice in being the ambassador of my brethren .to you. That three years have passed since you retired
from the position of Grand Master; and that, after this lapse of time, your brethren
ahould now co~te ~o you with this manifestation of their affection and good will, but
~nders more_s1gmficant the gift• . Thr. delay proves at least that they are not acting
m mere obedience to some establtshed usage, and that this testimonial is the result
of oalm and mature consideration.
The Imperishable nature of this solid silver, its untarnished lustre aud intrinsic
value, and the chaste and delicate designs or ihe artist, are illustrative at once or
on.r re~ard f~r you, of your private and Masonic oharacter, and of the l!delity and
skill with which !on h~ve performed every task we have ever imposed upon you.
On the prlnc1pal piece we have caused to be placed this inscription-'• To the
X.-. W.-. WILLIAM A. DAVIES, Past Grand Master, this, with five accompanying pieces
of 1Uver, was presented by the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of Cali!ornia, at its Annual
IJommunicatiou in October, A. L. 5871, as an evidence of its fraternal esteem and
regard ":-that as it goes down to your poste~ity 'from generation to generation, it may
llllently rndeed, yet eloquently, reveal to Vtem the high regard in which you were

presenting me with this beantiful testimonial, and it more than taxes all my powers
to find words for the expression to my brethren, in fitting terms, ot my appreciation of this evidence of their friendship and good will.
When we look aronnd us on occasions like the present, we are reminded of other
days, and we almost expect to see in their accustomed seats many who·have long
since passed over the dark waters never to return to ns again. And Yet the Grand
Lodge of California is the same body as when presided over by Grand Masters STEV·
ENSON, HOWARD, CURTIS, BELCHER, or CLAIBORNE. "Not for a day or generation,
but for all time,'' is the motto legibly written on her standard. Still, we have seen
among oar numbers, daring the present Communication, so many new faces that we
are admonished that we, too, of the elders, shall soon be called from oar labors on
earth to join the" innumerable throng," and yon, brethren, who are here for the first
time, participating in our labors, will be called upon to occupy our places.
But we live again in our children, and it is this, M .'. W.·. BJother, which makes
this testimonial to me of inestimable value. To be able to tralsmit to my children
so distinguished a mark of the favor of the Grand Lodge of California is to me. a
gratification beyond all measure-a reward which to have lived twenty years to
deserve is as being paid an hundred fold-the evidenpe of a good will which to con·
tinue to deserve during the years God in His providence shall allot to me here, will
be ample compensation.
M. •• W. ·. Grimd Master: For the fr11.ternal and kindly manner in which you have,
in too flattering terms, been pleased to address me , I return my heartfelt thanks;
and to my brethren of the Grand Lodge, through you, I olfer a feeling of gratitude
for which no language at my command has the power of expression.

ADOPTED OCTOBER, A. L. 5871.
Section 3, Article ill, Part ill, is amended so that it shall read as follows:"SEO. 3. No Lodge shall ballot npon soch application, (except by dispensation
from the Grand Master, as provided in Sec. 1, .Art. I. Part II,} until it shall h11ve been
referred to a committee, whose duty it shall be to make strict examination into the
moral, mental, and physical qualifications of the applicant, and to report thereon at
the next stated meeting, unless further time be granted. No application shall be
withdrawn after reference to a committee. The report of the committee shall state
the facts of the case, and if, for any reason, it be unfavorable, no ballot shall be had,
bot the Master shall, upon the reception of the report. declare the candidate rejected·
If the report be favorable, a ballot shall be had and it shall require a unanimons
ballot to elect. If but one black ball appear in the ballot-box, the Master, without •
declaring the result, may at once order a second ballot f'lr the purpose of correcting
a possible mistake; but in no case, after one ballot has been had, shall any discus·
sion be permitted in the Lodge before the second ballot is had, nor shall the second
ballot be postponed to another meeting of tbe Lodge."
·
· The 10th subdivision of Section 1, Article IV, Part II, is amended so that it shal
read as follows:"10th. To trammit to each Lodge within the jurisdiction, once in every two
months, a list of all rejections, (with the causes thereof,) expulsions, suspensions, and
restorations of which he shall have been notified by the several Lodges."
Section 4, Article VIII, Part I, is amended by striking out the 2d clause thereof,
which now reads as follows:" 2d. For each member it &hall have received by affiliation during the year, the
sum of one dollar:"
Thus abolishing the dues to the Grand Lodge for affiliations.

three-fourths of these cases I have been obliged to return the certificates of the Sec.
retaries for amendment, such certificates fa.iling to show either that the required
notice had been given, or that the requisite vote was had. The correspondence of
the Grand Kaster has been thereby very much increased, and, to avoid unnecessary
labor for my successors in office, I take occasion now to call the attention of Masters
and Secretaries to the fact that the Uniform Code provides that these amendment!!
can only be made by a two-thirds vote, after one month's notice, and that in all cases
the Secretary's certillcate should show both that such notice was given and that
such majority was had. Ia this connection, and as in some measure germain to the
subject, let me suggest that a more careful perusal of our Constitution and Regulations by Masters and Secretaries, generally, would save a large amount of labor.
Applications for dispensations are, as a general rule, insufficient for some such reason
as above stated, and mast be returned with instructions to the applicant. So a
large majority of the questions of law, usage, and jurisprudence every year presented
to the Grand Master for solution, are so unmistakably answered by the plain letter of
the written law, that he who reads that law could not err in his conclusions.
I do not complain of any necessary or useful labor. Wherever there was room
for a doubt, I have taken pleasure in suggesting to inquirers my own interpretation of
the law, and have been pleased at the anxiety manifested to be correct. But let it
be remembered that there are nearly two hundred Lodges existing in this jnrisdiotion, and it will be seen that if there is only an occasional letter from each, the labors
of the Grand Master in answering all mast be very considerable in the aggregate.
Oar law is so fall and complete that very much of this labor may be avoided if Masters will, as it is contemplated that they should do, make themselves thoroughly conversant with that law, and then, as it is their business to do, carefnlly superintend
the work of their own officers.
Several of the Lodges proposed so to amend their by-laws as to make the monthly
dues payable at the end of the quarter, instead of in advance. The Uniform Code
recommended by the Grand Lodge makes the dues payable in advance, and Article
XIII of that code provides that in certain enumerated cases each Lodge may amend its
by-laws. If, by enumerating certain cases in which amendments may be made,
.Article XIII is to be conatrned as inllibiting amendments by Lodges in all other cases,
then it is incompetent for any Lodge to make yie amendment suggested, for it is not
one of the enumerated cases; and such change should originate in the Grand Lodge
as an amendment to the Uniform Code, and not in a particular Lodge, as an amendment to its own by-laws.
While I have some doubts upon this proposition, I am inclined to rt>gard it as the
fair intendment of Article XIII. Be that as it may, I think I see other sufficient objeo·
tions to such amendment by individual Lodges. Uniformity of by-laws, as far as practicable, seems to have been the steady aim and purpose of this Grand Body. Bat all
semblance of such uniformity would be speedily destroyed if the subordinate Lodges
were once permitted to enter upon the work of amending generally, and in other
respects than those designated in Article XIII. Besides all this, the ellect of
making snch an amendment in a few Lodges, while the many retained the provision of the Uniform Code, would be to keep the members of those few Lodges
in good standing on easier terms than those which the members of other Lodges
enjoyed. The member of a Lodge which had adopted snch amendment, would
be entitled to admission in a Lodge which had not adopted, it on easier t.erms than the
members themselves of the latter Lodge. Its operation would thus seem to be to
that extent partial and unjust; and for these reasons I refused to give my approval.
I doubt if the provision in question is very rigidly enforced, and perhaps the amendment in itself is not objectionable. But, if made at all, it should be general, applying
to all Lodges, and thus keeping all in that respect on the same footing.
Several Lodges have also asked my approval of amendments creating separate

392

Procee<l;i;ngs of the

[Oct. 8,

fonds for special purposes, or creating Boards of Trustees, other than the officers
of the Lodge, to take charge of the funds. I have also refused to give my
approval to all such amendments, on the general ground that these purposes
could be just as eftectnally accomplished by a simple resolution of the Lodge, thus
preserving intact the uniformity of the Code. It Is perhaps an objection to the latter
plan, that a mere resolution might be rescinded at any stated meeting without ~?tlce,
and by a bare majority vote, when but l'ew members were present, whereas, ID the
form of a by-law, it could only be changed after a month's notice, and by a two·
thirds vot.e. But I do not apprehend that any serious evil ls likely to result ftom
such causes, and, thongh disinclined to interfere with the discretion of Lodge3 in this
respect, and readily conceding that each Lodge is likely to be the best judge of the
propriety of such action, I have still persisted In withholding my approval. And I
now report my action In the premises, that this body may inquire, if it choose, whether
It Is advisable to alter the Uniform Code in any or these respects, or to enlarge the
field for amendments by each subordinate Lodge. I have already sufficiently Intimated my own opinion, and have only to add that I shall cheerfully accede to whatever your superior jndgment may dictate.
Four dispensations only have been issued for the formation of new Lodges, and two
Lodges have surrendered their charters. I regard these facts as healthful rather than
discouraging indications. We have heretofore been making Lodges, as well as Mason@,
altogether too rapidly. Organization into Lodges is of comparatively recent date,
and, while furnishing facilities for enjoyment, not otherwise attainable, it is by no
means essential to the prac~e of Masonic virtues. It is far better that individuals
should forego for a season the pleasure which Lodge lnterconrse affords, than under·
take the burdens and expense of maintaining a Lodge until there is enough of mate·
rial of good quality, easily acce81lible, to give at once an active, vigorous, and
healthful existence. .A. Lodge should serve some other purpose than the gratification
of personal ambition by making indifferent Masters and sending its representatives. to
the Grand Lodge. I hail the surrender of every charter, by a feeble and decaymg
Lodge, as an evidence of returning sense and wisdom rather than declining zeal; and
the action of Paradise and Mount Oa~ Lodges wonld be wisely followed by a
dozen others within the jurisdiction. There are at least that number whose existence
is simply a useless burden upon the members, without any corresponding benefit. or
advantage to them. They periorm no charities and do no work. Zeal and devotion
cannot long survive Inaction, and · they become Masonically dead. One year ago I
called your att.ention to the condition of these Lodges, with a suggestion that the
Grand Lodge take the necessary steps to hasten the extinction of such as came fairly
within the views then expreBSed on that snbject. Without repeating the reasons
then assigned, I again call your attention to that portion of my last year's report,
and renew the snggestion therein contained.

Grand Lodge seems to have been actuated by the same thought iii fr~ its regulation on this subject; for, after reciting the requirements, it adds, as if by way of

conform literally to what the several degreos respectively require of him." .A. man
with bnt one eye certainly is not perfect. The loss of one of those organs is a maim
and a blemish. Yet he can conform literally to all that Masonry requires of him, and
can learn and do all Its work as readily as with both eyes. Besides, since Masonry
has oeased to be operative, thl' moral and mental are far more important than the
physical qualifications; and, ~ile we onght to adhere rigidly to the landmark!! and

make a most excellent and exemplary Mason, and become an ornament and blessing
to the Craft. While I.have a strong feeling against all imperfections in oandidatea,
and nnderstand how difficult it will be to find a stopping place if we once depart from
the requirement of substantial physical perfection, yet I could see no really good reason for holding the candidates in question diSqnalilled, nor did I think that a fair and

they have already been made Masons. Yet I confeBS that I should not regret to see

At your last Annual Communication, Section 3, Article III, Part ill, of your Consti·
tntlon, was so amended as to dispense with a ballot.for the degrees, upon an unfavor·
able report being received from the investigating committee. Under this amend·
ment Masters of Lodges have found themselves In donbtwhat course to pursue where
one only of the committee reports unfavorably, and the majority favorably. I am not
surprised that Masters have been some what embarrassed In snob cases ; yet an unfavorable report by one,of the committee is, until withdrawn, as much an objection to the
initiation of the candidate, and is as likely to lead to bad practices upon the ballot
being taken, as if snr.h report was concurred In by all; and hence the reason which
dispenses with the ballot, when the whole committee report unfavorably, applies with
equal force when any one of snch committee so reports. Bnt the report of one is not
the "report of the committee ;" and hence such a case, though plainly within the
evil intended to1be cured, is not within the letter of the amend~ent. While my own
judgment Is that there ought not to be a ballot when any one of the committee reports unfavorably, yet I had grave doubts whether the language of the law could
fairly be so construed; and I accordingly advised Masters to take the ballot in such
cases, until the Grand Lodge should make the rule more definite.

commissioners. I did not think it competent for the accnser, at his caprice and withont consulting the Lodge, to dismiss charges once preferred. The accnser is not the
only one Interested in such cases. Uumasonio conduct is not a matter pertaining
solely to him. It Is not his personal allair, to be hnshed up, compromised, or adjnsted,
as he alone may fancy. The honor qf the Fraternity may be Involved, and every mem·

is the accuser; and the Lodge might well retnse to allow the accused to go unpunished simply because he had in some way quieted his accuser. Any other ~e, It
seems to me, would open the way for disreputable practices. ~at the Lodge itself
may at any time dismiss charges upon the application oftbe accuser'. I have.no doubt.
A dismissal by 11he commissioners, without investigation, would not, m my Judgment,
be ·final until reported to and concurred in by the Lodge. The Lodge might very
properly, in a given case, send the charges back to the commissione:s with ln~truc­
tions to proceed. The whole subject was disposed of in accordance with these Views,
and I now submit my action in the matter for your final determination. .

Several questions have been presented which involve the .a uthority of subordmate
Lodges In the control and disbursemettt of their funds. I confess to have experienced
some dilllculty and embarrassment in disposing of these questions. On the one hand
is the abstract proposition, founded apparently in justice and natnral right, that each
Lodge should have the power to dispose of itB own according to itB own judgment
and discretion. But this, however, should be subject to some limitation; for a corrnpt,
immoral or other absolntely nnmasonic nse of funds wonld be ntterly indefensible,
and, I a~prehend, should call for prompt rebuke and 4iscipline. The difficulty is In
determining in each case the propriety or Impropriety of the appropriation. I have
always supposed, howev~r. that Lodge funds were provided for the purpose of meeting the expenses of the Lodge, aud for uses purely charitable ; that such funds shonld
be carefully gnarded and sacredly preserved for such purposes, and for no other ; and
that it was entirely competent for the Grand Lodge to inquire of its subordinates at
any and all times whether they have made such proper use of their fonds, or otherwise.
I have found however, that some of my brethren entertain very different views upon
t~ subject.' aud are disposed to regard any inquiry in that direction as unauthorized
and impertinent. It would perhaps be timely and appropriate to have some expres·
sion upon this subject, in general terms at least, from the Grand Lodge its.ilf, that
there may be an end of doubt and controversy.
In one Instance, I was informed that some two hundred dollars had been taken
from the funds of a Lodge, by no means wealthy, to pay carriage hire in transp~r~ng
the brethren and their families to a place of entertainment. Sur.h an appropriation
was, in my judgment, absolutely inexcnsable nuder any circumstances. There are
some poor brethren in every Lodge who cannot attend, or do not care to aue~d, such
entertainments. Bot they have contributed to create the Lodge fund and it is a part
of their reliance if misfortune and adversity overtake them. To appropriate such
fund to such purposes is indirectly to compel these poor members to contribute to
the amusement merely of their more opulent brethren. Instead of this, the fund
should have been preserved to meet some call for charity, liable to occur at any time;
and finally, if not so needed, it would at least enable the Lodge to reduce its dues,
and thus relieve its needy members from a part of the burden imposed upon them.
In another case a Lodge had been tor a long time paying a nurse for waiting on a
sick brother who was himself possessed of abundant wealth. Now, the pervading
spirit of Freemasonry is charity, relief-not indemnity, or insurance, or compensa·
tion. But there is no charity and no relief in giving to the man of unbounded
wealth. In my judgment, this was not merely unnecessary and uncalled for, but
something more. It was absolutely wrong and unmasonic. It was taking from the
poor brother to give to the rich-eCJmpelling him who toils for his daily bread to

1872.]

395

yield up a part of his hard earnings, not to relieve a sull'erer, but to add still more to
the wealth of one &!ready wealthy.
In another cue a Lodge had donated something over two hundred dolla.rs, the
built of its ava.ilabl~ funds, to aid the organiz&tion of a concern known Bl! the
I. 0. A. R. What these formidable lett.ers signify I have not yet inquired. But I
understand that they relate to one of the various orders of so-called side degrees of Masonry. This I. 0. A. R., whatever it is, may be a worthy and enjoyableaesooiation. I do
not propose to criticise it, for I k:ilow nothing of it. But the appropriation of the
funds of a Lodge to such a purpose waa in my judgment so utterly wrong, that my
first impulse was to call for the c~ter of the Lodge. But, as the evil was already
done, and as your Communication was near at hand when I received the firstauthentlo
information, I thought it best to content myself with simply reporting the matter
for your consideration.
In another case a Lodge, ill supplied with the implemenia and appurtenances for
doing its work, and excusing its set of be.tt.ered tin jewels on the ground of poverty,
had borrowed one hundred dolla.rs for the purpose, as entered on its minutes, of giving a "sumptuous collation" to the newly-installed officers.
In several other cases Lodges have expended very considerable sums in the burial
of brethren who died under suspension, leaving abundant means for the support of
those dependent upon them.
I trust that you will not close your labors without some unmistakable declaration as to the propriety of these various appropriations. The facts above set forth
have been disclosed through the system of inspection ad<!pted two yea.rs ago; and
these disclosures are in themselves a sufficient reBl!On for continuing that system,
unless some method of supervision still more efficient can be now devised.
The following question as to advancement wae presented for decision : A candidate
had been elected to receive the three degrees in a certain Lodge and had received the
first degree therein. Removing to another part of the State, the Lodge in which he
had been elected ant! initiated requested the Lodge where he had gone to reside to
confer the remaining degrees. The latter Lodge was about to pass the candidate,
when a member thereof objected to his advancement. I was of the opinion that such
objection should be disregarded; that it could only be made by a member of the
Lodge in which he had been elected, and that its sufficiency must be tried and determined in such Lodge; and that the Lodge which had been requested merely to do the
work for another, though it might decline to do it at its option, ought not to assume
to pass upon the quality of material which the other had already accepted. Still, it
is a matter in which all Masons, as well as the members of the Lodge electing, are
lnierested; and, perhaps, som!lthing might be said in support of such objection.
I have also been called upon to consider whether a dimitted Mason may affiliate
with a Lodge other than that within the jurisdiction of which he resides. I think
the int.endment of our Constitution to be that he should apply to the Lodge where he
resides, though it is not SQ expressly stated, and possibly affiliation anywhere m.ight
be a compliance with ite terms. The latter construction, howeTer, might lead to
curious results; for,if the applicant may go t.o a distant Lodge in this State for affiliation, I do not see why he may not apply to some Lodge out of the State. Indeed,
in the very caae presented, the brother, fearing that he would be rejected in the
Lodge within whose jur:isdiciion he resided, was about to seud his dimit and petition
to his mother Lodge in Tennessee. Without exactly deciding the question, I di&couraged the ent.erprising brother with so much energy that be abandoned the project of afllliating in Tennessee. I should be glad, however, to have the question
settled authoritatively. An impression prev&il.s, I think, that a brother may affiliate
with any Lodge he may select. I am sure that such ought not to be the rule, and I
hope that it ia not in this jurisdiction.

A number of Lodges failed to hold any meeting on the day fixed for their annnal
election of officers, In conseqnence of the violent storms and impassable condition of the
streams and highways which many of yon have occasion to remember only too welL
In all snch cases, with one exception, prompt applications were made for dlspensa·
tions to elect at other times. In the exceptional case the Lodge chose not to hold
any election, but to permit the former officers to bold over another year. In its internal polity, I have always regarded Masonry as essentially democratic. If not required
by the plain letter of our written Jaw, the spirit and genlns of its government, at
least, require the annual selection of olftcera to rule and govern the Craft. The
Lodge in question was accordingly advised that, prima facle, it was at fault in failing to bold its election at the appointed time; and that, unless the proper steps were
promptly taken to remedy and excuse the omiSBion, it would be regarded as a willful persistence In the fault and be dealt with as a case of insubordination. The
subsequent proceedings of the Lodge, I am happy to say, showed conclusively
enough an anxiety to do right and to avoid the appearance even of disregarding any
requirement of the law.
Another difficulty arose from these failures to elect officers at the appointed
time. The installation in such cases could not take place nntil after January, 1872;
and a resolution bad been adopted at yonr last session Inhibiting the installation of
any Master after that date, withont the certificate of the Grand Lecturer, or of the
Inspector of the District in which the Lodge was situated, that snch Master was competent to give the work and lectures of the three degrees. In many cases the
Inspectors had not yet been appointed and the situation of the Locfges in some cases
rendered it practlcaliy lmpoBBible for the Masters elect to procure sncli certificates.
It was so perfectlyobvions, moreover, that it was the intent of the Grand Lodge, when
adopting that resolution, to permit all Masters for the then ensuing year to be
installed without such certi6cate, and that the month of January was named because
it was presnmed that all the Masters would be installed within that month, that I felt
justified by the necessities of the case in construing the resolution by the light of that
plain intent; and I accordingly advised those concerned that they would incnr no risk
by proceeding with snch installation. Indeed, the power of the Grand Master tp grant
dispensations to bold the e !actions at a period other than that fixed by the Constitution, would seem to carry with it the power to permit snch officer to be Installed when
elected, notwithstanding the apparent inhibition of the resolntion. Otherwise the
dispensation to elect wonld be vain and nugatory. Still there are clearly two sides
to the propoB!tion, and I confess that it seemed like straining the prerogative of
Grand Master to a considerable extent, as it was disregarding the letter of a resolntion
of this body, by virtue of an implied power only.
During the year inquiry has been several times made as to the right to visit, and
the right and effect of an objection to the admission of a visitor. Our Constitution
seems plainly enough to contemplate that the objecting party should state the ground
of bis objection, and that the Ml!oBter of the Lodge should thereupon determine its snf·
:fl.ciency. I have no doubt that such is the law of tbisjnrisdiotion, and I have so advised.
But my own judgment is that the rule ougft.t to be changed. I do not think a member ought in any case to be driven from bis own Lodge by the admission of one who
is not a member ; and jnst this state of things may readily result from the preeent
rule. It may well happen that a member can not sit in Lodge with a proposed visitor, and yet the reasons may be of so private and delicate a nature that be would
su1fer any inconvenience rather than state them to the Master of his Lodge. Still,
under the preeent law, be must state them or bis objection must be disregarded.
The visitor is admitted and the member retires. Thia is all wrong. The right of
the member as against a mere visitor should be held more sacred, and as between
them no third party should be called in to exercise bis judgment upon the matter.
The Master can not place himself in the position of the objecting brother, and un-

Early in the year 11 circular of special instructions was issued to the Inspectors
of the various districts, calling their attention in detail to various matters which I
deemed it desirable that they should investigate. An abstract of this circular was afterwards forwarded to the M:11Bter of each Lodge, accompanied with duplicate blank
forms prepared by the Grand Secretary, designed to faci.J.\tate the task of making 11
financial statement by each Lodge. The Secretaries were requested merely, not
required, to fill these blanks. In most cases it has been promptly and cheerfully
done; a.nd the statements thus returned throw much light upon the transactions of
the Lodges, and furnish a great deal of valuable, and some, perhaps; rather curious
information. I most heartily recommend that a tabulated statement of these reports
be published in your proceedings tbis year, that the brethren throughout the jurisdiction may learn the :financial status of the fraternity, what use is made of its
revenues, whiit we are doing in the cause of charity and humanity, and what it is
oosting us to do it. In 11 few instances, to my great surprise, Secretaries declined
to make the desired statement. If their books were properly kept it would require
but little labor to comply, and the failure to do so is suggestive of something
mong. It can only lead to a suspicion, more or less potent, that there is something
which they do not care to disclose, and I recommend to the Masters of those Lodges
a careful inquiry into the causes of such failure. It is quite poBBible: that, if such
statements had always been required, we should have muoh better ordered books in
some of the Lodges, and perhaps several cases . of defalcation would have been
avoided. And, .tt.ally, I now recommend that each Lodge be required, the ensuing
year, fu return such statement to the Grand Secretaey or to the Inspector of the
bistrict.

Particular!y was thls the case, perhaps, in the •sixteenth district. I think it desirAble
that these reportB should be published with your proceedings. They are generally
concise and well written, and will add but little to the expense of publication, while they
will be found of interest and benefit to the Craft ; and, moreover, their publication will
incite future Inspectors to still greater zeal and diligence. When the right man
shall have been found for the position in all the districts, the operation of the sys.
tem will be found as beneficial as its most sanguine supporters have ever anticipated.
Indeed, the good already effected is almost incalculable. I can conceive of bat one
plan which would surp1188 it. The most perfect system undoubtedly would be for
the Grand Lodge to select some one who is thorough master of the work of Masonry,
and, at the same time, well veraed in its history, traditions, literature, and jurispra·
deuce, and pay rum a sufficient salary to command his entire time and attention·
He should then be endowed with enough of authority to render his services
elfective, and should visit every .Lodge in the State without any expense what·
ever to the Lodges, remaining as long as he might find it necessary iu order to cor.
rect all errors and leave each Lodge ia perfect condition. If this system could be
adopted even for two or three years-long enough to make one such visitation to
every Lodge in the State-it would place this jurisdiction above and beyond any
other on the continent; and the Lodges being once brought up to such a standard, it
would be many !years before another such visitation would be really required. This
has been my ideal system from the beginning. But to put it in operation and to
command such service would require at least four or five thousand dollars per yeara large sum for the Grand Lodge to pay. And yet perhaps it would be found, on
careful inquiry,, that the salary now paid the Grand Lecturer and the amounts paid
by subordinate Lodges to Inspectors and lecturers would aggregate very nearly
that sum. Without advising any hasty action, I subllllt such plan to your deliberate
judgment. It is not necessary that it should be adopt.ed this year. Think it over
carefully-take a year if you choose to consider it-but be sure of one thing, my
brethren, if you finally adopt and carry it out, you will at no distant day have
abundant reason to be most proud and happy over its results.
I recommend that the Grand Lecturer and the Inspectors of the several Districts
be again constituted a special committee on the whole subject of work and
lectures, that they may consult together over the various reporill, and present
such modifications and suggestions as their united experience and observation may
commend. And I suggest to them that, if the system of Inspectorsis to be continued,
provi!iou should be made to pay their expenses in attending the Grand Lodge, as
other officers are paid, and that some rank and station should be assigned them in this
body.
Let us turn now, my brethren, from these business considerations and forget the
hopes and ambitions of the future while we contemplate for a moment the sadder
incidents of the year's experience. I have to announce a sorrowful event which
none of us codld have anticipated twelve months ago, when an esteemed brother was
so active in our midst, so filled with life and vitality and with all the hopes and
aspirations of his middle manhood. JOHN SHERRILL WA.RD, a Past Senior Grand
Warden of this Grand Lodge, a faithful officer, a zealous Mason, and a noble citizen,
has p888ed the portals which open on the shadowy and unseen land. Let us pay.the
offering whlch his memory deserves. Kind, tender, truthful, and compassionate, he
posseS11ed in an eminent degree the virtue qf personal fidelity, and drew nearer and
nearer to himself all who were worthy of his friendship and regard. Of him It may
be truly said that he was one whose heart beat quick for others' woe~ good, true
man and faithful friend. He needs no other eulogy-no sculptured marble to per·
liia remembrance.
