Some thirty or forty volumes- principally the bound transactions of other Grand
Lodges-have been added to our library, which now contains over six hundred volumes of purely Masonic literature, a complete catalogue of which will be pnblished
with the proceedings of the present year. All are handsomely and uniformly bound,
and it is believed to be the largest and best collection of Masonic books to be found
upon the continent.
The sea.I of our Grand Lodge has now been in use some twenty-two years, and is
much worn. It never was " a thing of beauty," and it is suggested that, as a new one
should at once be provided, it would be well that it.a design be one more appropriate
and significant. A sketch for a new device has been prepared under the direction of
the writer, which is herewith submitted for consideration, and which may be briefiy
described as follows : A shield, quartered;-the first quarter charged with the arms of the State of
California, for the jurisdiction of our Grand Lodge ;· the second, with the arms of
the Grand Lodge of England, for our descent from that progenitor of all the American Grand Ledges; the third, with the arms first used by the Freemasone at York,
for the rite which we practice; and the fourth, with the two implements of the Craft
which are it.a principa.l symbols in every land, for the universality of our Fraternity.
Supporters- Dexter, a female figure representing Faith; and Sinister, a female figure
representing Hope. Crest-the upper portion of a group of figures representing
Charity, surmoumted by the All-Seeing Eye with diverging rays of light. Motte>"These three, but the great.est of these is Charity;" and the whole surrounded with
~e inscription, "Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons,-California."
' The description has not been written in that language of heraldry, which, perhaps,
should properly be employed concerning blazons of arms, for two reasons : :fl.rst,
that the undersigned is in grave doubt whether he remembers enough of the venerable slang of the Herald's College to so present it; and second, that if he did, very
few, probably, would understand a word of it.

solicited Bro. ORBIN Wn1T00111e HoLLBNBBOK, Master of Eureka Lodge, No. 16, (in

only been sarpaeeed by that prodaced by the manner in which he has discharged the

to the credit. of its members that, finding the proceeds of the sale, with the email

The Grand Lecturer presented his .Annual Report to the Grand
Lodge, as follows:To the M.-. W. ·• Grand Lodge of California: In accordance with a resolution of the Grand Lodge I respectfolly present the
following report of my official acts dnring the past year : Owing to circumstances beyond my control, it has been impossible for me to visft
as many of the Lodges as I had intended and desired. I have, however, in company
with the Grand Master, visited six or the Districts, comprising fifty-two Lodges, in all
which the evidence of improvement in the work of Masonry was manifest. The
Districts visited were the second, third, filth, sixth, ninth, and sixteenth. I also
visited Lodges Nos. 55, ~7, 134., and 201, in the eleventh District, and No.156 in Jhe
twelfth. Io most of the Districts visited, the officers exhibited a creditable degree of
proficiency In the work and lectures, yet in some instances instruction was greatly
needed, and in such cases the errors were pointed out and the proper corrections
made. Wherever I have been; I have found the officers of Lodges ready and eager
to receive instruction and ambitious to render themselves perfect in the work and
lectures ; and the great improvement already made proves the efficacy of the system adopted by the Grand Lodge for the dis.eemination of the work.
In teaching, I have not confined myself wholly to the recitation of the ritnal, bnt
have endeavored also to demonstrate the proper manner of conferring the degrees, in
order to make a suitable impression npon the mind of the candidate, and to illustrate
the great principles or Masonry in their application to individuals and to the gen·
eral conduct and government or the Lodges; and I have reason to believe that my
efforts in this direction have not been nnprodnctive of beneficial results.
.A.side from my visits to the Lodges, a great portion of my time has been given to
the instruction of Masters, Wardens, and other officers of Lodges visiting the city
for the purpose, most of whom required to be taught the entire work and lectures-a
labor which in many instances required no small amount of patience and perseverance ; and I have been more careful and assiduous in my instructions to those who will
most probably be called to fill the Oriental chair, in consequence of the resolntlon
or the Grand Lodge at its last annual commnnication, requiring Masters of Lodges,
before their installation, to produce a certificate of their competence to confer the
several degrees and deliver the lectures appertaining thereto.
I have received reports from the Inspectors and Depnty Grand Lecturers of the
following Districts, viz: From Bro. JoRN A. WATSON, of the First District; Bro

Bro. JAMES H. LANDER, from the special committee to whom had

He e.lso named the following brethren to fill the vacancies in the

Grand Lodge of OalifO'l'nia.

'

7b the M.·. W.·. Grana Lodge of Oalifomia :Your committee, to whom was referred the Address of the M.·. W.·. Grand
Master, respectfully report as follows:We despair of making this paper approach in excellence to its subject, but, in
humble imitation and admiringly emulative concmTence, take as our text its wordsunimprovable by us-" do and develop." No three words could better express our
duties and the result of their performance. Let us first, as the opening words of the
AddreBB suggest, offer to the All-Giver our reverent thanks for the season of genera.I
prosperity with which he has crown0d us. To the real, true duties of a Mason, as
beautifully expressed in the AddrEJse, we invite and recommend the obedient attention
of the Craft. Its perusal will convey and inculcate more than this report, though, with
emphatic approbation of the Grand Master's opinions and suggestions, we urge a
higher standard for our initiations and a more rigid enforcement of our discipline.
Read it, brethren, when the words of tho AddreBB, its counsels and precepts, shall
have passed the hands of the printer; and let Masters of Lodges haoe it read, as it
will do our subordinates more good than a score of sermons.
.As to feeble, inert, and inoperative Lodges, we concur with the Grand Master. Let
them su beide ; and let their members, struggling against an efilux of population, a paucity of members, and want of material, surrender their charters and assume new affiliations. Your committee fully appreciate how hard it is to give up a
long-issued charter, how fondly the few remaining brethren cling to it, and how its
surrender in their hands implies almost a Masonic delinquency. But the integrity•
and welfare of the Craft at large require a wai.ver of such feelings, and we recommend that the Grand Master, during the coming year, exercise diligently his plena.ry
powers in regard to Lodges of the class alluded to.
As to visiting brethren,-" Three, and the greatest of these is Charity." The
reception of visitors is an off-shoot of this, our cardinal principle. Let visiting brethren have a more cordial welcome than has heretofore been offered in many of our
Lodges.
On the matter reported in the Address relating to the suspension of the Masters
of Santa Rosa and Inyo Lodges, we recommend reference to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
We hail, with approbation and pleasure, the advancing desire of Lodges to
punish delinquents and enforce the moral law. Thia committee, at your last Communication, made its appeal and invocation for a more strenuous exercise of discipline and for the assertion of a higher staud&rd of conscience. Be it, or be it not,
referable to euch action, the present Address assures us that a material and gratifying advance has been made in that direction. Still, however, do we press the
urgency of a faithful, unfaltering application of discipline on the part of Masters
and Wardens. The father of a family does not, if he does his duty, pass by the
delinquencies of hie children; equally, nay, more, should the Master, having charge
of a family where adult years imply discretion, be held to a rigid accountability in
the government of his Lodge.
All action reported for the year, relating to permission given for public processions,
etc., inasmuch as the same requires no reference and the power has been most prudently exercised, is respectfully recommended for approval. Public processions and
displays are the only methods of proselytism allowed as, and no over-use in this
respect appears to have been permitted. The joinder of our brethren of the Scottish
Rite in our ceremonies, we fraternally hail and acknowledge.

In the matter of the petition of Na'f!al. Lodge for permission to appear In
pnblic ceremonies In subordinate association with another society, occurs an
opportunity for this Grand Lodge to assert what this, its committee, deems
to be Its dignity and the call of Its antiquity. As between Odd-Fellowship and
Masonry, we adopt, and heartily, the sentiment and the words of the Grand Master:
"Between them there can be no gronnd for rivalry or jealousy; each has in view the
common purpose of doing good and improving and edncating the human family."
Bot our coadjutors of that Order will forgive us when we sustain the Grand Master in
asserting Masonic precedence. If a decedent-a member of our Order and of some
other society-is to receive Masonic burial, the rites of the Craft mU8t have the precedence ; and so should it be with all other ceremonials. Our age demands this
tribute from aU societies, and our repute has not forfeited, and, we doing oar duty, will
not forfeit the claim.
All matters ln the Address relating to by-laws and amendments thereof, we recommend to the Oommittee on By-Laws. This portion of the remarks of the Grand
Mll!'ter ale~ sngg~sts some deficiencies on the part of Secretaries, to which we call
the1r attention, with the hope that no such notice will be necessary for In the coming
year.
Such portion of the Address as relates to dispensations for new Lodges and surrenders of charters, we recommend to the Committeee on Charters.
The portion-no inconsiderable one-of" qnestlons and decisions," it is not the
~ovlnce of this committee to pasil upon; and we, congratulating the Craft npon the
wisdom and clearneSB which appear in these ennnciations of Its Head, recommend their
consideration ·to the Committee on Jurisprudence. Among this business lies the
qnestion as to the course to be pursued In the event of an adverse minority report on
an applicant for the degrees. This committee believe and state, pasBfm, that In this
case the minority has equal cogency with the majority; bot the matter lies for the
consideration of the commitee mentioned. Also, we draw the at.tention of that com·
mittee to the question suggested by the Grand Master in regard to the disposition of
charges when once presented.
In respect to the misnse of funds by snbordinade Lodges, the Grand Master presents
question most difficult of solution. Certainly it does not belong to us to decide, and
while we give it prominent notice, we leave it to yonr consideration and that of the
appropriate committee. We take occasion to say, however, that, .while every
Lodge is the controller of its own treasury and may abuse that power to the detri·
meqt of its poorer members, the Grand Lodge has ample power, on proper representation, to correct such abuse. Let this go to the Committee on Jurisprudence ;
and we strongly call its attention to the expressed desire of the Grand MastPr to
procure an opinion of the Grand Lodge upon this subject.
To the same committee we commend full consideration of a correction of cases
like that, the recital of which brought tears to many an eye in this Grand Lodge.
Let some amendment of our laws be made which shall not leave the widow of a
brother comfortless and his children doubly orphans. Such things should not be,
and we leave their correction to the brethren of the Committee on Jurisprudence.
The report of official visits we recommend for approval. Their beneficial results
are beyond question and doubt; and the zeal and assiduity of onr Grand Master
in this work deserve emphatic recoguitlon and grateful, 11pecial thanks. The hospitable welcome by the Lodges honored by his presence is bot a well-merited return
for his services, and evinces proper appreciation. The whole system of District
Inspectorship and instruction has operated so beneficially that we heartily recommend the continuance of that system, under snch amendments as the Grand Lecturer
and the Inspectors may suggest.
While we do not altogether coincide with the reasons of the Grand Master for the
requirement of a financial report from each Lodge, we are of the opinion that such
requisition is healthy. It puts a check on extravagance and improper, nnmasonic

disbnrsements. Published reports announce the comparative expendltnres of Lodges,
and declare who bear the burdens and who rightfully claim assistance. We have

fact that this is their first occasion, and, as Imperfection Is a necessary accompanl·
ment of jnvenlllty, we think the Grand Master's recommendo.tlon for their pnblication

The Grand Master's opinion as to "cheapness" of official services and a possibly
mistaken economy partakes in definition and In essence of finance ; bot, as the
address seems to request a special investigation in this respect, the Committee on
Finance will excuse us for presenting the recommendation that the accounts of the
Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary, not only for the past year, but for the whole
term of office of the present incnmbellts, be referred to a special committee. Investigation by that committee, we are assured, will in its results be a fraternal rebuke to
those caviling brethren who, not knowing, or ignoring the amount of official work
performed by the officer last named, have fallen into the error of assuming that his
salary is excessive. "The laborer ·is worthy of his hire." With this text, and a
most thorough examination ·or the work of the officers, we commend this matter to
the rigid scrutiny of the committee suggested.
The traveling and other expenses of the Grand Master we recommend for
reference to the Committee on Finances.
In relation to onr last year's Chicago contribution, the remarks of the Grand Mas·
ter need no comment nor addition. Sym11athizing with the calamity of onr Illinois
brethren, fraternally we held out our hand. We did our duty, no more. The recognition ofour aid is a matter of heart-felt pleasure; and may that day not soon oocnr that
shall call for reciprocity. ~
Again we recommend to the Committee on Finances snch action as may tend to
assist the San Francisco Roard of Relief. It Is the centre of Masonic charity in the
State, and justly claims aid from the whole of this jurisdiction. Snch appropriation,
however liberal, as that committee may suggest, we heartily approve in anticipation,
and pray its confirmation.
All matters in the address relating to work and lectnreR we recommend for reference
to the Grand Lectnrer and Inspectors as a special committee.

Grand Lodge, removed by the Almighty to a higher sphere, be repeated on a monm·
ing page of the printed proceedings of this communication.
To our worthy, faithful, and efficient chief, let this Grand Lodge, in the adoption
of this report, earnestly, fraternally, and affectionately express its deepest gratitude
for diligent service, and for healthy, acceptable, and conscientious government.
Most Worshipful! beyond mere form of words and your Masonic title, we feel and
know that this committee's respectful salutation finds response in every bosom here.
With warm thanks for your past good gonmment-long may it continue I-we
offer our prayers for your future welfare.

Bro. WILLIAM H. Hn.L, from the Oommittee on Correspondence,
presented the following report, the reading of which was dispensed
with, the members being furnished with printed copies thereof:To the M.'. W." Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :Against the earnest wish expressed at the close of our last year's report, hut lu
obedience to the command of our Grand Master, we again resume our pen and labor
in tbe preparation of the fifth annual report It has been our fortune to snbmit to the
Grand Lodge. In one sense this Is a task-for the careful perosal and jndicious review of the proceedings of nearly fifty Grand Lodges is no occupation for RU idle
hour now and then which may be snatched from the pursuit of daily and pressing
avocations. It is, in every sense of the word, labor and toil. So, at least, have we
found it, and our brethren in other jurisdictions say _the same as to themselves. But
there Is pleasure as well as toil in the work. One is brought, as it were, Into personal contact with his brethren "wheresoever dispersed around the globe," and reads
of their prosperity and trials-of the continual growth of the Institution of Masonryof it'! good workR of Brotherly I.ove, Relief, and Truth-of the giving way of antiquated prejudices, even though some men of small intellectual and moral calibre
are busily engaged in again striving to kindle the flame of discord, envy, and hatred,
hoping that the fire will consume our Fraternity instead of their own rubbish-and
in the reading of all these there is true pleasure. Permitting the one consideration to
balance tbe other, so far as personal feelings are concerned, we again devote ourselves to the work before n!!. We are not satisfied with the specimens heretofore
furnished. But we thank our brethren for the kind reception ever given to those
already submitted. As heretofore stated, we do not seek to be either Solomons or
Solons in Freemasonry, nor even lawgivers or law expounders, in any respect. We
rather seek to take our indulgent readers with us, in our walk through the field of
proceedings, and with them gather a few of the many buds and flowers of beauty
and interest to be met with in every quarter. That others could be more witty, profound ,and grave, we readily admit; and we sincerely hope that our next Grand Master
will give some other brother the opportunity to ventilate his wisdom and skill In this
matter. We feel that honors enough have been heaped upon our unworthy head.
We have received and reviewed the proceedings of forty-five Grand Lodges, and
several of these for more than one year. Our list is complete with the exception of
Ohio and Rhode Island,.which had not reached the Grand Secretary at the latest
hour to which the publication of this report could be. delayed. Those reviewed are

ARKANSAS.
The thirty-third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas was held
In the city of Little Rock, on the sixth of November, 1871, the M.-. W.-. 8AMUEL W.
WILLIAHS presiding as Grand ¥aster, and the R.-. W.-. Lma; E. BARBER being Grand
Secretary. Representatives were present from one hundred and twenty-nine subordinate Lodges. (Thanks to the R.·. W. ·• Grand Secretary for stating that fact and
saving us the trouble of counting the long list, to ascertain the number.)
The Grand Master wields a graceful and well-pointed pen, and his address amply
repays for its perusal and study. We most give one or two of the opening gems:We are again permitted as a Grand Lodge to assemble aronnd onr Altar and
exchange greetings. Since we last met a year has gone to take its place with the
thousands that have preceded it. Its humane actions done, sorrows suffered, and joys
experienced, are garnered in the store-house of memory, with those of the years that
have gone before. The acts of men and of nations have become history, and have,
for good or evil, made their impress upon the fntore, to control or regulate and intlnence hnman destiny. In many a home where one year ago was gladness, the wail of
the sorrow-stricken Is heard, becanse loved-ones are not.
Time has laid his hand npon the strong man, and the vigorous form Is fallen ; it
has touched gentle woman, and the sparkling eye is dim.
A year has come and gone, and its conrse has sent its millions to their last resting
place in the dark and narrow house. The year has given to history new stories of
blood and carnage ; new battle-tlelds, where the strength of armies has been riven,
as empires struggled for mastery; where now the untrodden grass grows green above
those who one year ago walked above it, living men.
What has the year been to each of os? Where are its hopes? How many have
ended in fruition ? How many been blighted? What of its sorrows and amictions ?
What of Its joys! Are they not alike now they are past?
As a people, we have been signally blest in the year that has just closed. While
other nations have been amicted with war, and the invasion of "hostile armies, and
internecine strife of the most bloody and cruel character, peace has been ours.
While famine, with gaunt, hungry mien, has stalked through other lands and claimed
his victims by thousands, until the motber has sold her child for food, and the grave
has answered the requisition of the hungry, and the corpse of the starved has become
the food of the starving, plenty has crowned our boards. While the pestilence that
"walks in darkness and waste th at noonday," has poisoned the breath of cities and
nations elsewhere, God has given us pure air and joyons life. While the fire-fiend
has melted cities to ashes elsewhere, onr homes are spared. We have been blessed
witb a most bountiful harvest, giving us promise for lhe futnre. Amid such surround·
ings, there can be no occaeion iso appropriate In which to review onr Masonic life,
to recall those duties and obligations which, as Masons, we owe to God and to each
other.

BRITISH COLUMBIA.

In announcing, three years since, the formation of a Grand Lodge in British
Colombia, we were inadvertently led into error. The proceedings sentns seemed a.II
right on tbeir face, bot in fact they only affected the Lodges subject to the Grand
L•>dg~ of England or Scotland, we do not now remember which. We were not aware
at that time, it being our first work at the reviews of the Communications of our
brethren throughout the world, of the divided allegiance that prevailed in British
Columbia, and had also been manifest in all the other British-American Provinces,
prior to the establishment of Grand Lodges in each in torn. We understand the
work to be so diffe rent in the two home jurisdictions as to make it exceedingly distasteful for either class to give op wholly to the other, or for the two to mPet half
way upon some common ground. If correctly informed, the Scottish work is much
nearer to that in the American Grand Lodges, than to that in England. We may, however, be in error. Our impression comes from conversations with British Columbia
brethren of both jurisdictions during a visit to Victoria le.et winter. But to return to
our writing. The Lodges in British Colombia are equally divided between English
and Scotti~h Lodges, and all attempts to harmonize opinions and ,form one Grand
Lodge, have failed op to this year, when all obstacles were removed both at home
and abroad, and the brethren now literally" dwell together in unity." We have now
before ns for revie w the" Proceedings of the Convention to organize, and of the
first Grand Communication of, the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of F. and A. M., of [ritish
Columbia," and while we procr.ed to give an analysis of what was done, we cheerfully extend the right hand of fellowship and recognition, and bid o:ir northern
brethren of the Pacific Coast an earnest God-speed.

OANADA.

We have received the proceedings of four special Communications of the Grand
Lodge of Canada, held, respectively, September 23, 1870, May 11, May 2', and J~ly
l, 1871, (each called to Jay the corner-stone of some public building), and of the sixteenth Annual Communication, held at Ottawa, July 12, 1871. Tbe M.-. W.'. ALEX. A.
STEVENSON presided In the Grand East, or " on the throne," as our Canadian brethren express it, and the R.·. W.·. THOMA.B 13. HA.RBIS was Graud Secretary. Representatives were present from two hundred and one subordinate Lodges.
The buildings for which corner-stones were laid at the several special Communications were the new Court Honse at Ottawa, the "Canada Air Line Railway
Bridge'', across the Grand river at Cayuga, the Provincial Asylum for the Blind, ai
Brantford, and a public hall at Thornhill.
The Grand Master delivered an address of not unreaijonable length. The greater
part, however, ls devoted to correspondence, to congratulation• with the retiring and
Incoming Noble Grand Masters of Englllnd, and to the Quebec case.
He had granted diepensatiq_ns for eighteen new Lodges during the year, and two
dormant Lodges bad been resuscitated. Applications for the establishment of three
other Lodges had been declined, for good reasons to the Grand Master.
The Grand Master calls attention to the evils and difficulties growing out of the
rule in Canada which permits the same brother to be a member of two or more
Lodges, and suggests a repeal or essential modification thereof. We should think it
was high time for such action, and somewhat wonder that a rule like that should
have prevailed In any jurisdiction.
The Quebec matter ls so thoroughly discussed in the Report on Correspondence
that we make no synopsis of the Grand Master's comments upon the same, save to
say that individually he Inclines to the opinion of those who would prefer to have
things remain as they are, "trusting to time and the good offices of brethren concerned to heal at no distant d11y the breaches which have been made in our ranks."
The address was referred for consideration to the " Board of General Purposes," a
sort of ad interim Grand Lodge, or, as an eloquent counsellor of our acquaintance
is accustomed to say" lmperium in Imperio."
Quite a. space in the proceedings is devoted to the reports of District Deputy
Grand Masters for the several districts. They generally report a state of good feeling and of prosperity, but the incumbent for the Montreal district bad encountered
divers difficulties growing out of the Quebec matter-for there both Grand Lodges
claimed jurisdiction, and each was quite snre that the members and work of the
other were clandestine and irregular.
The "Bpard of General Purposes " submitted Its annual report, from which we
learn that the receipts of the year had been $9,793.88, and the expenditures $9,149.85.
The Grand Lodge holds at its disposal fonds amounting to St2,3t5.26, of which $10,454. 76 belongs to the "Benevolent Fund Investment Account," and $5,376.31 to the
"Masonic Asylum Trust Fond.'' The Board bad presented a donation of $250
"towards alleviating the distress, regardless of nationality, amongst members of the
Fraternity," growing out of the Franco-Prussian war. A truly Masonic act.
The rank of "Past Grand Chaplain" was conferred opon Rev. Bro. C. P. BLISS,

CONNECTICUT.
The eighty-fourth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Connecticut was
held in the city of Hartford, Mny 8, 1872-the M.· . W.·. JAMES L. GouLD, Grand
Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. JOSEPH K. WHEELER being Grand Secretary, with
representatives from one hundred and six Lodges.
The Address of Grand Master GoULD Is first-rate-being well written, plain
Rpoken, and eloquent, as might be expected from one who confesses that he Is editor
of a daily new•paper. The address occupies eleven pages of the pamphlet, and
then there is a" tail to the kite." twenty pages long, consisting of correspondence
on several topics, from the great fires of the West to the great banquet of American
and Eoglieh Masons in the District of Columbia. Of the former, we will say a word
or two ; the latter can only ~e laid up in the archives of the Lodge for reference
thereto by the curious. The Grand Master pays a glowing tribute to the memory of
Dr. DAVID E. BOSTWICK, of Litchfield, who was an eminent Mason, a good man, and
upright citizen. He was Grand Master of the jurisdiction in 1864. General prosperity had marked the Craft during the year, nothing having occurred to disturb the
peace and. harmony of the sobordioates.
In noticing the report of the Grand Lecturer and District Deputies. the Grand
Master suggests, as of great importance to ensure uniformity of work, that "some
competent representative of the Grand Lodge should visit, annually, each Lodge
within the jurisdiction, to correct little irregularities, and, in many cases, to give
mnch·needed instructions in the work and general detail of the Lodge economy."
We doubt not bot this plan would work well in a jurisdiction so limited In geographical dimensions as Connecticut; bot he would be a "live" man, truly, who
could do that work in California, that has some twenty ooonties, " more or less,"
each larger than the little "oblong square" on the borders of Long Island Sound.
The Grand Master regrets that he could not accepi all the invitations received by
him to visit Lodges. He thinks that, though " marrying a wife " or "buying a yoke
of oattle," were not deemed valid excuses in the "Great Light," the being "editor
of a daily newspaper" should be a mantle of charity ample enough to cover a
"multitude of sins." We concur-having been there ourselves. He refers notably
to a singular bot well·devised festival which he attended in Birmingham. It orig!·
nated with King Hiram's Lodge, the object being to gather at a hanqnet, held in
the afternoon, all the old veterans of the Lodge who were prevented from attending
its stated Communications on account of advanced years, bodily Infirmities, or
remote residence. Some three hundred guests were at this banquet, of whom
twenty-one were of ages varying from sixty-one to ninety-one ; seven being over
eighty and seven others over seventy. Rome of these old veterans came from distances of ten, fifteen, and twenty miles. The total age of these twenty-one patri·
archs was sixteen hundred and twenty-two years, or an average of seventy-seven
years each. As may be expected, it was a glorious affair throughout, and this
Lodge has resolved to have such banquets annnally.

The Annual Communication was held November 8, 1871, the same Grand Officers
appearing, with representatives present from eighteen Lodges.
The address of Grand Master STANSBURY is a business-like document, well written
and to the point. Thanks are returned to the " Masonic Choir" (which appears to be
a permanent as well as useful Institution), for having accompanied the Grand Mas·
ter in his visitations of the several Lodges, thereby adding great interest to the otherwise dry work of exemplification and lecturing. Eminent brethren accompanied the
Grand Master and delivered formal addresses or lectures to the Lodges. Eighteen
of these are named. Why cannot we inaugurate and carry out some such plan in
California?
Thr great fire in Chicago called out the practical sympathies of the brethren. The
sum of $2,868.40 was contributed and conveyed to Chicago by a special committee.
Commendatory notice is given of the work of the "Masonic Mutual Relief Associa·
tion" of the District, which, commencing with seven members in 1869, now numbers
six hundred and eighty-eight, and had contributed during the year $2564 for the relief
of the families of deceased brethren. It is a kind of life insurance that has thus far
worked well.
A committee appointed the previous year had held meetings of conference with
a like committee from the Grand Lodge of Odd Fellows upon the subject of precedence or courtesy in cases of funerals of brothers conducted by both Orders. The Odd
Fellows claimed that" when deceased were more prominent in Odd Fellowship than
in Masonry, they should have precedence in conducting the funeral.'' The commit·
tee recommended, and the,Grand Lodge conc urred, that each case be left entirely in
the discretion of the Mastet of the Lodge having charge of the funeral.
·
The Report of the Committee on Correspondence is from the pen of the Chairman, Bro. W.R. SINGLETON, and fills one hundred and fifty pages of the proceedings.
It comprises a review of forty-one .American and nine foreign Grand Lodges. California, for 1670, receives its full meed of notice. Liberal extracts from Grand Master

as tne Grand Lodge of California is indeed thus located, ready at a moment's notice
to fulfill that poetical idea advanced in Congress, that the ;, Occident will kiss the

We thank our brother for his kindly notice of our own report, and" acknowledge
the corn," in that palpable hit about long messages. There are exceptions to all roles,
good brother, and when a thing is enper-excellent, one can hardly get too much ofit.
There •re many things in this report which we would be glad to copy but have

The address of Grand Master P ABCO is a well-written document, valuable for its
sound and practical Masonic advice as well as for the details of his work during the
year. He thinks with us that morality a!1d temperance are as much parts of Free·
masonry as is the ability to rehearse the rit ual and lectures. Would that all the
brethren would " take due notice and govern themselves accordingly."
The Grand Master had visited officially many of the Lodges in the jurisdiction.
Florida is not yet over supplied with railroads, and sometimes the Grand Master was
fatigued by "long and tiresome drives over sandy roads and pine forests." But he
always met with a hearty welcome, and the " refreshments" set before him, consist·
inir of "a wild turkey from the woods, fine oysters from the Gulf, and huge potatoes
from the garden," amply repaid him for the fatigue endured in reaching such hospitable abodes.
He had granted dispensations for the formation of four new Lodges, one of which
was named after himself. The Grand Lodge approved of this, but then passed a resolution that hereafter no Lodge should be called after a living man. Good for F lorida;
and we hope to be able to say the same in the future of California.
The Grand Master spoke a kind word in behalf of the sufferers by tire in Illinois,
Wisconsin, and Michigan. Degrees of latitude make no difference in a Mason's
charity or sympathy.
The Committee on Education reported that several Lodges were at the ex pense
of educating their Masonic wards; bnt the free -school system, and the " Peabody
Fund" did away with the necessity for such charity on the part of most of the
Lodges.
The receipts of the Grand Lodge were $4,058. 75, and the expenditure& $2,113.15.
The report of the Committee on Cortespondeoce is again from the pen of Bro.
DAWKINS, Grand Secretary. Last year he only gave a brief synopsis, and hardly
that, of the work reviewed, being induced thereto by a clamor about the cost of
printing the report. But as a majority of the brethren requested him to give no in ore
installments of such lean feed, he returns to the old style of full review, and now
gives us interesting sketches of the proceedings of forty-four Grand Lodges, our own
for 1870 and 1871 among the number.
Io 1869, as Grand Master, Bro. DAWKINS granted a dispensation to a certain Lodge
to elect a new Master. For this he was taken to account by Bro. GBAY, of Arkansas,
and others, they alleging that the true Masonic doctrine is that the Senior Warden
must, "under all circumstances, go to the East." Bro. D. now fights manfully for his
former action, and contends that when a Senior Warden is notoriously incompetent,
and the Lodge, knowing that faot, petitions for a dispensation, a new Master should
be elected. We will not review this controversy. Bro. D. makes out a strong case
for himself, but still we think the law is with his opponent. The better way for
Grand Lodges to do, is to walk right up to the line and forbid the installation of
either Maater or Warde ns, until they are known to be competent to confer the
degrees, deliver the lectures, and preside with Me.sonic dignity over the Lodge. We
have tried half the experiment, and the rest will probably follow in due time.
Bro. DAWKINS favors California with an extended and generally favorable notice.
He is very complimentary to Grand Master PBA1'T for his address, and to our humble
self for what we were responsible for in the proceedings. Io 1871 he is ditto, and also
highly praises the excellent oration of Bro. BROWNE. When speaking of our donation
to Chicago, Bro. D. says : "California Masonry is evidently of the very best quality,"
and of one of our officers, remarks that " the Grand Secretary is ABELL (able) Lo steer
the finances right, and does do it."
·

We have the proceedings of the last Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge

nothing here of the use of the scissors-that potent editorial weapon! We like to

that those Postmasters, or others, who cabbage these extra reports will be benefitted by their perusal, and so come to " repentance and a better mind " that in future they will permit at least one extra copy to reach California.
The Commnnication was held in Mac<Jn, October 31, 1871, the M. •. W.·. SAMUEL
LAWRENCE presiding as Grand Master, and the R.·. W.-.J. EMMETT BLACKSHEAR being
Grand Secreta1·y. Representatives were present from two hundred and twenty
Lodges.
The address of Grand Master LAWRENCE, as is everything that comes from his
fluent pen, is an excellent, and even eloquent, production. Will not these truthful
passages, which we take from the opening of the address, repay au oft perusal?The period of our Annual Communication has again arrived, and we are once
more assembled around onr altar, my brethren, with hearts, I trust, full of gratitude
to the Architect of the universe for the abundant mercies He has bestowed on us dnring t'he year just past. If He has atllicted and made us to suffer, He has also reproved and comforted us. Thus seems it good unto him to make us perfect.
However others may consider the duty of rendering this homage to the High and
Holy one, whose habitation is in the Heaven of Heavens, but whose presence is
everywhere, even now in our midst, we Masons cannot neglect or ignore it. We are
taught by our sacred princirles to cherish in our hearts love to Him, and we should
ever be ready in our genera assemblies, with one voice, in united acclaim to shout
the final words of the grand old anthem of centuries, "We praise Thee, 0 God, we
acknowledge Thee to be the Lord," while each heart should breathe the spirit of
the Psalmist: "I will praise Thee more and more."
No longer do men point to our Institution as a mere social, or even eleemosynary
Society, bnt recognize and own in it far nobler and grander objects-objects, in
the attainment of which, all those are added. It shonld be our pride, my brethren,
to be privileged to contribute to this result.
A t'ew, in their blindness, are yet heard to grumble, and object that their elevated
view of Freemasonry has a tendency to evangelize it. They seem to be atllicted
with some terrrible dread of that word eoan1.elize. But they are yet in darkness, and
know not of what they speak. llJvangelize l! reemasonry ! Why, it is already evange·
lized to their hand. What is it in its inception, in its objects, and in its work, but an
"EVANGELION," a good message of good tidings to mankind-the giving of light
to the blind? And what are we, my brethren, each and all of us, every one who has
truly received onr mysteries, but evangels in the best sense of · the word, messengers of good tidings, bearing on and sprea1ling ever, as on the winged winds of
Heaven, to the four corners of the earth, the good message : "Glory to God in the
highest! on earth peace, good will towards men."
The Grand Master utters an indignant protest against the acts of the Grand Orient
of France and Grand Lodge of Hamburg, and hopes that the resolutions of non-intercourse will not be idle threats merely, but" a stern and inflexible refusal to recog·
nize as Masons any and all who claim to hall from tlie interdicted jurisdictions."
This may be a hardship in some individual cases, but it is justice.
He speaks feelingly and eloquently of the Wayhington Banquet given to the
Grand Master of England, at which he was present and one of the speakers.

and elsewhere, will heed and follow :Masonry, althongh teaching all virtnes known to the breast of man, makes it one
of the highest principles of the Order to speak well of a brother, and to recognize
all mankind as a common band of brothers.
·
Slander, under ordinary circumstances, among people who do not snstain toward
each other any nncommon relation, is one of the lowest offenses against social or·
der; it involves falsehood, malignity, and cowardice ; but to calumniate a brother
Mason violates the fundamental laws of the Brotherhood, and destroys the principles upon which it is built. The slanderer is a disgrace to our Order, and its enemy.
The maxims of Masonry prescribe the method in which evil reports should be
bronght to the knowledge of those whom they affect, and for whose mjury they were
invented; this dnty should be discharged in all kindness, and while it places the
party injnred on his guard, mnch pain and trouble may be avoided.
Profanity is more an indecency than a vice, more a mark of bad breeding than of
depravity ; the idle nse of 88cred names does not add force to trnth nor emphasis"to
expression.
Yo Society, no Order of men, no Rank, no Sect, appears to be free from a vice
which should, above all others, be denounced in this presence-it is Intemperance.
Rere, before this Alt&r, and with the obligation of.my office upon me, I am called
npon to exhort Masons, and all men, to abandon the nse of intoxicating drinks, as the
cause of a thousand vices and follies, as the worst enemy to all that is beautiful and
good.

The Committee on Grievances submitted an elaborate report on matters referred
to them. It is qnite evident that their position was no sinecure. We shonld judge,
from reading this report, that they had some queer Lodges and remiss brethren in
Indiana, as well as in. California. They still keep np, in Indiana, what should be the
exploded system of trying a brother before the whole Lodge ; and we find a curious
specimen of the practical workings of that system in the report before us. One
Lodge, having a membership of fifty-two, tried a member for fighting, to which he
pleaded guilty. Bnt when the Lodge met to try, or rather receive the plea, only
four members were present besides the accnsed. They expelled the offender; bnt
the committee and Grand Lodge reversed this action and ordered a new trial, on this
gronnd, which is nndonbtedly correct:We hold that no Lodge is competent to transact bnsiness without at least seven
members. It requires seven members to constitnte a Lodge. A charter cannot be
granted to less than that number, nor surrendered so long as seven members vote
against it; and it follows that no bnsinesa, snch as passing the ballot for any purpose,
can be transacted withont the presence of at least seven members. Hence any
action taken in this cause when less than the constitutional number were present
was unconstitutional and void, and the farther fact, that by the report of this Lodge,
made on the first day of January, 1871, only seven and ei11;ht months prior to the
time of this trial, this Lodge contained a membership of fifty-two, shows that at a
meeting called at any reasonable time, and with any reasonable notice, it would not
have been difficult to have insured the presence of more than four members.
In another case, a Lodge took a vote and expelled the accused before having
prononnced him guilty. They were kindly permitted to go back to first principles
and can but try again. If stupidity were a contagions disease, we should say that some
of the brethren in Indiana bad been within catching distance. But in one case, we
think that the committee went a little too much into the hair-splitting business. It
appears that a certain brother entered Into corresp'ondence with one of those thieving rascals in New York who propose to furnish an unlimited amount of connterfeit
greenbacks for circulation. He paid express charges; but when a large box came
to hand, for some reason, be dropped the matter and coucluded not to go any farther
In that specnlation. The committee held that it was not proven that he intended to
utter or circulate the counterfeits, and so they reversed the action of bis Lodge in
suspending him. Perhaps it was so, technically, but we should snspect the honesty
of any man or brother who entered Into snch correspondence for am!.18em811t'8 sake.
An old Maryland judge was wont to have all horse thieves, brought before him,
sonndly whipped by the constable, and then, to remedy all errors, grant the whippee
a new trial! We make no particnlar application in this case.
A resolntion looking to the establishment of a "Masonic Widows' and Orphans'

From the very able and eloquent oration pronounced by the W.·. Grand Orator,
Bro. GEO. B. COBKHILL, we cnll the following gem, only wishing th\t we had room
for the whole document : Masonry inculcates no special doctl"ines of theology; it has no political tenets ; it
"'quires of its votaries no pledge as to form of government, as to theories of science,
or personal vocation. It sweeps in the vast arena of its power the entire inhabitable
globe; it treads beneath the canvas wigwam of the untutored savage ; its music
sounds through the arches of the temples of China; its votaries of every age and
Clime, of every color and condition, jostle each other thronghont the limits of the
lands of the W'lrld ; its magic signs and mystic ties link heart to heart and hand to
hand, when language becomes a burden and identity is forgotten.
The future of Masonry no one can tell; as it has lived through the countless years
of the past, so comin~ time will honor and prosper it, unless its votaries •hould fail
of the high destiny within their reach. The institution is nol>le enough in its origin,
grand enough in its conceptions, to command the respect of the earnest men of the
present or any succeeding age. And so long as we are trne to the lessons that are
taught ns, true to the commanil.s that are laid upon ns, trne to the obligations that
we assume, our success and prosperity is certain.
The onward march of civilization, the general dissemination of the great principles
of the Christian religion, the elevation of humanity, but widen the field of our influence and open the way to success. Have we not, then, all a duty to perform-each
individual member for himself, and for the world in whioh he lives? Your first dnty,
It Is trne, is to yonr brethren. The individual prosperity and happiness of each
brother should be the care of every Mason; but yonr sympathy and your labor should
not be restricted to those of yonr own order.

The Address of the Grand Master is well written, of reasonable length, and
devoted mainly to the discussion of local matters. We find, however, some troths
so happily expressed In the opening paragraphs, that we are tempted to transfer the
same to oor own report :You are not here for display or pastime, or revel of any kind, or to be feted or
feasted, but for the annual necessary legislation of the most important and control·
ing part of the Masonic Order. This assertion is too true to be considered either
novel or startling, and every Royal Arch Mason, Knight Templar, or Scottish Rite
Mason Is directly interested In remembering and recognizing the controling reality,
that the Blue Lodge is the root, the magnificent trunk-growing In symmetrical
bean,y, while all contained in Capitnlar, Templar, or Scottish Rite Masonry, are the
branches and twigs of the parent tree, the special prosperity of each depending upon

The worshippers at that shrine, as.an organization, are withont·territorial posseesions, have been gathered from the four quarters of the world ; they are together
for mutual Improvement, are taught to meet on the level and learn the lesson of
Jove, that a brother can be found lo the Jew and Gentile, Turk and Christian; they
have no coercive political power; morality and virtue are the executive offices whose
zeal and fidelity have enabled them to survive the wreck of mighty empires, and present a proud contrast with the nations that fionrished when the Order was in its
infancy, and now in the continued but later days of its glory, they are almost without token of remembrance.
The symbolisms and allegories of Masonry are still all-powerful, the concentrated
principle whereof is the humanizing des!re to promote the happiness of mankind and
dignify humanity by the exercise of a living faith, and the Hope that hopeth for all
that is just and wise, that triumphs over evil, is the friend of truth and prophet of
the good time coming ; that adorns the sandy desert of life with a tranquil beauty
that shall never fade, embellishes it with a wealth of thought, feeling, and action ;
that forgiveth seventy and seven times and is still rich in the treasure of pardon;
that smooths the pillow of the dying, drops a tear wlth the mourner, speaks peace to
the aftlicted, in a voice sweeter than honey, and administers its power with hands
softer than the down of the dove ; that needs no eulogy, carries out their designs
with successful energy, and requires all within the fold, who wish to be happy, useful, and beloved, to cherish, cultivate, and extend their glorious purpose.

against secret societies, hot we have not space for farther qnotations.

in ao equivocal position with their Masonic neighbors of Texas, and with the sojourning brethren in Metamoras, naturally desire to be received under an acknowledged
Masonic authority. I advise the reference of this subject to the appropriate committee.

have found means) to give and " worthiness" to receive.
In a city like ours, holding communication with every portion of the globe, frequented and sought by the denizens of every clime, there is bot too much opportunity afforded for the exercise of the kindly offices of charity; and I can testify, from
my own experience, that" charity is twice blessed-it blesseth him that gives, as
well as him that takes," and in the gratitude which the relieved cherishes for the hand
which helped, when help was so aeeded, our Relief Lodge, and those who enabled it
to di~pense its aid, found a reward-the noblest in the wide field of Masonry.
Satisfied that my successor will strive to excel me in zeal and faithfulness, I bnt
trust that those of our honored Fraternity who have hitherto, whether as Lodges or
individuals, upheld the Relief Lodge, may likewise seek to surpass themselves, and
enable our entire jurisdiction to preserve and increase its fair fame for brotherly and
Masonic actions, abroad and at home.

I cannot permit the opportunity to pass without a few brief words of counsel and
advice. The signs of danger have already appeared in the horizon, and we shall be
wise if we put our good ship in condition to withstand the shock of the approaching
storm. Ignorant and deluded men are envious of our increasing popularity, and the
timid and foolish are fearful of our growth and prosperity. Already combinations
are being made against ns, and outside parties are blindly cnltivating a· hostility which
may possibly eventuate in another era of darkness and gloom. It is a fact, however,
that cannot be disgnised, no matter how earnestly we may strive to do so. that onr
most dangerous enemies are within onr own lines. The great battle is to be fought
with ourselves; and the victory, if it is won, must be in us and of us. Intemperance,
profanity, avarice, envy, malice, and all the long train of social and moral evils, are
endeavoring to undermine onr institntion; and it will reqnire the earnest and nnited
efforts of all ll'Ood and faithful Masons to prevent the strnctore from tottering and
crumbling ta the earth. We cannot overcome the prejudice of the outside world by
arguments or altercations, nor is it oeces•ary that we should do so. Bat we may add
materially to the reputation of oar fra~ernity, and comJlel the respect .and !JOn!ide!lce
of the community, by conformmg our hves to the teacqmgs of oar anment mstitutioa.
Thus may we do oar part toward continuing the order in its original purity, and feel
the glorious satisfaction of having done our duty to oar brothers and ourselves.
One more injunction, not new but none the less important, I wish to impress upon
you-Guard toell the outer door. Masonry is judged, to a great extent, by the character of its individual members, and it is of the utmost importance, that none but honest and upright men gain admission. That your committee can find nothing agai_nst
a candidate is no reason why he should be admitted. He should possess sterling
qualities of mind and heart, without which no man can be a good Mason. Give this
subject the attention its importance demands, and for the future firmly determine to
raise the standard of your Lodges by guarding well the outei: dom·.
The Grand Master publishes some ten of his decisions. We quote only two. The
fifth is iu conflict with the rosltion taken by oar own Committee on J arisprudence
and Grand Lodge, (as we sh1dl note further on), and the seventh is somewhat novel
tons, but it appears to be sound both in its law and equity.
V. Applications from candidates over whom the Lodge has no jurisdiqtion, or
who are physically disqualified, should be returned without a ballot, and the facts
entered upon the record.
VII. A Mason claims to be a member of a Lodge, and proves that at a certain date
he was actually a member. The books are lost, and the Lodge has no record evidence that he was ever dimitted or deprived of membership. The burden of proof
is on the Lodge, and they mnst show that he is not a member. The fact that he has
neglected to pay dues for many years is not conclusive evidence that he is not a
member, bot would be entitled to considerable weight, especially if snpported by
other facts pointing in the same direction.

The committee, now that an objection is formally raised, say they consider such

that the action of the power of a Rite, whether dogmatic or administrative, can not
legally extend, except to Masons of that Rite, obedient to the jurisdiction of that
Body." In reference to t he same principle, and the action of certain Grand Bodies
thereupon, the committee state the fact that the Grand Lodge of England has a Provincial Grand Lodge at Buenos Ayres, within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of
the Argentine Republic; that the Grand Lodge of Scotland ha.a its Lodges in Venezuela and Peru; and that of Ireland its Lodges in Portugal. Not perceiving, therir
fore, any Ma.sonic interference with or violation of the rights of the Grand Lodge of

Rite of Masonry within its proper jurisdiction."
We have thus noticed this matter at some length, because the same questions may

the opinion tha.t the establishment of rival Lodges in a. foreign country, though ~f
different rites, is fraught with danger. Collisions a.re imminent, and action in all
such cases should be marked with great ca.ution. As the Hawaiian Kingdom we believe, is the only foreign country where our Grand Lodge claims jurisdictio~, there
is but little risk of our coming into collision with foreign bodies. But we may learn
a.nd practice caution nevertheless.

Some Lodges may find that this plan will work well, and it is certainly a very simple one, but we question very much whether it would do as a general role. Something was said in our own Grand Lodge last year abont the unmasonic charact.er of
requiring the payment of does in Lodges-that it was a departnre from Ancient Landmarks and usages, and did away with true Masonic charity. This, as we were told
by some old Masons, was done in former times by Masons putting their hands in
their pockets and relieving the wants of all distressed brothers, whether members of
their Lodge or not. We listened with pleasnre to these arguments and admired the
principle, and from our own hearts could wish that all Masons woold act upon that
idea, and BO would they were we now in the midst of that Millennial Glory where
man shall be freed from the imperfections of common life, and do good unto all for
the glory of God. But, as this poor world ii now, we can not shut onr eyes to the
fact, that men (even though Masons) ,do not live up to their professions or duty, and
too often throw upon more willing brothers the burdens which all should share.
Onr own experience and observations are, that when we wish to raise money for a
suffering brother or his family, even in & large city, where there are hundreds of Ma.sons, we can almost count upon our t.en fingers those brethren upon whom it is safe to

opinion that the system of compulsory dues has still some merit, for it compels A.
as well as C. to do something in the line of his duty. We sincerely hope the good
time of the Millennium is not far oft', but we do not as :(et perceive sufiicient evidence
of its proximity to base legislation, Masonic or otherwise, upon snch a contingency.

The fifty-fourth Annual Communication of the Grand. Lodge of Mississippi was
held at Holly Springs, January 22, 1872, the M.·. W.·. GEORGE B. FEABN being Grand
Master, and the B.·. w... J. L. PoWER, Grand Secretary. Two hundred and thirteen
Lodges were represent.ad.
The Grand Master's address is brief, and ma.inly confined to the business of his jurisdiction. We copy this appropriate tribute to the memory of two illustrious Masons,
whose fame was not confined to their own State, the venerable Bros. GILES M. H ILLYER
and GEORGE H. GRAY, Sen. Both transmitted a name and renown of which their
descendants may well be prond. But death le.gs not with his work for any man, and
"the great as well as the small mnst go when he sounds the ale.rm:"
Our gifted brother, GILES II{. HILLYER, Past Grand Master, after a painful. pro1racted and wasting illness, departed this life at Vicksburg, on the 22d of April last.
To those of us who saw him in last Grand Lodge this sad event was not unexpected.
His once manly form, wasted and worn with disease-his eye, still bright, yet soft.ened
and subdued by the near approach of the final end-his voice, still eloquent, yet echoing with the hollow cadence of the tomb-warned us that for the lru!t time we had seen
him in our midst. .A.nd yet, when the sad tidings reached us that the end had come-that Brother HILLYER was no mor&--0ur hearts were stunned by the heavy blow of
the great calamity, and even now it is he.rd to realize that we shall see bim and hear
him no more.
While this great weight of sorrow was yet fresh upon us, the 111&.Ronic heart was
aga.in bowed in grief, and its wounds again opened, for our venerable Father. GEORGE
H. GBAY, Sen., had suddenly been summoned to his long home. Devoted to Free-°
masonry, because he regarded it a beautiful and harmonious science, calculated to
ennoble and elevate its votaries in the scale of morality to a position second only to
that attained by the sincere Christian, he was, through a long and active life, a living
exemplification of the principles he professed, and gave all the resources of a mind
well balanced, acute and discriminating, to the elucidation of those principles for the
benefit of hie less informed brethren , and enjoyed the reputation of a sound Masonic
jurist, not confined to the limits of this State. At the time of his death he filled ~e
position of Grand Treaanrer of Grand Lodge, e.nd for several years had acted as Chauman of yonr Committee on Masonic Law and Jurisprudence.
While we mourn our sad bereavement, may we not forget the impressive lessons
which death continually teaches us; may we rather ever r emember the beautiful
words uttered by Brother HILLYER, but one short year ago: " My brethren, the duty
we owe the dead is performed. It remains that we who are alive should so live, and
by our actions attend \be coming of the Day of Fate, that we neither be surprised,
nor leave our duties imperfect, nor our sins uncancelled, nor our persons unreco~­
olled, nor our God unappeased, but when our bodies in their turn descend to thell'
graves, our souls may ascend to the regions of eternal light wherein is the Holy H ouse
of the Heavenly Temple of the I..ord."
Dispensations had been issned for the formation of eight new Lodges.
The receiplB of the year were $10,31117, and the expenditures $10,288-66.
The DaptislB of Mississippi, who had established an " Orphans' Home,'' made
propositions to the Grand Lodge to tum the same over to its supervision and control.
A committ.ee was appointed to consider the offer and accept the same if thought expedient.

recommend them t.o become members of their Masonic family. They commit a
wrong not intentionally, but from want of thought. We all may be more or less
subject to such reproach, and all will do well t.o ponder over this abuse, which can be
so easily corrected.
We get the" good fellows" int.o the Order, and what is often the result? What
good do they do us, or we them? What becomes of them? Perhaps we never see
them again ; they did not find the gew-gaw they were looking for, and at once abandon the Lodge for more congenial associations. Perhaps, resolved to find a plaything, they make one of our solemn mysteries ; or worse, use them for selfish and
unholy purposes, thus bringing scandal on the Order-and then we have t.o get the
"good fellows" out. That makes trouble in the family, and no good whatever has
been accomplished. We have sown the seed on barren ground, lost both it and the
labor, and have also suffered some in the opinion of the world. Let us acknowledge
the truth, and face it. FreemBBOnry is becoming too popular, and this very popularity is a foe to its stability t.o be feared, unless the current of favor is guided and controlled within legitimate bounds. It is threatened with a patronage which amounts
t.o invasion. Its attractions are snch that our doors a.re 15esieged with the popular
impulse t.o become Masons-not Master MBBOns only, for many of these outside admirers have already fixed their eyes, as they suppose, on a pomt fa.r above the basement story. They merely want t.o pass through, and go up stairs and climb the
steeple, if there is a steeple t.o climb.
Bliould our plain and orderly apartments of " Three Degrees" of Ancient Craft
Masonry be used simply t.o minister t.o such aspirations as these? And yet such aspirants do get in, and J>ass through and climb. The worst of it is, they &'Ct through
with very little knowledge of what they have seen and heard-so little mdeed that
they could not prove their claims as Masons away from home, and a.re seldom seen in
the "Blue Lo<fge" after. There is, however, one grain of comfort in connection
with their thorough ignorance of Masolilry: they could never divulge its secrets if
they tried.
No one admires our srstem of Masonic rites, in all its grades and degrees, more
than I do. I love the whole of it t.oo much t.o stand by and see any branch o:£ it
s~hted or abused without regret. This is the reason I object to our Three Degrees
bemg me.de merely a thoroughfare. We are t.old, and wo teach, that Masonry is a
"progressive science;" but this kind of progress is no advance towards the end it
has in view. It is all true, and good, and beautiful. It is eJllworth being, and knowing. Let us realize these facts, enjoy our Masonic privileges as men, and not trifie
with them as thoughtless boys,
" Pleased with a rattle, tickled with a straw."
Let us grasp it, as we receive it, with intelligence and understanding, and with
honest, earnest hearts and hands, work out its mighty moral purpose.
Should any danger threaten our Order in the future, it will strike from within.
We have nothing t.o fear from the outside world, RO long as we remain true t.o ourselves and our trust. The mutterings of an anti-masonic st.orm, which we hea.r in
various quarters, come from the clouds of disappointment that have gathered from
these very mists of igilorance to which I have referred. They are at present impotent
t.o harm, for the vital principle is not in them. Their pretensions ·are conglomerate
of falsehood, and their lightning is a sham. Bee t.o it that no spa.rk of truth gets int.o them, or a thin vapor, no bigger than a man's hand, may overspread the sky, and
then will break the storm.
Great prosperity always begets a careless sense of security, and cheap commodities, though of the best qualitv, a.re never priz.ed at their real worth. Let me exhort
you to doubly guard your doors against the popular pressure, lest the human sea
break through, and sweep into our castle walls, leaving nothing but a wild waste of
waters. Let me conjure you t.o place the true value upon our treasures, that none
may squander or throw them away because they are so easy of access, and so cheap.
Rea.lize but this truth: we are making too many Masons, and are making them t.oo
fast: and the infallible Masonic instincts will avert the only danger that can threaten
the st.ability of our beloved Order. We will .also render secure those other Orders t.o
whom we furnish all their materials, and who build their structures on our foundations.

The report of the Committee on CorTespondence is again submitted by Bro. R. H.
TAYLOR, aud in saying that, our readers may have the assurance that it is No. 1, for
Bro. TAYLOR in that line is hard to beat. He Rees the salient points in the various
Grand Lodge proceeding11, and presents them in a pleasing style. He, too, is never
afraid to" speak out in meeting," and there is never any doubt where he stands on
any new question that he discusses. In this report he reviews the proceedings of 38
Grand Lodges, beginning with oar own for 1870. He speaks in the highest terms of
the address of Grand Master PRATT, and quotes liberally therefrom, though not at all
times con earring folly with him in hiR expressed opinions. Bro. T. is also highly
complimentary of our own report, and copies therefrom. He is pleased with the
final action of our Grand Lodge on the subject of the burial of suicides, in regard
to which he and the writer have measured lances in times past. But all Is "peace
and quiet on the Potomac now." Only this, however, in addition-we like to see
consistency where it can be practised, and we mean to stir up our Grand Lodge untll
it will grant the same privilege to brothers who have died while guilty of no greater
crime than of owing to their Lodges the sum of SS, which, ic many cases, they were
too poor to pay, and too proud to ask for or receive a remittance of does as a
charity. And yet, our Grand Lodge so adjudges and acts at this present writing·
We hope that Bro. TAYLOR will lend us the aid of his pointed pen in this effort or
oars to bring our Grand Lodge to "repentance and a better mind."
Bro. TAYLOR, having been charged by Bro. Wmi:BLER, of Connecticut, with pro·
lixity in a former report, thus " rises to explain," wherein we heartily concur, and
say, Amen!
We plead guilty. That report was prolix. We "rise to explain." Ju the first
place, we think it the duty of each Chairman of Committee on Correspondence to
give the proceedings or every Grand Lodge a "thorough J!erusal," so that nothing of
general interest may escape him. In the matter of " liberal comments" we have
only to say that when the subject treated of requires comment, the reviewer's re·
marks should be given with sufficient f~l.lness to .allow the reader to know his opinion. It may, or may not, be of some ut1hty. If 1t provokes thought upon a disputed
point, it is of service. These reports should have an aim, and that aim should be to
Increase the stock of Masonic knowledge. By courteously discussing the questions
which arise, we shall arrive more nearly to uniformity in matters of Masonic Jurisprudence and usage; we shall obtain a better knowledge of Masonic landmarks, and we sh11ll
help to elevate the standard of Masonic Intelligence. These discussions oftentimes
require" liberal extracts," that we may fairly present the views which we attack or
endorse. Even in matters of mere ornament-the graces of language applied to
speculative t.orics-the p~etry of Masonry i wherever we find passages which in our
judgment wtl tend to withdraw the mlnu of the reader from the dull, plodding
actualities of every day life, and give new scope and strength to his imagination we
most confess it is difllcult for Ull to refrain from quoting tliem. We tru~t that Bro.
WHEBLER will not consider our explanation too prolix.
We copy the following remarks on the subject of affirmaticma in M~sonry, not
that we concur or have reason to dissent, bnt because of the valuable information
imparted in relation to the origin of the practice. Bro. T. is answering some critl·
cisms made by Bro. DRUllllOND npon the position maintained by him in a former
Report:" We have been quietly making some Investigation Into the matter referred to in
the last two paragr!Lp~s,. and may hereafter give. the result. Suffice it to say here
that in some of the Jnr1sd1ctions affirmations were ID use llfty years ago, and had been
for a loug time (indefinite) before that. Of hoto recent origin are they in courts, &o.?"
Our statement was" modern" not "recent." Now, a brief reference to history
will show that we were correct. In the latter part of the reign of CHARLES I, namely,
fn the year A. D.16-17. GEORGE Fox founded the" Society of Friends," in England,
and they were called by that name until the year 1660, when, Fox being brought
before the magistrates of Derby for preaching there, and telling them to "quake at
the name of the Lord," GERVASE BBNNETT, one of the magistrates, caught up the
word, and called Fox and bis friends Quakers, by which name the " Friends" have
ever since been known to the world. ~·rom the time they were founded until after

Grand Lodge of Oalif07'nia.

1872.J

489

the accession to the throne of J~KB II, Fe~ruaq'" 1686, the QoakerR were subjected to
many disabilities and perseont1ons. Their evidence was held inadmissible. For
refo•ing to take a leg~I oath they were treated as obstinate offenders, and subject
to penalties. JAKES, ID 1687, issued a pr~lamatlon by which he declared his resolu·
tion that, as he would not force ~he conscience of any man himself, neither would he
allow any man to force the consc!ence of others: Still, the persecutions and disabili·
ties of the Quakers, and other dissenters, contmued. In 1688 he ordered the proc·
lamation to be republished, and appended to It an additional declaration stating bis
unalterable resolution of securing to the subjects of the English crown,/ freedom of
conscience forever," and of rendering thenceforth merit, and not oaths the qualifl·
cation for office. That this declaration might be more generally know~ au order
was sent to the several bishops, enjoining that it should be read by th~ clergy in
their respective ch arches, at the nsoal time of divine service, in London on the 20th
and in the country on the 27th of May. The bishops di•obe,red the order, for which
they were tried-seven of them-at Westminster Hall. Great public excitement
prevailed. Mnltitodes came f'rom the country to the metropolis to attend the trial.
Within the court the officers were unable to maintain the nsoal forms of decorum.
'l'he feelings of the audience burst through every restraint, and repeated cheers of
approbation encouraged the witnesses ana the counsel for prisoners. The jury were
out all night, which they spent in lond and violent debate. In the morning they returned into court and pronounced a verdict of not guilty. It was received with
deafening shoot!! of applause; the enthusiasm communicated itself to the crowd
withont the )!all ; it was rapidly propagated to the extremities of the metropolis.
This contest with the bishops It was, which, more than anything else, led to the revo·
lotion, by which JAKES was compelled to abdicate, to be succeeded by WILLIAM
and MARY, Prince and Princess of Orange, who began to reign February 13th, 1689.
Bui the entering wedge had been applied, and a part of the hardships which the
Quakers had .been compelled to undergo were removed by the Toleration .Act which
was passed in the first year of the reign of WrLLIAM and lllARY, (1 Wm. & M. c. 18,
§ 13,) which first allowed the Quakers to make a declaration (or affirmation) of their
fidelity to the State, Instead of taking an oath of allegiance, and exempted them
f'rom all pains and penalties on their making, if required, certain other declarations
there prescribed. By another Statute, which passed about six years after, (7 & 8
Wm. III, c. 34.,) their solemn affirmation in courts of justice was admitted in civil
oases, to have the ~ame effect as ao oath; but they still continued to be ~xcloded
from giving evidence in criminal cases nntll 1829, when by the .Act of 9 George IV,
o. 82, Quakers and Moravians were allowed to give evidence upon their solemn affir·
mation in all cases, criminal as well as civil. Still later, in 183,, by 3 & 4 Wm. IV,
c. 82, a similar statutory provision was made in favor of a sect called " Separatists."
But, in England, the full privilege of making affirmation, instead of being sworn,
was not extended so as to embrace all 'persons unwilling to take an oath, until the
reign of the present Queen. VICTORIA began to reign June 20th, 1837. By 17 & 18
Viet.. c. 125, § 20, it was enacted:" If any person called as a witness, or required to make an affidavit or deposition,
shall refuse or be unwilling, from alleged coosclentions motives, to be sworn, it shall
be lawful for the Court or Judge, or other presiding officer or person qualified to take
affidavits or depositions, upon being satisfied of the sincerity of such objection, to
permit such verson, instead of being sworn, to make hie or her solemn affirmation or
declaration.'
So much in support of oar statement; and now, granting that" in some of the
Jurisdictions affirmations were in use fifty years ago, and had been for a long time
(indefinite) before that," does that fact tend to prove that this Is not an innovation?
Does our brother think that at the time of the _Promulgation of the Gotblo Constitn·
tion, .A. D. 926, Masons were allowed to be obhgated by allinnation? Is it permitted
in England-from whence Masonry was transplanted to this country-even now?
This Is an interesting question, and we hope Bro. DRU!dllOND will not fail to give us
the result of his investigation, as he intimates he may do. In the meantime we refer
him and others who may feel an interest in the matter, so far as the history of the
•Introduction of affirmations in courts and legal proceedings is concerned, to HUHE'B
History of England, vol. vi, p. 316, et seq.; LINGARD's History of England , Reign of
JAns II, p<l8$im; Enclyclopredia Britannica, article "Quakers;" 1 PHILLIPS on
Evidence, Ch. IIL

Grand Lodge of New York protested against this illegal and unwarranted invasion
of their territory, and appealed for protection to the other Grand Lodges In the
United States.
The result of this appeal was, that ever7 Grand Lodge, I believe, then In existence jo the Republio, discontinued Masomc intercourse with the Grand Lodge of
Hamburg. Yet, notwithstanding this combined action, and notwithstanding the
renewed and continued protestations of the Grand Lodl{e or New York, the warrants

flaunted the black ftag of Masonic piracy and lllibusterism in the face of the Masonic
world. The doctrine of Grand Lodge supremacy and exclusive •overeignty within
well defined and established territorial limits, is llOl7!Rtimeit called an .Ameri-Oan
doctrine. I do not regard it as an exclusively American doctrine. It is a uninersal
Masonic doctrine. I do not believe there is a Grand Lodge In the world which would
not Indignantly resent a similar illegal Intrusion upon its jurisdiction. Ir the Grand
Lodge of New Jersey were so base and unmindful of its Masonic doty and obligation,
as to establish a snbordinate Lodge within the jurisdiction of Hamburg, I have no
doubt that that body would vehemently protest against the irregularity.

and unaided, to protect itself in the premises. What the great State of New York,
with ite constant communication with Bamburg, bas failed for twenty years to effect,
New Jersey cannot expect to accomplish.
The history of the former conduct of Hamburg assures me. that the protest which
I have issued, and any nrotest and remonstrance which this Grand Lodge may issue,

Masonic instincts of Amity and Fraternity, not to consider the less noble instinct of
eolf-preservatioo, will induce the Grand I.odges of the United States to stand shoulder
to shoulder with the Grand Lodge of New Jersey in resisting this illegal invasion of
territory exclusively masooically occupied.
I can see bot one means of protection to ourselves, and at the same time to all the
other Grand Lodges of the Union. The individual action of the Grand Lodges of the
United States has been tried in defence or the Grand Lodice of New York. and has
failed. I believe that the united and combined action of the entire Craft of the
United States will alone abate the evil.

workman and overseer, and neglected no part of his wide extended jurisdiction or

He congratnl11tes the Fraternity npon the Masonic prosperity of the past year,

give such recreant brethren a "hauling over the coals."
Nearly a page of this address· is devoted to feeling allusions to the death of a

former died in oftlce, and of him Grand ·Master ANTHON says: "On his deathbed,
after a full profeBBion of his religions faith, he said to a Masonic friend standing near:

Could a better eulogy be pronounced npon any man !
