NORTH CAROLINA.
The eighty-fifth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of North Carolina
was held in Raleigh, December 4.th, 1871-the M.·. W. •• CHARLES C. CLARK being
Grand Master, and the B.-. W.-. DONALD W. BAIN, Grand Secretary. Representatives
were present from one hundred and fifty-three Lodges.
The Address of Grand Master CLARK Is a nobleprodnction. Would that all "whe
are in high places" would be eqnally explicit and plain in their condemnation or the
violation or the " perfect points " of Masonry. At the risk or being charged ourselves with a desire to ride hobbies, we will quote these eloquent words of the Grand
Master:·
It should be, and doubtless Is, a cause for self-congratulation, that the Grand
Lodge of North Carolina has, at all timP.s, and under all circumstances, recognized
this mission of Masonry ; and, by word and deed, endeavored to constrain the individual Mason to be true and faithful in his allegience, and" to live and act agreeably
to his profession." No corrnpting habit, no debasing immorality, no polluting vice,
hllll here received aught bot the severest condemnation-while subordinate Lodges
have been exhorted and required to vindicate the character of our moral institution,
by a prompt and thorough expurgation or moral offences, either by reforming the
offender, through good counsel and timely admonition, or by cutting him off, as a
diseased lim\J, that would destroy the vigor and ruin the health of the whole body.
And hence it is, tbat the arch enemies to all social peace and personal purity-Profanity and Drunkenness-have been boldly and deterll!-i~edly aSl!a~led by tbe reeol!ltions of '68, which proclaim to the world the true epmt and genius or Masonry, m
the enactmentlst. That profani'Y and drunkenness are among the highest MasoniO crimes.
2d. That subordinate Lodges in this jurisdiction are directed to vindicate the law
in relation thereto.
It would certainly be a work of supererogation to attempt to prove that these
resolutions are in perfect accordance with every Masonic precept and doctrine.
They do not make acts offences which before were not offences. They are simply
declaratory of the law. The Mason Is taught, even at hie Masonic birth, never to
mention God's name "but with that reverential awe which is doe from a creature to
his Creator;" and always to subject the appetites and passions to that due restraint
"which renders the body ta.me and governable, and frees the mind from the allurements of vice." The fact is, the moral law ill the Masonic law; and he who violates
the one violates the other. Hence the most eminent Masonic jurists, submitting

As a matter of history, as well as of general Interest, we copy somewh11t at length
the account of the peaceful close of the controversy between Oregon and Wash·
ington. May "Canada" and "Quebec" be equally fortunate :The Grand Lodge of Oregon will sanction all that oar Washington brethren have
said and done in the premises, and heartily nnite with tbem in celebrating thle grand
demonstration of peace. The terms npon which these Grand Bodies have joined
hands, and now salute their sister jorl~diction In the bonds of perfect union and fra·
ternal love, have no reference to the principle involved in the now abandoned
controversy. On this point our brethren say: ' While we hold that on these questions
honest differences or opinion may exist, still a mere difference of opinion cannot warrant non·intercoorse as a proper cause of ill feeling between Grand Bodies.'
In -view of the fact that our Washington brethren were of onr household in days
gone by ; that their Grand Lodge was formed oat of members of our family • that
they have borne, with their Oregon brethren, the burdens and fatigues of establishing
:Masonlo Lodges in early days, as well as in pursuing the industries of a perilous
pioneer life in this new land ; that oar respective Grand Bodies were, for a pleaaant
period, band in hand, and heart with heart, laboring in the Masonic field, scattering
goodly seed, reaping and distributing the fruits of oar beneficent work among· the
husbandmen and those d~peodiog npoo tbem, until, we regret to say, a heavy cloud
arose oat of a spirit of contention, and obscured the light from those avenues in which
we were wont to meet, causing a separation-the one party turning to the right, the
other to the left; that this dark spectre remained in oar horizon as a signal of dis·
pleasure for a long, too long a season; that now it is dispelled by the aid of the great
light in Masonry, and the eon of other days has once more shed its bright and mellow
ray~ upon our walks; that these Masonic treasures now in our keeping were left
with us for our own improvement in moral science, and advancement in all things
beneficial to our race, requiring always unaffected charity, without which our efforts
avail nothing, by those who have gone before ns, some onto an advanced natural life,
and others far beyond ; that we should receive them in trust daring our day of Ma·
sonic nsefulness, and band them over nnimpaired to those who shall succeed to onr
places at our departure from the scene of Masonic labor; that onr lives are too short
to bear an angry spirit that stirreth up strife, or take delight in unprofitable conten·
tlon ; 'that there is room for all in Solomon's Porch.' In view of all these things,
we repeat, we cannot bnt exclaim, with oar Washington brethren, • Let as hasten to
· the realization of the Masonic and religious assurance, ' how sweet and how pleasant
It is for brethren to dwell together in unity.'

That the Petitioner was regnlarly initiated into that Lodge on the first day of

The Address of the Grand Master fills fourteen pages of the proceedings. After
noticing the fact that his Grand Lodge had already been recognized by twenty-two
Grand Lodges, he says : These Grand Bodies represent nearly half a million of Freemasons, amongst whom
are a host of illnstrions brethren whose well-deserved fame extends over both hemispheres.
These and other no less eminent brethren (whose Grand Lodges also will soon
recognize ns) have, in their heroic advocacy of the cause of Quebec, from their rich
and varied stores of learning, poured a flood of light on the history, traditions, customs,
laws, and constitutions of our Fraternity anent the regular formation and rights of
Grand Lodges.
The great care bestowed by these brethren upon the consideration of the questions
at issue, the patient painstaking to ascertain all the facts of the case, the prompt
recognition by some Grand Lodges, the delaying of final action for a time and for
various reasons, on the part of others, and the manifest determination on the part of
all, to arrive at, and abide by, a just decision, have been most honorable to them as
well as most 11ratifying tons, and have given to their deciRions in onr favor, a Masonic
and moral weight and force which can neither be gainsaid nor resisted.
In reference to the Grand Lodge of Canada, he remarks:Although compassion dictates the exercise of the virt.ue of silence anent the doings
for the past year of the Grand Lodge of "Canada," yet candor compels me to say
that most of the evils which have afflicted the Cran in these two Provmces during the
past twenty-two months have been almost wholly dne to her nnfraternal course.

afford magnanimously to practice charity which sutfereth long; and to trnst in the
Great Architect of the Universe so to order his good providences that the day might
not soon, if ever dawn, on which forbearance on our part would cease to -be a virtne.

ing this Grand Body, duty to the numerous Grand Lodges which have already recognized us,-and the maintenance of the doctrine of exclusive Grand Lodge jur1sdic?on

sacred meetings of the brotherhood. Around many a hearthstone there hangs to-day,

As to-day we meet to renew the associations of former years, let us realize more
than ever the nature and binding force of those. ties which link us together as a band
of brothers/ossessing in common joys and sorrows, hopes and fears, pleasures and
pains. An amid the strife and turmoil of life, and the manifold infirmities of our
being, who does not need and feel the want of the fraternal sympathy which blesses
him who gives as well as him who receives-of that fraternal voice which speaks
words of comfort to the sad and sorrowing, and of that fraternal hand which gently
leads the wearyl'ilgrim safely through the dangers of life's rugged path to the refreshment and rest o the Upper Sanctuary. H these sacred ties are pronlptly and practi·
oally recognized by the Fraternity, the unity and usefulness of our beloved Institution
will be established, and her name and fame perpetuated to the end of time.

others had been denied, chiefly for informality.
He recommended the recognition of the Grand Lodge of Quebec, and the Grand
Lodge concurred.
Among the decisions of the Grand Master we note the following as being correct,
and worthy of all acceptation :6. Candidates for the degrees of Masonry must be able to read and write, and
sign the petition in their own handwriting.
7. That charges against a brother do not, before trial, render him ineligible to
office or suspend him from office, he being entitled to the presumption of innocence
till the charges be proved.
8. That an abuse of the right of ballot for candidates by a brother is a disci·
plinable offence ; and if a brother waive his privilegn of secresy, and avow an un·
worthy motive for balloting against a candidate, he is subject to charges.
9. That the obligation of all Masons requires them to abstain from gambling,
profane swearing, intemperance, and evil speaking, and that the habitual practice
or these vices demand of the Lodges prompt discipline.
The Grand Treasurer reports the receipts ot the year at $7 ,609 61, and the expenditures $7,552 44.
Seven pages of the proceedings are taken up with the report of the Committee
on Appeals, upon a case which became very oomplioated in its progress through
the inferior Lodge, but which was only of local interest to that jurisdiction.
The corner-stone of the new .Masonic Temple was laid during this Communication, and in relation thereto we find this noteworthy incident:Bro. J.B. KERSHAW tendered for the use of the M.'. W.". Grand Master, for bis
nse in laying the Corner Stone of the new Masonic Temple, a silver trowel made for
the use of W.'. Bro. the Marquis De LA FAYETTE, and employed by him io laving the
Corner Stone of the Monument erected at Camden to the memory of w,., Bro.
Major General the Baron DE KALB, March 9th, 1825, and bearing an inscription to
that effect; manufactured by our late W.". Bro. A. YoUNG, P. M. Kershaw Lodge,
No. 29, and placed at the disposal of the M.·. W.·. Grand Master through the courtesy
of the widow of a worthy brother, late a member of that Lodge.
The Report on Correspondence is by thl' Grand Secretary, bot instead of the
usual elaborate and Interesting document, which was wont to issue from his grace·
ful pen, we have the merest skim of dry etatistics. The worthy brother gives as
his reason for this the resolution adopted by the previous Grand Lodge " to reduce
the annual expenses of the Grand Lodge." This was Indeed" saving at the spigot."
Let our brethren take care that their new .Masonic Temple do not prove wasteful
"at the bung."

TENNESSEE.
The fifty-seventh Annual Commnnication of the Grand Lodge of Tennessee was
held in Nashville, November 14, 1870, the 21!.-. W.·. JOHN W. PAXTON being Grand
]\faster, and the R.·. W.·. JOHN FRIZZELL, Grand Secretary, with representatives from
284 chartered Lodges, and 20 U. D.
The Address of Grand Master PAXTON is very short, but well written. He pays a
feeling tribute to the memory of several eminent Masons of the jurisdiction, who
had been called away by death during the year, among them the R.·. W.·. Gra.nd
Treasurer, W. H. HORN, and Bro. Lucms J . POLK.
Generally, peace and harmony had preva.iled, and fraternal relations with all other
Grand Lodges had been unbroken.
He he.d granted dispensations for.the formation of eleven new Lodges, and finds
the work of the Grand Master so arduous that he recommends the appointment of
additional Deputy Grand Masters or Inspectors.
He objects decidedly to the practice becoming quite common, of Lodges seeking
for acts of private incorporation, and recommends a.n inquiry into that matter by the
Grand Lodge. We think he is about right. A clashing between the two powers-civil and Masonic-will be almost sure to come at some time.
The Address of the Gra.nd Orator, W. ·. Bro. ANDREW B. MARTIN, was delivered in
public, and is published in the proceedings. It was an eloquent production, a.nd we
regret that we have not room for some extracts therefrom.
The special committee on the subject of "non-affiliation," submitted a most elaborat.e report, reviewing the action of nearly all the jurisdictions therein. The report
was adopted by the Grand Lodge. We have or;Lly space for the concluding sentences
and the resolutions:We hold that \it is the positive duty of every Mason to be affiliated; that when
a brother takes a'dimit and remains non-affiliated he materially errs; bat he is still
our brother, and our dnty to him is to win him back by kind words and loving looks,
not to drive him again from the family circle with threats and blows.
We firmly believe that this gentle treatment will al least succeed better in accomplishing the object than harsher measures. We do not mean to leave non-affiliates
severefy alone, but to hold out inducements to tttem to return to their Lodges, and
make these Lodges so agreeable to them as to induce them to remain there.
With this view, then, we first "Propose the abolition of all affiliation fees; let
there be no impediment in the way of the return to the Lodge.
Let every brother Mason treat every other with the same consideration and attention, and so act toward the non-affiliate as to make him sensible that he is a member
of a great Brotherhood, and feeling this every day of his life, he will soon come to a
natural sense of the shame of his own position, and manly self-respect will bring him
to apply for reception.
But many will urge that they have applied for affiliation and been rejected.
This is easily remedied. Let the Secretary be instructed to issue such brothers a
certificate of rejection. This•wm show at le11st honest intention on his part, and the
fact that snch a dem11nd will be issned by the Lodge, will render its members more
cautions in the use of the black-ball for frivolous objections.
And when the brother is in the Lodge, keep him in by kindness, excite his Interest in Masonry ; if he is a rich man, do not trouble him by the presentation of every
case of charity to him, and thns bore, annoy him, and make him dissatisfied ; if ho
is a poor man, do not hurt his feelln~s by asking him to contribute ; and if he is very
P.oor, excuse him from Lodge dues; If he is a peculiar man, bear with bis weaknesses;
If he is an ambitious man, satisfy his ambition-it is easily done.
Never let the non-affiliate feel that he is beyond the pale of Brotherhood, bot
rather be extra courteous, and yon will win him back. Here is the grand talisman
of Freemasonry-.J ustice is its security.
We therefore recommend tbe rejection 'of the resolution referred tons, and sub·
stitote the following :-

"1. ResolTJed, That non-affiliation does not deprive a brother of his individual
rights as a Mason, bot only of such additional rights as are acquired by Lodge
membership.
"2. Resolved, That the M. W. Grand Lodge of Tennessee hereby again recommends the abolition of all fees for affiliation in the Lodges of its jurisdiction.
• 3. Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of Tennessee considers it to lie .the duty of
every Mason residing within its jurisdiction to be a member of a Lodge and frater·
nally urges all non-affiliates to attach themselves to some Lodge without delay.
"4. Resolved, That should a brother apply for affiliation to any Lodge of the jurisdiction, and be rejected, he be entitle!! to receive a certificate of the fact from the
Lodge so rejecting him."
The receipts of the year were S13,361, and the expenditures Sl2,180 70.
The Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence, as with us, was constituted a standing
committee, and authorized to take cognizance of matters during tbe recess of the
Grand Lodge.
Quite a number of Representatives from other Grand Lodges presented themselves and were appropriately received. Onr own is represented by W.·. Bro. TOWN·
SRND A. THmus, who will be recollected by many of your members who in years
past were accustomed to meet with him in the Communications of this jurisdiction.
The Report of the Committee on Correspondence was submitted by Bro. GEORGE
S. BLACKIE, and is an elaborate, well written review of the proceedings of nearly
ah the Grand Lodges. We willingly give place to, while we heartily endorse, the
sentiments of this, one of the opening pare.graphs of the report:At home we find that the Craft was never in a more flourishing condition than at
the present moment ; at least this is so as regards numbers, seeing that in almost
every jurisdiction a large increase of members is reported. If numbers give strength,
ihe institution never rested upon so sore and firm a footing. But we unite with those
of an enlightened culture who rather fear these numbers ; wbo dread lest a strength
in numbers only is bot a fallacious strength, that it is an element of weakness rather
• than strength; for with the numbers comes a proportionate amount of ignorance
and prejudice. Too true it is tbat Masonry is becoming too popnlar,too fashionable,
as we have said before, like church-going. Men of every kind and degree are knocking at the door for admittance , and we sadly fear that the sentinels at the outposts
are not carefnl enough in their inquiries, bot permit many a wolf in sheep's clothing
to enter the fold and to learn Its ways, and then, consciously unworthy, to glory in
the name of Mason. We fear that year after year the requirements for qnalilication
are lowered, that lectures and ceremonies are~ abridged, that moral teachings are
pot olf to a more convenient season, training to a proper understanding of Masonic
principles is neglected, and discipline disregarded, or not even thought of among
the members. If such be the case, woe to Masonry! woe to Masons! for the instiiution has its foundations as sorely undermined as the Temple of Dagon when Samson bowed himsell with its pillars, and the fall will involve all those who rest therein
In fancied security. Watch, then, this enemy. He is in our temple, chained and
blind, perch1mce, but watching his opportunity with one mighty throe to crush him·
self and all his foes. Vigilance, strict vigilance over ourselves and our brothers, is
our only hope, and never was it more necessary.
Our brother's notice of California is very brief, yet complimentary of the documents ema.nating from Gra.nd Master PRATT, Bro. PIXLEY, and our humble self.
The Canada and Quebec matt.er is fully discussed by Bro. B., he inclining decidedly
in favor of the former.

He had granted dispensations for seven new Lodges. Rela.tions with the Grand
Lodges of the American Union were of the most amicable and satisfactory character. Trouble very nearly arose with Kentucky, on account of a complaint made
by a border Lodge, that residents of Tennessee had been made Masons in Kentucky Lodges. But the correspondence that ensued developed the fact that both
Grand Lodges had agreed for yea.rs, to concede each to the other, to receive applications from and ma.ke Masons of the residents of the other State who r0eided nearer
to Lodges in said jurisdiction than in their own, and so the matter was left, and the
practice is to be continµed. Might we not adopt some such rule--l!upposing it to be
reciprocated-in relation to Oregon and Nevada? We see no hBl'Dl therein, and it
would save action on individual applica.tions, which have been grant.ed heretofore.

This amendment to the Grand Lodge Constitution we.a adopted, and it strikes us

petitioning for dispensation shall produce a certifica.te from the Worshipful Masters

correctly.

With such facts as these before them, who ce.11 have e. doubt of the nuiverse.llty
of Freemasonry?
Me.soury is e. live body, not e. dead ce.rce.~s. Its mlsalon Is to propagate knowledge; teach the libero.I a.rte and sciences; to guard with watchful eye the morals of
the people ; to oppose any and ail orgaulzations that would pull down the pillars of
the temple of liberty, and despotically rule the miuds and consciences of the people•
to watch over and protect the best interests of society at large. Therefore it should
and does take the lead in all benevolent enterpriRes, in all educational mevements
for the enlightening of the world, In ail good plans for the bettering of society.
And faithfully adhering to this doctrine, to its three grand tenets of Faith, Hope,
and Charity, and governed by its three great lights, It is bonnd to accomplish the
aim it he.s in view-the nnion of men of all religions creeds, and all shades of poi:tlcal opinion, to work in the canse of Charity, and for tile alleviation of human suffering.

TEXAS.
The thirty-fifth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Texas ~81J held in
Houston, June 12, 1871,-the M.'. W:. CLIJ<TON W. W1NKLEB being Grand Master,
and the R.·.
GEOBGE H. B&INGBUBST, Grand Secretary. Eighty-five Lodges
were represented at the opening, but this number we.s nearly doubled before the

w.·.

close.
The Address of Gtand M&1Jter WL'iKLEB is quite long, but a business-like document. He gives abstracts from the reports made to him by the several District
Deputy Grand Masters-SOme of whom reported rather curious proceeding&, but
characteristic of that border jurisdiction. The Grand Lodge applied the corrective
to prevailing evils with an nnsparing hand, and yet Texas has more than its share of
queer Lodges, and much more queer Masons. We shall allude to some of their
transactions by and by. But here is one good thing that we do not believe that California can match : Bro. DoWELL, who lives in the extreme western border of the
State, writes that he has not been absent from a single meeting of his Lodge fur the
last twehie yea.rs I The ·Grand Master is right in saying that this faithful brother
"looks well to the West."
The Grand Master had granted dispensations for the formation of nine new
Lodges.
The Deputy Grand Master also submitted a report showing faithful work in visiting and inspecting Lodges during the year.
The receipts of the year were $25,087 07, and the expenditures $24, 752 56.
From the reports of committees we should think that some of the Texas brethren
resort to charges and trials in Lodges to secure the collection of ordinary debts. The
Grand Lodge showed its appreciation of such nnmasonic work, by reversing the
action of every subordinate Lodge that had lent itself to that kind of bnsin8811. In
another C&1Je, where two Masons had been engaged in a. most disgra.Ceful and bloody
brawl, the Lodge to which the most guilty brother belonged, acquitted him, a.lthongh
the acts were confessed ; the Grand Lodge reversed its action, expelled the brother,
and &lTested the charter of that Lodge. That will do. There we.s no homooopathy in
that dose, a.nd we hope that other naughty boys will take warning a.nd behave themselves.
Another C&1Je excited a smile as we read about it. A schoolm&1Jter (a M&1Jon) had
punished a. girl in his school severely, whereupon her gna.rdia.n (another M:&1Jon) gave
him a thrashing. The Lodge tried to reconcile the brothers, but in va.in, and so forgave the man who avenged the pupil, when he W&IJ willing to confess that "he W&IJ
sorry if he had done wrong." The ma.tter came up to the Grand Lodge, wh'l.ch dismissed the same, thinking enough had been said and done.

Ever since 1858 the brethren in Virginia have been feeling their way towards the
erection of a grand Masonic Temple. A good lot has been secured, and stock taken
by the Grand Lodge, other Grand and subordinate bodies and individuals, to the
amount of $53,925. Efforts are to be made immediately to raise $100,000 more, and
then the corner-stone will be laid. The contemplated building is to be one hundred
and thirty by one hundred feet, and four stories in height-the firet. and second stories
to be for public use, and the rest for Masonic purposes. The Board of Trustees express the opinion that the stock in this Temple will pay a good dividend. We trust
that, after waiting so long and patiently, the expectations of our Virginia brethren will
be realized.
The Grand Master was requested and authorized to appoint a" Historiographer
of the Grand Lodge," to collect and arrange all materials available to throw light
npon the history of Masonry in Virginia.

A Masonic trial for an otrence of which profanes were witnesses, is not and should
never be a matter to be concealed. If there be am.mg ue a wolf in sheep's clothing,
and to strip him of his disgnise the testimony of a profane be needful, we must have
that testimony. The disguise may never have been cast otr among ns; bot when It
has been thrown aside before profanes, hav~ we not suffered? ~nst the s?ndal continue to be our cross, and the finger of pubhc scorn and opprobrmm be pointed at us
nntil some brother can be witness of a fact which will enable him to confirm the conviction which notoriety in the community has impressed upon us all, before we can
cast the wrong-doerl'rom among us? Not at all. We are nnder the highest obligations to protect the reputation of a brother unjustly assailed, and no man deserves
recognition as a Mason who would not extend the charity of every reasonable doubt;
bot there is a correlative obligation reetln!f upon each and all of us. The world can
only know Masonry by those who profess its principles; and when the man rightfully
commands no confidence from the public, the Mason is rightfully entitled to no fraternal privilege in the Lod~e. If he. be !' f!O?d Mason, and the o.ccasion .or n~deeerved
reproach, he will not sbrmk from 1!1qu1ry, 1f ~e do not court tnal. If, ID his Interest
the testimony of pr.ofanes be obJected t<!, 1~ Cl!-n only be to p~rpetuate the wrong
which his presence ID and Lodge necessarily rnf!icts. If, In the mterest of Masonry,
the testimony be objecte to, it mu~t impress the public with an idea which is false m
fact and most pernicious in result. It is not necessary to produce the witness before
the Lodge. The commission nsnallr. resorted to, sits not as a Lodge. But if the trial
be had in open Lodge, there is no d1mcnlty in taking, upon sumcient notice, the depo·
sltions of witnesses who cannot be present at its sessions; and if exception be
taken to any action of tbe committee before whom such deposition is taken, it can be
considered and determined in the Lodge.
It appears that there are twelve Lodges still owing allegiance to the Grand Lodge
of Virginia, which are situated geographically within the State limits of West Virginia.
These are all in the counties of Berkeley, Jefferson, Greenbrier, and Monroe-conn·
ties where, as our brother says, "the sympathies, avocations, convictions, and feelings of the controlling elements of population are conceded to be adverse, Intensely
adverse, to separation from Virginia." By common consent, in the adjustment of the
difficulties between the two Grand Lodges of Virginia ar.d West Virginia, the alle·
giance of the Lodges in these counties was not changed. In a short time, however,
as Bro. W. thinks, the "accomplished facts of history'' will be recognized, and these
Lodges will surrender their charters and accept new ones from West 'Virginia. Mean·
while, we sincerely coincide with our brother in the hope that friendly relations may
not be disturbed. He says :Until, however, they do so volnntarfly, they arA brethren ofonr household, entitled
to and assured ever of receiving a greeting as brethren tried in a furnace of' trial,
and fonnd always true and trusty, and our daughter Grand Lodge will be the last to
ask us to violate our pledged faith to them. The brethren of these two Grand Lodges
dwell side by side in harmony and peace. Among them no contention exists, bot that
noble contention, or rather emulation, of who can beet work and best agree ; and he
little appreciates the true principles of Masonry who would seek to sow in either
happy honsehold the seeds of discord and strife.

A somewhat novel question having arisen in the Jurisdiction during the year, we
will refer to it with some partlcnlarity. Charges of groee onmasonic and Immoral con·
duct were preferred against the Depnty Grand Master, by Walla Walla Lodge, of
which he was a member. The Lodge, doubting its power to try an officer of the
Grand Lodge, wrote to the Grand Master for advice, who instructed them that the
office of Depnty Grand Master was no immunity for crime, and directing the Lodge to
proceed with the trial. His orders were : "Prefer the charges, take the evidence,
and report yoar findings for my d~cieion." The Committee on Jurisprndeuce decided
that no euoh appeal to the Grand Master was necessary originally, bot hatiiflf] been
made, that gave the Grand Master anthority in the premises, and henceforth the
Lodge conld only act as he directed. The Lodge, npon certain of the charges having
been confessed by the delinqnent, proceeded to au spend hi m ind¢finiLely, and then
anbeeqnently reinstated him. This, the committee are of opinion, they conld not do,
but that the Grand Lodge could alone pass sentence, the Grand Master having submitted
the whole case to its decision. The Grand Lodge diF!Spproved of the action of WaUa
WaUa Lodge in the reinstatement, and declared the offending brother to be indefinitely snspended.

FOREIGN GRAND BODIES.

We have many hundreds of Masons in this jurisdiction who are of foreign birth or descent. Some, probably, were once members or Lodges in Europe, or elsewhere, outside
the bounds of the J.'ederal Union. Such, we feel s!IBored, still take an interest in the
welrare of the Fraternity in their old homes beyond the seas. For their benefit, and
for that of others too who realize the cosmopolitan extent and character of Masonry, we
compile a few items or information touching the growth and prosperity of our beloved
Fraternity lo the old world. Not having the original" proceedings" before us, or the
ability to translate them if we had, we shall avail ourselves of the work of b~other~
SooT, of Louisiana, BLACKIE, of Tennessee, CA.BB, of Kansas, and GouLEY, of M1ssoon,
who have all executed their work in a neat and workmanlike manner, sod to whom
we here rrankly acknowledge our indebtedness. We must very much abbreviate
their extended notices of the transactions of these foreign Bodies.

We pass now from pleasure to sadness. At the installation ceremonies of October
18, the Grand Master referred, in very affectionate and sorrowful lan~age, to the
illness of brother L.\URIE, the Grand SecretR1·y. On the 26th, this distinguished
brother died of congestion of the lungs, at the mature age of seventy--0ne years. He
succeeded his estimable father as Grand Secretary in 1831, and he has ever since
11.lled the office with great credit, U';ltil of la~, w~en bad health an~ olu age made
him a. poor correspondent. But his lllaaomc wntings had made his name a honeehold word througnout the world, and in far diatant lands the news of his death h.1111
been received with genuine sorrow. He was a great antiquarian, and a. man of much
taste and literally ability. His place has been filled by the appointment of brother
AI.Ex. J. STEWART, the able RecOrder of the Chapter General of the Knights Templar.

IRELAND.-Grand Lodge.-At the meeting of the Grand Lodge, held on the Sd
of June, 1869, it:! attention was called to the matter of inserting in the local newepapel'll reporlB of the proceedings of ordinary and refreshment meetings. This was
regarded to be a violation of the strict secrecy with which the Grand Lodge requires
all Masonic business to be treated; therefore a law was p88Bed that the transactions
or proceOOing• which occur in any meeting of the Grand Lodge, or of private Lodge,
or any Masonic committee, or any comment thereon, or referred thereto, shall not be
printed or published without the permission of the Grand Lodge or of the Grand
Master or the Deputy Grand Master.
At the Quarterly Communication, held on the let of July, 1869, the order was
made that, from and after the 24th of June, 1869, Past Masters shall not be entitled
to vote in Grand Lodge, or in any Provincial Grand Lodge, until duly registered as
Past :Masters, and their certificates 88 snch taken out ; and that the Book of Constitutions be altered a.ccordingly.

FRANCE.-The proceeding& of the Grand Orient are given lut. Owing to the impending relations existing between that Body and &11 the American Grand Lodges,
we only copy the &ooexed paragraphs, for which we &re &lso indebted to our Tennessee brother : Our report on the important events which have occurred in this jurisdiction
during the put year is of considerable length, and, while we think the information
it coma.ins is of great interest t.o the Fratemity of Tennessee, and of great importance t.o the future history of the Craft in all parts of the world, yet the objection
has been raised that, as we are not in correspandence with the Grand Orient, our
proceedings should not be burd!Jned with its history. lo deference to the vi-s of
the brethren who take this position, we have struck out several pages which discusa
the following t.opice: The abolition of the office of Grand Master; the persistent adherence t.o the recognition of the spurious Masonic body iu Louisiana ; the citation
of the King and Crown Prince of Prueei& before & Masonic tribunal in &besieged
city t.o answer t.o irrelevant charges; the actiun taken thereon in the French Lodges;
the astounding vagaries of the brethren on April 12, 1871, when the views of a Commune were adopted &s the Masonic programme of peace; the intertwining of the red
flag of anarchy with the banners of Masonry; and the erasure of the name of Gov
from the documents of the Order.
The conclusion t.o whieh the discussion of these t.opiee leads us is, that the Grand
Orient of France, and the Masons of its obedience, are not now, whatever they may
have been, entitled t.o be regarded as members of the same Masonic system to which
we so proudly and gratefully adhere, and that the mere correction of the error int.o
which the Grand Orient fell when it recognized the Louisiana body will not be sufficient t.o place the Grand Orient on that footing which would entitle it t.o our recognition and friendship. We say so with regret, but we say it e&rDeetly: the Frater. nity in the Grand Orient of France are not Masons.
l3ut this remark must not be construed t.o refer to &ll the Masons of France.
There a.re yet in that country tens of thousands of good and true Masons, who have
not" bowed the knee t.o Baal," men who are entitled to all our love, all our respect,
all our recognition. These are the Masons owing &llcgience t.o the Supreme Council
of France, who are in every respect regular, and who &re recognized as such by all
parties who have t&ken the pains t.o inquire into their history and doctrine.

SECTABIAN llcTot.ERANOE.-Bro. GouLEY furnishes us with a translation of the
following docUDlent, which is certainly a curiosity. If Roman Catholics rely upon
llUCh sources for their information in relation to Freemasonry, we do not wonder at,
while we can but pity their ignorance:During the ~t year the Roman Catholic priests have not failed to carry on
their accustomed warfare against the Freemasons, and their mouth-pieces, the

"All honest, rational, Christian, and Catholic people, and the majority are such,

&pron.' All intellect, all virtue, every merit, springs from Freemasonry. Whoever
h•s not clipped his finger in this kettle of sorcery must eke out the miserable life
of a poor. degraded, hounded, plundered dunce in free Italy. The Freemaaons alone
u.re the privileged rulers, treasurers, tax--001lectors, and gormandizers, who live upon
the fat of the land, and now and then a few crumbs are dropped to the rest of
Italian•. You are an ass I No matter; if yon are only a Freema~on, you may become a professor. You have robbed and cut people's throats! No matter again;
you may become a judge, president, or prefect, if you only wear a little apron of the

a finaer."

CONCLUSION.
Our work for'1872 is now ended. We have done what we could. We have spoken
freely, but always kindly. We thank our brothers of other Commit.tees for the
uniformly kind and courteous words they have written of our reports. We hope the
present may meet with a like reception.
As usual, we append our table of statistics. They are necessarily incomplete, a.s
some Grand Secretaries gave no statement whatever of members or work, and we had
to take last year's figures. From our table it will appear that the number of FrOO:
masons in the United States and British Province3 of this continent is 524,412, and
that notwithstanding the lose by deaths, suspensions, etc., there hu.s been an actual
increase of 22, 761 during the year.

anthority of the Supreme Conncil of Charleston? I refrain from entering into details on
this subject, because considerations foreign to Freemasonryseem there to have pla.ved .
a. very considerable part. But I cannot help remarking that the unfortunate cootllct,
...-h now eecupies our attention, would never have had existence if the Grand Orient
of France had not at that time talllm part against the Supreme Council which sat at
New Orleans.
When, In 1868, the decree of the Grand Master renewed the relations broken oft'
since 18.55, sevoral of the Masonic Powers of Europe had aaeady solemnly recognized
the Supreme Council of Louisiana. The Grand Orients of Italy and Helgium had
exchanged with that power guarantees of friendship. The Grand Lodges of Hanonr,
Holland, and Hamburg had already entered into correspondence with it. Nothing
·up to that time had excited the extreme snsceptibilites which a little later began to
manifest themselves. If the conflict could have been for~een, it certainly would have
been avoided. The Grand Orient of France feels for its brethren and allies too strong an
atfection to expose itself, for any trilling cause, to ruptures with them which would be to
it a source of great sorrow. It does not ignore the importance of American Masonry,
and the interest which the Masonic· Powers of Europe have· to continue on friendly
terms with it. To·day, the desire to renew those interrupted relations is stronger
than ever before; but questions of principle are raised, aad the Grand Orient of
France has been compelled to examine and answer them. Questions of interest
must disappear whee questions of principle arise.
Will the Grand Orient, in consequence Of declarations of noa·intercourse, with·
' draw the recitals of the decree of the fifth of November, 1868, which were Intended
to sustain those who proclaim the equality of men without distinctions of nationality ,
race , or color? Will It, in the face of reason and the law of progress, recognize the
doctrine that any Masonic authority h11s or caa have the so~ and p erpetually excln·
slve right to exercise all Masonic power in the State in which it is established? Wlil
it proclaim, as au article of faith, that only one rite can be practiced in each State?
These are the questions to be coaeidared in this debate. I cannot avoid thinking
tbat their det.erminatioo has been settled in advance , and I have a firm hope that the
Masons of America will soon coincide with us in opinion. Above the constitutions
attribnted to the King of Prussia, above the particnlar organization of Grand Lodges,.
there is the rigbt and the real interest of Freemasonry, which must control onr
minds and consciences, ana which, ia the last resort, mnst triumph.
.
I conclnde with the recommendation that the Grand Orient of France express Its
sincere regret to the Masonic Powers which have broken oft' friendly relations with it,
in consequence of the decree of the fifth of November, 1868 ; that it du1Difest the ear·
nest hope that those Powers may reconsider their decisions; but that it declare that
it cannot reconsider or change the conclosione of that decree.

The doctrines of the foregoing report are probably sufficiently hnmanitarian and
progre99lve to suit the notions of the most zealone advocates of progress ; but they
are not Masonic. At least, they are in direct antagonism with the well established
laws of Masonry as understood and universally recognized In the United States and
the Dominion of Canada. If we understand correctly the pretensions of the Grand
Orient of France, as set forth In this report, they arelet, That that Power will not recognize the right of any Masonic Body, under
whatsoever name organized-whether Grand Lodge or Grand Orient-to maintain
and exercise exclusive jurisdiction and control over the first three degrees of M'8onry
within any State or Territory over which it has assumed and eetahlish edits authority:
2d, That a Grand Lodge, within the United States, practicing the York Rite, can
not prohibit the establishment of another Masonic Power within the same territory
which may confer the symbolic degrees according to tbQ Scottisl1 Rite : and
3d, That whenever any Grand Lodge or other Masonic Power adopts regulatlona
not in accord with the philanthropic and progre99ive notions of the Grand Orient of
France, that body has the right to Invade the territory of eoch Grand Lodge and es·
tablish therein subordinate Lodges which shall work according t.o its views.

render tnto my h~nds the charter so unwo~thily. held. In brief, that the Lodge
must properly pomsh the ollenders, or be pomshed itself for the om issiou.
There ban be no doubt about the duty of the Ma.ster to bring snch offenders to
trial. He most see to it that his own household is kept in order. But, where charges
have been preferred against an offending member, the law prescribes what shall
then be done. It directs the election of commissioners to try the case and gives
them full power to hear aod determine as to the guilt or Innocence of the accused.
If they are false to their trostthey should be punished; if they err in judgment, there
is an appellate tribunal with ample authority to revise and correct their determina·
tious. The board of commissioners is an independent body-as Independent as any
court that sits to determine the guilt or innocence of one indicted by a Grand Joryand its members alone a e esponsible for their own acts. It will not do to say that all
the members of the Lodge are guilty-that the Lodge itself ls guilty-of a breach of
irnst, because a board of trial commissioners have rendered a wrong verdict, whether
such verdict was the result of misjudgment or of a wilful disregard of the trust reposed
in them. There was a time when judges controlled the judgment of jurors and
arbitrarily punished such as did not reader such a verdict as pleased the court ; but
that day has fortunately paased away, aod Jurors act opoo their oaths as men, with
no authority to coerce or compel a verdict against, or even in conformity with, their
own convictions. Trial commissioners, in a Masonic court, most act upon their own
convictions io determining from the evidence as to the guilt or Innocence of the
accused, and they alone are responsible for their own action. The Master presides
as judge and declares the law; the commissioners are the sole judges of the facts
proven, and, ordinarily, they are accountable only to their own consciences for the
motives by which they are actuated.
In a clear case, however, like that presented by the Grand Master, when the facts
are admitted and the law is plain, only one verdict could be h.oriully reached, and it
might well be said th~t commissionera who should, in disregard of the duty they
owed to themselves, their Lodges, and the great body of Masons, render a verdict
or acquittal in such a case, were no longer worthy to wear the badge of a Mason.
Charges might properly be preferred against them, for, by their perfidy, they had
shown ihemselvea deserving the severest punishment known to our law. But it is
•lfficult to conceive even of a case where the Lodge shonld he held responsible for
the faithlessne88 of a board of trial commiBSioners, over whose acts it neither can
ner ought to have any control.

Now, as th ~ law stands, your committee do not see how the conclusion of their
predecessors could be avoided. The applicant, ignorant of jurisdictional lines, pre.

receives the petition and refers it to a committee. The committee report that th;
Lodge has no jurisdiction, by reason of the non-residence of the applicant. What is
to be done? His petition cannot be withdrawn, but must be acted on. The petiiioner most be rej.ected, becanse his petition, undesignedly bot falsely, stated his
residence to be within the jurisdiction. He cannot present another petition to the
proper Lodge within the time limited, because, if In the form prescribed, it would be
false. The fault was with the applicant in failing to make proper inquiries as to
jurisdiction, and he must suffer the conseqnenr,es. Yonr committee agree entirely

han1h the consideration it deRerves. They therefore make no recommendation on
the subject.

to take objection. It Is addressed to a particnlarperson-requeeta his attendance at

the then approaching session of the Grand Lodge-tatee, In elfect, though In very modest terms, that strong elforts would be made to defeat the reelection of the writer

·
.&ny member of this Grand Lodge bas the undonbted right to aspire to any office
within Its gin, and to announce to every Mason of the jurisdiction that he is an aspirant, If he so desires to do. Under ordinary circnmetances, the modesty and good
taste of the party who should make such an announcement would not be as consplcnons as some other le88 commendable qualities, and he would stand in about the same
relation to the office sought as GsoRGB FRANCIS TRAIN does to the Presidency. Be
would see it in a vision afar o!r. But it ie qnite another thing when one who has
occnpkld for many years a position like that of Grand Secretary, and desires to be
reelected to the same position. Be has an undoubted right to desire to be reelected,
and to make known his desire to every member of the Grand Lodge, in any proper
f.lrm; and if be learns that strong elforte, or any efforts, are being made, or are to be
made, to defeat hie reelection, be may, without any impropriety, inform his friends,
or those whom he enppoeee to be hie friends, of the fact, and reqnest their attendance-In the reasonable expectation that they will support him and use their influence,
in all proper ways, to lndnce their friends also to enpport him.
Thie circular letter le not an official paper and does not purport to be ; bot is simply a private letter, printed for the convenience of the writer, annonnoing, inferentially, the facts of bis ca~didacy for reelection and of the opposition which would
probably be made to him, and requesting the attendance in Grand Lodge of the par·
ties to whom it was addressed. No word ie said as to the character or motives or
those in opposition-no reqneet is made, by implication even, that the parties to whom it was addree~ed should nse any nndoe influence or do anything more
than make him properly known to their friends. U this can be called an" electioneering docnment," It le certainly a very mild one.
The 4th subdivision of instructions to the committee directs them to inquire
"whether any officer or this G. L. . may wlthont violating any law insert in
an official paper report or address any matter intended directly to influence an
election!'' This contains an ioeinnation' that the officers of this Grand Lodge hatJe
need their official positions to influence elections, and hatJe Inserted in their addressee,
reports, and official papel"1', addreBBed to the Grand Lodge, matters foreign to the
proper subjects of each addressee, reports, or p11pers, for the pnrpoees of inflnencing
and controlling its elections. It is an insinuation and not a direct charge-as It
should have been if there were any occasion for It-against all the officers of the
Grand Lodge, that they had availed themselves of their official positions to gain a mean
and dishonorable advantage over their opponents by inserting in their addreBBeB,
reports, and official papers, matters foreign to the properenbjects and objects of each
addresses, reports, and papers, solely for the purpose of inflnencing the elections of
this Grand Lodge.
Although thie was bot an insinuation, and not a charge, your committee have taken
upon themselves the labor to make a careful examination of the addres~es,reports, and
oftlcial papers of Grand Officers for the last five years, in order to.dlecover, if possible,
whether there was any gronnd whatever for such au ineinnation; and if so, to report
when and by whom the address, report, or paper was made, and where it might be
found. Although there is n.o law forbidding such a thing, yet It would be so mean
and contemptible for any one holding official position to prostitute it to so base and
dishonorable a purpose, that your committee would have felt amply repaid for the
labor to which they were subjected, by being thereby enabled to expose such meanneBB and dishonesty. Bot, aner the most careful examination, they have been unable

7b th.e .Jl.'. W. ·. Grand Lodge of Oalifomia :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of FGNWICK FIBBER from the
action of Abell Lodge, No. 1'6, in snspeoding him from all the rights and privileges
of Masonry, have had the same under cooelderatloo and report as follows : The first error complained of le, that the commissioners erred In not granting a
continuance, as asked by the accused; bnt it has not been made to appear to your
committee that any injury was done to the aconeed by the refusal of the commiseioners to grant the oontionance.
The second error complained of Is, that the offenses with which the accused was
charged are not violations of any Masonic law. Though the charges are not as spe·
cifically and technically drawn as they should have been, they are sufficient to
apprise the accused of the nature of the offences charged against him. The first charge
is habitual Intemperance and gambling; the second, obtaining money from a brother
by promising payment from a particular source, which promise was violated.
Temperance Is one of our cardinal virtues, " aJd should be ihe constant practice
of every :Mason." " From onr duty to ourselves result all those virtues, the practloe
of which enables ns to discharge the obligations we owe to society, onr family, and
our friends. In neglecting this duty, by abusing the bounties of Providence, by impairing our faculLiee by Irregularity, and by debasing our profession by iotemperaooe,
we violate the moral la.w and are guilty of Masonic crime." Gambling is also

declared to be a Masonic offense In the old charges. The ancient charge on this
subject, at the making of a Freemason, was that " a Mason must be no common
player at the cards, dice, or hazard."
That the second charge contained a Masonic otrense no one can doµbt, for "to be
good and true is the first lesson Wft are taught in :Masonry."
The third error complained of is, that the accused was debarred the privilege of
producing any rebutting iestimony. It is trne that the aroused did not prooiuce any,
but he had the opportnnity to do so, as he was regnlarly summoned to trial, though
he did not attend. He had also the opportunity of being heard before your commii.
tee. The object of your committee being to do even and exact justice, it has been
the Invariable rnle always to hear and consider any additional evidence that may be
adduced before them, either on the part of tbe accuser or the accused.
The fourth error complained of is, that the commissioners elected to try the case
were not all present, and that the board did not consist of the requisite number, as_
ordered by the Lodge. Seven was the number of the commissioners determined
upon and elected for the trial of the charges,-!onr of whom attended at the trial
and concurred in the findings and sentence. The Constitution of the Grand Lodge
does not require the attendance of all the commissioners to constitute a court. If it
did, we fear that there would be very few or the courts under the Constitution legally
held. Its only requirement is that "tbe judgment of a majority of the commissioners
shall be taken as the decision of the whole," and that we have in the present case.
The fifth error complained of Is , that the evidence was insufficient to warrant a
conviction ; bnt your committee find that the answer of the accused filed in the case,
In connection with the oral testimony, was sufficient to sustain the findings of the
oommissiooers; and they see no good reason for interfering with the sentence.

Bro. WILLIAM C. BELOHEB, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following report : 2b tJae M. ·• W. •• Grand Lodge of California :Y onr committee have given careful consideration to the amendment to Bee. '•
Art. IT, Part V, or the Constitution, proposed by Bro. WILLIAK H. HILL, and report
111 follows : ·

566

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 10,

That section now reads: " For non-payment of his dues a member may be suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, in the manner provided in Sec.
9, Art. III, Part III." Bro. HILL proposes to add: "But in case of the death of a
member while thus suspended, it there be no other Masonic otleose established
against him, his Lodge may, in its discretion, bury him with the customary Masonic
honors." As the law now stands, a Mason may be suspended for non-payment of
his does, but he ought not to be ~o suspended unless there is culpable neglect on his
part. If he be, for any good reason, unable to pay his duea, we take it t.hat no Lodge
would suspend him, bot wouJ.I rather remit his dues and give him such encouragement and help as his circumstances might require. The law, in saying that he may
be suspended, implies that he ough~ not to be, unless, being able, he has refused or
culpably neglected to pay. If he has been culpable in this respect, the law ordains
that he may be suspended. In the matter of the suspension the Lodge can and
ought in all cases to exercise Its discretion with great care. It is true that Sec. 9,
Art. III, Part JI[, directs that a member, more than six months in arrears for dues,
shall, after notice, be suspended onleHs cause be shown why he ought not to be ;
bot that does not mean that the party notilied must in all cases himself show the
cause, and that he must personally answer the notification r.nd show that, by reason
of his own sickness, or that of his family, or for some other good reason, he is
unable to pay. Except in large towns, every member of a Lodge knows every other,
and knows his circumstances and condition in life ; and in all cases the Master ought
t<J know, and the Lodge ought to be inform~d. whether the party notified to show
cause should be suspended or not: atrd if Master or Lodge, without knowledge or
inquiry, allows a member to be suspended, the Master and every member of the
J,odge participating in the action are culpable. The fair presumption is that the
Lodge has in all cases exercised its discretion in the first instance with proper caution ; and that, if any member should, through inadvertence, be suspended who
ought not to be, the Lodge would take the earliest opportunity to remedy the wrong
It had snlfered to be done, by remitting the dues or giving time for their payment,
and thus restore the injured party to his standing.
We are aware that au opinion prevails to •ome extent among Masters that when
a member of a Lodge has been once suspended for non-payment of dues, there is bot
!Jne way for his restoration, and that by the payment of all arrearages. But that is
clearly wrong. The Lodge may at any time remit his does, and by that act restore
the standing of the party as elfeotually as he could restore himself by payment.
There can be no doubt that the Lodge can at any time make amends for a wrong or
injustice inadver.tently done.
Your committee think that Lodges should exercise their discntion towards the
living ; and that when they have allowed their members to remain under the ban of
suspension so long as they lived, the time for their discretion has passed. Let them
be more careful how they exercise their discretion towards the living, and there will
be no occasion for it towards the dead.
Your committee recommend that the amendment be not adopted.
All which is respectfully submitted by
WILLIAM: C. BBLCHl!R, }
CHA.RLBS M&RSH,
.
WILLJA.ll A. DA.VIES,
Commiite6.
MORRIS M. ESTEB,

Hasons ont of moneys owing them. The mere fact that a Mason is unable to pay his

Masonic censnre, the case mnst ipvolve a willful and deliberate disregard of moral
and Masonic dnty, and an Intention, knowingly and wilfnlly, to cheat and defraud a
brother." (Gr. Lodge Proc. Vol. VI., p. 360.) The evidence which appears in the

day of Augost, 1871,-the date of their first meetlng,-until the 28th day o( August,
1871, and, at the close of the proceedings on that day, the commissioners adjourned

January, 1872, a new Master and Secretary having been elected and installed, a meeting of the commissioners was held, three only of those who had attended the former
meetings being present, together with one who had not attended the previoos meetings. The Master, Secretary, accuser, and accused were also in attendance, the latter
for the first time. At this meeting no testimony was taken. The accuser stated that
" so far as he was concerned, he was willing to drop the matter where it was ;" but
the commissioners decided that the charges could not be dropped in that way, and
the accuser and accused were then, acoording to the transr,ript, " excused fr6m being
present;" but one of the commissioners, wishing to ask the accuser some questions,
he was brought in and some questions asked him, in the absence of the accused.
The commissioners then dismissed the accuser and proceeded to vote ou the question
of guilt or innocence.
Under Sec. 7, Art. IV, Part VI, of the Constitution, when the commiBBionei's failed
to meet on the 13th of November, pursuant to adjournment, and no forther time was
granted them by order of the Master, the court was, ipso facto, dissolved ; and thos,
the meeting of January 26th, 1872, was entirely without authority, and its proceed·
inga were absolutely null and void.
It was erroneous for the commissioners, after dismissing the accuser and accused
from further attendance, to recall the accuser and examine him in the absence of the
aocosed.

Bro. Jo~ H. MoKUNE, a minority of the committee la.st named,
presented the following report :B W G. L. Califarnia :A. minority of your committee to whom was referred a memorial from JESSE C
Louis BRESSE J E PURDY and others from certain Lodges located at San

REED

Francisco .composing the Masonic Board of relief of Sau Francisco begs leave to
Report that he can not unite with the other members of the committee in recom·
mending the formation of a State Board of relief. The objections to such action
are radical. The memorialists complain that such Board is called upon to relieve the
neceBBitiea of sojonrning Masons from every portion of the Globe to an extent entirely unequal in proportion as compared with other Masonic bodies. Whilst this
may be true to a limited extent it is not proven by any statistics. It is mere matter
of opinion. The Boards of Masonic Relief at Stockton Marysville and Sacramento
have not considered their bodies as a part of this Grand Lodge. They have not re·
ported their action here and we can not make a comparison with them. Neither
can we tell how many sojourning brethren have been relieved by each or any Lodge
not contributing to a Board of Masonic Relief so no comparison can be instituted
between the several Lodges not so contributing and the entire Fraternity at San
Francisco.
I might expreBB the opinion that in proportion to the wealth and membership of
the several Lodges located outside of San Francisco each Lodge has contributed its
proportional share to the relief of sojourning brethren. But as this can not be veril!ed I forbear. Each Lodge and the members the1·eof have severally contributed
according to their means. In many instances this relief has come directly from the
pockets of the Masoos present when the case was reported no record of which
went on the minutes.
A record was kept of the disbursements at San Francisco Sacramento Stockton
and Marysville and this Lodge ought not to assume that Lodges not r eporting here
have been remiss in their Masonic duties.
The question then recurs shall this Grand Lodge tax the Fraternity throughout
this jurisdiction 11 cenain sum to b e collected and disbursed under the auspices of a
committee?

572

Pr~dtilngs of the

[Oct. 10,

It will be recollected that our borders extend from Oregon to Mexico and the
border of i)le State of Nevada to the ocean. Emigration reaches us by steamer
Railroad and other land travel and sojourners are not confined to San Francisco.
In the largest four of our cities we have boards of Relief. Masons acquire a habit
of referring distressed brethren to such Boards. Thus they forget it is more blessed
to give than receive. None of that consciousness of a good action done which is so
sweet to the true Mason can arise from his mere contribution of fifteen cents per
month for e. purpose he never knew what.
Not so with outside Lodges. A Mason is in distress the brethren open their purse
strings and contribute according to their several means. No account is made of it •
no charge to another Lodge for such charities. To compel such brethren to pay ~ .
monthly stipend to be disbursed by others for purposes they know not what for objects they might not approve would be in my jnllgment to do a great wrong.
.Again charity. so far as po~sible should be given by the man who owns the
money. How mnch easier to disburse the money of others than ones own. Thus
State and county officers and the Legislature are proverbially munificent. Give a
central power e. right to levy assessments and they become munificent. Objects of
charity become more numerous and the merits of each case are less carefo1ly scrutinized. ' Masonry instead of being charitable becomes an insurance office against
distress.
This is not its legitimate purpose and if persisted in and such a tax enforced its
injustice will be felt by the brotherhood and the prospects of the Order injured.
I have thus far left out of view the impossibility of framing machinery to disbnrse
properly.
'
The money if raised must be paid out by some central power. If left to every
Lodge to determine in each particular case and it is allowed tll'draw on e. Treasury
it will be easy to Bankrupt such Treasury. Nothing can be a protection except to
allow the giver to judge of the object himself and give to that pat'ticnlar brother.
Thus we avoid centralizing power and keep it where it can never be abused That is
to say in the subordinate Lodges or in such boards of relief as such Lodge con·
senta to belong to.
Again the severe.I Lodges in this jurisdiction do contribute directly to the fonds
of this Grand Lodge and such fonds are distributed to the four Boards of relief.
Last year the sum was$--, this year$--. For e.nght that appears to the con·
trarv this sum is amply sufficient to cover any excess paid by these several Boards
of relief over individual Lodges elsewhere for relief to sojourning Brethren.
I therefore recommend that the matter under discussion be indefinitely postponed.
J. H. McKUNE of the Gommitiee.

The W. -. EnwARD E.W. McKINBTBY, Grand Orator, then addressed
the Grand Lodge as follows : MoST WoRSHll'FUL GRAND MASTER AND
BRETHREN OF THE GR.A.ND LODGE : -

Your labors in this chamber have been seasoned by the generous delight of
renewing your fraternal vows. Hand in hand, eye to eye, and heart to heart, you
have breathed those sentiments of regard and affection, without which your Order
itself wonld be but a mockery and a snare. Nor, in the midst of this interchange of
kindly greeting, have yon forgotten those who are with us in the spirit. and, through
the sympathy engendered of Masonic love, made partakers of this joyous scene.
The expanded vision, therefore, beholds not only those actually present, bu.tall good

Gr(ltl'l,d Lodge of OaUforn~.

and trne Masons within this jurisdiction, gathered in one vast assemblage, while in
tones falling far beyond the feeble words I utter, is repeated the chant of DAVID the
King:Behold how good and how pleasant it le for brethren to dwell together in unity ·
A• the dew of Hermon, tbat deecended upon the mountainl! of Zion ;
For there the Lord commanded the bleeeing, even life for evermore.

'

It is to this unuy that I would speak, for, in default of this, your pretended symbols
have no archetypes, your formularies are but empty words, your very antiqnlty a
gray ruin-picturesque indeed, but furnishing no shelter for the weary and unfit for
any homely use. It is this unity which illumines the interior of the Temple and feeds
the sacred fiame upon the altars of your sanctuary. · It is therefore no part of my
purpose to enter into a dissertation upon the history of Masonry, and, before entering the portal, I shall pause but a single moment to contemplate the grand old tower~ whose venerable exterior excites the reverential awe of every beholder.
Among all nations he. been exhibited a disposition to give credit to au individual
for the creation of polit1 . or legal institutions-really the development of time
and circumstances. Engh, vriters have often assumed that Alfred the Great was
the founder of all useful law
own to the Saxons; and, actuated by e. like feeling
Roman authors have attribi. ~d their corporations of builcl~rH to their typical Jaw:
giver, Numa Pompilius. In truth the origin of the collegia-which, for want of a
better name, we may call corporations-seems lost in the mist of ages; but, what·
ever their origin, it is certain that, during the latter days of the republic and the
more fortunate period of the empire, they contributed powerfully in propagating
the Roman customs, sciences, arts, and laws. '
The societies of architects, which have left throughout Elll'ope such gigantic memo·
rials of medimval art, were directly derived from the Roman coUegia fabrorum, for
the" ancient laws" of the arc_hitects, confirmed by King Athelste.n, A.D. 926, (and
still preserved at York), are said to agree with what is found relating to the coUegia
in the Corpus Juris Romani. Now, as in the societies of architects of the middle
ages, moral training was combined with professional apprenticeship, nothing was more
nature.I than that when, in progress of time, such associations of practical workmen were
abandoned, others ·should be substituted-with objects purely speculative-which
retained the working tools of the builder's art as apt emblems for enforcing the lessons or the masters. Masons claim a still more ancient origin, but, as onr accounts of
the discipline of the workmen on Solomon's Temple are traditionary, this is not the
occasion to do more than refer to them. Indeed, it -is not very material, perhaps,
whether certain of our work is based upon authentic tradition or is the embodiment
of an idea-serving to illustrate the steadfast loyalty of the martyr to principle. In
either case, the inoral is impressively rendered and the fact remains that, at a dis·

might at any time refuse to obey or be gnided by its direction. The Lodge has now,
nnder the laws of the State, all the power reqnisite for the management of its own
concerns ·1 and your committee think that the creation of a corporation within the
Lodge, fo r the managem~ntof any of its funds, would be not only impolitic but of dangerous tendency. They therefore · recommend that the proposition by Bro. HELLER
be disapproved.

Bro. WILLLU1 C. BELcHEB, from a. majority of the Committee on
J urisprndence, presented the following rei}ort :To the M. •• W. •• Grand Lodge of Oal.ifomia :At the last Annual Communication, the C.>mmittee on Jurisprudence was divided
on the qnestion of the legality of the formation, and the recognition by this Grand
Lodge, of the newly formed Grand Lodge of Quebec, and two reports were presented
thereon. No definitive action was taken by the Grand Lodge on those reports. The
majority of that committee arrived at the cooclosioo that the Grand Lodge of Qoebec
was not legally formed and ought not to be recognized, and presented their reasons
at considerable length. Your committee is again divided on the same qnestioo, and for
that reason, as well as by reason of the very grave importance of the questions pre·
sented, the undersigned members of the Committee on Jnrisprudeoce have again given
the whole subject their most careful consideration and have reviewed and re-examined
their report of last year, to correct its statements if anything was there misstated, and
to test again the correctness of the conclnsions then arrived at. The facts are correctly
and folly stated In that report; and a re-examination of the facts and a reconsideration
of the law applicable to them lead them irresistibly to the same conclusions arrived at in
their former report, and leaves them no room to doubt as to the duty of this Grand
Lodge in the premises. It is not a question of policy, but of right. The Grand Lodge of
Canada had, in 1869, and 'for fonrteen years prior thereto, a well-defined territorial
jurisdiction, embracing Upper and Lower Canada. In that year certain Lodges cf
the lower Province threw off their allegiance, declared themselves independent,
formed themselves into a Grand Lodge, and asked os to recognize the body thus formed
as a jnst and legal Grand Lodge; thus to declare to the Masonic world that, whereso·
ever rebellion to regularly constitoted Masonic aothority raises its head, we will join
hands with it, will recognize the right of rebellion, and will foster and encourage the

,

Grand Lodge of OaUfornia.

spirit of rebellion. As long ago as l %5 this Grand f,odge, by its edict of non-inter·
coorse with the Grand J..odge of Hamburg, declared that it would not maintain
friendly relations with any Grand Lodge that sooght to interfere with the jorisdic·
tional rights of any other. In that case, the Grand Lodge of Hamburg songht only to
establish and maintain two or three Lodges subordinate to itself within the territorial
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of New York ; and qnite recently our amicable relations
with the Grand Orient of France were intenopted by a like edict becaose that Grand
Orient recognized and sustained the formation of a so-called Masonic body in the city of
New Orleans, in violation oftl}ejnrisdictiooal rightB of the Grand Lodge ofLooisiana.
It is trne that we did extend recognition to the Grand Lodge of West Virginia, bot
that was done wit.hoot much consideration and nnder peculiar circoIDStances. West
Virginia was erected into a State by the Congress of the United States at a time when
that portion of the State of Virginia wa& loyal to the Government, and when the remain·
ing portion of the State was not only in open and active rebellion, bot was the most active
theatre of war-the place where were massed the armies of the rebellion-when intercourse between the newly formed State and I tB parent State was not only dangerooa
in the extreme, bot was prohibited by positive statotes and the roles of war. At such
a time the Grand Lodge ~f West Virginia was formed, and it is not strange that it was
recognized without at all considering the l'ights of the Grand Lodge of Virginia. Bot
if a case like that of West Virginia were to arise in time of peace, when the voice of
the mother Grand Lodge could be heard, we think that this Grand Lodge shonld hesitate long before it extended recognition to the newly formed Grand Lodge nntil
recognition had been extended by the mother Grand Lodge.
But, whatever might be the decision in such a case, shoold one arise, we need not
ioqoire, for it could form no precedent for a case like that of the Grand Lodge of
Quebec. As stated in oor former report, the political condition and standing of a
State of the United States and of a Province of the Dominion of Canada are entirely
different. On the one hand, the British Parliament is the sopreme head, possessing all
governmental power. It creates the Dominion of Canada as a State snbject to itB
supreme control and direction-divides it into sobdivisions of Provinces, recognizing
and retaining Provincial bonndaries as they have existed for a long time-gives to
the Dominion a Legislatnre and investB it with certain general and special legislative
powers for the whole State-gives also to the Provinces Legislatnres with strictly
limited and defined municipal powers. On the other hand, the Federal Government
is one of limited powel'!l-cooftned strictly to Its grant of aothority-while the States
possess all original governmental power and authority. They are the sources of
power, and retain and can exercise all snch power except in so far as it has been
delegated to the general government by the Federal Coostitntion. A State sobdivide9
it9 territory into municipalities of greater or less territorial extent, and gives to each
such legislative power for monicipal porposes as It may choose ; bot it remains the
source of power and can at pleasure recall the gift or change or modify it. The
State is sovereign; the Province a municipality.
We repeat some part of our argnments in regard to the political sitnation of the
Province of Quebec, not so much because the decision of the case rests upon that, as
because it has been discussed by our brethren of other Grand Lodges of the United
States, and the standing of the Grand Lodge of Quebec made to rest on the political
standing of the Province ; and because, as we think, they have )'rrived at a wrong
cooclosion !\'om a failure to ascertain and consider the facts. They assume that the
Province of Qoebec is an Independent State like one of the States of the United States
-possessing independent and original power-whose territorial limits can be changed
or modified only by its own consent-and upon that assumption assert that it is the
American doctrine and has become the common law of Masonry that, whenever an
independent State is formed, the Lodges within it are at liberty, and possess the absolute right, immediately to throw off their former allegiance, to form an independent

Grand Lodge, and to compel all Masons and Masonic ,Lodges within the territorial
limits of the new State to abandon allot.h er allegiance and tO swear fealty to the new
Grand Lodge. This is practically the rule in the United States, because no Grand
Lodge in the United States institutes Lodges outside the territorial limits of the State
in which it is located, except for temporary purposes , or claims to exercise exclnsive
jurisdiction beyond the territorial limits of its own State.
We base our conclusions upon higher ground-upon the ground of a~solnte right
which we ought not to ignore-that, when a Grand Lodge has establisher. its jnrisdic·
tione.J limits, and has, for a series of years, claimed and exercised jurisdiction withln
those limits, its subordinate Lodges cannot, without its consent, throw off their allegiance and set up for themselves. That is the right of revolution, and we cannot
acknowledge it.

Bro. CHARLES MABBH, from a minority of the same committee, presented the following report :Tu the M.·. W. ·. Gi•and Lodge of CaUfornia :In the matter of the recognition of the Grand Lodge of Qnebec, action upon which
was deferred at the last Annual Communication, the undersigned, of your committee,
after a careful review of the action had by a great majority of the American Grand
Lodges, are more than ever co~viuced of the justice and correctness of the conchisions arrived at in their report made last year, and can find no sufficient reasons for
changing the recommendation presented therein.
The question as to whether Quebec is a sufficiently independent political sovereignty to admit of the formation of a Grand Lodge is most positively answered in the
fact of the formation of the independent Grand Lodges of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, adjoining pro·viDces, having exactly the same political stalus in regard to government as the Provinces of Quebec. and Ontario. The Grand ·Lodge of Canada
claimed and exercised the same right, in its organization in 1855, in the form common
to American Grand Lodges, and by which form the Grand Lodge of Quebec was regularly organized in 1869, only it has been cnstomary, and a practice so universally recognized, for the Grand Lodge holding the original jurisdiction to relinquish the same,
upon the successful maintenance of the new Grand Lodge, that the action of the
Grand Lodge of Canada in this matter is in the highest degree nn~haritable and unjust.
It acquired its own prerogatives and powers by the same mode of pr-0cednre, but has
ungenerously treated the Grand Lodge of Qnebec as a rebel, and endeavored by petty
annoyances to bring discredit upon its organization and prevent it from occupying
the political bonndaries which it is by right entitled to.
Your minority committee, fully believing that the Grand Lodge of Qne bee was properly organized nuder the rule which has prevailed in the orl!janization of American
Grand Lodges, and that the opposition and factiuns interference shown and persisted
ill by the Grand Lodge of Canada is in the highest degree contrary to the spirit of
charity and forbearance which should ever characterize the condnct of Masons; and
believing further that, by joining with more than thirty of the Grand Lodges of our
country who have already extended the hand of fraternal recognition, we may much
more effectually assist in allaying the strife which, on the part of the Grand Lodge of
Canada, is impotent for aught but the promulgation of such edicts as a dethroned
STUART might issue to the people of the British Empire, and a continuation of petty
annoyances which rellect no credit upon Masonry, respectfully ask that the resolution
a.c companying their report, presented at the last Annnal Communication, be adopted.
