To the M. •• W . .: Grand Lodge of Oalifomia :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. Gioa.GE WooD from
the action of Nanal Lodge, No. 87, in acquitting Bro. SAMUEL W. HERRICK of charges
preferred against him, have had the same under consideration and report as follows:Upon the facts, as they appear in the transcript, no other conclusion could have
been arrived at. But the accuser assigns specific errors and grounds of appeal, and
these areFirst.-That the Lodge proceeded contrary to law, in that all the members were
not notified of the trial. The accuser doubtless means that all the commissioners
were not notified. Only one of the commissioners was absent at the trial, and there
is no evidence before your committee that he had no notice of the time and place of
trial. Had he heen present the result would have been the same, as the other !Ix concnned in the finding and signed the record, so that no injnry has been done.
Seoond-That one of the commissioners elected was absent during the trial. In
the case of FENWICK FIBBER, of Abell Lodge, No.1'6, reported on at the prese~t Com·
munication, your committee say : " The Constitution of the Grand Lodge does not
require the attendance of all the commissioners to constitute a court. If it did, we
fear that there would be very few of the courts, under the Constitution, legally held.
Its only requirement is, that ' the judgment of a majority of the commissioners shall
be taken as the decision of the whole,' and that we have in the present case."
Third-That the accuser would object to four of the six who did attend, as jurors in
any court of justice. In the case of WILLIAM MILLING, reported in the 'th Vol. of
the Grand Lodge Proceedings, page 363, your committee say: " It is too late to challenge the commissioners after tht-y have assembled for trial. Were such a rule to be
admitted, there might never be a trial under the present system. b is the duty of the
members of the Lodge who desire an impartial trial to be had, to attend at the special
meeting of the Lodge and see that no biased commissioner is elected; and, should
such an one be chosen, to have him set aside and an impartial one substituted." In
·the record in the present case, there is nothing to show that any objection was made to
any of the commissioners in any stage of the proceedings prior to the rendition of the
verdict; and a party cannot be admitted, after snbmitting his case to the court and
the rendition of an adverse decision, to object to the competency of the court. It is
entirely too late.
•
Fourth-That the accuser has learned, since the trial, that the accused had made
a false statement in his evidence before the commissioners. But there is nothing before
your committee to sustain that point, although any evidence that the accuser might
have adduced would have been heard by the committee.

To th.e JI.'. W.·. Grand Lodge of Oal!fomia :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of J.C. JOHNSON from the action of Palmyra Lodge, No. 151, In suspending him from all the rights and privileges
of Masonry, have had the same under consideration and report the following : The commissioners, at their first meeting, elected a chllirman and, although the
Hast.er was present during the trial and rnled upon the legal questions which arose,
yet, upon the conclnsion of the testimony, he retired, leaving the commissionen to
deliberate upon their finding and sentence. A court thus oonstitnted Is not constitutional, as the fundamental law of the Grand Lodge makes the Master the presiding
officer in all stages of a trial.
The Constitution provides that" any Master Mason in good standing may • • •
appear as oou11Sel." In the present case the Master rnled that one who presented
llimself as snoh could not act as connsel for the accused on account of his being a non.t.fliliated Mason. The mere fact of being non-a11lliated does not always disqual.ify a
brother from acting as counsel, for, though on-alllliated, he may be in good standing;
but here the standing of the party does not appear, and it is therefore to be pre·
aumed that the Master was right in his decision and that he was ruled ont because
he was not in good standing.

7b the M." W. ·. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :Your Committee on Grievanoes deem it necessary to report that, from the appearance of several of the so-called transcripts of records of trials placed in their hands
they strongly s11Spect that the papers sent up to this Grand Lodge, in some of th:
cases, are not transcript.a of the records of the trials, bot are the original records
themselves. The Constitntlon provides that the record of the trial shall be filed for
safe keeping among the archives of the subordinate Lodges, and that a tranacript
~ereof shall be sent to the Grand Secretary in certain cases. It would be singular
1f the Lodges could not understand so plain a provision, and could not distinguish
between an original and a copy, which is what the word transcript signifies· bnt in
order to insure a compliance with the provisions of the Constitution in
fut~e
oases, yonr committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution :.RuolTJed, That the Grand Secretary be, and he is hereby, instructed, npon the
receipt from a subordinate Lodge of what purports to be the transcript of a trial
record, to examine the same, and, if he has reason to snepect that it Is tile original
record itself, to enter immediately into a correspondence with the Lodge npon the
anbject and obtain a compliance with the requirements of the Constitution.

Bro: WILLIAM: H. HILL, from the special committ.ee of Inspectors,
presented the following report :7b th.e H. ·. W. ·• Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :The special committee, consisting of the Grand Lecturer and the Inspecton of the
several Masonic Districts, to whom were referred the report of the Grand Lecturer
and certain portions of the Address of the Grand Master, have given to both careful
consideration and report as follows :First, The only point presented in the Grand Lecturer's report reqnlring special
notice is that in reference to the work of the French Lodge, La ParfaiJ,e Union, No•
17, In this city, in which it Is a well known fact that an entirely dilterent kind of work
is practiced from that which, by the edict of this Grand Lodge, has been imposed
upon all the other Lodges in the jnrisdictlon. Your committee cannot see the propriety of this distinction. If the nearly 200 Lodges working in the English, German.

588

Procedilnge of the

[Oct. 11,

and Italian langnagee are reqnired, nuder penalty, to conform strictly to the established work, why should the one working In the French language be excepted?
Tbere appears to be no sufficient reason therefor, and yonr committee feel it to be
their duty to recommend t.hat the Grand Lodge do now declare, by Its adoption of
tbis report, that there most hereal\er be no exception made as to compliance with
its edict in regard to uniformity of work within this jurisdiction.
Second-The Grand Master recommends that the reports of the Inspectors be pnb·
llshed with the proceedings of the Grand Lodge. While the Inspectors appreoiate his
compliment as to the value of their reports, and while they admit that some good
would be done by such publication, they are nnanimonslyofthe opinion that this year
it would be Inexpedient. The de~ire to keep down the expenses of the Grand Lodge is
one consideration ; another is, that the publication in full of what some of them have
felt it their duty to say of the acts and work of a few of the Lodges, in their respective
districts, might be productive of more harm than good. Another year this consideration may not have so much weight. In almost all cases the delinquent Lodges and
officers promised amendment In the future, and your committee would give them the
opportunity to folfill their promises without the mortification of pnbllc exposure. At
the same time, that a check may be kept npon all, it is recommended that the reporta
of the Inspectors be kept in the hands of the Grand Master for snch fntnre action,
If any, as he may deem to be neceesary.
Third-The suggestions of the Grand Master as to the appointment of one compe·
tent person, at a remunerative salary, to perform the dnties of inspection and lnstrnc·
tion throughout the State, Is worthy of serious consideration, and it is hoped that the
fraternity will give to it its foll weight. But it)s not thought by your committee that
it would be beet to recommend its adoption at this Communication. They think that
the present system should have a further trial, and that, at lewit for one or two years,
we shonld wait and see what will be the pra<ltical operation of the provision, here·
after to be enforced, that no Master shall be Installed unless he produce a certificate
from the prescribed authority that he Is fully competent to perform the work and
deliver the lectures in the three degrees.
Fburtli.-The well known modesty of the members of your committee, if no other
consideration, leads them to refrain from the endoraement of the recommendation of
the Grand :Master that the expenses of the Inspectors in attendance upon the Grand
Lodge should be paid, and that some definite rank and position should be assigned to
them upon Its floor. Whatever this body shall de~rmine upon either or both of those
points, will be perfectly satisfactory to them, and doubtless also to their successors.
Fifth-Your committee recommend that the third resolution, to be found on page
195 of the Proceedings of 1871, be so modified as to apply to :Masters in this State
only. The reason for excepting the Lodge In Arizona and those in the Sandwich
Islands is obvious, and they therefore recommend such exception.
Sixth-The Inspectors for Districts Nos. 20 and :II are of the opinion that those
districts should be divided and new ones formed. Your committee therefore recom·
mend that the Grand Master be authorized to divide the same, and also to divide any
other district, as he may deem necessary, and to appoint Inspectors and Deputy Grand
Lecturers for such new districts. No addition ,1 expense to the ftaternity would be
incurred, and It is uot seen that there can be any objection to granting this power to
·the Grand Master.
Your committee woold further recommend that five hundred copies of the " :Moni·
torlal Work," published nuder the direction of the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer,
be republished and bound In cloth-the same to be sold by the Grand Secretary to
Lodges and officers of Lodges at the price of twenty-five cents per copy.

To the M.•. W.·. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :Your committee, to whom was referred the petition of JOHN H. BuBNs, expelled by

Progress Lodge, No·. 125, Jone 25, 1866, praying to be restored to all the rights and
privUeges of Masonry, have had the same under consideration and report as follows:ProgrBB8 Lodge being extinct, oo action could be had on au application by the
Lodge which expelled the petitioner, aod your committee are left to act independently.
The offense for which the petitioner was expelled was that of falsely and fraudulently
alleging io a petition, presented by him to ProgrUtJ Lodge, for the degrees of
Masonry, " that he had resided in the State of California more than one year, aod in
the City of Sao Francisco more than six months next preceding his application, and
that he had oot within twelve mouths been rejected by aoy Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons;" whereas, in troth aod io fact, he had resided in the City of Virginia, State
of Nevada, for some time previous to, and within two mouths of, the presentation of
said petition, and had been rejected for the degrees by Escurial Lodge, No. 7, in the
State of Nevada, within three months of the date of his application to Progresa Lodge.
In the petition for restoration it is stated that" the offense as charged was true,
but it was committed through ignorance, not having fully read the ,petition when
signing." The same excuse was offered by the petitioner before your Committee of
Grievances, oo his appeal from the action of Progress Lodge io expelling him, (see
Grand Lodge Proc., Vol. VII, page '13,) bot the committee found that the excuse was
not snstained by the record of the trial ; for, io his aoswer to the charges before the trial
commissioners, the petitioner set forth " that discovering that his legal residence was
Ban Francisco aud that therefore the reception of bis petition by the Lodge in Nevada was improper aod illegal, and having been informed that a rejection under such
au illegal reception was a nullity aod left the petitioner just precisely where he was
before he had applied, • • • • • he signed the petition." This was the tech.
nical defense the petitioner made upon his trial, showing that he bad knowingly and
wilfully signed the petition; aod your committee are of the opinion that any one who
could be guilty of such falsehood and deception, in order surreptitiously to obtain
admission to the Order, is altogether unworthy to be a Hasoo. Your committee
therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution :-

Tu the M. •• W. ·• Grand Lod,ge of Oal.ifornia :Your committee have considered the suggestions of the Gra.nd Master upon the

rule would have been so stated as to include the case under collllideration. I could
not see any rational distinction between the two cases which should make the
voucher good in the one case and not in the other, and my decision was pronounced
accordingly.
' A misapprehension seems to have prevailed to a considerable extent as to the status
of colored Masons and their right to visit. The question hae been several times
presented to me, and, as it is likely to occur more frequently hereafter until the matter
is fully understood, I think it advisable once for all to have it settled in this jurisdiction. I have invariably answered that the color of the skin is a consideration to be
eiitirely disregarded. It is surprising that, with the general intelligence of the Fra-

1873.J

Grand Lodge nf OaUfornia.

25

ternity in this State, there should be any occasion to reiterate the fundament&l doctrine that Masonry recognizes no such distinction. It is simply a question of regularity and standing, and whether the skin be. black, red, or yellow, the applicant to
visit is to be tried by those tests, and those only, which are applied to his white
brethren. In one case the Master ot' a Lodge informed me that one of his subordinate officers, whom he highly esteemed, had declared that he could not sit in the
Lodge with a black man, and that if the visitc.r was admi~ he himself must retire.
To this I replied that, although it was the duty of a Master to preserve, if possible, the harmony of his own Lodge, yet he also owed a Masonic duty to members
of other Lodges than his own; that they had some rights entitled to recognition, and
that he did not owe to the members of his own Lodge any such special duty as called
upon him to regard an absurd or unmasonic objection to a visitor; and that, if I
were Master, and a member of my Lodge based his objection on the sole ground of the
color of the visitor, I should disregard such objection and let the over-sensitive and
offended member retire if he chose to do so. If, however, a member should object
"without assigning any reason, that would present another question, upon which I expressed my opinions one year ago, and they need not be here repeated. A colored Mason sat in this Grand Lodge from day to day at its last Communication, and I have
yet to learn that any body's manhood has been seriously impaired thereby. I have
but little patience with that Masonry which adopts any other tests than those of regularity, character, manhood, and intelligence, and it is time that there was an end of
this child's babble about colored Masons.
·
I cannot ref~ from again expressing to you the pain and humiliation I have
more than once experienced !'t the want of attendance on Masonic funerals. From
this Temple I have seen the dead borne away to their last resting place with scarce
enough of followers to lift the body from the hearse and lower it into the grave.
Thie is not Masonic burial. The very term implies something more. The pauper
from the almshouse and the felon from the sca:ffold ar<3 attended more respectfully
than this. Let us remember that it is the last service which we shall ever be called upon
or permitted to render to the departed, and let no trifiing considerations of business
or convenience interrupt the performance of this duty. If brethren cannot be
awakened to a proper discharge of these rites by their own consciousness of right
and wrong and the admonitions which have been given them already from this
Body, it only remain& for Masters to enforce their attendance by imperative summons-for our dead must be respectfully and decently entombed.
The correspondence of my office has again fallen off--0nly one hundre4 and forty.
six official letters having beeu required of me during the year. This is doubtless
attributable to Masters becoming more thoroughly acquainted with the law, and
needing less advice; and this, in turn, is attributable, in a great degree, to the system of inspection, by which discussion, in.formation, and advice, are brought directly to their doors. While it indicates advancing intelligence and familiarity with
duty, it has been a great relief to the Grand Master.
There have also been much less than the usual number of amendments to bylaws, and the certificates of such amendments have been more generally correct in
the first instance, though many have been sent back for insufficiency.

In one case I was indneed. for the time being, to lay a.side my own sense of propriety and fitness, by permitting a Lodge to take the name of a living man ; and I

former occasion I had absolutely refused a dispensation until the petitioners selected a.nother no.me; but in that ca.ee it was my own name which wa.e proposed to
be used, and I felt entirely free to pursue my-own judgment, a.a no one'!( sensibilities

to select some other name: A number of Lodges in this State have been already
na.meq for living men, but I think the practice an imprudent one, and that it
ought to be discontinued. Until the end of iife there is no certainty what may
be done by the beet of us, and no knowing how soon the deepest odium may

earth, if we have been faithful to the end, it will be soon enough for us to receive
such honors. Borne expression of the sentiment of the Grand Lodge upon this
subject would, perhaps, save my successors in office from embarra.esment, and many
of us, perhaps, from some nnplea.sant reflections hereafter.

One year a.go I called your attention to the expenditures of this Grand B~y, a.nd

be well practiced in some other direct.ion also. In my intercourse with the Fraternity I hear, as I wish to hear, and ought to hear, all their various complaints. There
is still a general feeling that the expenses of the Grand Lodge are too high. I sympathize in that feeling, or rather, I should state the proposition more correctly by
saying that the Grand Lodge disburses too much money. That you all wish to be

some of you· have fallen into two materia.l errors: first, in assuming that all
moneys paid by this Body a.re on account of Grand Lodge expenses ; and second, in

pa.ye or expends one dollar of Grand Lodge f!nnds without your order. The reform,
then, must commence with yourselves. The remedy is in yonr ha.nds, and in yonr
hands only. If, in the haste of your yearly sessions, and without much consider-

I know that there is a venerable theory among certain Ma.sons that Ma.sonic Lodges
ought not to accumulate money; that its care and investment tends to draw attention away from the true purposes of the Order; and that the "true and ancient charity
consists only in individual contributions whenever want and need present themselves.
As a theory, this is as grand and beautiful a.s it is in fa.ct impracticable and
absurd. Whatever may be my practice, no man h(LB a Jceener appreciation of that
which is good and beautiful and true in more.ls, ethics, and religion. But we must
dea.l with the world a.s we find it, and not a.s we might wish it to be; and the age
has become intensely praotica.l and utilitarian. Money, whether rightfully or
wrongfully so, ha.a become the grand lever which moves the universe. Any atte111pt
to ignore its uses in Freema.sonry would be as vain and idle a.s to reject it in the
secular affairs of. life. It is its abuse only that is to be guarded against, and nothing
is more desirable in a Lodge-Grand or subordinate-than a well stored exchequer.
I would make Ma.sonry a.s practica.l a.s is the age in which we live. I would have
you put in practice, day by day, in ell the wa.lks of life, the beautiful lessons and
sublime theories to which you listen with such rapture in the Lodge-room; and poverty
and dependence are not the agencies through which such ends can be accomplished.
I would have you do something for the unfortunate as well a.s give him magnificent aphorisms and words of comfort and encouragement. I wo.;ld not have yon
bid the hungry to be fed and leave him without food. I would not have you tell th.i

Another vacancy in the numbers heretofore ewting upon our registry has
occurred, making thirty-nine in all. On the sixth day of September last, by a resolution adopted unanimously, J>iamond LOdge, No. 29, at Diamond Springs, El
Dorado county, proposed to surrender its charter, stating e.e the reason therefor that
so many of ita members had removed from its jurisdiction that it was no longer
possible properly to carry on its work. Bro. CHA1\LE8 F. IllWIN, e.n old and esteemed
Past Master of the Lodge, was suggested as a proper agent to wind up its affairs, and

for that purpose. There baa not been sufficient time to receive or give any further
information in this case, and the only pa.per concerning it accompanies this report.
The chartered Lodges which have appeared upon our register have borne numbers to two hundred and twenty-two. Of these, thirty-nine have been erased by surrender, forfeiture, or the establishment of new Grand Lodge jurisdictions, leaving
in actua.l existence one hundred and eighty-three. To these a.re to be added one
Lodge, the dispensation to which was continued at the last Annual Communication,
and eight to which dispensations have since been iesued; me.king the whole number
of existing Lodges one hundred and ninety-two.
On the tenth day of June last, the hall of Harnitos Lodge, No. 98, was destroyed
by fire, and with it was lost its furniture, books, jewels, papers, and the charter of
the Lodge. With commendable mal and promptitude the property lost has been
replaced so far a.a was poesible, and the Lodge now presents a petition for the issue
of a duplicate of the charter destroyed.
Of the proposed amendmenta to the by-laws of Lodges which have been received
during the year, the approvals of the Grand Master in the cases .of thirty have been
filed in this office, and information thereof has been given to the Lodges, their action
in all these cases having apparently been in consonance with the law upon that subject. But information in regard to the la.st named fact has, in mlllly inetanoes, been
obtained only after repeated letters from the Grand Master or the undersigned,
which would have been unnecessary had the Bl)cretaries, in the first instance, properly presented the applications for approval. The law requires that llll amendment
shall be proposed at a stated meeting of a LOdge; shall, at a subsequent stated meeting, be adopted by a vote of at lelll!t two-thirds of the members then present; and
shall then be tr11Usmitted to the Grand Mllllter for hie approval. It ie probably true,
that in most, perhaps in all, cases the action of the Lodge he.e been exactly in
accordance with the law; but the Secretary, in many instances, simply sends

information, in brief, that a certain amendment has been adopted, without stating, hi
terms, a.a he should, for the proper information of the Grand Mllllter, that it has
been adopted in the manner which the law prescribes. That fact, then, has to be
ascertained by e.n otherwise unnecessary further correspondence between the Grand
Master or the undersigned and the Secretary; and the subject ie presented here in
the hope that some of the Secretaries will note ~is published suggestion, and thus
spare themselves and one or other of the Grand Officers a needless addition to the
now plentifully sufficient amount of neceese.ry letter writing.
Of the thirty amendments above mentioned, eight, being from Lodges Noe. 45,
99, 138, 206, 207, 217, 219, and Solano, U. D., propose changes in the times of meeting; eight, being from Lodges Noe. 2, 10, 41, 66, 102, 128, 138, and 188, propose to
abolish the fee for affiliation; eight,"being from Lodges NOB. 19, 50, 64, 68, 88, 129,
188, and 198, propose a reduction of the quarterly dues; two, being from Lodges
Nos. lll 11Ud 128, propose an increase of those dues; two, being from Lodges Nos.
191 and 209, propose a reduction of the fees for degrees; one, being from Lodge No.
124, proposes llll increase of those fees; and one, being from Lodge No. 128, proposes
a single ballot for the tbfee degrees. The approval of the Grand Master being but a
temporary authorization, the foregoing amendments, as required by our laws, are
now submitted to the Grlllld Lodge for final action ; as are also the books of by-laws
of the eight Lodges whlch have been established bydiepeneation since the last Annual
Communication.
During the pllllt year, by a Vflry persistent correspondence, the undersigned has
been enabled to complete his collection of the by-laws of all the Lodges, with all
amendments thereto which have been approved to this date ; and a tabular statement
accompanying this report will show for each its day of stated meeting, its fees, respectively, for the three degrees and for affiliation, and the amount of dues per annum required from its members. From this it will be seen that for the affiliation
fee (now proposed to be abolished) seventy-one make no charge; that twenty-six
oharge only one dollar, being the all!-ount heretofore, but no longll!", required by the
Grand Lodge for each affiliation; that twelve charge sums from two to four dollars;
that seventy-one charge five dollars; that nine charge sums from six to fifteen dollars; and that two, possibly with the benevolent wish to turn the current of affiliation to less populous Lodges in this city, have advanced their charge to fifty dollars.
It will also be seen that the fees "he.rged for the three degrees vary from fifty to one
hundred dollars, and that the duee required from members range, with five exceptions of lesser sums, from six to sixteen dolle.rs per annum. An appended note will
also show the eight Lodges which, of all the one hundred and ninety-two now in existence, still adhere to the old custom of requiring a separate ballot for each degree ;

The Grand Lodge did one act of stern justice that will probably admonish others
of the error of their ways should they attempt to imitate the offense committed. A.
certain Lodge found a brother gnilty of a gross Masonic crime, and yet refused to
affix any penalty except a reprimand. The Grand Lodge reversed its action,
expelled the offending brother, and openly censured the Lodge.

The Grand Lodge then assembled pursuant to adjournment-the M.·: W.·. Grand
Master, SJ.HUBL W. W1LLIAHS, presiding, an<l the R.·. W.• . LuKE E. BJ.RBJ;:R being

The Grand Master submitted an able, elaborate, and interesting Address, full of
words of wisdom and good connsel most fitly expressed. " The Mason," he says,
"who has net-the moral courage to condemn and war against vice is the moral poltroon. The Mason who is addicted to and influenced by vice, and lends himself to
prevent discipline, is the traitor and ~PY of the enemy." Plain words those, and the
Grand Master proceeds to give them additional point and force by the following,
which we quote for Masons outside of Arkansas :We find Masons in formal good stan ding in their Lodge, who are grossly intern
perate; who encourage this worst scourge of humanity, by dealing ont death to the
body and damnation to the SOOJ a.t BO much eer glass, who haunt the gambling bells
and moral sinks of our towns and cities. This shonld not be.
It Is sometimes said the brother must follow a certain calling to soppo rt his
family, and that he keeps atdecent, orderly place. And it may all be trne. Bot
cannot his brethren assist in setting him up and sustaining him In some calling that
Is more consistent with the teaching of Masonry, and woold, or shonld be more
agreeable to the feelings of a good Mason?

Gambling is another crying evil of the age. It is not necessary merely to refer to
the card-table, the faro bank, keno, or any other of the gambling devices which are
exhibited to decoy the young and nnwi!'ry; nor do I supp.ose that many M!'sons .are
addicted to this gross and more revoltmg form of gambling. It presents ~tself ID a
more insidious and dangerous form, and even the church is not free from its cursed
taint-the lottery, re.me, prize scheme and gift enterprise. We find these heralded
upon every corner, practiced everywhere. Even good-meaning le.dies at a church
fair will ask ns to take a chance in some re.me for the benefit of the church. Do we
wonder that the infidel, Train, proposes to invent a game of Holy Poker for the nse
of churches? Railroad companies allow young boys to sell, upon thei~ trains, p~ize
candies, and practice other gambling schemes to corrupt the more.ls of this generation.
At bottom, tbis love of gambling is fed by the inordinate love of money prevalent
at this day.

On the preceding 30th of J nly, a Special Commnnication of the Grand Lodge was
held in New Westminster for the purpose of laying the corner stone of the Mortuary
Chapel of the Masonic Cemetery at Salferton.
The ceremonies vlere conducted by the Grand Master, and were in substance
those in use in onr jurisdiction. The corn, however, was in a cornucopia, the wine
in a vase, and the oil in a flask, and the words spoken were : "As I strew corn npon
the stone, the emblem of plenty, so I poor wine on it as the emblem of cheerfulness,
and I anoint it with oil as the emblem of comfort and consolation."
At the Annual Communication, Grand Master POWELL delivered a well written
Address. He congratulated the Fraternity upon the cordial reception of their Grand
Lodge by sister jurisdictions; the only formal ones lacking being the Grand Lodges of
Indiana, England, and Scotland, ·none of which had, however, objected, and their
assent would be forthcoming, doubtless, in good time. He had visited all the Lodges
in the Province except that at. Ce.riboo, the most northern one in the world.

COLORADO.
The twelfth Annual Commnnication of the Grand Lodge of Colorado was held in
Central, September 24, 1872,-the M.·. W.·. HENRY M. TELLER being Grand Master,
and the R.·. W.·. EDWARD C. PARlllELBE, Grand Secretary. Representatives were
present from twelve Lodges.
The Address of Grand Master TELLER is brief, being entirely confined to the
bnsiness of the jurisdiction. He apologizes for not lia.ving discharged more of the
duties appurtenant to the position of Grand Master. He had granted dispensations
for two new Lodges, and referred a third ,application, in relation to which he was in
doubt, to the Grand Lodge, by whom a charter was ordered. It was one of those
cases of concurrent jurisdiction, often embarrassing to decide in a new and sparsely
settled region. It"shows 'that distance from a Lodge is not always an unanswerable
argument for the establishment of a new Lodge. Tue Grand Master cites the case
of an over-zealons brother (FRAZIER) now dead, who traveled regularly fifty miles
to attend the stated Communications of his Lodge, he being an old man, and Colorado
not being blessed with the best of roads or conveyances.
Complaints had been made that in many places the brethren did not manifest that
zeal for Masonry, as exemplified in the attendance upon Lodge meetings, that they
did at first. The Grand Master is of the opinion that the reason therefor is that
there is too much of the mere routine of work in the Lodges and not enough of
attention given to refreshment and sociality. There is something worthy of thought
in this suggestion of the Grand Master, which we submit for the consideration of
the brethren :"The only excuse for this is tbat we have n,o time. All our regulars and frequent
specials are required to confer the-degrees on candidates and attend to business of
the Lodge. But, brethren, it will be better for us to make fewer Ma.Rons and attend
strictly to the duties WE1 owe to each other and the Lodge. We must remember that
we have other duties than making Masons; that we owe something to those who are
already Masons. Let us see to it during the coming Masonic year that we make our
Lodge-rooms attractive to the brethren, both members and visitors. J,et us make it
a home for the brethren-a. place where all Masons will find a hearty welcome. Let
us occasionally throw open the doors of the Lodge-room and have the mothers,
wi!ves, sisters and daughters of Masons meet us in a social way. and thus cement the
ties. of Brotherly Love in a true Masonic way. We shall find the labor of the Lodge
rest more lightly on us, and we shall realize the truth we so often repeat, that
"Masonry conciliates true friendship among those who might otherwise have remained at a perpetual distance."
·
The Grand Lodge receipts for the year were $2694 48, including a balance of
$1418 from the previous year. The expenditures were $765 25.
Resolutions were adopted prohibiting Masonic intercourse with any Masou coming
from either the Grand Lodge of Hamburg or th& Grand Orient of France.
The Report of the Committee on Correspondence was submitted by the Grand
Secretary, and is a very brief and cursory review of the proceedings of forty-four
Grand Lodges, our own for 1871 being one. Our good brother does not do justice
to himself in being thus concise. He writes so well that we would be glad to read
much more from his pen. Be more free, good brother, with both it and the scissors,
hereafter.
There are nineteen Lodges jn the jurisdiction, with a membership of 1079: There
were 95 initiated, 89 passed, and 84 raised during the year.
The Grand Master and Grand Secretary were both reelected.

In Joly the Grand Master attended a double celebration, which was decidedly
unique in character, so far as our knowledge of Masonry is concerned. This was the
laying the corner-stone of a new hall, and the dedwatinn of the hall at the same time.
By way of explanation we are informed that "a space had been left in the north·
east corner of the building for the stone and the appropriate deposits. Physically,
and inasmuch as the corner- stone is now more of a symbol than an actual support of
the bnilding, we can well see how all this might literally be. But, then, what a bnrlesqne npon the very fundamental idea of a " corner-stone upon which the future
superstrncture is to be reared." We wonder what Solomon or Hiram wonld have
thought of the suggestion to lay the corner-stone of the Temple and have the services
of the dedication at the same time I We are aware that Maspnic tradition has some
thing to say about a missing stone, but that, we believe, was the key of the arch
and not the" sure foundation stone of the corner." We cannot bot think, therefore,
that little Delaware has made a new discovery in the way of economizing time and
expense of ceremonies. The nearest approach thereto which ever came under our
observation was at the laying of the corner-stone of an African Methodist Church,
we being merely a looker-on. The sable brethren and sisters went through with all
the D,.ecessary motions, including music, exhortations, &c., and then the corner-i!tone
was r.arefully conveyed to an adjoining building, to remain for several days, nntil the
workmen should get the wall ready for it!
The Grand Master was present at the banquet given to the Grand Master of England in the City of Washington. He had granted a dispensation for the formation of
one new Lodge.

night. He thinks, however, that one Lodge in Delaware could, if permitted, discount
all that had ever before been heard of. A Worshipful Master sent to him this telegram : " Please grant to - - - Lodge dispensation to pass and raise a brother of our
Lodge, a mariner. Answer by telegraph." As no name was mentioned and the
Lodge had forgotten to send the five dollars fee by telegraph, the Grand Master, for
those, as well as other reasons, did not "answer by telegraph." We wonder what
request will next be made of a Grand Mast.er!

anything, the right to be bnried with honor-not a title to be grndgingly fol\owed to
the grave by a corporal's guard of unwilling and mortified brethren, who feel that

casions, when I have seen the evidence of a forgetfulness of our duty in this particular regard, because I have felt that those who had a right to expect the consolation
of respectful attention and sympathy were justly disappointed and grieved ; and that
a reproach might thus be brought upon the Order of not acting up to its principles of
fraternity. Especially have I felt so when I have noticed that the attendance seemed
to be graduated by a consideration of the Masonic and social position of the deceased
brother, in apparent forgetfulness of that fundamental maxim or our Order, that in
Masonry we meet upon the level of our common humanity, and that death detects the
fallacy of pride and does away with the artificial distinctions of a heartless society.
This dereliction of duty has not merely fallen under my own occasional notice.
It ' has been repeatedly brought to my attention by the Masters of Lodges, who are
always expected to attend and officiate, however meagre and discouraging ma1 be
the attendance of the members. Every .member of a Lodge ought to recognize 1t as
a duty to encourage and.support the Master in the performance of this as well as
every other official ministration devolved upon him by his position. The hour when
we may need sympathy and consolation is likely to come to every one of us. How
desolate In such an hour the feeling that no one cares for our sorrow, or is wi\lin' to
take the least pains to lighten our bereavement I Brethren, let it not be cast as a nst
reproach upon ns that we desert our brother when he lies helpless in death, an refuse to his family the solace of our sympathy.

The Grand Master gave another of his excellent Addresses. Those " scissors "
will go throngh what comes from his pen, do what we can to prevent. For instance,
who could resist the temptation to copy such paragraphs as these, which constitute
the opening gems of the address : In entering npon the pleasant task of preparing my usual Address, my mind has
reverted to the first time I attended this Grand Lodge. It was eight years ago. The
dark shadows of war still hung over the land like a pall. Many of our oldest and
strongest Lodges were not represented. Petitions came up for new charters for
Lodges whose halls and furniture had been reduced to ashes, or ravaged by a hostile
soldiery. Jackson Lodge, in whose hall we were assembled, had been but recentll
surrendered to the Lodge by the military government. In the outer world, mens
hearta were sick with despondency and uncertainty of the future. But twenty-four

A few of our venerable brethren, whose names are historic in our annals, still
lingered among ne. Past Grand Master BROWN paid his last v)sit here, and In person
presented, as Ohairman, the report or the Oommittee on Foreign Correspondence ;
his mind still in its vigor, though his frame was bowed with age and jntirmity. It
was the only time I ever saw .him. ~ remember the deep impression made upon me
as he entered and was received with the honors due to his rank and character.
Many of the members were but recently from the camp, or prison , and were still
clad in the rough garb of gray, which association had made HO dear to our eyes.
And In many cases side by side with the ex-soldier in gray was one who wore the
blue; no longer a foeman. but a brother, who had learned the eame sacred lessonR of
Faith, Hope, and Charity that we had been taught, who had united in the same vows
that we had made, and who was with ns to prove that he remembered these lessons
and vows, and to renew hie obligations at the altar of Masonry. What a beautiful
lesson was thus presented to us ; what a delightful exhibition of the Heaven-born
infi11enqes of Freemasonry. How well adapted to all periods of the world's history
to all circumstances of man's career. If those soldiers, then still in arws, could grasp
our hands as brothers, the thousands of Masons whom they represented still acknowl·
edged the tie that bound us; and in spite of the terrible scenes t he country had
passed through, a lasting peace and an entire reconciliation were possible.
There are many who still see nought but gloom and darkness in the future, but I
can trace a steady and constant improvement in our affairs since those days and if
the spirit of Freemasonry had been more prevalent, the whole conntry wonid long
since have been reunited as firmly as our beloved Fraternity. But my purpose is to
corurlder our own progress and advancement, not that of the outside world.
One by one nearly all the old Lodges have been restored-new ones are constantly
springing up, and we now number sixty-five, thirty-four of which were actually represented at the opening of this Grand ·communication; and within this jurisdiction
we have a total of more than twenty-one hundred Master Masons.
God bless our right-thinking brother, and may all Masons, like him, thus extend
the right hand in token of perfect and perpetual friendship. He had granted dispensations for the formation of four new 1.odges, but had nniformly said " No " to all

The respect the world entertains for Freemasonry is founded and mnst depend on the
lift: and condoct of ~ts _disciple_s. Boastful ~n.d. proud claims for great and good

actuated by the same motives and practicing the same rules of condnot. Every link
in this chain is an integral pa.rt or the whole. Tarnish one link and yo1' tarnish the
chain, and fn so far detract f'rom the pleasing effect the beauty of the whole. The
individual brother, then, is responsible In a. <legree, for the general character and in

Every brother, in this sense, is the keeper of his brother. And if we cannot inspire
a failing brother with sufficient self-respect and love and regard for the Institution to
make him avoid evil and shoo those things which a.re calculated to bring dishonor and
reproach on ns, it is onr duty to cot him oft and disown him altogether. If a link lo

be cut ont and cast away, lest the rnst and the canker commnnicate to the rest. and
the whole chain become contaminated and foul.
It is the duty more especially of the inspectors of the chain, the Worshipful Me.sters
of the Lod!Jes, to see to this; but It is no less the duty of each brother to note every
defective hnk, and not only to keep himself at all times ready for inspection, bnt to
report any link he may discover in need of polish. Thns, if all wonld act, the antire
chain will be kept bright and shining, and there will be no point for envy or malice to
attack, and the prosperity and perpetuity of the Institution will be secured.

The Grand Master had iaaued dispensations for the fonnation of sixteen new

We find quite a number of cases of discipline reported, some of which (the
offenses we mean) did not reflect much credit npon the offending brethren. In Illin011, as well as here and elsewhere, the discipline of the Lodge is sought for the
enforcement of mere business contracts and transactions. But the Grand Master
very aptly and truthfully says : " I do not understand that a Masonic Lodge Is the
proJler place to enforce the payment of debts, whetjier lncnrred on account of a
• corner in wheat.' or on account of a failure in a newspaper enterprise, or because
of any other purely business transactions." In another case, a Lodge had pnbllshed
a non-affiliated brother in the Masonic Trowel as "a Masonic impostor.'' The
brother satisfied the Grand Master that he was a member of a Kentucky Lodge in
good standinf and free from reproach. The Lodge was advised of this fact and
urged to rep1ur its error, but it obstinately refused to do anything iu the premises.
Whereupon the Grand Master closed the Lodge and submitted the whole matter to
the Grand Lodge, which endorsed his action, and continued the forfeiture until the
Lodge saw flt to make amends for its uujnstifiable course.
In quite a number of cases where an offending brother had been found guilty of
gross unmasonic conduct, deserving of expulsion, or suspension at the least, the
brethren had only voted a reprimand. Upon appeal to the Grand Master and Grand
Lodge these errors were promptly corrected, and full justice done to the culprits.
The Grand Master had been called npon to give decisions upon points of Masonio
law in "several hundred cases," most of which, he quietly and almost satirically
remarks," could have been determined by referting to the printed oode.'' He publishes only eleven of these decisions, all of local interest, and requiring no further
notice from us.
Upon the topic of" Grand Lodge Sovereignty," the Grand Master comes out
squarely on the "Canada and Quebec" question. He, too, as we have already
remarked was the case with another Grand Master, recommends non-intercoune
with Canada, unless she retreats from her present position and fully acknowledges
the Independent sovereignty of Quebec. Here is what he sayB:The dimculties existing between the two Grand Lodges referred to, are matters
which at this time we cannot consider. They have long since been duly weighed
and ably discussed by a number of Grand Lodges. It is sumcient for us to know
that we have been appealed to by the Grand Lodge of Quebec, to assist her in maintaining that which we have declared her entitled to, and that which we claim for
ourselves, viz: supreme Masonic anthorit1. over a lawfully defined territory. It
appears to me therefore that it will be neither consistent nor prudent, in view of
our oft repeated declarations upon the subject of Grand Lodge sovereignty, to suffer
the appeal of the Grand Lodge of Quebec to p688 without some response. While
we are not without hope that the Grand Lodge of Canada will heed the popular
Masonic voice as manifested by the unmistakable admonitions of a !lumber of her
peers; yet this Grand Lodge would be derelict in its dnty should it fail to lend lta
aid in the maintenance of law and order, by at least joining in these fraternal warnings. It is therefore with sincere regret that I feel called upon to recommend that
in case the Grand Lodge of Canada refuses to wecede from her present position
towards the Grand Lodge of Quebec, the Grand Master be requested to revoke the
commission of the Representative of this Grand Lodge near the Grand Lod~e of
Canada, and that he 'be authorized to proclainl that all Masonic Intercourse and fellowship between the said Grand Lodges cease, and be discontinued until the Grand
Lodge of Canada shall renonuce all Masonic authority over the recognized territory
of the Grand Lodge of Quebec. I would further recommend that no Masons who are
members of Lodges in the province of Quebec, who are working under the authority
of the Grand Lodge of Canada, be recognized In this jurisdiction. In making these
recommendations, I do so after mature deliberation, and a just realization of their
importance; aud with II fnll measure of sadness at the necessity of sundering the
fraternal ties which have existed so long and have been so cordial.

for thirt year, our good brother is so complimentary that modesty almost forbids fnrther allusion. We had asked how it was possible for a Grand Lodge like that of
Illinois, with representatives from five hundred and thirty Lodges actually present,
and casting nearly one thousand votes for the Grand Officers, to transact its business
in three de.ye? Bro. ROBBINS gives us the solution in the following paragraph from
one of his former reports, from which it appears that (as It should be) nearly ail
the business of the Grand Lodge is done by its committees, and that, before the
commei;icement of the Annual Communica.tion .: In Illinois, the committees are all appointed for a long time beforehand, and
each member is notified to appear for duty at a certain day-say four, three, two, or
one-before the meeting of the Grand Lodge, or on the day the Grand Lodge meets,
according to the apparent amount of work to ·be done. The Committees on Appeals
and Grievances, Chartered Lodges, Lodges U. D.. and Mileage and Per Diem, meet
four days beforehand, e.nd in the absence of bustle and confusion, with the ready
and intelligent assistance of the Grand Master, Grand Secretary, and his Deputy,
proceed steadily and surely with their work. The Committee on Appeals resembles
a regular trial court, and every case is thoroughly examined. The Committee on
Lodges U. D. have an enormous work; but after settling principles and rnles of
proceedings, the work is pa.reeled out, and every item of busmess, nsage, or work is
thoroughly overhauled, and when ready to report, the Chairm&n takes Lodge by
Lodge, and makes up a terse , clear, and pointed report and table of statistics. The
work i~ Committee on Chartered Lodges is. immense, bnt no µoi~t !s neglected, e.nd
the entire mileage for every officer, committeeman, and Lodge is m readiness. So
of all other committees. Everything that can be reported on is ready when the
Grand Lodge meets. If all this work were to be carefnlly and safely done during the
sittings of the Grand Lodge, it would take a session of four or five days. By the
system now pursued, the revenue, which is less per member than in any other corresonding Grand Lodge, is suffici,ent to meet expenses, and mileage and per diem, and
eave a surplus, while at least one half of the aggregate time is saved to the persons
attending upon the Grand Lodge.
Jn theory we have almost the same thing in this jurisdiction, where nearly e.ll the
committees a.re standing over for the year, aud are 1upposed to do most of their
work during the recess ; but in practice, we a.re sorry to say, that the lion's aha.re is
eft for the actual sessions of the Grand Lodge, and we find it difficult to close before
the fifth day, and sometimes not even then. In one thing further, too, we have often
thought that our own Grand Lodge could with profit imitate the example of that of
Illinois ; but om good brethren are quite sure that there is a large feline in the meal
tnb every time the proposition is me.de, and so no reform ce.n be effected. · Instead
of sitting like five hundred and odd dummies, to listen to the always tedious cO'Unting
of the votes, twelve tellers are appointed who receive the ballots and canvass them
in a.n ante-room, while the Grand Lodge proceeds meanwhile with its legitimate
.
bnsiness, and thus saves instead of wasting a. day.

MASONIC CALENDAR.
ANCIENT CRAFT MASONS commence their era with the creation of the World
calling it Anno Lucis (A . L.) "in the year of Light."
SCOTCH RITE, same as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish chronology is used, .Anno
Mun.di, (A. M.) ''In the year of the World."

72

Procw:lings of the

[Oct. 14,

RoY AL AROB MASONS date from the year the second temple was commenced by
Zernbbabel, Anno lnventionis (A. Inv.) "in the year of the Discovery."
RoYAL AND SRLEOT MASTERS date from the year in which the temple of Solomon
was completed, Anno .Depoauionis (A. Dep.) "in the year of the Deposit."
KNIGHTS TEMPLAR commence their era with the organization of their Order, Anno
Orainis, (A. 0.) "in the year of the Order."
RULES FOR KABONIO DATES.
1. Ancient Craft.-Add 4.000 to the common time. Thus: 1872 and 4.000=5872.
2. Scotch Rite.-Add 3760 to the common era. Thus: 1872 and 3760=5632.
3. Royal Arch.-Add 530 years to the vulgar year. Thus: 1872 and 530=2402.
4.. Royal and Select Masters.-Add 1000 to the common time. Thu.s : 1872 and
1000=2872.
5. Knights Templar.-From the Christian llra take 1118. Thus : 1118 from 1872
=754..

We have also received, in a very handsomely-bound pamphlet of one hundred
and sixty pages, a detailed report of the· transactions of the Masonic 11,.elief Com-.
mittee, in the reception and disbursements of the charities contributed by the Fraternity at large for the relief of the imlferers by tl\e great fire in Chicago on the 8th
and 9th of October, 1871, when so large and valuable a portion of that beautiful city
WBS laid in BShes. We have perused this report with great interest. It has increased
our love for our noble Fraternity. It furnishes one of those delightful episodes in
life that tell us, that after all poor human nature is not qnite so bad as some of the
gloomy ascetics in religion would maintain. There is, at least occasionally, a silver
and even a golden lining to the dark cloud of selfishness and crime, and long will
thousands, made happier by these contributions of Master Masone "throughout the
world," bless Masonry for what it is and what it does. We point to this one glorious
record of facts as a triumphant answer to all the sneers· and opposition of the " antlSecret Society" mawworms; at least, until they can show a brighter or an equal
record. We would be glad to copy this report, with its accompanying tables entire,
but have not the space, and so must. content ourselves with meagre references here
and there , with perhaps an occasional extract. The pamphlet is entitled "Blessed
Charity," and is thus dedicated: "To the Ancient and Honorable Fraternity of Free .
and Accepted Masons throughout the United States, Canada, and elsewhere, whose
fraternal kindness and spontaneous generosity so g~eatly assuaged the misfortune
and distress of their brethren, as well as the widows and orpllanJl of deceased Masons who were rendered needy by the awful calamity of the ever-memorable 8th and
9th of October, 1871, this report is gratefully and alfectionately submitted." The
details of the work here given, bring to mind the truth of what Shakspeare said:"The quality of mercy ie not strained ;
It droppeth, as the gentle rain from Heaven

Upon the place beneath; it is thrice blessed;

We note one case of discipline worthy of mention: The Master of a certain Lodge

charter of the Lodge therefor.

A Chaplain of a Lodge in one of the country parishes, who was also a clergyman,
declined to use the prayers laid down in the Trestle Board and Monitors in use, as he
could not conscientiously approach the Most High except through the mediation of
the Redeemer and Saviour. Being anxious to give this subject all the consideration
which its importance demanded, I referred the matter to our reverend Grand Chaplain, whose decision of the case met my full approbation and would seem to settle
the question. R.'. W.-. Bro. CARPENTER writes as follows: "I would say to any
brother Chaplain that on page 323 of the ' General Ahlman Rezon,' there is a prayer
whlch can not be objected to by either Jew or Gentile, and I presume that this
prayer would be acceftable to all, while any Christian Minister can offer it fer·
vently from the heart.' T.he prayer referred to is the Lord's Prayer.

brother" mentioned was accustomed to visit. We ask for further information:In answer to a communication from a brother in San Francisco, a member of
a Lodge in this jurisdiction, stating that upon visiting a. regular Lodge in that city he
had there met a man of color, said to have been regularly made in a Lodge under the

A report from the Committee on Jurisprudence .Presents a peculiar case, of which
we will give a synopsis : Oriental Star Lodge, No. 21, at Livermore, wl\s chartered
by the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts in 1811, and had, by prudence, accumulated a
sm~ll fn~d amounting, in 187.0, to $2000. In 1872, certain members of the Lodge
residing m Canton, at s01_ne dIStauce from the Lodge, petitioned for a new Lodge at
Canton, and received the approval of Oriental Lodge. A resolution was then offered
in the old Lodge to donate $1000 of the above fund to the new Lodge, under certain
oonditions, which was adopted by a vote of thirty-nine to ten, many of the petitioners for the new Lodge being present and voting in the affirmative. Protest being
made against such action, the matter came before t he Grand Lodge. The committee
repbrted that the action was invalid, "l. Because members voted upon the question
who had no right to vote on account ·of pecuniary interest in the question. 2. The
proposed appropriation is beyond the power of the Lodge to make, without the con~ent of the Grand Lodge." The report was adopted, and then the Grand Lodge gave
its formal consent to any future action on that snbjeot which Oriental Lodge might
choose to take.
We believe the committee were right in their conclusion. We have, however,
seen so muoh trouble and bickering arise out of the attempted partition of a Lodge's
"reserved fund," that we sometimes wish it were illegal for such a thing to exist
either in a Grand or s ubordinate Lodge.

and not he decided by a snap judgment
For one, we heartily wish that the custom were introduced of nominations in
Grand and subordinate Lodges prior to elections, and of confining the votes to such
nominations. Then brethren would know who ·were the aspirants, and better still,
who were most fit for the offices indicated. And then no brother's name could be
used without his consent, as is often now the case, with the result, frequently, of
placing him in &.n unenviable position, which he would not occupy on any consideration were his own wishes consulted. So far from any Ancient Landmark being violated
by the adoption of the course here suggested, if we are correctly informed, nominations
for some considerable time prior to the election are positively required in the Grand
Lodge of Scotland, if not in that of England. We are somewhat familiar with the
workings of Lodges, Grand and subordinate, in another Order, where nominations are
in order and the votes confined tO such only as do not decline, and are satisfied that
it is a wise provision. Ail to the diecuSBion of the character or fitness of candidates,
either pro or con, our opinion is decidedly against its permission. We believe that
more harm than good would result from the practice, If generally allowed.

The Grand Master dellverjld an excellent address, not particularly marked for its
brevity, for it occupied twenty pages of the proceedings, and a startling array of asterisks informs us that all was not printed that was read. A few· of the opening sentences on" Brotherhood " are so well expressed and trnthful that we venture to clip
a paragraph or two :·
Among the hundreds of faces before me are many I know-faces of those with
whom I have taken sweet counsel-and there are some I do not know ; bu1; by those
means which a Mason understands I do know that you are all Masons, and, being
Masons, I know you are my brothers. We are brothers, not by race or by blood
bnt by spirit-a brotherhood which gratifies our social nature, mitigates onr mentai
distress, ministers to onr physical feebleness, follows us to our silent grave, and then
shelters and cherishes the loved one& we leave behind us.
Brotberhoad involves equality, and notwithstanding official stations, designations
and duties, we meet on the level of brotherhood, to be equal partners in all the
pleasures :ind benefits which Masonry bestows. •
Brotherhood also Involves fatherhood; and to onr Great Master and Father it becomes us to render hnmble and hearty thanks for the blessings of the year that has
passed, and from Him to seek wisdom and guidance and continued favor for the time
that is to come. His all-seeing eye, as well as the eyes of our brethren, have been
upon each one of ns durillg all the year; and while our outward acts have been visible to them, our motives and secret acts have been known only to him. He will
jndge rightly, and it becomes us to judge kindly.
The twelve new Lodges chartered at the last Communication had all been" consecrated and constituted" and dispensations had been issned for the formation of five
.more.
The Grand Master bad personally visited and inspected thirty·two Lodges, and
comments freely upon their work and standing. Here are some roles which he laid
down in·regard to the manner of keeping Lodge records. From what we have seen,
In our official capacity as inspector, we would recommend a like law in our own jurisdiction:·
I have made the following orders or snggestions in regard to the manner of keeping Lodge records.
l. That in addition to a record of work and ordinary business, the book should
show the receipts of each evening, whether fees or dues, and the names of the brothers paying the same, and all snms received by the Secretary during refreshment to
be entered in the proceedings of the next regnlar meeting.
2. That when an account is allowed, the nature of the claim and the amount allowed should be entered.
3. That the reports of the Secretary, Treasurer an.d Finance Committee should be
made in detail, and should show the source of all receipts, the object and amount of
all expenditures, and, when approved, shonld be recorded at length.
4. The fee deposited with a petition shonld be entered in the record, as other
receipts, and paid over to the Treasurer, and in case of rejection.an order should be
immediately drawn for the amount.
5. That the record, when approved, shall be signed by the W. Master.
6.- I have also directed that each Lddge keep an alphabetical list of its rejections,
with the date of each; and that a like list be kept of all rejections by contiguous
Ludges, of which proper notice may be received.
The Grand Master Is opposed· to the undue multiplication or Lodges. They had
now one for about every eight hnndred male inhabitants over twenty-one years of
age, and he thought that at least thirty per cent. of those now in existence were not
required. It was not at all necessary or expedient that every" village or every fonr
corners In the State should have a Lodge." A carefnl and extensive observation had
t&nght him that " very muoh of the bad material found In our Lodges is due to the
fact that :M:~onry Is too much used to snbserve mercenary purposes."

pression. A few modern Grand Lodges, in adopting a regnlation that the 'decision

The proceedings of the fifty·second Annual Commnnication of the Grand Lodge
of Missouri come to us in a handsomely printed pamphlet, or volume rather, of about
three hundred pages, rivaling in bulk and neatne88 of typographical execution our
own issue for 1872. The Communication was held in the city of St. Louis, October
15, 1872-the M.·. W.·. Tnoiu.s E. GARRETT being Grand Master, and the R.·. W.·.

The Addre88 of Grand Master GARRETT is very long, occupying some thirty pages
of solid matter in brevier type. Yet it is a well written and able document, and
contains matter of such interest to the Craft in that large and important jurisdiction
that it will well repay a perusal by Masters and brethren. He opens by congratnla·
tione to the brethren upon the flourishing condition of the Order throughont the jn·
risdictfon. He says : The good yon have done is an anchor of safety. The good yon may yet do is a
beacon of hope. You are fnlly alive to the position you occupy before the world,
and do not shrink from its responsibilities. Yon recognize the fact that the design of
our Order is not only to promote each other's welfare, but to advance the interests
and improve the tone of society at large.
A proper and feeling eulogy is pronounced upon Past Grand Master GEOJ!.GE
WH1Tco11111, who had died during the year. He was Grand Master in 1862, at a time
when the w!J.ole State and our Fraternity were in "the ntmost confusion" on ac·
count of the horrors of the civil war. It needed a sound judgment, a cool head, and
nnflinching firmness, combined with a kindly and friendly demeanor, to guide the
good ship safely through the narrow and sometimes crooked channel, and avoid the
breakers on both sides. These elements were combined in a good degree in Grand
Master WH1TCOM11, and ft was but true to say that under his administration the good
craft came safely to. port, with scarcely a sail torn or a spar injured, and sound in
hull. Would that such Grand Masters conld always be found to preside over the
Craft.
Grand Master GARRl!'I'l' "devotes several pages of his address to some sound, plain
spoken and wholesome advice to those Masons who are wont to carry too much of
their business into Masonry, and unwisely strive to nse its power and machinery for
the mere collection of debts owing by one Mason to another. This has been often
tried in our jurisdiction, bnt has uniformly received the censure of our Committee
on Grievances and the Grand Lodge. It was with pleasure that we pernsed the ex·
cellent and cogent suggestions of the Grand Master of Missouri. These closing
words are all that we have room for at present, bnt they will suffice. We hope that
all good Masons will lay them well to heart and "govern themselves accordingly":Leave collecting debts to .agents, constables, and courts. Let business be strictly
business and Masonry remain purely Masonry, and do not mingle the incongruous el·
ements of the two to make one snbserve the pnrposes of the other. Grant business
accommodation• only at their par valne and dispense Masonic charity freely. Pursne
this straightforward course and the Lodges will be spared au infinitude of trouble in
conducting trials of a character that should never come before them.

and adds: " We cannot refrain from saying that we believe California is entitled ·io

Our worthy brother is rather obtuse. Has he forgotten the well known law

case as in the other. And, then, a• to the equities of the case, we ask if exact justice would-flot more probe:bly be done by seven or nine brethren, charged specially

Texas? We do not claim perfection for our plan, but it is immeasurably superior to
a trial before the Lodge, which, in nine cases ont of ten, is but a broad farce.

those means be employed in commemorating for all time the name and fame of our
greatest national benefactor. In what way, more agreeable to themselves and more
acceptable to their country, conld the Masons of the Union testify their appreciation
of the Government under which they live, than by crowning the century with the
completion of such a work in 1876 ! As yet, Masonry has no memorial more durable
than paper inscribed with the glorious name of Washington. His portrait adorns our
Halls, and we point to him as the grandest illustration of the incorruptibility of our
institution-having no prouder boast than that he was an active Mason and the Master
of a Lodge. Why, then, when the opportunity offers for doing so, and the time more
fitting now than it can ever be again, should we d~lay an act of tardy justice to his
great memory?

other way the Grand Body can do fnU justice. We do not take into account the
question whether he left a widow, or children, or father, brother, or sister. He left
behind him, if he was nnjnstly or unlawfully expelled, the entire Masonic Fraternity
as his brethren, and what injnres his standing at death, injures them. He left to
them also, In that case, the charge of ais reputation, dearer to him, perhaps, than
life itself. " He cannot come to us, bnt we shall go to him;" and how can we say,
in the light of all onr Masonic teachings, still more In the Guu LIGHT ever ftamlng
on onr altars, that we are not" onr brother's keeper," not only in his person, bot In
bis repntation; as well while living, and able to claim and protet•t them himself, as
when death has deprived him of this power.
We notice this decision more particularly because we think it has become quite
a common thing for Lodges and Grand Bodies to consider that, if a Mason dies under
suspension or expulsion, that is the end of the case; and all hta Masonic history and
rights and all the dnties and obligations of our fraternity toward him are bnried with
him in his grave I
We do not so read Masonry, and deem that method a narrow and contracted view
of the liberal and comprehensive principles of onr Fraternity.
•

aot.ion was other than a mere error in judgment-a mistake of the brain, and not
from any coldneBB of the heart of that noble jurisdiction.

Home is not yet bnilt, bot the Trnstees thns annonnce their intention as to the

however it may be erected hereafter, shall never, with onr consent, be built into a
great Masonic poor houee. We intend to prevent the possibility of its association
with every vestige of eleemosynary charity and of indigent protection. So far as

Home where the griefs of a disrupted heart can be lolled into relief-a Home where

school, the field, and the workshop; where they may be morally, mentally, and
physically edncated-a permanent, protecting Home of frngality, propriety, indnstry, and activities, that will in time become self-snstaining and self-enlarging ;-a
Home that will be recognized as the Masons' rightfnl heritage, whenever bnsinese
exigencies, the disasters of fortune. or the hand of God compels them to seek its
shelter:- home that will illustrate the genins of onr Order, the dignity of this
Grand Lodge, the loving brotherhood of onr Frater:nity, and, as a work of Masonic
beneficence, be worthy to rank with the pnblic benefactions of the great and powerful State in which it is located.

from recommending any person for initiation, or serving on any committee, and let

a spectator in its meetings, and entitled to Masonic charities and benefits otherwise,
as when in foll fellowship. Let this continne say three, fonr, or five years (the time
to be fixed by each Grand Lodge). and then if the dues are not paid, expel him. In
the meantime, pay Grand Lodge dues on him until expelled.''

OREGON.
The proceedings of the twenty-second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Oregon come to us in a handsomely printed pamphlet of nearly three hundred
pages. The Communication was held in Salem. June 24, 1872-the M. ·• W. •. WILLiill
D. BABE presiding as Grand Ma!lter, and the R.·. w.·. J.E. HURFORD being Grand
Secretary. Representatives were present from thirty-nine Lodges.
The Address of Grand Master HARE is well written, and has the ring of true metal.
If our brethren of the "Webfoot" State will give heed to and follow his excellent
advice, both he and they will have occasion to feel proud of the grand and noble institution. He opens with a grateful tribute to that good Providence which had so
blessed them during the year. "Enterprise and thrift," he says, "are seen on every
hand, and this, our beautiful State of Oregon, is rapidly advancing in wealth, population, and educational civilization." All of which it gives us great pleasure to learn,
for the prosperity of any one of the Pacific commonwealths is the prosperity of all.
Here, too, are some of the well digested, finely expressed words of tl\e Grand
Master:.ours 1s a grand an~ h~ly alliance; her votaries are not only admonished, but reqwred by solemn obhgat1on, to keep the moral law. What a power for good is this
organization of ours! What a blessing it should be to the world. I maintain that a
Lodge of Masons should not only be a benefit to its members, but to the community
in which the _sam.e !s ~ituated; ~y compelling, if needs b~, by the enforcement of
p~oper Masowc discipline, all of its members to square their lives by the square of
virtue.
And that the brethren in this jurisdiction might be at no wistRke as to what he
understood Ma.sonic virtue and duty to be, the Grand Master, ou assuming the duties
of his office, issued a circular to the subordinate Lodges, the salient points of which
we give below :1 have written this letter in a spirit of fraternal kindness, for I would do good to all,
more especially to the household of the faithful. I desire to call your attention, and
esp~ally the attention of, the sev~ral Mqsters of subordinate Lodges under thia jurisdiction, to one or two prevalent vices which, I am sorry to say, exist to some extent in
most of our subordinate Lodges, which, if tolerated or practiced by our bretheren
must cease and be discontinued. I name them in their order:'
1st. Profane swearing-the taking the name of God in vain. This, you all know
is a Masonic olfense, violative of/our solemn obligations, and is destructive of th~
ground work of Masonry. If any o you are addicted to this ungentlemanly and unmasonic practice, I pray you, if you have any regard for your plighted honor, or the
welfare and honor of Masonry, let such a practice forever cease. Brethren, we cannot
alford, in this s]jort life, to live beneath our privileges or violate our vows; and I hereby
enjoin the duty upon aU Masters of 11Ubordinate Lodges under this iurisdiction, to see
to it that this o.fff!Tl,Se against Masonry shaU cease under this jurisdiction.
2d. lntemperance.-By this I mean the use of intoxicating liquors as a beverage
to an excess. This vice is not only unmasonic, but is degrading to our Order. Let
this, also, cease: This question has been asked of me: What is the pens! code of
Masonry? This question I propose to answer here, so that no one shall plead or pretend ignorance thereof; and thus I answer: That every violation of the Moral Law,
to-wit: profane swearing, drunkenness, idleness, brawling, fighting, cheating, gambling, engaging in any bu8iness that is irreligious or that tends in any way or manner
to corrupt the public or private morals, the violation of the Statutes of the State,
embracing moral turpitnde, are Masonic olfenses, and are forbidden by Masonic law.
Brethren, let us apply ourselves to the wiping out of all blemishes upon our Masonic
character, and make of ourselves lively and polished stones in our Masonic Temple.
"I have reason to believe," adds the Grand Master, "that this letter has been attended with good results. I call your attention to the injunctions therein contained,
and submit to yon the propriety of enforcing the same throughont this jurisdiction."
He had granted dispensations for the formation of fonr new Lodges. The new
Masonic Temple in Portland had been completed, and the Grand Lodge accepted an
invitatioll. to'be present at and condnct the ceremonies of its dedication.
The Grand'Lecturer, Bro. LBMUEL LYON, had died during the year, and the Grand
Master and Grand Lodge paid appropriate tribute to his memory.

Under the head of Alabama, Bro. CHADWICK, quoting one of the decisions of that
Body, says:Ma.sons should not plead the statute of limitations, it strikes us, in any case. Stat·
ntes of this class are never looked upon with favor by the courts. Then why should
Masons avail themselves of them? Statutes of limitations give the privilege to do
that which of moral right ought not to be done. We think nothing should be offered
to excuse a. Mason from paying his jnst dues except poverty.
We concur in all this as a. general proposition, but we can hardly indorse these
few words," in any case." We have known of instances where a worthy, strnggling, industrious brother, with a family dependent upon him, was so tightly held in
the grasp of mercenary and" pound of flesh" demanding Shy locks, that we wonld
have blamed him if he did not plead the statute of limitations, if he could not otherwise release his throat from their iron, unyielding grasp. " Let every tub (or case)
stand upon its own bottom," good brother, and justice and equity will generally be
done, even if law be occasionally pnshed one side an inch or two.
