We find some excellent remarks· and suggestions in a report from the Committee
on Jurisprudence, which we qnote for the benefit of onr own readers. The items of
Masonic history here given are worthy of note :6. Are funeral honors a matter of right, or of courtesy merely! If a matter of
right, what constitntes "good standing," entitling a member to funeral honors?
.Answer. Strictly speaking, no Mason is entitled to it as a matter of right, growing
out of his relation to the Fraternity. It is a matter of courtesy-a free-will offering
to the memory of a deceased worthy brother, whose l<lllS we deplore, whose life we
are not ashamed of, and whose virtues we c0mmend to the world.
"Good standing," in reference to visitation and dimits, technically means free
from Masonic censure, and not under charges ; when need in referenee to burial
honors, it means a worthy member, free from censure.
The old charges and regulations make no reference to Masonic burials, and there
is no aneient law on the subject binding npon Masons of the present day, so that the
whole subject is within the control of the Grand Lodge, with one ancient example
and modern usage for its gnide.
.
Funeral rites, in honor of distinguished persons, and those whose virtues have
commended them to the esteem and affection of the living, have been practiced in all
ages, and in all civilized countries, differing in forms according to the rank of the
individual and the prevailing customs of those offering the tribute. It is the verdict
of the living IlJ.>On the character and merits of the dead.
In conformity to this nsage, as well as to the legend of our Order, distingmshed
Masons, and those of great skill and merit, were doubtless interred with Masonic ceremonies at a very early period in the history of the Order, but such honors were not
common nntil modern times, and have never been indiscriminately bestowed, except
in the United States.
In Continental Europe, it is still practiced in conformity to the symbol of our ancient legend, and only in honor of prominent officers and distinguished persons. In
Germany, it is rarely observed. The practice has been more general in England, and
in countries in whir.h England planted Masonry. In E11gland, no Mason can be
interred with Masonic honors unless it be at his own special request, and then only
by dispensation from the Grand Master, or Provincial Grand Master. And, but for
the geogrophical extent of our jurisdiction, it would be well to confine the privilege
to .the discretion and authority of the Grand Master. But as this is impracticable, we
should have some definite regulation on the subject.
t;everal of our sister jurisdictions, with some of our best Masonic writers, have
declared that suicides (except in particular cases), and others whose atrocity And
manner of death bring discredit on Masonry, should not be interred with Masonic
honors.
The committee believe it would be an ontrage on pnblic sentiment, and a prostitution of Masonic rites, to pay Maaonic respect to the memory of those whose lives have
been an open violation of the cardinal virtues of our Order. Such a practice tends to
cheapen virtue with our own members, and degrades Masonry in the eyes of the
world.
We desire the Grand Lodge to take such action in the premises as that every
Mason who is no.t living in the discharge of his Masonic duties may look forward to
the certainty that, however he may escape the discipline of' the Craft whilst living,
his merits and demerits will be passed on by the Lodge when he dies.
To the worthy Mason, snch a discrimination will "be an incentive to press on to
higher excellenmes, knowing that when he dies the honors and respect paid to the
ancient artificer of the Temple will be awarded to him •
We therefore recomm1md the following rule:It shall be the duty of each subordinate Lodge to bury a deceased worthy member
thereof (if deemed worthy bl the Lodge) with Masonic rites; if requested bJ" the decedent, or by his near relatives after his death; in all other cases, snch Masonic
honors may be granted, or withheld, as the Lodge may deem best.
Our Tennessee brethren take high moral grounds on two important subjects, in
which all who really understand what Masonry is, and what it teaches, will heartily
concur:Resolved, That for a persistent habit of profane swearing, it is recommended that
suspension or expulsion he invariably adopted.
Resolued, That the disreputable occupation of keeping a tippling saloon for the
purpose of retailing a.rdent spirits, is destroying to the character of a Mason, and that
when any Mason is known to be engaged in such bnsiness, and refuses to abandon
the same when requested and admonished by his Lodge or brethren, he should be
suspended or expelled.

TEX.AS.
The thirty-seventh Annual Communication of the Gra.nd Lodge of Texas was held
in the city of Houston, June 4., 1873-the M. •. W. ·• W111. BBAMLETTE presiding as
Grand Master, and the R.·. W. ·. GEORGE H. BB INGBURST being Gra.nd Secretary.
Representatives were present from one hundred and fifty-nine Lodges.
The Address or Granll Master BBAll!LllTTE is of great length, occupying some
twenty-three pages of the proceedings. It is well written and able, and discusses
some questions, to which we shall more particularly allude, with a freedom and point
that is refreshing. The Grand Master has certainly an exalted view of the moral
status of Freemasonry, and he seems determined, so far as lies in his power, to bring
the Fraternity in his jnrisdiction np to the same high level. He meet& with some very
obstinate elements in his crusade for truth and right, bnt he never quails nor
turns aside. We trust that his mantle may have fallen upon a worthy successor.
Proper notice is taken of the death of Past Grand Master E. B. NJCROLB, who died
November 30, 1872. He had granted dispensations for the formation of twenty-two
new Lodges, and had refused applications for eleven more. One of these last was for
" .Bramlette Lodge," at Beardstown. " It involved a principle," remarks the Grand
Master," that I have always opposed-the naming of Lodges for living men. When
a brother is distinguished, both for his knowledge of :Masonic lore and the practice of
our virtues, It might be well thns to honor him; but this honor is too frequently con·
ferred upon brethren at their own request or suggestion, when, perhaps, they do not
merit it. Beally, I think a Mason is unworthy the honor of the name of a Lodge
when thus brought abont by his own intrigues. I have known several instances or
brethren having been thus honored who afterwards conducted themselves to the disgrac\ of their namesakes."
Upon the general principle here announced we concur with the Grand :&laster, and
are sorry indeed that the honor when conferred iii Texas has been sometimes abused.
We are quite sure that our California brethren can not yet say this of " Curtis,"
"Claiborne,'' and" Abell" Lodges, and may the day be far distant when such a re·
preach shall come upon our jurisdiction.
We have this reason and argument given for hisrefneal of a dispensation in a given
case, both of which commend themselves to general approval. We once saw a
comer-stone laid in Cahfornia with two holes in it-one for the Masons to fill and the
other for the Odd Fellows-and if ever there was a botched-up piece of busineBB that
wasit:1 deemed it my duty to refuse dl~peneation to Paris Lodge No. 27, to participate

The Committee on " Grievances and Appeals " submitted several elaborate reports.
As heretofore, we are struck in reading them by these two facts, which are apparent:
first, that in this south western border State, brethren and Lodges are often extremely
blameworthy in their Masonic action, but that, second, the Grand Lodge is reinorse·
lessly severe in its ministration of discipline therefor, thus teaching the Fraternity
that they may not with impunity defy the laws of God and man, which are the laws
of Masonry as well. We would be glad to quote from several of these reports in
proof of this, but our limits will not permit.
A Past Grand Master's jewel was presented to Grand Master BRAMLETTE on his
retiral from office. The Building Committee of the new Masonic Temple reported
that the whole amount thus far expended had been $25,603 57 in currency and
$90,318 72 in coin. The Temple was appropriately dedicated during the Communication. A short but eloquent oration was delivered on the occasion by Past Grand
Master F. B. SEXTON, l'rom which we select the following, which briedy notices the
beginning and progress of Freemasonry in Texas:The ceremonies of th.is day, my brethren, can not fail to bring to our minds a con·
sideration of the history and progress of Freemasonry in Texas. Little less than forty
years ago, five brethren, whose names deserve to be here repeated- ANsoN JoN111s,
JOHN A. WHARTON , ABA BRIGHAM, JAMES A. E. PHELPS, and ALEXANDER RuSSlllLLwhose uam es are on record in our Grand Lodge-names that are historic with the Republic and State of Texas-and which I hope will never fade from the mem9ry of
Texas Masons, inet in a laurel grove in Brazoria county to concert measures to organ·
ize the drat Masonic ·Lod11:e in Texas. They subsequently organized Holland Lodge,
No. 1, which, now meeting in th.is city and in this Temple, is the oldest, the most prosperous, and the most respected Lodge in the State, including among its members distinguished gentlemen, enterprisiug and public spirited citizens, devoted Christians,
worthy , ingenious, and faithful craftsmen, who are constantly engaged in doing good
unto all men-albeit, they may "remember it more eepecially to the household of the
faithful." A little later, on the 20th of December, 1837, the Grand Lodge of Texas
was.formed in the then town of Houston. The five who met in Brazoria, and those
who organized the Grand Lodge , have all been gathered to their fathers; but" their
works do follow them.'' They have labored , but we have" entered into their labors."
The laurel grove in Brazoria has been exchanged for the splendid apartments now
occupied by Holland. Lodge in this building, whlle the Grand Lodge, which formerly
was glad to beg accommodation in the counting rooms of country storekeepers, now
meets in this magnificent Temple, which we have to-day in the name of God, set
apart to purposes for His glory and the good of man. Instead of meeting with members not enough to fill its official stations, unless by borrowing from a subordinate , or
from non-affiliates, it now numbers over 300 Lodges subordinate to ils jurisdiction,
whlle 300 or more brethren representing morally, socially, and intellectually the very
best elements of Texas population, the high and the humble, the distinguished and
obscure, rich and poor, old and yonng, the blacksmith who forges, and the farmer
who drives the plough, the carpenter who shoves the plane, merchants, members of
learned profeBBions-meu of all creeds and all vocations, are eager to receive its instructions, to do its work, enjoy its social pleasures, and wear its high honors. From
the small beginning to whlch I have referred, we have grown, until incense now
arise• from more than 300 Masonic altars in Texas, and more than 10,000 faithful
brethren now minister In the duties of Brotherly Love, Relief, and Truth,
Whatever may be said of Masonry in the past, or whatever may be its future fate ,

UTAH.
The proceedings of the first Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Utah
come to us in a very neatly printed pa.mphlet of over one hundred pages, bearing the
imprint of a Se.It Lake City office. It is the day of small things with this our youngest
sist.er; but who can t.ell what will be seen after the lapse of a score of yea.rs! About
that time in the pa.st California commenced her Grand J,odge existence with but
three subordinate Lodges, the same number that gave birth to that of Utah. And
now we call ourselves o~e of the great ones of the land, having on more than one
oocasion polled over five hundred and fifty votes at elections for Grand Officers. Bo
may it be with the future of this "little one" struggling into being and active life,
amid the at present untoward infiuences of the sinning saints of BBIGRill YoUNa's
t.oppling dynasty.
The Communication waa held at Se.It Lake city, October 7, 8, and 9, and by adjournment, November 12, 1872,-the M.·. W.·. OBED F. STRICKLAND biiing Grand
Ma.at.er, and the R .·. W.·. JOSEPH F. NommAN, Grand Secretary. Representatives
were present from the throe Lodges of the jurisdiction.
The Address of Grand Master BTiucKLAND is brief, but ably written. Here are the ·
opening paragraphs, which, as a beautiful specimen of word-painting, can hardly be
excelled:Sitnated as we are In the valleys and foothills of the moootains, near the River
Jordan and the Dead Bea. surrounded by mountain heights covered with perpetual
snow "The Beautiful Snow," that in shrinking, moist-ered modesty at the face of the
sun, iiiakes verdant twenty thousand cottage homes, shaded by the morning shadows
of the Wasatch; homes of a people who believe in prophets and prophecies, that they
came up into these mountain valleys at the instance and direction of the Almighty;
a people engaged in building a temple as a future dwelling-place of the Lord; a peoJ.>le who believe in and practice many dogmas of the Israelites in their yalmy days;
1t is not unlike the topol!'raphy of the country or the belief and practice o the people
in ancient days, when Masonry , like a" silver lining" to the great black cloud of religious superstition and licentiousness then enveloping the earth, came forth and
formed the first living nucleus of cosmopolitan idea.a, around which new thoughts
could rally with an assurance of protection, until strong enough to go forth among th.e
nations commanding and demanding respect.
Our 'ttrst Great Master, in his wisdom, well knowing that cosmopolitan ideas were
heresy among those who claimed that they were the chosen people of the Lord among ,
all the nations of the earth, devised Masonry, with its secrets and its penalties, as a safe
depository where the seeds of progressive human events might find she~ter, until the
ground was fitted for the sower to go forth and sow broadcast the mllm facts upon
which the foundation of all civilized nations now rest; the existence of one God and
the universal brotberhood'of man.
This is the broad platform of Masonic belief and Masonic practice ; a belief and
practice that go hand In hand; a belief in which the good Mason "thanks God he Is
like "Other men; " a practice in accordance with the dictlltes of the human heart,
when not perverted by the bitterness of partizan creeds, or over-persuaded by the
gaudr. trappings of some aristocratic route to heaven;. a belief in the world as we
find 1t· 11. practice that will, to the best of our ability, put to riithts what we find
awry ·'a belief and practice 1hat has lately culminated in a friendly arbitration betweeil two great nations of their disputP.s and misunderstandings, a result due to
Masonry and Me.sonic teachings more than any other source.
Peace, harmony, and prosperity had a.ttended the Craft during the year. Dispensations hlld been granted for t.wo new Lodges. The Grand Master was absent from
the jurisdiction for some time, during which the Craft was in the care of the Deputy
Grand Master, Bro. T.oUIB CoRN, a worthy namesake of our own genial Past Senior
Grand ·warden in California. Some little ill feeling had been engendered because one
of the.Lodges in Salt Lake City had burled a non-aftiliated Mason with Masonic honors, when the officers 'of the other two older Lodges declined to do so on the wellgrounded belief that the recipient was a suspended Mason, and hence had forfeited
all his rights. The matter was referred to a committee of the Grand Lodge, who
found th e facts to be as stated by the Grand Master, but who came to the conclusion
that the offending Lodge had not intended any violation of Masonic law or usage.
The future was provided for' by the passage of the following resolution :-

VIRGINIA.
The Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Virginia was held in Richmond, December 9, 1872-the M.·. W.·. ROBERT E. WITHEBB presiding ll8 Grand
Master, and the R.·. W,·, JOHN DoVE being Grand !:lecretary. Representatives were
present from one hundred and twenty-four Lodges.
Grand Master WITHERS submitt.ed a well written Address, giving an account of
his work during the year, and containing much good counsel and excellent.advice.
H e had granted eleven dispensations for the formation of new Lodges, and hav.ing
pretty thoroughly visited the Lodges in the jurisdiction, w!IS enabled to say that the
Fraternity was "in a healthy and prosperous condition." The Grand Orient of
France and Grand Lodge of Hamburg receive just scoring for their outrn«eons interference with Masonic affairs in the United States.
The Grand Master publishes twenty-three of his decisions, most of which command our hearty assent. But we are compelled to dissent from some. For instance:
"7. 'llhat public installations of officers is improper." And why, we humbly ask?
We certainly have found no inconveniences or improprieties resulting from the practice in California. Again : " 17. That a Lodge can elect as its Master a MllBon nat at
the times. member thereof." We once heard it argued, and quite ably too, that a
branch of a legislature, if destitute of suitable materials among it.s members, could
elect an out.sider as its presiding officer, but even that struck us as a novel doctrine.
To apply it to a Masonic Lodge appears to us as 11 manifest absurdity. But we will
not argue the question. The Grand Lodge of Virginia seemed to take the same view
of the matter, and, on the report of its able Committee on Jurisprudence, reversed
this decision of the Grand Master.

paid a high tribute to his zeal, ability, and success.

Lodge owns bonds and stocks valued at $45,309.

coincides with our own views on this vexed question that we copy the same entire,
only expressing our pleasure that Old Virginia speaks so plainly and well:From the report of the Committee on Masonic Law and Jurlsprndenoe, which was
approved and ailopted, we cite the following decisions :" Que.,tion. Bro. A. charged with perjury, and having made oath before a negrb
justice of the peace that he would abstain from drink for a certain time. The evidence to substantiate this cha~e was simply the certificate of the negro J.P., which
was ruled out by the Master. Was the ruling right?.
"Answer. It was right, in our opinion.
.
"Q1'elftion. A Mast.er Mason is eharged with violating his oath to the Fraternity
in pledging his word as a Mastor Mason to a negro who claims to be a member of the
negro Lodge in N·-· The only evidence to substantiate this charge was the verbal
and written stat.einents of the negro, which were ruled out by the Worshipful Muter. Was the ruling right, and is negro t.estimony to be taken again't Masons
charged with Masonic offences ?
"AnatDer. We answer the ruling was right, and we give it as our opinion that
negro testimony ought not to be taken in the case mentioned."
If the committee did not mean to hold that negro testimony was inadmissible on
all occasions, we regret that they were not more explicit; and if they did, we regret
it still the more. The spirit of modern legislation has been every where brea.king
down the restrictions aforetime imposed upon the compet.ency of witnesses, and we
believe the ends of justice have been subserved by authorizing even parties to the
controversy to testify in their own behalf-leaving their testimony to be valued as to
its credibility by the Jury or the court. During the exist.ence of slavery, nine-tenths
of the negro population were Rlaves, and the negro was excluded from the witnes~­
box not so much from an1 distrnst of hiK capacity to testify truthfully, as upon his
own account to relieve him from the embarrassment in which he miii:hi be placed
between the commands of conscience and the law, on the one side, and those of an
unprincipled maater upon the other. Similar principles even now deny the wife or
husband capacity to testify for or against each other. Since the abolition of slavery
these reasons no longer exist, and the legal capacity of the negro to testify in all the
civil courts is an established matter of public law; and we believe redounds to the
promotion of justice. We see no good reason why Masonic Lodges should not follow
the civil courts in admitting all testimony which may tend to enlighten the tribunal
upon the matt.er of controversy. The burthen of determining the credibility and
weishing the value of testimony may be increased, but the occasion of complaint for
domal of a fair hearing is removed, and before an intelligent and honest tribunal the
result is much more likely to be just to the parties in interest and satisfactory to the
public. We can not, therefore, recognize any: just principle on which negroes should
be now excluded from testifying other than that which would exclude nll profanes.

The fifteenth A.nnual Communication of the Grand Lodge of the Terrhory of

the R.'. w... THOMAS M. REED being Grand Secretary. Repr086ntatiTilf! were present from fourteen chartered Lodges.
The Grand Master's Address is a well written paper, ma.inly devoted to the e.ft"aire
of the jurisdiction, but still containing remarks on topics of deep interest to all the
Fraternity. ••Death," he remarks, "has been bu1y in our ranks. Our returna will
show an unusual mortality-ibis time, not alone in the rank and file. We have had
this hall draped in mourning, for Death has stricken down so great and so good a
man as our Past Grand Master BK!IJAllIN E. LoMBABD. Eminently virtuous and
chivalric, without fear and without reproach in the discharge of his duty, he was
erer"ready to commend the worthy and reprehend the erring."
The Committee to whom the subject was referred, reported an elaborate and eloquent, but doubtless truthful eulogy to the memory of this departed Mason, in
which the Grand Lodge concurred. Bo, one by one, are the fathers iaken away.
May their sons, by uprightness 'and zeal, make good their place in and about our

Yorn: committee apent several weeks of ~he past year in the city of Dublin,
and desires to state that, as the Representative of Tennessee Masonry in Ireland,
he waa received with the utmost cordiality by all the officers-from the Deputy
Grand .Master, down. He had the pleasure of seeing a great deal of work, ann
had the honor of being specially entertained at their banqueiB by the Irish
Masone. Nothing was left undone that could have made his visit more pleasant
and happy; and everywhere in Ireland, as well as in the other British Islands,
the utmost respect and affection was displayed for American Masone and the
Grand ;Lodge of Tennessee. He aJso attended the annual meeting of the .Masonic
Orphans' School for Girls, and was much delighted with the neatness, order, and
excellence everywhere exhibited, as well as with the superiority of the intellectual
~~ moral training. The school was established in 1792, for the purpose of providing a shelter for the female orphans of deceased Freemasons. It is supported entirely by voluntary contributions, ihe Grand Lodge subscribing £125
per annum, in addition to the collections at Grand Lodge and the fees payable by
Grand Officers. The children a.re fed, lodged, clothed and educated. Their relI!lloua and moral training is most carefully guarded. They are thoroughly instructed
ID all the branches of a sound English education, the rudiments of French, German,
and drawing, and music to such ae evince a natural taste for it. They are taught all
the practical details of household economy, and particular attention is paid to plain
needle-work. The pupils make up their own clothes, and perform the principal
portion of the domestic work of the house. They are trained to habits of order,
neatness, and regularity, so that they may become useful members of society when
they ~eave school; and it is most gratifying to be able to report that many of its former IDmates are now comfortably and respectably settled, and some have shown
their high appreciation of the value of the institution by contributing regularly to its
support. several of the pnpils are sent annually to the Continent, where they obtain
~tuatione ~ school8 as English teachers, and ar.e thus enabled to perfect themselves
ID the continental languages and other accomplishments. Not one pupJ.l.of the institution has ever been known to go astray, as we we..re informed by the Deputy Grand
Master. The number of pupils at the time of our visit was forty-two-the majority
of whom were the orphans of brethren belonging to country Lodges; and by far the
gre&ler number were the offspring of parents whose position in life gave them little
reason to apprehend that their children would ever De thrown on the charity of the

At the annual assembly of the Grand Orient, held in September le.st, a report was
submitted which we reproduce as a matter of history, thus:·
'.'Your committee hes been obliged to examine a voluminous correspondence and
important documents; we have also been obliged to revert to the history of the question submitted. We bring you the result of our labor and a proposition which we
trust may put an end to the dissonance which separates two great countries so well
calculatea to m&llltain friendly relations-to wit, France and the United States of
America.
"But before entering npon the history of the question and presenting our resolution, we are happy to be able to state that, in no letter, in no protest, have we
found that. the Grand Lodges of America reproach the Supreme Council of Louisiana for the admission of colored men into M!UlOnry. On the contrary, the Grand
Lodge of New York, under date of Feb. 27th, 1869, expressly says: •American Masonry hes no law forbidding colored men to be made Masone.' All the Lodges are
satisfied with protesting against the decree of Nov. 5th, 1868, because it implies recognition of an American :Masonic power which they style irrregular. Your committee hes been gratified in observinf? that, cfficially at least, a.II the Grand Lodges pay
homage to that principle of equality which France was the first to proclaim in declaring free every man who touches the soil of France. Not one of them de.re protest
openly against the initiation of colored men, and if any restriction be hidden in
the hearts of men, which I cannot believe, it must be admitted, that this hypocrisy of
sentiment is nevertheless homage r.aitl to the great philanthrophic principles which
take refuge under the tri-color of ~ranee, and under the starry flag of the Union.
" Moreover, the Freemasons of the States which have fought so gloriously for the
abolition of slavery-the compatriots of LINCOLN--Oould not deceive our hopes, and
if a few personal letters, some individual relations, raise this question of the indignity of race, all the Masonic centres reject it, and are in perfect accord with the
Grand Orient of France. We repeat it, we are happy to state that the Freemasonry
of the great American people is in a.ccord with French :Masonry in being directed and
lerl by the great principles of tolerance and equality, which are the foundation and
the glory of our order.
"Without entering into all the transformations undergone by the Supreme Councils of the Northern States of America, it will answer our purpose to ca.II attention to
the fa.ct that, a.ccording to the grand Constitutions given- JS pretended-by FREDERICK II., King of Prussia, two Supreme Councils only ca.n c0--0xistin North America.
We will not now inquire whether the Constitutions of May lat, 1786, were really the
work of Fm:DEBICK the Great, or whether he had the right to make them ; we merely
state the fact. Two Supreme Councils of the Scottish Rite constituted, one at
Charleston, the other at Boston, direct the Hite, and live in peace .with the Grand
Lodge• professing the York Rite. It appears that in 1839 these two Supreme Councils in Boston and Chariest.on ceased labor. A Consistory of the 32d degree had been
established in New Orleans; in this Consisoory were Mesons possessin!I'. the 83d degree. They established a Supreme Council, which the1 ornamented with the name
of •Supreme Council of the United States of America, and gave notice of its existence to the various Masonic powers.
"On the report of Bro. TARDIEN, December 24th, 1842, the Grand Orient recogniz.ed it, and in the Calendar of 1843, alongside of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana,
we find: 'New Orleans, Supreme Council of the United States of America.'
"These fraterna.l relations contiDued until 1855, when the a.ctive members of the
SuJ?reme Council of America arranged with the Supreme Council of Charleston,
which had resumed labor, a concordat, or treaty, by which the seat of the Supreme
Co.uncil was removed to Charleston.
"From that time relations with the Supreme Council of Louisiana were interrupted, and the dissenting members of that body only reorganized in 1868, at which
time they asked to enter anew into relations with the Grand Orient, which request,
on the report of Bro. REXES, was refused b:v the then Grand Mester.
"In 1868, on a fresh application, and following the example of Italy and Belgium,
the Grand Master on a favorable rel?ort of a member of the Council, signed the decree of November 5th, 1868, which 18 the basis of the present discussion.
"By a SUSOO,Ptibility, which we understand, the American Powers see in this
decree an invasion of the Masonic affairs of America by the Grand Orient of France.
"But it is necessary to bring things back to their real basis ; it must be admitted
that the Grand M!Ulter only wished to re-establish ;previously existing relations, and
in no wise to impose upon the Lodges of the Umon the recognition of a new Supreme Oouncil. He acted in the most complete good faith, and the Grand Orient

the majority of said powers."
It is only necessary to remark on this report that like its predecessor at the hands
of CAUBET, it distorts and ignores historical facts, and avoids altogether ·the reel
question at issue. Grand Lodges are not competent to pass upon the regularity or
irregularity of Supreme Councils, and if they were they would not do it, for the reasons that their business is confined exclusively to the affairs of Symbolic Masonry.
The Grand Orient must resolve to meet this question on its own merits, and not
otherwise. It must say, without equivocation or any possible reservation, that it
approves and will stand by the doctiine, that a lawful Grand Lodge in the United
States has full and entire control over the Lodges and Masons of Symbolic Masonry
located in its territory, before there can be any possible debate between us And, •
having settled this question our way, for we will assent to no other, it will then
remain for it to show that it is a Masonic organization-having no Grand Masterand that it is proper for us who hold that the Grand Master is an indispensable part
of a Masonic governing power, to bold Masonic correspondence and relations with a
power, ignoring one of the very initial propositions of regular Masonic existence.

On the 25th of May, 1871, a conference was held, over which the Crown Prince

and hold the same relation to the Prussian Grand Lodges as that of the other existing German Grand Bodies, viz: the Grand Lodge of Hamburlil", at Hamburg; the
Grand Lodge of Saxony, at Dresden; the Grand L!Jd,ge "Zur Emtracht,'' at Darmstadt; and the Grand Lodge " Zur Sonne,'' at Bat,renth.
They also recommend that the five "isolated ' Lodges, heretofore recognized, be

zu den drei Reissbrettrettern,' at Altenburg; "Archimedes Zurn ewigen Bunde,''

In answer to the question " what might seem to be the proper attitude of the
German Emperor to the German Grand Lodges?" they respectfully request bis
"Imperial and Royal Highness graciously to condescend to assume the ProtectoraiJ" over them.
.
As to the Lodges in Alsace and JLorraine, they recommend that ihey be imperatively ordered to sever their connection with the Grand Orient of France and unite
themselves to a German Grand Lodge. There are seven of these Lodges, viz.: "FideliM,'' at Colmar ; "Amis de la Verite,'' at Metz; " L'Esperance,'' and "Parfaite
Harmonie,'' at Miihlhausen; "Progres" at St. Marie aux Mines; "Vrais Amis!' at
St. Saugemiind, and "Freres Reunis,'' at Strasbourg.
Such is the substance of the report. It must be remembered that Masonry in
the Prussian dominions exists merely by the consent of the government, which exercises a strict surveillance over it, and it is scarcely necessary to add that the "Most
Worshipful Protector," the Emperor and King William "graciously condescended"
to accept the Protectorate of the Grand Lodges in the other German States, thereby
extending the same system over the WQole German Empire. The war of 1866 between Prussia and Austria resulted in the annexation of Hanover to Prussia, and by
a cabinet order dated ~'ebruary 17, 1867, the Grand Lodge of Hon over was dissolved ..
The reason assigned was, that by an edict issued by a former King of Prussia. October 20, 1798, only three Grand Lodges could be permitted to exist in the Prussian
dominions; but the Grand Lodge of the Ecletic Union, at Frankfort-on-the-Main,
and the Lodge No. 351 of that city working under a charter from the Grand Lodge
of England, were not disturbed and it was supposed that they would be permitted to
contmue their labors. Action, however, appears to have been -0nly postponed. For
some reason not explained, but which is not difficult of solution, the Grand Lodge of
the Eel ctic Union is now recognized, and all Lodges holding charters from foreign
Grand Bodies imperatively ordered to connect themselves with a German Grand
Lodge or dissolve their organizations.
On May 28, 1871-three days after the conference at which the Crown Prince presided--the annual mooting of the Grand Masters was held at Fnnkfort-on-the-Main.
The eight German Grand Lodges were represented bv their principal officers, and
M.·. W.·. Bro. WARSATZ. Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Saxony. submitted a
projet for the formation of the Deutscher Grosslogen-Bund, or National Grand Lodge,
under the Protectorate of the German Emperor, which, after mature deliberation,
was adopted. The object of the organization is to secure a closer union of tlie German Grand Lodges, thereby promoting their harmony and co-operation in assUilling
a "common Masonic attitiide" toward the Grand Lodges ou~ of Germany; but, at
the same time, recognizing the autonomy of the several German Grand Lodges (subject to certain minor restrictions), and tile existing systems, or Rites, as practiced by
them-but no other.

Lodges of West Prussia had a reception at the old Castle of Me.rienburg, by the
Emperor WILHELM. The representatives pregented an address to the Emperor
expressing their allegiance and Masonic devotion to the High Protector,-nd the
Emperor replied as follows :-'''I find with great pleasure in your address the expression of true Masonic spirit
and feelings. My ment and reward in relation to Freemasonry lay in the fact that!
successfuly promoted a very intimate brotherly intercourse among the Lodges of
Prussia, and as far as possible between all German Lodges.
"When I was requested to join the Fraternity of the Freemasons I bad a kind of
prejudice against the institution, because a.11 secret manners and things were obje<ltionable to me. But once initiated, and knowing e.nd appreciating the spirit of the
Craft, I devoted myself to itB aims e.nd destiny with all my bee.rt. I found, however,
that brotherly love; in as far 118 it relates to the opinions and views of the disciples of
the several systems e.nd jurisdictions is very often only on the lips, and not always
in the bee.rm of the members, because each svstem of work considers itself as the
only right mee.ns to reach our common aim . '.rherefore it seemed to me e.n important object to effect conciliation among the systems, and especially through a friendly
intercourse and discussion on the views of the prominent members of the Craft.
You know I was successful not only with the original Prussian Lodges, but also, after
the annexation of He.nover, with the former Hanoverian Lodges, and even mostly
with the other German Lodges. We came nearer to the South-German Lodges, and
have with them, notwithstanding their peculiarities, an intimate intercourse,
al though they do not recognize me as their Protector.
"The increased number of Lodges and growing number of their members give
me proof that the Fraternity is propagating and promulgating the true spirit of
Masonry, and meets with success. Please do your best as men and Masons to diffuse
and realize our doctrines also in profane circles. Of course our advel'!laries, who
make us responsible for all the evil of our times, even for the ' Commune,' will never
acknowledge our operations and effects; but we can quietly indulge them in their
opposition, if we a.re satisfied with ourselves. It is impossible for me to come now
so often as before to the Lodge meetings ; but I give you my son as my substitute,
who will be active in the same spirit in Freemasonry as myself."

CONCLUSION.
Our yearly stroll through the field of American Freemasonry is again ended. We
trust the flowers and fmit gathered here and there by the we.yaide may be e.cceptable
to the Fraternity, to whom we now present our specimens and samples. Perhaps
we have occe.sione.lly encumbered our traveling bag with useless, if not worthless
matter. And then age.in,. full many e. re.re gem may have escaped our notice and
may still be among the rubbish. Tbe.t others could have done the work better, we
freely admit. But such as we have e.ccomplished we humbly submit, invoking the
indulgen ce of a kind constituency.

Bro. WILLiill C. BELCHER, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following reports:To the M. ·• W. •• Grand Lod3e of Gall{ornia :At the la.st .A.nnua.1 Communication, on motion of Bro. WILLIAM H. HILL, so
much of the report of the Committee on Correspondence as related to the status of
Masons coming from the provinces of .A.lsace and Lorraine, was referred to the Com.
mittee on Jurisprudence, with directions to consider and report1st-Whether this Grand Lodge can, consist.ently with its resolution of non-mt.ercourse with the Grand Orient of France, exempt Ma.sons coming from the above
named provinces from ite edict; and 2d-If eo, whether it is expedient to make such
exemption.
'
Your committ.ee have carefully considered the matt.er referred, and report that,
in their judgment, this Grand Lodge could not coneist.ently exempt ~ny :Mason
owing allegiance to the Grand Orient of F:rance from its edict of non-mt.ercourse,
and that it would not be expedient to ma.ke such exemption, even if it could be done
consistently.
.
•
The politica.l allegiance of the provinces of Alsace and Lorrame has been transferred from France to Germany, but that can in no way affect the status of ~e Masone of those provinces who yield a.llegie.nce and obedience to the Grand Orient of
France. .A.ny Mason yielding allegiance to that Grand Orient, !10 matt.er whence he
comes, who would avail himself of such an exemption while that edict stands,
would be unworthy to receive any favors or attention at our ~n_de. .A. ~~nt respect
for himself and hie brethren would forbid hie seeking or receivmg CIVlhtiee or att.entione while we declined intercourse with hie Grand Orient.
But if there are Lodges in the provinces of. .A.leace and Lorraine, or in any of the

our edict does not affect them.
To the M.-. W." Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :The Grand Ma.st.er, in hie Address to the Grand Lodge last yea.r, report.ad severa.l
instances in which Lodges of our jurisdiction had used their funds for purposes not ~
genera.lly recognized as strictly Ma.sonic, they claiming the right to dispose of their
own funds for such purposes as seemed good to them, and polit.ely hinting to the
Grand :Master and the Grand Lodge the propriety of attending to their own bmsinees.
In one case a Lodge gave a " sumptuous collation" to its newly-installed officers,
and borrowed a hundred dollars to do it with; in another, a Lodge gave two hundred
dollars to assist in the organization of a society for conferring some side degree or
degrees; in another, a Lodge pa.id two hundred dollars to hire C&l'l'~ee ~convey its
members, witll their families, to some pl&ce of ent.erta.inment ; and m still another•
a Lodge hired nurses to wait on.one of its members who was abundantly able to pay
hie own bills.
.
The Grand Master thought that the use of Lodge funds for such purposes was
a.Itogether improper, and desired that the Grand Lodge should take some action on
the subject. That portion of the Address was referred to the then Committee on Jurisprudence, who failed to report at that Co11;1.1nunica.tion ; and it has been, with other
unfinished business of that committ.ee, placed in the hands of the present one.
Your committ.ee have given the subject careful consideration, and fully con= in
the remarks of the Grand Ma.st.er. A Masonic Lodge is established for certain pur-

-

·Grarul Lodge of Oal,ifornia.

175

poses of charity and society, and gathers its funds for the promotion of tlioee purposes. For such purposes it has the ina.lienable right to expend all its available
funds, and, if need be, to call upon it.s members for unusual contributions. It holds
its funds in trust for those purposes and none other, and whenever it uses them or
allows them to be used for any other, it becomes false to its trust and should be held
to strict account.
It is humiliating to know, an~ knowing, to confess, that there could be found a
~ajority in any Lodge in this Bt&t.e, with so little appreciation of the spirit and obJects of Masonry, and with so little regard for the welfare and good name of their
Lodge, as to consent to divert its funds from their legitamat.e uses and employ them
for their privat.e amusements and gratift cations. It is well enough, if the members
of a Lodge choose to give dinners or oollatione to their newly insta.J.led officers, and
can afford to pay for them, that they should do so ; but it is simply shameful for
them to take the funds of the Lodge to pay the bills, and particul&rly so to borrow
money in the name and on the faith of the Lodge for such use.
There is objection to the so-caJied "side degrees" at aJ1 times; but if members of
Lodges can find amusement in them and desire to seek amusement in that way, let
them foot the bills they contract, and seek for some place beyond the precinct.a of the
Lodge-room in which to confer them. If they are too poor or too penurious to pay
the piper, let them forego the dancing.
It may be very pleasant for brethren to go to theatres and otller places of amuse_
ment, and t&ke their wives and sweethearts with them, and go in carriages. This is
all well enough if they can afford it, but it is inexpressibly mean for those who can
afford11uch amusements to rob the charity fund of their Lodge to pay the11cot. If they
cannot afford to ride, let them wa.lk ; and if they cannot afford to pay the bill, let them
beware. how. they contract it. Those who would be~ to use the funds of a Lodge

To the M." lV.-. Grand Lod.ge of Oalifornia :The Committee on Jurisprudence have considered the question proposed by Bro.
CHAIILES L. Wm<UN ae to the proper meaning of the word "notified," in Sec. 9,
Art. ill, Part ill, of the Constitution, and report ae follows:Sec. 4, Art. II, Part V, provides that "for non-payment of his dues 11 member
~ay ~ suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry in the manner provided m Sec. 9, Art. ill, Pe.rt m." Thie last section is as follows :No Lodge ehall expel a member for the· non-payment of hie dues· but in case
any .mem00r shall have refused or neglected to pay hie regular dues durlng a period
of BI~ mof!the, h~ shall be no~.fied by the Secr!lte.rY, that unless, at the next stated
meeting, either his dues be paid, or sickness or inability to pay be shown ae the ca.use

182

Procedngs of the

fOct. 15,

of euoh refusal or neglect, he will be suspended from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry. If neither of these things be done he shall be so suspended, unless for
special reasons shown the Lodge may otherwise determine.
The law imposes the duty of paying hie dues upon every member of a Lodge and,
for wilful or culpable neglect to pay them, prescribes a penalty. Thie necessarily
implies that the party shall have hie da.y of hearing, and shall not be subjected to the•
penalty until he h88 been advised of the facts chs.rged ag&llist him and has had an
opportunity to be heard. It is like the prooeedinge in a court of justice. There, in
civil C88ee, a complaint must first be filed to give the court jurisdiction of the subject.
Then the party against whom the action is brought must be notified of the pendenoy
of the action, and that judgment will be taken against him if he neglects to show
cause within the time specified in hie notification why it should not be so rendered ;
but this time does not begin to run until the service of notification has been made.
Such service in all C11Bes must be person.al, unless the law provide some other form
in C88e the party to be served is absent from the State or ca.nnot be found therein.
Notice must be either actual or constructive, and there can be no constructive notice
unlees the law provides for it and prescribes how it shall be made, for such notice is
always a substitute for actual notice,
Section 9 simply decla.res that" he shall be notified by the Secretary," and this
means actual notice, because no other is provided for. The Tyler is tlie proper offi·
cer of the Lodge to serve notices, as is the Secretary to prepare them, and your committee think that, under the provisions of Sec. 9, no member of a Lodge can be
lawfully suspended for non-payment of dnee nnleee he has in fact been notified, and
has had a reasonable time after such notification to pay or show cause why he can
not; and that the writing of a notice by the Secretary and depositing it in the poetoffice, prepaid, to the address of the delinquent, is not a notification, within the meaning of Seo. 9. If the delinquent resides within the territorial jurisdiction of the
Lodge, the notice should be served by the Tyler, or by some brother specially deputed by the Master for that dnty, and service by mail can not be in any case considered
notification nnless it be known that the letter was actually received ; and no member
should be declared suspended for non-payment of dues until he has bad a reasonable
time to pay, or show cause why he does nbt. Bee. 9 prescribes one month as the
time, when members reside within the territorial jurisdiction of the Lodge and have
had actual notice, for the law presumes that the Secretary and the Tyler will be prompt
in the discharge of their duties; but in case the delinquent resides outside, or happens
to be outside the jurisdiction at the time, and notice has been by him actually received,
no time is prescribed, and a reasonable tim,e, dependent in each case upon the peculiar circumstances attending it, should be allowed.
'
Your committee further think that no Lodge should suffer any one of its members
to be suspended without knowing that he h88 been wilfully or at least culpably negligent in the matter of paying his. dues, for it is a grievous wrong to declare and
publish a Mason as suspended when there is no just cause for such suspension. Theoretically the Master and Wardens are supposed to know the condition and circumstances of eyery member of their Lodge, and it is only just that they should cause
proper inquiry to be made before any one is suspended from his privileges for any
cause. It is true that the law declares that he shaJJ, be St18J>ended if no cause is shown
why he should not be, after he has bj3en notified, but it is so declared upon the presumption that some member of the Lodge will know the circumstances of the delinquent, and will show cause for him if he can not do so for himself. The Loage, before allowing any one of its members to be declared suspended for non-payment of
duee, should be certain of three things:let. That he h88 been in fact notified, otherwise he can not, or should not, be so
declared:
2d. That, if notified otherwise than by service of notice by the Tyler or other

1873.]

Grand Lodge ef Ou1Jifornia.

183

person properly deputed for that duty, he h88 had a reaaonable tiine within which to
show cause why he should not be suspended : and
3d. That he h88 the ability to pay, and that his neglect is wilful, or at least culpable, for otherwise he ought not to be suspended.
· The membe~ owes duties to his Lodge, but the duty is not all on one side. The
Lodge owes duties to every member, which are very poorly perlormed when it allows
any one to be suspended for non-payment of dues without knowing or inquiring
eve_n, whether ~s n~gleot arises from disreg&rd of Me.sonic duty or fro~ some cause
which renders it.en~ely excusable, and might perhaps make it the duty of the Lodge
not only to re=t hie dues but to render positive aeeistance ·to relieve distress It

The Grand Lodge was called on at 10 o'clock, the Grand Master presiding.

The Grand Secretary ·presented a petition from JAMES LoNGSHoRE,
heretofore suspended for non-payment of dues by the late Progress
Lodge,' No. 125, praying that his arrears of dues be reinitted; which
was referred to the Committee on Finances.
He also presented a communication from Doric Lodge, No. 216,
relative to the proper construction of a resolution of the Grand Lodge,
adopted at its last Annual Communication, concerning certain funds
of the late Progress Lodge, No. 125 ;
Also a printed memorial from sundry brethren relative to the
right of visit ;
Also a question from Bro. JORN A. ODELL, as to the right of an
accused brother to object to a cominissioner elected to serve upon his
trial;
Also a resolution offered by Bro. ELISHA B. RoBERTSON, proposing
to rescind the resolution of 1871, which requires Masters to furnish
certificates of their qualification before installation ;
Also a question by Bro. WILLIAM BERRETTA, as to whether the petition for degrees of a person who has served a term in a State prison
for grand laroeny, even though there were doubts as to the justice of
his punishment, should be received:All which were referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.

To the M.·. W.·. Grand Lod,ge of California:Our relations with the Grand Orient of France have again been the subject of
oonsidera.tion by the Committee on Jurisprudence, in connect~on with the report of
a committee in respect to the " Supreme Council of Louisiana," accepted by the
Grand Orient, in General Assembly, at the Annual Convocation in September, 1872,
of which the following is a translation :VERY DEAB BBETHREJc-Your committee has examined a voluminous correspondence and some important documents, and has re-ex.a.mined with some care the
history of the question which is submitt.ed to you; and it now presents, as the result
of its labors, a proposition which it is hope.d will put an ~nd to the ~~ements
now separating two great countries so well intended for friendly relations with ea.ch
. other as France and the United States.
Before ent.ering upon the history of the question, and bringing to your notice its
conclusions, your committ.ee is happy to state that in no letter uor prot.est have .the
Grand Lodges of America charged, as an offense against the Supreme Council of
Louisia.na, that it received men of color in its Lodges. On the contrary, the Grand
Lodge of New York, under date of the 27th of February, 1869, formallrdeclared that
.American Masonry haB no Zato which f orbid• the reception of men or color as Ma,.
80118. All the Grand Lodges content themselves with protesting a.g..mst the decree
of November 5th, 1868, because it implies the recognition of a Masonic power in
America. which they regard as irregular. ·

196

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 16,

Your committee is pleased to notice that, officially at least, all the Grand Lodges
render homage to that principle of equality which France was the first to proclaim, in
declaring every man free who touched French soil. No one dares to protest openly
against the initiation of men of color, and if any reservation is concealed in the depths
of any heart-which I do not wish to believe-it must be confessed that even this
hypocrisy of feeling is an homage rendered to those great philanthropic principles
which shelter themselves beneath the tri-colored standard of France and the starry
flag of the Union.
Besides, the Freemasons of the States who fought so nobly for the abolition of
slavery-the compatriots of LINCOLN-could not deceive onr hopes, .and if some
individual letters, some special reports, raise that qnestion of inferiority of race,
all the Masonic Centres repulse the idea and are in perfect harmony with the Grand
Orient of France. I repeat that it is with great pleasure that we state that the Freemasonry of the great American people is, like the Freemasonry of France, directed
and animated by those grand principles of tolerance and equality which are the foundation and the glory of Our Order.
Without entering into a recital of all the transformations to which the Supreme
Oouncils of the States of North America have been subject, it will suffice to recall to
,ronr attention that, according to the provisions of the Grand Constitntlons, given, as
18 pretended, by F&Bnl,!RIC II, King of Prussia, only two Supreme Councils of the Scottish Rite can exist in North America. We do not desire to inqnir<> here whether the
Constitutions of May 1st, 1786, are really the work of the great FRBDERIO, or whether
he had authority to make them. We simply.state a fact. Two Supreme Councils, e·stablished respectively at Charleston and at Boston, ruled the Scottish Rite and lived
in harmony with the Grand Lodges which practiced the York Rite.
It appears that in 1839 these two Supreme Councils, of Boston sud of Charleston,
ceased their labors. A Consistory of the 32d degree had been established at New
Orleans. In this Consistory were several members of the 33d degree, and they established a Supreme Council to which they $'ave the name of "The Supreme Council
of the United States of America," and notified the various Masonic p owers of its
existence. The Grand Orient of France, upon the report of Bro. TARDIEU on the 24.th
of December, 1842, recognized it, and in the Masonic Calendar of 1843, by the side of
the Grand Lodge of Louisiana, we find: "New Orleans: Supreme Council of the
Uuited Stat~s of America. S. G. Com. Ill. Bro. SANTIAGO; Representative near the
Grand Orient of France, Bro. Juax, and near the Council of America., Bro. MoNTlllAIN."
These fraternal relations subsisted until 1855. Bro. JUGE, as Representative, was
replaced by Bro. JoBERT, who, under that title, appeared upon our calendar till the
Supreme Council in Louisiana ceased to be inscribed there and was replaced by the
Supreme Council of Charleston. At that time the active members of the Supreme
Council of America concluded a concordat with the members of the Supreme Council of Charleston, which had then recently been revived, by the terms ot' which the
seat of the Council was removed to Charleston; and from that time our relations
with the Supreme Council of Louisiana were interrupted. Some of the members of
that Council were dissatisfied wjtl1 the concordat, and in 1858 reorganized their
Council. In that year they asked to return to their friendly relations with the Grand
Orient of France, but their request was refused by the then Grand Master on the
report of Bro. REXES. In 1868 a new application was made, and the Grand Master,
upon a favorable report made by a member of th~ouncil to whom the subject had
been referred, and following the example of the Grand Orients of Italy and Belgium,
signed the decree of the 6th of November, which is the subject of complaint by the
American Masonic Powers.
Through a sensitiveness which we can well understand, they 11aw in this decree an
interference with the Masonic al!klrs of America by the Grand Orient of France.
The fact· was, however, that the Grand Master wished only to renew with a Masonic
Centre the friendly relations which had theretofore existed, and did not desire, in any
way, to impose the recognition of a new Supreme Council npon the Lodges of the
Union. He acted with the most entire good faith. The Grand Orient is in the same
position. It cannot alone decide as to the regularity or irregularity of a great Masonic family or Power; it can only conform to the decisions of' the authorities which
govern the Scottish Rite. The action <!l the Grand Master and that of the Grand
Orient of France are thus explained in the most natural manner, and ought not to
cause any serious diflerences among brethren who should loTe and esteem one
another. To put an end to such differences, your committee propose that the
Grand Orient of France address these explanations to the Grand Lodges of America
and to the two Supreme Councils of Charleston and Boston; and it Is hoped that
they will restore union and fraternal relations between the Masons of France and
America. Your committee, therefore, has the honor to propose the following:Whereas, the decree of the 5th of November, 1868, was only the renewal of one
which had been issued in 1842, by which friendly relations were established between the Grand Orient of France aud the Supreme Council of America, (now called

1873.]

the Supreme Council of Louisiana,) which, withont complaint, appeared for twelve

Whereas, that decree, which cansed no dilferences and was followed by t~e

.
Whereas, by that decree the Grand Master did not intend to. encroach either

acquired, or thinks it has acquired, under the Constitutions of 1786 ; and
Whereas, the voluminous correspondence between the Grand Orient of France
and the Masonic Powers of America clearly shows that they accept and share the
philanthropic principles to which the Grand Master alludes in his decree ; and
Whereas, it is our earnest desire to convince the Masonic Powers of America
that the Grand Orient of France has never wished to intermeddle in the discussions
within the American T,odges which have misunderstoQd its purposes, but sincerely
wishes that friendly and fraternal relations should never cease to exist between the
two ~reat republics of America and France : It is
Resolved, That the Grand Orient of France, in its .Annual Convocation 1LBBembled,
directs the Council of the Order, at present its representative with foreign powers,
to inform all th e Grand Lodges.of America, and the Supreme Councils of Charleston
and Boston, of its friendly and fraternal intentions and its firm purpose never to interfere in any wa,r in Masonic questions exc~pt such as are international in ch.aracte~.
The Grand Orient wishes to respect the rights of every country and every Rite, as 1t
wishes to have its own respected; and if Scottish Masonry, represented by all the
Supreme Councils of the globe, declares the Surreme Council of Louisiana to be
irregular, the Grand Orient (the Supreme Counci for France and the French c<!lonies) , will conform to the decision ot the majority of the Powers of the Scottish Rite.
This report Is more conciliatory than that of Bro. CAUBET to the Supreme Council of the Order, of which we presented IHranslation last year; but it evades the true
issue. The Grand Lodge of Louisiana claims exclusive jurtsdiotion over the first
three degrees of Masonry in the State of Louisiana. All the Grand Lodges of the
United States join with her in the assertion and enforcement of such jurisdiction.
Her complaint is t.hat a Body, professedly Masonic and styling itself the Supre111e
Oouncil of Louisiana, has been organized in that State, which asserts as among its
prerogatives the right to confer, or to authorize its subordinates to confer, 11pon profanes the first three degrees, and which has established Lodges which appear to have
conferred those degrees upon many persons within that State ; and that the Grand
Orient of France has publicly and formally r ecognized that " Supreme Council of
Louisiana " as a just sud legally constituted Masonic Body, acting within its legitimate power and authority, and has upheld it in its usurpation of rights and powera
which belong exclusively to the Grand Lodge of Louisiana.
The jnrisdictional claim of all the Grand Lodges of the United States is the absolute and excl11sive control of the degrees of Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft, and
Master Mason; and they will not hold fellowship with any Masonic Body, of any Rite,
which seeks itself to encroach, or which upholds and fosters the encroaohment of
others, npon such claimed jurisdictional rights.
It is not a question to be left to the arbitrament of the Powers of the Scottish Rite,
or the York Rite, or any Rite, or all the Rites. It is a question already decided and
settled. The Grand Lodges of the ·United States and the Supeme Councils of the _
Northern and ~Southern Jurisdictions thereof are in harmony upon this and all o~her
questions. The first recogni~e the jurisdiction of the last over the degrees peculiar to
the Scottish Rite, as coextensive with the territorial limits of the Government of the
United States. Those Supreme Councils have declared this so-called Supreme Council
of Louisiana to be spurious, and it seems to us that the statements of the report to the
Grand Orient show it to be so. The report states that the "Snpreme Council of the
United States of America," organized prior to 1842, was consolidated with the Supreme
Council of Charleston in 1866, and that certain dissatisfied members of the forllljlr,
after some years, organized the Snpreme Council of Louisiana. The Supreme Council of which they had been members had ceased to exist; its existence had been
merged in the Supreme Council of Charleston, being that of the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States; there was nothing left to be revived or reorganized; and

198

the dissident members of that organization had no authority to institute a new
one. But we need not undertake a defence of the rights of the Supreme Council of
Charleston, whose jurisdiction has been invaded. We have only to do with the intrusion upon the jurisdictional rights of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana. Those rights
have been invaded and the Grand Orient of France bas encouraged and given aid
and comfort to the invaders. We were grieved that anything should occur to disturb
onr friendly relations with that Grand Orient and the Masons of France under its
jurisdiction, and are now most earnest in our desire to see those relations restor~d ;
bot the question at issue is one of vital importance to us, and will admit of no compromise.

whom the transcript in the case was referred, recommended that the action of the
Lodge be reversed and set aside and that the case be remanded for further proceeding&, because the commission which tried him was not legally constitnted; which reoommendatlon was adopted by this body. It appears, however, that the case had been

in 1870, and, upon the report of that committee that the testimony in the case was
amply sufficient to sustain the charges preferred, the action of the Lodge was confirmed. Upon the facte coming to the knowledge of the Grand Master, he declared
the action of the Grand Lodge in 1870 to be a 11.nality, and the rnling of the Grand
·Master has governed the action of the Lodge. The petitioner now bases his applica
tion upon the fact that the commiBSion which tried him was not legally constituted.
Formerly all charges for Masonic offenses were tried only in the General .Assemblies of Masons, but upon the organization of Grand Lodges the jnrisdict.ion devolved
on them. For convenience I.bis Grand Lodge has delegated to its subordinates power
to try otrenses; and, in-the exercise of this power, the subordinates and the commissioners they select act, not from any inherent power, but for and on behalf of the
Grand Lodge, which retains complete control of and supervision over all the proceedings. This delegation of power to the subordinates is not exclusive, for the Grand
Lodge can not divest itself of thll, one of its tnndamental rights, bnt retains the power
to try and punish otrende.rs by the action of ite own body. The committee of 1870, it
appears, deemed the case of the petitioner a proper one for the exerclae, by the
Grand Lodge, of ite inherent power; and, finding that the accused had attended the
meetings of the commissioners during the taking of the testimony and that there
was no more evidence to be Introduced, regarded the commissioners as haviD{l taken
the testimony on behalf of the Grand Lodge, and proceeded to try and determine the
case. Finding that the "testimony was amply sufficient to sustain the charge
preferred," they made the action of the commission their own, and their recommendation was adopted by the Grand Lodge. It is true that the manner in which it was
done Is somewhat informal; but the substance is there-a conviction upon sufficient
testimony, on proper charges, and with adequate sentence; and If the oommission,
acting nuder delegated power, was not prop11rly constituted, certainly no exception
can be taken to the tribunal by which he was 11.nally sentenced. " The action of
the Grand Lodge in 1870 was a finality," the same as if the charges had originally
been entertained by the Grand Lodge.
The fact that a second review of the case was had by the Grand Lodge resulted
from a duplicate transcript being sent up, which was referred to a committee composed
entirely of ditrerent members from the committee of 1870. Yonr committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resolr1ed, That the petition of J,ua:s MATSON In the premises be and the same is
hereby denied.

was used in the erection of a dwelling; that the accused employed counsel to prevent
the collection of the debt, and finally sold the house for $3600, but did not pay the
first dollar of the bill for the lumber. No excuse whatever is shown for not ·paying
th~ debt out the proceeds of the sale of the house, and your committee, believing that
the facts proven established a case of willful and deliberate fraud, cannot see that the
commissioners erred. Had the sentence been expulsion, they would not have interfered with it.
An objection was made by the accused to the specification upon which he was
convicterl, on the ground that It was not softlciently specific; but all that part of the
specification in which the insufficiency was alleged to exist can be stricken out, and
yet leave agood and valid specification of fraud. Mere technical objections cannot
avail here. The object of the Fraternity is to do strict justice, and when tllat has
been done, without the infringement of any of the rights of the accused, technicalities
cannot stay the judgment.
The evidence objected to went merely to that part of the specification which might
with propriety have been stricken out. Its admission, therefore, as it has no bearing
on tile result, could not be a ground of reversal. Your committee recommend ihe
adoption of the following resolution:-

·

accused was not notified of the meeting for the election of commissioners. Of this
we have merely the allegatlon of the accused, whilst the record of that meeting shows

part of the trial who had not heard all the evidence. Without admitting any validity
in the objection, the fact that the findings and sentence were the judgment of the
majority of the commissioners, who had heard all the evidence, is of Itself sufficient
to sustain the action of the 1.odge. The other objections appear only in the points
presented by the accused. Your committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution : Resolved, That the action of Ferndale l.odge, No. 193, in expelling WILLIAM Enw ARD RILEY LocB:wooD from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the

accused bases his defense on the allegation that the brother Is unworthy to be a Mason 11.ud should be expelled. The old York constitutions enjoined that "every Mason
shall cultivate brotherly love" - "A want of courtesy and kindness to the brethren,
speaking calnmniously -of one behind his back, or in any other way attempting to
injure him, is each a violation of the precepts of Masonry." This Grand Lodge, in a
case where the charge was that very abusive language had been used by one brother

such expressions as those complained of are in plain .violation of its spirit and tt"e.chings."....:(Vol. IX, p. 447.) Aud in another case this Grand Lodge says: " No circumstances will justify the application of vile and abusive epithets by one brother to

sufficient to afford ample redress for all cases of grlevanoe."-(Voi. IX, p.427.) If a
brother is unworthy to be a Mason, he should be expelled; but so long as he remains
a member of the Fraternity, he must be treated with kindness, courtesy, and br~th­
erly love; and any brother who speaks disparagingly of him is amenable to Masonic
punishment. The proceedings of the Grand Lodge abound in cases where brethren
have been reprimanded, snspended, and even expelled for such offenses; and, as the
specifiQJ1,tions in the pr~sent case are clearly proven, the accused was properly convicted and sentenced to punis1unent. He may be t hankful that the sentence is not

·

another question. Ordinarily, for soch language we would not consider the punishment sufficient; but there is a circumstance attendant upon this case which, though
neither justifying nor excusing the offense , is rather p alliating. And, though the evidence does show something of a vindictive spirit in the accused, yet , as the commissioners, who knew him, deemed it sufficient to sentence him to be reprimanded only,
we are somewhat inclined to think that his impulsive zeal for the good of our Order
prompted him to do and say that which upon sober r eflection he can not fail to.regret.

mend the adoption of the following resolution:·

To the M." W." G1"a'Tl4 Lodge of Oalifornia :Your committee have oaref'ully considered the papers placed in their hands concerning the confilcting jorlsdlctional claims of the Grand Lodges of Canada and Quebec, and that portion of the AddreBB of the Grand Master relative to that subject.
The dilferences beflveen those Grand Lodges seem at this time much farther from an
amicable adjustment than they were at the date of our report last year. Then there
were mutual propositions for compromise, but since then the Grand Lodge of Quebec
has IBBued an edict of non-intercourse with the Grand Lodge of Canada and the Masone
of that jurisdiction, and have sent to all the Grand Lodges in its correspondence an
appeal requesting them to join in the interdict and become active participants in the
conflict. Since then, too, the Grand Ledge of Canada has held its Annual Communication at the city of Montreal, within the Prcnlinceof Quebec. The Grand Lodge of Vermont, apparently eager for a fray, IBBued an edict of non-intercourse with the Grand
Lodge of Canada before th"e appeal of the Grand Lodge of Quebec was published,
and even before its edict in regard to Canada had been iBBued; and subsequently the
Grand Lodge of Illinois has presented to the Masonic world a similar instance of most
unneceBB&ry and Injudicious lntermeddling.
Your commi~e heartily indorse that portion of the Addre88 of our Grand Master
wherein he expreBBes his disapproval and condemnation of those unwise acts of hostility on the part of the Grand Lodges of Vermont and Illinois toward the Grand Lodge
of Canada; and did they think that aoy words more forcible than those presented
in that AddreBB were neceBBBry to express their disapprobation of the course of the
two Grand Lodges named, they would not be slow to supply the deficiency. The act
of those bodies is overbearing, unauthorized, unmasonlc, and utterly unworthy the
high character and standing which hitherto they have borne; and it is to be hoped
that few or the Grand Lodges of the United States, whatever may be their opinions
of the question of jurisdiction at issue between Canada and Quebec, will follow eo
pernicious an example.
The views of your committee respecting the rights of the contending parties were
very fully expreeaed in their reports made last year and the year before, and need
not now be repeated. The question then before them was-Shall we recognize the
GTand Lodge Of Quebec as a just and 'legally formed Grand Lodge, and enter into
friendly relatlons with It as such! The committee were divided, and the Grand
Lodge decided the question in accordan~e with the views of a minority of the committee. The question now would appear to be-Shall we leave the belligerents to
fight their own battles, or shall we join actively in the hostilities!
In the judgment of your committee, this Grand Lodge did all that could be rea.sonably asked, in recognizing the Grand Lodge of Qnebec as a just and legally constituted Grand Lodge, and may now maintain f'rlendly relations with both the parties
to the contest. Long ago we refused even to recognize the Grand Lodge of Canada
whilst that Grand Lodge was in conftict with its mother Grand Lodge of England.
But, If we had recognized the Grand Lodge of Canada while the conflict was pend·
Ing, it would not have followed as a necessary sequence that we should have declared
hostilities with the Grand Lodge of England because she did not immediately accept
our views of the situation and yield what she claimed as her right. That would have
been Quixotic In the extreme, as it woold be now for us to sever our friendly rela·
tions with the Grand Lodge of Canada becanse It did not accept and act upon our apparept advice in regard to Its relations with the Grand Lodge of Quebec. We will
continue to hope for a speedy and mutually satisfactory adjustment of the dift'erences
between Canada and Quebec; but, while the strife continues, we will stand aloof &om
it and will at all times welcome as brethren the Masons In obedience to either one
or other or the contending parties. ·
The Grand Lodge of Canada might perhaps regard our action of last year as hoe·
tile, and declare all friendly relations between us at an end. So too the Grand Lodges

208

Procoodings qf the

[Oct. 17,

of England, Ireland, and Scotland, and with them the Grand Lodges of Massachnsetta,
Pennsylvania, New J ersey, Virginia, and Missonri-the oldest and most conservative ,
of the Grand Lodges of the United States- if they sh:ould take the same view of onr
action in respect to the Grand Lodge of Quebec as we did, and do, of the action of the
Grand Orient of France with respect to the Snpreme Council of Louisiana, might interdict all further Intercourse with ns.
The Grand J,odge of Canada established, and for more than tea years maintained,
jurisdiction and claimed exclusive jurisdiction over the territory now embraced in
the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec. It bad established more than thirty subordinate
Lodges in the Province of Quebec, and still claims J,orisdiction over t!!ose Lodges and
over that Province. The Grand Lodge of Quebec was organized and, asserting for
herself exclusive jurisdiction over the same Province, absolved certllin Lodges which
had been obartered by and bad theretofo1·e borne; allegiance to the Grand Lodge of
Canada from their allegiance, and established new Lodges. We recognized the Grand
t
Lodge of Quebec.
The Grand Lodge of Louisiana established, and for many years maintained,jurisdiction over the territory of the State of Louisiana and claimed exclusive jurisdiction over that territory. The Supreme Council of Louisiana, wor)dng io the Scot, tiah Rite, was organized in that State and establi!lhed Lodges therein, autho1izingthem
to confer the degrees of Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft, and Master Mason.
The Grand Orient of France recognized the Snpreme Council of Louisiana as a just
and legally constituted body, rightfnlly exercising powers claimed by the Grand Lodge.
We regarded the act ot'reoognition as hoetile , and suspended intercourse with that Grand
Orient on that account. The consistency of oar action in the two cases may not be
very apparent; bot in the latter case we have no doubt of its correctness, and as to the
former we can certainly afford to maintain oar friendly relations with ibe Grand
Lodge of Canada if she still holds oat to as her right hand. We have no cause of
complaint.
If the Grand Lodge of Qnebec had once acquired and exercised eult1Bi1Je jurisdiction over the t.erritory claimed by her, and the Grand Lodge of Canada had invaded
that jurisdiction, a very ditlerent case would have been presented from that of the
one before us. The question is now, not of an invasion by the Grand Lodge of Canada of territory over which another bad acquired jurisdiction, bot whether, having
once acquired jurisdiction and established Lodges, she had the right, in the presence
of another Masonic power claiming jurisdiction over the same territory, to maintain
the Lodges established by her and the juriadiction acquired. As against both the
Grand Lodges.of Canad& and Quebec, the Grand Lodges of England, Irel&lld, and Scotland have st.eadily maintained that right, and, as we are informed, each of them still
maintains one or more Lodges in the Province of Quebec and in the Province of
Ontario. Quite recently, too, the Grand Lodge of MaBB&ehusetts has asserled t!'te
ea.me nght in refusing to surrender to the Grand Orient of Chile her authority over
the Lodges established by her in that republic. Those Grand Lodges, and the Grand
Lodge of Canada with them, may be ·&ltogether wrong in this matter, bot they seem
to be honest and earnest in their claim of right; and, as we have ever found them
very pleasant friendl, yve can well afford to maintain our friendly relations and leave
them t" grope along in the po!!8ible darkness which envelops them until they shall
discover the right and see it as we are supposed to do.
