But is it possible that a mai<Jl"Uy or a Lodge wonld thus vote, without any cause,
or for such oauses? And yet I can not resist such a conclusion, for you tell me that
no member of your J..odge can now procure a recommendatory certificate ; and there
must be 11<1me membere age.inst whom no excuse for such refusal can be alleged. This
indicates a most unhappy and Indefensible disposition among you-a condition of affairs which no circumstances can jnstil'y; and I admonish you now that it must be
corrected and that yon must act upon reason in the disposition of all such applioations.
Again, you advise me that, when it was proposed to remove from yoor old hall
to another, an exciting and unbecoming discussion took place ; tbat when yon
proposed to build a home for yourselves, wrangling and serious disaffection resulted; that some deem themselves wronged by the action or the majority, and
in their resentment have so far forgotten their Masonic duties and obligations as to
no longer attend the meetings of the Lodge or participate in its business; and that others, still more censurable, seem to attend and participate only for the purpose of creating further annoyance and vexation.
.
My brethren, the remedy for all these afflictions is in your own hands; and I entreat you, with the most fraternal solicitnde, that you speedily apply that remedy. I
do not think that 1 have mistaken their real and underlying cause. Upon some ~ues­
tions of great interest and apparent importance, you have been almost evenly divided; and all your troubles come, directly or indirectly, from an unwlllingness of the
minority to acquiesce in the will of the majority. Let me say then to the disaft"ected
and protestant, that the will of the majority is the law or a Masonic Lodge, and that
he who does not yield a cheerful obedience to that will when fairly expl"t'ssed, pro't"es
himself unworthy ol the fraternal confidence and trust of his Jirethren. He who resists or impedes or embarrasses the operations or his Lodge, or does aught to impair
its harmony or prosperity because his judgment or wishes, or perhaps hie caprices.
have not been complied with, only establishes his own utter misconception of the Ma
sonic theory of government, the bigotry and narrowness of his own nature and disposition, and his unfitness to be a member of the Masonic household. And I submit
to you that he who would willfully cripple or destroy hie Lodge because other, and
perhaps wiser, counsels had prevailed in the administration of its affairs, is but a
breeder of mischief who should be stripped of the ancient and honorable badge he
wears and banished forever from your assemblages. Cao a minority expeot a majority to yield to them? M:aet they destroy because they can not rule ? Shall there be
strife, bickering, and contentiou, because judgments differ? I am not accustomed to
such conduct In Masonic Lodges, and it fflll81 not be.
Let me entreat yon, my brethren, to be wise and rational. Let me appeal to your
own consciences and better natures and implore you to be true to yourselves, to
your own manhood, and to the sacred trust with which Freemasonry has honored
you. If to some of you the decisions of the majority seem unwise. imprudent, rash,
or unjust, remember that it is still the will of the majority- the law of yoor house·
hold- and must be respected and observed. You are not to resist It, to withdraw
your allegiance because your views have not prevailed, to imperil the peace and harmony or hazard the prosperity of your Lodge ; but, patiently submitting, you are to
yield a cheerful support fo all things, and wait for time and season and wiser counsels
to bring your brethren to your own views and wishes.
Let there be mutual concession, and you, my brethren of the majority, be respectful to and considerate ol the feelings and wishes aud judgments of those who differ
with yon. Be careful that In the exercise or rower yon keep steadily in view the
best interests ot your 1..odge and the rights o the minority also. Let moderation,
forbearance, and brotherly love characterize all yoor proceedings, and, by a tender
regard for all who differ with you, retain their co-operation even in what they disa}>prove. No man is so wise that he may not err, and no Mason most be so proud or
self-willed as not to yield a cheerful and ready obedience to the fairly-expressed wish
of a majority or his brethren.
Finally, let me remind yon that, when opposition assnmea the character of active
resistance to legitimate decisions or resolves, or seeks to impede or prevent their execution, or when it manifests itself in ellorts to destroy peace and harmony, cripple
tirosperity, or impede in any way the legitimate work of the Lodge, it hl\8 become
insubordination, and must be punished and subdued. And while I ask you once
more, in all kindness and fraternal regard, to hasten to a reconciliation ot yoor differences and bring back the peace and harmony which onght never to have been interrnpted, I must at the same time remind {ou that, at last, a remedy quick, sharp,
decisive, and final will sorely be applied.

Bro. GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE, from the same committee, presented
the following report :To the M. •. W. ·. Grand Lodge of Chlifornia :At the Annual Communication in 1sn, Bro. MosES HELLER presented the following
question, which was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, viz.:Have Master Masons, Individually or as an association, th~ !ight ~ nee either the
name or the emblems of :Masonry for th.e purpose of advertl8log their business ~nd
thus inducing the public to believe that such business ia conducted nl!der the au.~pmes
of the Fraternity"! And, if not, are not all :Masons conn!lc1;ed with the so-.called
"Masonic Savings and Loan Bank" of San Francisco, violating the laws and edicts of
this Grand Lodge!
No report thereon was made at that Communication, bot at the succeeding one, in
1872, a report was presented which, after some discussion, was re-committed to the
Committee on J nrisprudence with instructions again to report at the present Com·
munication. Your present committee commence their report with the following
extract from the report of last year :. It Masons, being a hoot to engage, or already_engage~, in a priv!lte enterpri~e,
seek by any means whatever to induce the pubhc to beheve that their enterpnse 18,
or is to be, conducted nuder the auspices, or under the control and managei_nent, or
upon the credit and responsibility of the Fraternity of Masons, they are 1JU1lty of a
fraud upon the public and an outrage upon Masonry, and should be dealt with accord·
ingly. As to the public, they are seeking its confidence under false. pretences and
are unworthy to be trusted; and as to Masonry, they r~gard no~ its good .name·
among men, bnt,.for their own private gain! woul~ expose 1t to thens~ of beanng all
the odium neoe88arily attendant upon possible ID18management and failure.
t Buch is the opinion of your present committee as they have maturely studied and
learned the spirit and teaching of Masonry .. Every step taken, from poroh to inner
oourt, serves to emplulsiae the first declaration a Mason is required to make before he
is caused to knock at the door in his search for light. It is to be hoped that the declaration is always made with sincerity that he iB unbi.asseA by friends and unin:fl.uenced by mercenary motives, and that the favorable opinion oonceived of its objects
and purposes is formed in the light of the true spirit of that declaration, and in
no other.

We h•ve never failed to hear it inculcated that the true spirit a.nd object of the
Fraternity on this question is, not to enable us to ma.lie gain, but to lead its lovers
and followers to willingly help, aid, and 888ist those who, by force of adversity and
misfortune, make mute or expressed appeals to its humanities for relief. This spirit,
which we believe to be plain and clear, seems to us to denounce, as a mean perversion
of the ancient integrity and honor of our Order, every attempt that any Muon
may make in the direction to which the question submitted points, for the purpose
of filling his coffers or pockets. Its symbols and emblems, its signs and tokens, its
name and fame, its rank and l:tonorable titles, belong not to an individual for his own
use and benefit, but a.re talents intrusted to him to be used for special and exclusive purposes. These purposes are purely Masonic, and there is no reasonable
excuse for misapprehension of their true and lawful use. That Masonry, or anything
which is incidental to it, is intended or contemplated to be hawked about and used in
the business pursuits and struggles of men, aa capital for making money or for the
advancement of their mere. personal triumphs, is the grossest pe.rversion of noble
a,ims and the most cheating of populr.r fallacies. We know that its purposes are
higher, nobler,and le88 selfiah; and if we err in our strong convictions of wh•tFreemasonry truly means and plainly teaches, then we have been badly taught and most
ornelly deceived.
If asked, as we are in that branch of the.question submitted to us which 888Umes
conditions, if the "laws and edicts of this Grand Lodge" are being violated, we say
that the spirit of the law of univel'Blll Masonry, which the Grand Lodge itself can
not violate and still remain a just Grand Lodge, is violated by the act complained of.
Its unwritten law, its vital spirit imd essence, which is of far more worth than all
the illuminated manuscripts and parchments which slumber upon the shelves of ancient libraries, is against it-hostile and frowning. Simony in the church, and the
use of Masonic knowledge, advantages, or position by a Mason for the purpoee of
securing his gain and forwarding his business profects or worldly triumphs, are of the
same tribe and kindred. There is no "law or edict of this Grand Lodge" on this
subject now extant, nor do we believe that it is.necess.ry that any such law should
be enacted (for we are making more laWll than we tnudy and pay nispeot to); bm
nearly a score of years ago there was a law of this Body which declared the statement
of universal Masonryjn saying that such things were "open violations of the spirit
of Masonry." We have heard that the wise men of that day declared their opinions in the Grand Lodge that they could not mU:e a law stronger thim the admitted
and conceded unwritten law, which declaration was accepted as the general sentiment;
and so, in the making of a new Constitution, that law was left behind with many other
things declaratory of axiomatic truths.
Your committee present to the Grand Lodge their opinion that Master Masons,
lndJ.vidnally or associated, violate the true spirit and unwritten laws of Masonry when
use is made of the name or the emblems of Masonry for the purpose of advertising
their business; and further, that the Masons · connected with the so-called "Masonic
Savings Bank " of San Francisco do not violate the "laws and edicts of the Grand
Lodge," because no special law or edict upon that subject exists; but that the use of
the name " Masonic," for their corporation, violates the true spirit and unwritten law
of Masonry, and that it would be a correct assertion of Its dignity, and is due to the
Fraternity, that the Grand Lodge declare that it does not give countenance to and
has no sympathy with such misuse.
All which is respectrnlly submitted by

7b the M.·. W: •• Grand. Lodge aJ Califomia :-·
Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the .Address of the Grand
Master relative to retrenchment in the expenditures of the Grand Lodge, report that
they have carefully examined the subject and are unable to find any regular expenditnre made on the part of this Grand Lodge which is unnecessary or extravagant.
The salaries paid to the Grand Officers are not more than commensurate with the
services which they are required to perform, and, so far as the principal salaried
officer is concerned, the remuneration is by no means as much as his skill and ability
would undoubtedly command in other occupations. Justly, then, we can not there
retrench.
It has been suggested that we try an experiment of economy by the reduetlon of
our 'printing. In what respect! The Report on Correspondence occupies a large
space in our annual publioatlons, but is thete a member of the Grand Lodge who
would wish to see thli\t fund of information-that summary of the thoughts, reasonings, and actions of all the Grand Lodges.of the world with which we are in correspondence-ed'ace~ from onr proceedings, or so limited in its scope as to be only a
directory cf Grand Lodg6s and therefore useless! It is not too much to say that, to
the general Masonic reeder in our own jurisdiction, that report has more of interest,
perhaps, then all the remainder of onr publfostion; end, as to its import abroad, is
it not well that it should be known of men that we de~ire not only to collect and
profit by the lessons taught by so many of onr elder brethren, but, with such modesty es beseems our youth, to take some care that our own light shell not be entirely
hidden under the historical bushel!
Your committee have already expressed their views in regard to the "publication
of the lists of members of our Lodges, which also occupy a large portion of our
printed records ; and, as to the remainder, they are unable to perceive that they
contain more than Is necessary to subserve the proper purpose for which they were
intended-that of giving full information to the subordinate Lodges of all the transactions of the Grand Lodge.
Thus mnch for the printing of our annual journal of proceedings. .A.a to the incidental printing of blanks, circulars, forms, etc., your committee do not find ihat any
more hes been done than the law authorizes, or thsII necessity requires; and they
are well assured that this, as well as all other printing, has'been done at the lowest
rates which it was possible to obtain.
It may be true, and your committee need not _h esitate to say that it is true, that
the Grand Lodge has more than once exhibited extravagance, by voting away its
funds in spasmodic fits of thoughtless generosity or by the careless allowance of moonaidered claims recommended by its committees. But these are errors which the
Grand Lodge Itself alone can remedy by greater care and thoughtfulness in the future ;
and your committee have discharged their duty when they report, as they uow do,
that, in the ordinary business of the Grand Lodge, they see no extravagance of expenditnre and find no opportanity to recommend retrenchment.

of the Grand Lecturer and Inspectors, presented the following report:To the M~" W. •• <:Jrand Lodge of (]alifomia :.:....
The special committee, consisting of the Grand Lecturer and the Inspectors of the
several Masonic Districts present at this Commnnication, to whom were referred the
report of the Grand Lecturer and oertain:portions of the AddreBS of the Grand Master
relative to work and the system of Inspection, having carefully considered the several
subjects, report as follows:The observation and experience of the members of your committee enable them
to concnr fully with the Grand Master in the views expreBSed by him as to the benefits
which have resulted from the system of Inspection, and In hie recommendation that it
should on no account be abandoned. Many irregularities have been corrected, some
of which, though perhaps trivial in themselves, had a tendency to lead the Lodges to
greater and more serious deviations from the laws, regalatioBB, and customs of the
Fraternity. Some of the Irregularities to which the attention of the M&&ters and
Lodges have been called, and which they have promised to avoid in future, -.re not yet
entirely eradicated, and would, were the system abandoned, in consequence of changes
of officers be probably renewed. But as the system is something of a tax upon the
Lodges and as a large proportion of them are now working correctly, and as their
books and records have received a very careful examination and are In such condition
as not to require strict inspection again immediately, your committee recommend that,
during the ellSuing year, the Inspectors of the several districts be required to visit

Bro. JAMES LAmLEY offered the following resolutions:Resolved, That this Gtand Lodge cannot permit our Past Grand Master, Bro.
LEONIDAS E. PBATT, to retire from the chair which, during foar years past, he has so
ably occupied and so greatly honored, without offering to him its warmest, sincerest,
and most heartfelt acknowledgments of the untiring diligence and consummate ability which has characterized his superintendence of the Cro.ft during his long term of
office-of the promptness and impartiality of decision, the ready knowledge and application of the law of our jurisdiction, the aptitude with which his own good judgment
supplied any deficiency in that law when necessary, and the dignity of manner combined with gentleness of annunciation which have ever been exhibited when presiding
in this body-nd of the zeal, learning, and true Masonic feeling and spirit with which
his administration ha.s been con~tantly illnmina.ted.
Resolved, -'!'hat our retiring Grand Master be requested to sit for his portrait, and
that, when done, the Grand Secretary be instructed to have it suitably framed and
placed with the other portraits of the Grand Masters in the gallery of the Grand
Lodge.
Resolved., That the six elective Grand Officers be appointed a committee with
power to devise and procure & suitable testimonial expressive of the appreciation
which this Grand Lodge entertains of the eminent services of our esteemed and
beloved Past Grand Master, Bro. LEONID.ls E. PRATT, to be presented to him at the
next Annual Communication.

Which resolutions were unanimously adopted.

NOTE BY THE GRAND SECRETARY.

.A.t the .A.nnnal Communication in October, 1871, in accordance wi~h a recommendation or the Grand Master in his AddreBB of that year, a committee was appointed
to revise and amend the Constitution and Regnlatione of the Grand Lodge.
For varione reasons it was found impossible to assemble the committee during the
year following and, at the Annual Communication In 1872, it wee continued with
Instructions "that the revised Constitution, when completed, be distributed to the
subordinate Lodges -of the jurisdiction, that they may be prepared to vote understandingly on the question of its adoption at the next Annual Communication.''
During the past year the Committee on Revision performed, or endea.vored to perform, the duty assigned them, and fulfilled the instructions mentioned in the preceding
paragraph by transmitting to each Lodge of the jurisdiction a copy of the Constitution entire a.s proposed to be am.ended, .exhibiting every suggested erasnre, alterertion, or a.ddition in such a manner as to be readily comprehensible.
The instrument, thus proposed to be corrected, was presented at the late Communication. Many of the a.mendmente suggested by the committee were rejected,
as were also a number or others presented by the Committee on Jurisprndence an~
by individual members of the Grand Lodge. .A. number of other amendments were
adopted by a unanimous vote, and have now gone into effect as a portion of the
organic law; and still an additional number re~eived th~ votes of a majority, which
sends them over to the next .A.nnnal Communication for the further action provided
in onr Constitution.
The "Revised Constitution," as presented in the following pages, gives the original
text and all alterations and amendments which, having been unanimously adopted,
have now become the law, in roman letters. .All portions proposed by a majority
vote to be stricken ont, are given in roman also, enclosed in 'a parenthesis ~us) ;
and all additions proposed by a similar vote, a.re given in italia.
It was ordered that a sufficient number of copies of the Constitution, as thus
amended or proposed to be amendlld, to supply each of the Lodges wit h fonr copies
thereof, be printed and sent to them free of charge ; and that order ha.s been fulfilled
in the manner thought to be most ueefnl and convenient by publishing the Oonetitntion with the proceedings.

GENERAL REGULATIONS,
AS ABRIDGED AND AMENDED AT THE ANNUAL OOMHUNlOATION
In October, 1873.

I
-

1. The practice of dueling being repugnant to the principles of Freemasor:ry, in
all cases where two brethren resort to this mode of settling their disputes, it shall be
the ;duty of the Lodge or Lodges of which they are members, or within whose jurisdiction they may reside, forthwith to expel them ft-om all the rights and privileges of
:Masonry; and no brother who may fall in a duel shall be buried with Masonic honors.
2. (4.) ~is Grand Lodge, having recognized the principle that no one shonld be
initiated In.t o the mysteries of our Order enept in the Lodge nearest his place of
residence, (unless by its permission,) and having, by an established regulation, taken
care to avoid infringing the jurisdictional rights of others, will not tolerate that its
own be invaded; and it is therefore ordered that no Lodge, subordinate to the Grand
Lodge of California, shall admit to membership any person who, being at the time a
resident of this State, has received , or claims to have received, the degrees of )[a.
sonry from any source beyond its jurisdiction, without the proper permission, until
he shall have paid the Lodge to which he applies for membership, the foll amount
charged by that Lodge for conferring the degrees , less the sum paid by him to the
Lodge in which he received them.
3. (5.) This Grand Lodge recognizes no degree of Past Kaster conferred by any
authority not holden under a legitimate Grand Lodge-acknowledging only the Order
of that name as it exists in the ceremonies attending the installation of the Kaster
elect of a chartered Lodge; which Order shall be conferred only by a convocation
of Present or Past Masters, not less than three in number, who have thus regnlarly
'
received it.
4. (6.) All Masonic commnnication between the Lodges and Masons of this jnris·
diction and those acknowledging alleglsnce to the Grand Lodge of Hamburg, is hereby
forbidden, while that body shall continue its unlawfnl and reprehensible invasion of
the jurisdictional rights of the Grand Lodge of New York.
6. (7.) Such standard ofrevenue shall be continued hereafter as will afford an annual
excess over the current expenditures of at least one thousand dollars ; which excess
shall each year be set aside, as an accumulating fund, to be known as the Reserve
Fund, which shall be kept and increased for purposes ot emergency, and shall only
be drawn opon therefor. At each Annual Communication. a Board o!Trnstees, three
in nm~ber, shall be elected, whose duty it s!iall be judiciously to invest all moneys
set aside for each fond, and all moneys accruing from the interest on such investments•
and each member of said Board shall execute and fUe In the office of the Grand Sec:
retary, a bond In the penal sum of $5000, to be approved by the Grand Master,
Grand Treasurer, and Grand Secretary, conditioned that he will faithfally perform the
duties of his trust.
6. (9.) No Lodge under this jurisdiction shall be allowed to transact business
other than the conferring of degrees, with a less nnmber than seven membe~ present'.

7. (10.) The Grand Secretary is anthorized to charge the snm of one dollar, for
the use of the Grand Lodge, for eacb. copy of its printed proceedings for the current

at its next succeeding Annual Communication.
8. (ll.) All Ma.sons, heretofore stricken from the rolls of Lodges within this jurisdiction for non-payment of dues, who have not been reinstat.ed, are hereby declared
to be suspended, as provided in Bee. 9, Art. ID, Part ill, of the Constitution.
9. (13.) In addition to the dues prescribed in the ConsJ,itution, there shall be levied
hereafter upon the subordinate Lodges, for each Master Mason whose name is borne .
upon their rolls at the date of the annual returns, such sum as the Grand Lodge shall
prescribe at each Annual Communication, which shall .constitute a special fond to be
denominat.ed "The Representative Fund;" and it shall be the duty of the several
Lodges to pay the said sum at the time and in the manner directed in the Constitution
for the payment of their annual dues.
10. At the close of each Annual Communication, a committee, to be known as the
· "Committee on Pay of Members " and to consist of five, shall be appointed by the
Grand Mast.er, whose duty it shall be to ascertain, during the year succeeding, the
exact cost of transportation for one person from the location of each Lodge in the
State to the place of meeting of the Grand Lodge and back again; and, at the following Annual Communication, to report such cost of transportation as the sum doe to
the officers or representative in attendance from e!'ch chartered Lodge, which sum
shall be paid by the Grand Trensurer, such report being his voucher therefor, Bot no
payment shall be allowed for the officers or representative of any Lodge, the does of
which shall not have been paid in full.
U. (14.) The appointed Grand Officers and the chairmen of standing committees
shall receive payment for their necessary expenditures for transportation to and from
each Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, In the same manner as ordered for
the officers or representatives of Lodges; but no Grand Officer, chairman, or officer
or representative of a Lodge, shall receive such payment in more than one of those
capacities, nor shall he receive it unless he shall have been in attendance at such
Communication from the first to the last day thereof, inclusive, unless excused by the
Grand Lodge.
12. (15.) The work and lectures .Presented by the committee appointed for their
exa.rnination and revision, are approved, adopted,and made obligatory upon all Lodges
within this jurisdiction; and any Lodge which shall have had opportunity to obtain
instruction therein, and shall neglect or refoae to learn and use the same, shall, upon
representation of that fact to the Gra.nd Master, be liable to the arrest of its chart.er,
if, in his discretion, he shall think it proper.
13. (18.) The person who desires to be made a Mason must be a man; no woman
nor eunuch; 1\"eeborn, being neither a slave nor the son of a bond woman; a believer
in God and a future existence ; of moral conduct; capable of reading and writing ; no\
deformed or dismembered, bot hale and sound in his physical conformation, having his
right limbs as a man ought to have ; and able to conform literally to what the several
·
degrees respectively reqnire of him.
U. Whenever an appeal shall be taken from the jndgment of a sobordinat.e
Lodge upon the report of trial commissioners, any and all additional evidence, which
either the accuser or accoaed shall desire to have heard on the appeal, shall be talren
and rednced to WTiting within sixty days from the day on whi'ch the aunouncemeni of
the result of the trial shall Ile made by the Master to the Lodge, and all arguments
and representations which it is desired to have considered on the appeal shall also be
reduced to writing ; and no additipnal evidence, arguments, or representa.tions shall
be considered on the appeal unless the same shall be reduced to writing and transmitted to the Grand Secretary at least sixty days before the commencement of the
next Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge.
